4 *Ch 4, sc in next arch. Repeat from * 5 times to make 6 ch-4 spaces. (The arches in this round are slightly smaller—each one has only 4 chain stitches before the single crochet. When the round is finished, there will be 6 of these smaller arches.)

5 *Ch 3, sc in next ch-4 space. Repeat from * 5 times to make 6 ch-3 spaces. (Chain 3 for an even smaller arch, then single crochet in the next chain-4 space. When this round is finished, there will be 6 of the chain-3 arches.)

After the second time around the circle, the piece will begin to curve at the edges and gradually become bowl-shaped.

Makes a solid edge around the top of the net.

6 2 sc in same space as Step 5 finished. *5 sc in next ch-3 space. Repeat from * 5 times.

Step 6 is a bit different from the previous rounds, so here's a "plain English" translation of the instruction: Instead of chaining and moving on to the next space, work 2 more single crochet stitches right next to the one that completed Step 5. Now, with no additional chains, insert the hook into the very next ch-3 space, and work 5 single crochets there. Return to the *, and repeat again, 5 times.

Makes the carrying strap.

7 Ch 60, or to desired length for handle. Sc in same ch-3 space where Step 6 finished. Fasten off. (Make 60 chains or more, because the chain strap will be folded in half. Finish with a single crochet in the same ch-3 space where Step 6 finished, making a large loop for carrying the Water Bottle Net. Fasten off by doing one more chain, cutting the yarn with an 8" (20.5 cm) tail, and pulling the tail through the chain stitch.)

8 Weave in ends securely. (Use the yarn needle to weave the beginning yarn tail at the bottom of the net into the first round of arches, first in one direction, then back the other way. Also weave in the ending yarn tail through the round of single crochets, going in and out through the stitches in one direction for 1" to 2" (2.5 to 5 cm), then back the other way. Trim off the extra yarn with scissors.)

Crochet Language

An asterisk (*) in a crochet pattern indicates a set of directions that will be repeated several times over. Don't go to the beginning of the step, but look for the * and repeat from that point as many times as indicated in the directions. Some crocheters place a little sticky-note arrow, at the asterisk to help quickly find the spot. When the total number of repeats is finished, move the arrow to where it's needed next.

tip  When you need to keep track of a large number of repeats, it helps to use a pencil and paper, making a tally mark as you complete them. In this case, you could number the paper from 1–31 and then cross out a number each time you finish an arch by making a single crochet.

##   SOMETHING SOLID

### Single Crochet in Rounds

Now that you know what a crochet stitch looks like (with its V at the top) and the motions of making crochet stitches are becoming familiar to your hands, it's time to take it to the next level. In this chapter, you'll learn how to work a stitch into another stitch so you can begin to make solid fabric. You'll also learn how to increase (make the number of stitches grow), to count the rounds you've completed, and to use a stitch marker to help keep your place. Finally, in the second of this chapter's two projects, you'll learn a slightly different way to begin a project worked in the round. Both methods are common in crochet patterns, so it's helpful to understand both techniques. "Plain English" translations of the instructions are provided as needed, but the project patterns in this chapter through the end of the book are more like standard crochet patterns. Look for translations of tricky parts in the "tip" boxes and use the Glossary and list of crochet Abbreviations at the back of the book if you need help.

### Making a Stitch on Top of a Stitch

Begin with a practice piece, and when you are comfortable with finding the top of a stitch and making a new stitch there, you'll be ready to start one of the projects in this chapter.

**You Will Need**

_Yarn_

• worsted weight medium yarn

_Tools_

• hook in size a size comfortable for your hands

• scissors

• 1 stitch marker (see page 13)

Here are five rounds of single crochet (sc), without any increases to make the circle grow larger.

Begin by making 4 chain stitches, slip stitch in first chain to form a ring, chain 1, and make 8 single crochets in the ring.

A familiar starting place.

1 Insert the hook under both loops of the first stitch's top V, with the working yarn held at the back of the work.

2 Draw up a loop, as you've done before, with yarn coming over the hook, and then pull it through to the front of the work. There are now 2 loops on the hook.

3 Before continuing, be sure that the Step 1 insertion was under both loops. This is the standard way to make crochet stitches. There will be times when a special effect, such as ribbing or other texture, requires working into only the front loop (FLO) or only the back loop (BLO). But if this is not specified, patterns always assume that the hook is going into the stitch under both loops.

Completing the stitch.

4 Yarn over and pull through both loops on hook.

Checking for both loops.

Here's the first finished stitch, with its marker in place. The pointer shows where the next stitch will begin.

Once you've checked the first stitch, place a stitch marker in its top V, making it easy to find the first stitch of the round. To mark the stitch, simply insert the open part of the stitch marker under the front loop of the stitch, and turn or close the marker to keep it from falling off the stitch.

Now go ahead and follow steps 1–3 to make a sc in each stitch of the first round. Look for the next V to the left of the stitch you just finished. Stop at the stitch just before the marked stitch. There should be 8 sc in this finished round.

When making sc (single crochet) stitches into the stitches of the circle, the outside edge of the circle needs to grow larger to keep the circle flat. If the outside edge doesn't grow larger by adding extra stitches, the piece becomes a tube. You'll notice that now, after finishing just one round of stitches on top of stitches, the fabric already has a cupped shape. If you continue to make more and more rounds, your piece will soon look like a sweater made to fit a finger!

#### Crocheting a Flat Circle

To create a circle that lies flat as it grows, each round must have 6 more sc (single crochet) stitches than the round before it. Increasing means making more than one new stitch in the same place in the top of an old stitch. To practice increasing and get ready for the next two projects, start with a chain of 4, slip stitch to form a ring, ch 1 to start the next round, and make 6 sc into the ring. This step is just like the "familiar start" (page 39), except it has only 6 sc stitches, and you can use the same yarn and hook.

This second stitch doesn't need a marker because it's not starting a round. Move to the next stitch from Round 1, and work 2 sc stitches in it. Continue around, making 2 sc in each stitch, until you get back to the marker. Stop just before you insert the hook into the marked stitch. Round 2 is complete. When crochet work goes from one round to the next without using a turning chain, we use the term "working in spiral." Working in spiral is common in patterns for round projects that use only the single crochet stitch (and not the taller stitches you'll learn later), such as hats, bags, and some stuffed animals.

When you're ready to begin Round 3, take the marker out of the first stitch for Round 2 and put it into the first finished stitch of Round 3. Every time you start a new round, move the marker to the start of the new round.

Round 3 will have a slightly different pattern to the increases. Instead of increasing in every stitch (because only 6 increases are needed in each round), the pattern for Round 3 is *2 sc in the next st, 1 sc in the next st. Repeat from * 5 times. In plain language, that means that you'll be alternating—2 sc in a stitch, then 1 sc in a stitch, then 2, then 1, all the way around the circle.

As the circle grows larger, the space between each of the 6 increases grows longer. Patterns will state the number of individual stitches to make after each increase. Many different kinds of projects use this way of making a circle, including the two in this chapter: The Eenie Meenie Easy Beanie hat and the Trinkets and Treasures Drawstring Bag.

Rnd 2—Make a sc in the first stitch, and place a marker in the finished stitch. Now make another sc by inserting the hook into the very same place.

Rnd 2 now has 12 stitches.

Rnd 3 has 18 stitches. Fasten off the practice circle.

tip  In a pattern, the Foundation or Start is made up of the chain and the slip stitch to turn it into a ring, if the project is round. Round 1, which is abbreviated as Rnd 1, is made up of each of the stitches worked into the ring. The first stitch made into the top of another stitch is the start of Round 2. Make sure you put a stitch marker into the first stitch of Round 2 as soon as you complete that stitch.

### Eenie Meenie Easy Beanie

  What could be easier than the counting-off rhyme "eenie, meenie, minie, moe..."? Well, this hat is just that easy to make and fun to wear. You'll use some of the skills you've mastered, including starting with a ring, making single crochets in the ring, working spiral rounds of single crochet, increasing, and fastening off. If you choose a "long print" or "self-striping" yarn, the hat will produce its own stripes. Bulky yarn and a large hook make this hat both quick to make and extra warm to wear. Since a hat is made to fit part of a human body, this will be the first project in which gauge is important. To ensure that your hat is the desired size, the size of each of your stitches must match the size of the designer's stitches! The pattern teaches you how to measure gauge in a round piece and how to adjust if you find that gauge is not matching. Most patterns clearly state whether or not gauge is important for the project and provide the correct gauge when needed.

**You Will Need**

_Yarn_

• bulky or chunky yarn, 65–75 yds (59–68 m), ideally in a long-print or self-striping colorway, such as Paton's ColorWul

_Tools_

• hook size K (6.5 mm)

• scissors

• yarn needle

• stitch marker

• measuring tape or ruler

_Stitches and Abbreviations_

ch—chain

Sl st—slip stitch

sc—single crochet

st—stitch

sts—stitches

RS—right side—the outside of the project

*—asterisk shows where to repeat from, in each round

1 **FOUNDATION AND FIRST ROUND**

Foundation: Ch 4, Sl st to form a ring. Ch 1.

Rnd 1: 6 sc in the ring, place marker in first stitch—6 sc.

Rnd 1, complete, with marker in place.

The piece measures about 3" (7.5 cm) across. Notice the markers at 6 increase points.

2 **INCREASING ROUNDS**

Rnd 2: 2 sc in each st around—12 sc.

Rnd 3: *2 sc in next st, sc in next st. Repeat from * around—18 sc.

Rnd 4: *2 sc in next st, sc in each of next 2 sts. Repeat from * around—24 sc.

Measuring to check for fit, after step 2 is complete.

tip  The pattern of increases for Rnd 4 is 2 single crochet in the same stitch, 1 alone in next stitch, 1 alone in next stitch; 2 single crochet in next stitch, 1 alone in next stitch, 1 alone in next stitch; over and over around the circle. If you have stitch markers of different colors, you can use one color to mark the first stitch of the round as usual; use another color to mark the first of the "two stitches together" at each increase. For the rest of the increase section, you won't need to count stitches—just increase each time you come to a marked stitch, and move the marker to the new round, inserting it again into the first of the two increase stitches.

#### Measuring Gauge

When Rnd 4 is complete, lay the circle down on a flat surface. Don't stretch it, but pat it flat and then lay a ruler or measuring tape straight across the center, from one edge to the other. It should measure 3" (7.5 cm) across. If your piece is smaller than 27/8" (7.3 cm), it means your stitches are smaller and tighter than the designer's stitches. Start over with the next larger size hook or your hat will be too small and tight. If your piece measures more than 31/8" (7.9 cm), it means your stitches are larger and looser than the designer's and you need to start over with the next size smaller hook. It's very common to find that a different hook makes the right size stitches! It's always worth the time it takes to check gauge and start over with the hook that makes the right size stitches with YOUR yarn in YOUR hands. It's very disappointing to finish a beautiful project only to find out that it's much too big or much too small. In this project, you'll check gauge again after Rnd 7, making a different kind of adjustment at that point, if needed.

Rnd 5: *2 sc in next st, sc in each of next 3 sts. Repeat from * around—30 sc.

Rnd 6: *2 sc in next st, sc in each of next 4 sts. Repeat from * around—36 sc.

Rnd 7: *2 sc in next st, sc in each of next 5 sts. Repeat from * around—42 sc.

tip  Remember to move the marker to the first stitch of each new round as soon as you make that stitch!

Now it's time for the second size check. Lay the piece flat again and measure across the center from edge to edge. At this point, it should measure 6" (15 cm). Don't worry if it's off; you won't be starting over again! If your piece is smaller than 51/2" (14 cm), work 1 more round of increases, in which the pattern is: *2 sc in next st, sc in each of next 6 sts. If your piece is larger than 61/2" (16.5 cm), gently pull out the stitches of Rnd 7. The marker in the first stitch of the round will prevent you from ripping out too many stitches.

3 **SIDES OF THE HAT**

Rnds 8–18: Sc in each st around. Continue to move the marker to the first stitch of each round as you make that stitch. The sides will begin to "cup" toward you, forming a bowl shape, but the side facing you is actually the right side, or the outside of the hat. You can push the bottom of the bowl to see that you're working on the outside of the hat. You'll also notice that the 6 slightly pointed corners made by the increase stitches in Step 2 will gradually disappear. Many crocheters find it helpful to number a scrap of paper with the numbers 8 through 18 and cross off each number as that round is finished.

On the right side of the fabric, each round forms a ridge. If you lose count, start at the center (at the base of Rnd 1) and count the ridges outward toward the hook's current location.

#### Counting Rounds

At the end of Rnd 18, check the size of the hat one last time. Lay the hat down with the start (crown of the hat) at the top and the stitches of Rnd 18 forming the bottom edge. Measure from Rnd 18 to Rnd 1. It should be about 71/2" (19 cm). You can try the hat on, too, if you like. If you decide you want the hat to be longer, simply work a few more rounds, just like rnds 8–18. Each round adds about 1/4" (6 mm) to the length of the hat. If it's too long already, simply pull out a round or two.

4 **EDGING**

Rnd 19: With RS facing and final round of Step 3 at the top, Sl st in next st and in each st around. Fasten off, leaving 8" (20.5 cm) of tail to weave in.

Another use for slip stitch: making a strong, finished edge, slightly thicker than the rest of the fabric.

5 **FINISHING**

Thread the ending yarn tail onto a yarn needle and weave it in and out of stitches on the inside of the hat. It's best to weave it through 3 separate groups of stitches, about 1" or 2" (2.5 cm or 5 cm) long, in 3 separate directions: along a row in one direction, up through several rows in a second direction, and then back the first way across a row. Cut off the remaining little tail. Turn the hat inside out and repeat this process with the beginning yarn tail.

With the ends securely woven in, the hat is ready to wear.

### Trinkets and Treasures Drawstring Bag

  This little bag is so handy, whether used for holding game pieces, marbles, jewelry, or any other collection of small objects. The drawstring pulls the top tight to keep your tiny treasures safe. If you've worked your way through the previous chapters and projects, you know almost everything you need; but this project does offer a couple of small, new skills. You'll learn a slightly different way to start your project in the round—a way that eliminates the ring and its resulting center hole. You'll also learn to crochet "in the back loop only", to create a fold line where the bottom of the bag meets the sides. A variegated or ombre yarn makes the project fun, but a plain color will work just as well.

**You Will Need**

_Yarn_

• acrylic worsted medium yarn, such as Loops & Threads Impeccable or Caron Simply Soft, about 50 yds (45.7 m).

_Tools_

• hook size H (5 mm) or smaller, if needed to make the fabric nice and solid–see Gauge for details

• scissors

• yarn needle

• 1 stitch marker

_Stitches and Abbreviations_

ch—chain

Sl st—slip stitch

sc—single crochet

st—stitch

sts—stitches

PM—place marker—put the stitch marker in the indicated stitch

BLO—back loop only—insert hook under only the back loop of the stitch's top V, complete the stitch as usual.

RS—right side—the outside of the project

*—asterisk shows where to repeat from, in each round

_Gauge_

Exact gauge is not important for this project, but the stitches do need to be close and tight enough to create a solid fabric. Gauge in the sample: Rounds 1–3 = 11/2" (4 cm) across center of piece. If yours is more than 2" (5 cm) across, start over with the next smaller size hook.

#### A New Kind of Foundation

You've probably noticed that the earlier projects have all had a hole at the center, which was the foundation ring into which the first round of stitches were worked. But a hole is a bad idea when you're making a bag to keep small objects, so for this project, we'll create a solid foundation. With this technique, you'll increase to make the first round of stitches.

1 **A NEW WAY TO START**

Foundation: Ch 2. (That's right, only 2 chain stitches this time. The first one made is the actual Foundation, and the second one is the "starting chain" for the beginning of Round 1.)

Rnd 1: 6 sc in 2nd ch from hook. PM in first st. (Plain English explanation: there is a loop on the hook; don't count that one. Right below it is the first chain from the hook; this will become the starting chain for the round of stitches you're about to make. Right below THAT is the "second chain from the hook." It's actually the first chain you made, of the two. Now that you've found the right spot, insert the hook under 2 strands of yarn and make a single crochet stitch. Place the stitch marker in the top of this stitch as soon as it's completed, marking it as the first stitch of the round.

Now make 5 more single crochet stitches, always inserting the hook into that same spot. This is similar to the "2 stitches in one place" increase you've already done, but you're just adding a lot more stitches in that place. Don't worry about the crowding—they will fit, and will form a little circle.)

Making the first single crochet in the 2nd ch from the hook

Foundation and Round 1 complete.

2 **INCREASING ROUNDS**

Rnds 2–7: Follow the same directions you did for Rnds 2–7 of Project 4, page 44, ending with 42 sts in Rnd 7. Because the yarn is thinner and the hook smaller, the finished flat circle is quite a bit smaller than the one for the Beanie. This shows again the importance of gauge when following patterns—you may create the same number of stitches in each round, but if the stitches are smaller or larger, it will change the size of the finished piece.

These circles have the same number of stitches in each round. Keeping the same gauge throughout is important!

3 **FOLD LINE**

Rnd 8: Sc in BLO in each st around. (Plain English: In this round, you'll make 1 single crochet in each stitch, BUT you'll be inserting the hook in a slightly different place. Each time you start a stitch, insert the hook under only the back loop of the stitch into which you're working (see illustration, page 49).

Working in BLO—The "leftover" front loops create a ridge on the right side of the work; this is the "fold line" where the bag's flat bottom meets the sides.

4 **SIDES**

Rnds 9–20: working in both loops, sc in each st around. (Plain English: These 11 rounds are worked by simply doing a normal, "both loops" single crochet in each stitch, remembering to move the stitch marker to the first stitch of each round. This is the step where the project begins to take on its final shape.)

It's looking like a bag!

tip  Remember to move the stitch marker to the first stitch of each round, AND remember to stop and check gauge after Round 3.

5 **EYELET**

Next, you'll make the round with holes for the drawstring. To create the eyelet holes, make a chain after every 2 single crochet stitches, skipping (not working into) a stitch in Round 20.

Rnd 21: *Sc in each of next 2 sts. Ch 1, skip 1 st. Repeat from * around, ending with ch 1, skip the final stitch. (Plain English: Make a single crochet in the first and the second stitch, remembering to move the stitch marker. Chain 1, and skip the next stitch before you make a single crochet in stitches 4 and 5. Continue around the whole circle, ending with a chain 1 and leaving the final stitch of the round unworked.)

The end of the eyelet round.

6 **TOP EDGE**

Rnd 22: Sc in each st and in each ch-1 space around—14 eyelet holes. (Plain English: Make a single crochet in the first stitch and move the marker. Next, make a single crochet in the empty space or hole under the chain. Repeat these two all the way around, and you'll have 14 holes in Rnd 21.)

Rnd 23: Sc in each st around. Sl st in next sc to join. Fasten off. (Plain English: Make 1 single crochet stitch in each stitch around. Then slip stitch into the first (marked) stitch. Fasten off by making one chain stitch, cutting the yarn, and pulling the yarn tail through the chain stitch. Be sure to leave a 6–8" (15–20.5 cm) tail when you cut the yarn.

Working into a ch-1 space to complete the top of the eyelet hole.

7 **DRAWSTRING TIE**

Ch 75. Fasten off and weave in both yarn tails. (Plain English: Start with a new piece of yarn and leaving a 6" (15 cm) tail, make 75 chain stitches. Fasten off, leaving another 6" (15 cm) tail. Weave in each yarn tail along the chain.

Weaving in the yarn tails of the Drawstring Tie.

8 **FINISHING**

Weave in the starting and ending yarn tails of the bag.

Lace the Drawstring Tie in and out through the eyelet holes. Then tie an overhand knot at each end of the tie to keep it in place.

tip  In the Eyelet Round, it's important to make the chain stitches loosely. Each one should be just as wide as the top Vs of the single crochet stitches in the round.

##   ROW BY ROW

### Single Crochet with Turning Chains

Up until now, all your projects have been based on a circular shape created by working in rounds. The fabric, as you may have noticed, looks different on its right side than it does on its wrong side. Also, the right side is always facing you as you make the stitches. But one of the wonderful things about crochet is that there are so many different directions in which to work! This chapter will teach you how to work rows of single crochet back and forth. Working this way creates a fabric that looks the same on front and back. As you make each row, it still has a right side and a wrong side. The right side of the current row is still the side facing you as you work. But, since the work will be turned, like the page of a book, at the end of the row, the right side of Row 1 becomes the wrong side of the work when you start on Row 2. Switching back and forth every other row is what makes both sides of the fabric look alike—AND makes it much easier to create square and rectangle shapes. In this chapter, you'll learn a new way of starting projects, in which the stitches form a line as you create them instead of a circle. You'll also learn how to turn correctly, how to keep the rows from gaining or losing stitches, and how to count the stitches and rows in this new and different-looking fabric. You'll also learn how to felt a finished piece of crochet—creating a very thick and completely solid fabric. You'll make a felted phone pocket and a cute stuffed animal.

### Chain Foundation for Working in Rows

The chain that starts a row-based project is usually longer than the chains you've started with up until now. Generally, the starting or Foundation Chain is as long as the width of the square or rectangle being made. Imagine a winter scarf—if you start with a chain about 6" (15 cm) long and make MANY rows back and forth, you'll eventually end up with a long, narrow rectangle to wrap around your neck. Or, you could start with a very long chain and work a few very long rows to make the same shape. In other words, your rows can go across the short side of the rectangle or the long side. One way is not better than the other, but the two approaches create different looks.

Besides the length of the chain, another difference is in how the chain is used. Instead of making a ring and working the first single crochets into the "hole" at the center of the ring, this time you'll be making the first row of single crochet directly into chain stitches. Here is where it becomes very important to make the foundation chain loosely—the hook must go into each chain stitch without a fight. So, let's get going, chaining and rowing!

**You Will Need**

_Yarn_

• any worsted yarn in a light color, a few yards or small ball

_Tools_

• hook size H (5 mm) and I (5.5 mm), or J (6 mm) and K (6.5 mm)

• scissors

• 2 stitch markers

tip  Count the stitches at the end of each row (by counting the top Vs), to make sure there are 10. If there are fewer, look for a hole between two stitches, and see if you can find the chain that was skipped. It will be there between the two stitches on either side of it. If you have more than 10, look for a place where the work seems to bend in an "elbow"—that will be where you increased by working 2 stitches in the same place. If you can find the spot where the mistake happened, carefully pull out the stitches just back to that point, and then finish the row correctly. If you can't easily find the exact mistake spot, simply pull out that row—the marker in the first stitch will prevent you from pulling out too many—and do the row over again.

Many crocheters always make their foundation chains with a larger hook than they use for the rest of the rows.

Insert the hook under 2 strands of the 2nd chain from hook. It's easiest to put the hook under the back loop and bottom bump.

Complete the sc stitch as usual: yo and pull through both loops on the hook. The first single crochet into the chain is complete. Place a stitch marker in the top of this stitch.

Look for the very next chain loop to the left of the stitch just completed. Be careful not to skip a chain.

Finished row of 10 single crochet. Stitch marker shows the first st in the row.

**1 STARTING CHAIN AND FIRST ROW**

Foundation: With the larger of the two hooks, chain 11 loosely. Count the chains to double check, and then switch to the smaller hook.

Look closely at the chain you've just made. The loop on the hook does not get counted. The next loop below the hook is the "first ch from the hook" and is also the "turning chain" for a single crochet row. You will not work into it. The next chain beyond that is the "2nd ch from hook" and pattern instructions will tell you to insert the hook into it.

Continue across the chain, making 1 sc in each ch st.

Make 1 chain stitch, the "turning chain."

Insert the hook here to start the first stitch of Row 2 and work a single crochet. When the first stitch is finished, place a stitch marker in the top of it.

Row 2 is finished! The marker at the right hand edge will help in working the final stitch of Row 3.

Turn the work, just like turning the page of a book. Now the stitch marker is at the other end, because the first stitch of Row 1 will be the last stitch you'll work into in Row 2.

Locating the final stitch of the row—look for the stitch marker and make the last stitch of Row 2 in the marked stitch. As soon as you find it, you can remove the stitch marker to make it easier to insert the hook.

Using the hook as a guide in "frogging" to fix a mistake.

The pins are placed every two rows, to show how rows of single crochet are counted by "twosies."

#### Making the Turn

When crocheting in rows, each new row begins with a "turning chain." Some patterns will say to turn the work and then make the chain as you begin the next row; others will tell you to make the turning chain and then turn the work. The order in which you do these steps doesn't matter; some designers just prefer to write it one way or the other. What IS important is that you always remember to turn the work and to make the turning chain the correct length.

The length of the turning chain depends on what stitch is being done in the NEXT row. The turning chain must include enough chain stitches to equal the height of the stitches in the new row. A single crochet stitch is 1 chain stitch high, but there are other, taller stitches to learn later, and they will have longer turning chains—2, 3, or 4 ch stitches!

#### Onward and Upward—Row 2 and Beyond

Begin Row 2 by locating the first stitch. There is a loop on the hook; just below that is the turning chain, and the next loop is the top V of the first stitch of the row.

Now work a single crochet stitch in each stitch across the row. Remember to insert the hook under both the front loop and the back loop (under both arms of the sideways V) at the top of each stitch.

It's important to count stitches at the end of every row until your eyes get used to the look of the fabric. Counting stitches is the best way to figure out if you accidentally made two stitches in the same place (added a stitch) or accidentally skipped a stitch, leaving a little hole in the work (lost a stitch). If either has happened, insert the hook between the two top loops at the top of the last correct stitch before the mistake and then gently rip out stitches until you reach the error. The placement of the hook will ensure that you don't rip out too many.

Work several more rows, remembering to make a turning chain between the end of one row and the beginning of the next, using the 2 stitch markers to keep track of the final stitch in each row. You'll notice that the fabric has a different texture than the fabric that was made by working single crochet in rounds! When worked in rounds, as in the hat and bag, each round created one ridge or bump in the fabric. Now, working in rows, the ridges or bumps are more gentle, and it takes two rows to make each little "furrow." It's easy to count by twos when counting rows of single crochet.

When you're comfortable with crocheting in rows, you're ready for the next two projects—a felted pocket for keeping a cell phone or mp3 player safe, and a stuffed animal toy. Each of these projects will use the skills you already know, and also teach something new.

### Felted Phone Pocket

  Electronic devices are so handy... and so easy to damage! It seems a sure thing that phones and iPods get dropped from time to time, and replacing them is expensive and takes time. This handy pocket will help to pad a delicate device, cushioning it from bumps and bangs while in a purse or backpack. You'll crochet the bag first and then learn how to felt it. Felting is a process that turns the loose, holey crochet fabric into a solid, thick, dense felt (just like craft felt, but thicker). In order for the felting process to work, the yarn must be wool, or a blend made of at least 75 to 80 percent wool. Because fabric shrinks during the felting process, the crocheted piece must be made about one-third larger than its finished size. It's also important to use a larger hook than usual, so the stitches are fairly loose. Friction between the strands of yarn is an important part of the felting process. One benefit of the felting process is that yarn tails do not need to be woven in securely. The felting process ensures that no strand of yarn can come loose and begin to unravel the crochet.

**You Will Need**

_Yarn_

• worsted weight medium wool, about 50 yds (45.7 m) in color A (main color) and 15 yds (13.7 m) color B (contrast color). (sample was made with Paton's Classic Wool.)

_Tools_

• hook size J (6 mm), or K (6.5 mm) if you tend to crochet tightly

• scissors

• yarn needle

• 2 stitch markers

• 1 button 5/8" to 3/4" (1.5 cm to 2 cm) in diameter

• sewing thread and needle that will fit through button's holes

• 1 sewing pin

• pencil

• corrugated cardboard 6" × 6" (15 cm × 15 cm) (side of a packing box will do nicely)

• masking, packing, or duct tape

• top-loading washing machine with a hot water wash cycle

_Stitches and Abbreviations_

• ch—chain

• Sl st—slip stitch

• sc—single crochet

• st(s)—stitch(es)

• RS—right side; the outside of the project

• WS—wrong side; the inside of the project

**Directions**

_**Note:** The process of felting shrinks the crocheted fabric dramatically. The pocket will appear to be much too big until it's felted._

_Numbers at the end of a line of instructions indicate the total number of stitches in that row. A new "stitch count" number is given each time the number of stitches changes. If no new number is at the end of the line of instructions, your count should be the same as it was in the row before._

Rotate the piece and, working through one layer only, continue to sc, working 1 stitch in each original chain stitch of the Foundation Chain. This is the top edge of the front of the pocket.

**1 GETTING STARTED**

Foundation: With yarn A, ch 15 loosely.

Row 1: Sc in 2nd ch from hook, and each ch across. Ch 1, turn. Remember to place a stitch marker in the first stitch of each row, and to remove it when you use it to find the last stitch of the following row— 14 sc.

Foundation and Row 1 finished.

**2 MAIN SECTION**

Rows 2–42: Sc in each st across the row. Ch 1, turn.

The straight rows of Step 2 make the body, or main section, of the pocket.

**3 FLAP**

Row 43: Skip the first st; make a sc in the 2nd st and each of the next 11 sts. Ch 1, turn, leaving the last st unworked—12 sc.

Row 44: Skip the first st; sc in each of next 10 sts. Ch 1, turn, leaving the last st unworked—10 sc.

Row 45: Skip the first st, sc in each of next 8 sts. Ch 1, turn, leaving the last st unworked—8 sc.

Row 46: Skip the first st, sc in each of next 6 sts, leaving the last st unworked. Fasten off and remove stitch markers—6 sc.

Skipping a stitch at the start and the end of each of the next few rows will make a stair-step slanted edge for the flap.

Here are the shorter and shorter rows that make the flap.

**4 FOLD AND SEAMS**

Follow the photo captions to fold the crocheted fabric, and then crochet the side seams and front trim.

Rotate the work again and work down the other side, back to the fold. As on the first side, work through both thicknesses, making 1 sc in the side of each row end.

Fold the piece so Row 1 is lying on top of Row 40 (2 rows below the start of the flap's shorter rows).

Start at the fold and join yarn B with a single crochet through both thicknesses of fabric. Make 1 sc in the side of each row end until the end of the doubled side edge.

tip  Don't worry about the natural curl of the fabric. Curling up from the lower right corner is just what single crochet in rows does. It will not affect the final outcome of the project.

**5 FLAP EDGING**

Turn the pocket over so the back of the flap is facing you. With yarn color B, work a row of sc along the curved edge of the flap. Be sure to poke the hook under 2 strands of yarn in each stitch to avoid stretching out the stitches. Some of these edging stitches will be made into the sides of stitches at the end of a row, as with the seams in step 4. Some will be made into the tops of stitches in Row 46 of the flap. You'll need to increase around the curve by making 2 stitches in the same place a few times so the flap will lie flat. Here's how the direction for this step looks in regular pattern language:

Attach B with a sc in first row end at right hand side of back of flap. *Sc in next 3 sts, 2 sc in next st. Repeat from * 4 times. Sc in each of last 3 sts. Fasten off.

Because this project is going to be felted, there is no need to weave in the yarn tails. Simply trim them to about 3" (7.5 cm) long.

Increases in the edging row help the curved edge lie flat.

**6 FELTING**

Set the washing machine to its hottest wash water setting and select the smallest load size. Add a small amount of detergent and start filling the washer. Place your project and a couple of pillow cases, tennis balls, or old shirts in the washer. If the water heater is set for a temperature lower than 120°F (49°C), ask an adult to boil 2 qts (1.9 l) of water on the stove, and pour directly into the washer during the first hot water wash part of the cycle.

It's the combination of moisture, heat, and friction that go to work on the wool, causing the individual fibers that make up the yarn to attach firmly to one another. While the washing machine and hot water are doing their work, trace the shape of your cell phone or other device on to the cardboard. Cut 2 pieces of cardboard to this size and tape them together, making a cardboard size-model of the phone.

When the washer cycle is complete, remove the project. If it has become solid, with individual stitches no longer visible and no holes in the fabric, then felting is done. If not, re-wash, being sure to add the boiling water.

Stuff the cardboard model into the pocket and lay it flat to dry. Drying may take 24 to 48 hours. While the felt is still wet, the cardboard model makes sure the felted pocket doesn't shrink too much. If it has already shrunk, it can be stretched while still wet to fit the model. If the pocket is a bit larger than the cardboard model, that's fine—it means that there will be plenty of room for easy use.

Make a cardboard model.

You may need to be firm in stuffing the cardboard model into the pocket.

**7 FINISHING**

When the pocket is dry, remove the cardboard model. Follow the photo captions to finish.

Now your phone or mp3 player pocket is ready to keep an electronic device safe and snug!

Cut off all yarn tails—they will not unravel.

Cut a 1/2" (1.3 cm) slit (buttonhole) in the center of the flap, about 1/4 (6 mm) from the lower edge.

Use a pin to mark the spot on the front of the pocket that matches the buttonhole.

Sew the button in place. If you've never sewn on a button before, this is a great time to have an adult show you how.

### Monster Madness!

  With yarn and a bit of fluff for stuffing, you can make an endless variety of stuffed "critters" for yourself, brothers and sisters, and your friends. If you choose different colors of yarn, and felt or sewn features, each one you make will be different and special, whether cute and cuddly or "too ugly not to love."

You Will Need

_Yarn_

• worsted (medium) acrylic or wool blend, 100 yds (91.4 m) or less of color A, about 25 yds (22.9 m) of color B and scraps of black and any other desired colors for face embroidery. (Sample was made with Red Heart Soft.)

_Tools_

• hook size G (4 mm) and I (5.5 mm)

• scissors

• 2 stitch markers

• yarn needle

• polyester fiberfill stuffing

• 2 or more small buttons

• sewing thread and thread needle

• scraps of colored craft felt for face, optional

_Stitches and Abbreviations_

ch—chain

Sl st—slip stitch

sc—single crochet

st(s)—stitch(es)

RS—right side

WS—wrong side

_Gauge_

7 stitches = 2" (5 cm), 7 rows = 2" (5 cm)

Gauge is not crucial for this project, but use a hook that makes a fairly tight fabric so the stuffing will not peek out between stitches.

**Directions**

**_Note:_** Numbers at the end of a line of directions indicate the number of stitches in that row. If no number is given, the stitch count is the same as it was in the row before.

**1 CROCHET MAIN PIECE (HEAD AND BODY)**

Foundation: With color A and smaller hook, ch 16 loosely. (Use a larger hook if your chains tend to be tight.)

Row 1: Sc in 2nd ch from hook and place marker if needed. Sc in each ch across. Ch 1, turn—15 sc.

Rows 2–36: Sc in each st across. Ch 1, turn. At end of Row 36, fasten off.

Step 1, completed.

**2 ASSEMBLE MAIN PIECE**

Using color A yarn, start the seam at the left hand side where Row 36 meets the Foundation Chain. Make 1 sc in each row end, working through both thicknesses, toward the fold. This will join Row 36 to Row 1, Row 35 to Row 2, etc. At fold, fasten off—18 sc.

Attach a new color A yarn to the hook. At the opposite edge of the fold, sc through both thicknesses to close the other long side, making 1 sc in each row end, and continuing to keep rows straight and matched. Fasten off.

Fold the rectangle in half widthwise so that the Foundation Chain and Row 36 are together.

Starting the second seam by attaching the yarn on the hook to the work with a single crochet stitch.

**3 MAKE THE EARS**

Hold the Main Piece so that the folded edge is at the top and the open edge is at the bottom. *On right-hand edge, count down 5 rows from fold and place a marker in the seam. Count 5 stitches across the fold from the edge and place another marker.

Cut a piece of color A yarn about 18" (45.5 cm) long and thread it onto the yarn needle. Pull half the yarn through to create a double strand. Leaving about 4" (10 cm) of tail sticking out, sew a line of stitches from the first marker to the 2nd marker. Weave in the ending tail and cut it close to the crocheted fabric. Rethread the starting tail onto the needle (you can do the 2 strands separately if you need to) and weave it in as well. Trim it off close to the crocheted fabric. Repeat from * on left hand side of Main Piece for second ear.

Markers placed for ears.

**4 STUFF THE BODY**

Hold the Main Piece with ears at the bottom and the open edge at the top. Add polyester fiberfill stuffing a small amount at a time, tucking it down into the corners gently but firmly, until filled. Less stuffing makes a softer, flatter finished toy; more stuffing makes a fatter, firmer toy.

When stuffed, attach color A yarn to hook and sc through the thicknesses of both the Foundation Chain and Row 36 to close the seam. Fasten off—15 sc.

Now weave in any remaining yarn tails on the project so far.

Avoid lumpiness by adding the stuffing little by little.

Pull the edges together around the stuffing, and poke in the stuffing as needed.

Hiding yarn tails in the stuffing.

**5 MAKE THE LEGS (MAKE 2)**

Foundation: With the larger hook and color B, leaving 10–12" (25.5–30.5 cm) tail, ch 11 loosely.

Row 1: 2 sc in 2nd ch from hook, and 2 sc in each ch across. Ch 1, turn—20 sc.

Row 2: 2 sc in each st across. Ch 1, turn—40 sc.

Row 3: 2 sc in each st across. Fasten off, leaving 10–12" (25.5–30.5 cm) of tail—80 sc.

When both legs are finished, use the tails, threaded through the yarn needle, to sew them to the bottom edge of Main Piece near the outside edges, hiding the tails inside the stuffing. Trim tails off close to the surface.

The leg begins to curl with the increases in Row 1.

Two completed legs.

**6 MAKE THE ARMS (MAKE 2)**

Foundation: With larger hook and color B, ch 8 loosely.

Row 1: 2 sc in 2nd ch from hook. 2 sc in each st across. Ch 1, turn—14 sc.

Row 2: 2 sc in each st. Fasten off, leaving 10–12" (25.5–30.5 cm) tail. Weave in starting tail—28 sc.

Use the ending tails to sew an arm to each side of the body, halfway between the base of an ear and the bottom corner. The ending tail was left longer, so there's enough to sew across the width of the arm a couple of times in different directions, for sturdiness. After sewing back and forth, hide the remaining tail inside the stuffing and trim it off at the surface.

The arms are just like the legs, but smaller and a little less curled.

tip  If all the ends have been properly fastened off (with a final "yarn over and pull the tail through"), it's easy to simply poke them inside and hide them in the stuffing. To do this, thread a tail onto the yarn needle. Stick the needle into the stuffed piece and through some of the stuffing, then back out 1" or 2" (2.5 cm or 5 cm) away. Cut off the yarn close to the surface. Friction from the stuffing, along with the fastening off, will hold the end securely inside the toy.

**7 MAKE A FUN FACE**

Use the photo as a guide (or be bold and use your own imagination) to sew on buttons or glue on felt or fabric for the eyes, nose, and mouth. Be creative—who says your critter, monster, or alien must have two eyes? It could have 3 or 1 or 6! Use yarn to sew on a smile, a nose, or whatever other features in whatever colors you like.

tips It's best to sew on a leg with one tail and hide that tail inside the stuffing, then sew again with the second tail. This makes a more sturdy connection than a few stitches done at once with both tails doubled in the needle.

If the toy is to be a gift for a small child (3 years or under), safety requires that the face be embroidered with yarn. Babies and toddlers can bite off buttons and swallow them!

##   RIBBING

### Make it Stretchy!

"Ribbing" is a kind of ridged, wavy fabric that is extra stretchy. Many sweater sleeves, sock cuffs, hat edges, etc. are made with ribbing. When fabric is ribbed, it's not only stretchy, but also extra warm, because body heat is trapped near the skin in the air spaces under each ridge of the ribbing. Ribbing is easy to make in crochet simply by inserting the hook just a little bit differently at the start of each single crochet stitch. In this chapter, you'll learn how to create ribbed fabric, and then make a pair of fingerless mitts and a hat that instantly converts to a neck-warming cowl!

### Ribbing Basics

Ribbing is made by working the single crochet (sc) stitches "in BLO," or in Back loop only. As in earlier chapters, let's start with a practice piece, using scrap yarn and a comfortably sized hook.

### A Solid Foundation

**1** Ch 13. Sc in 2nd ch from hook and in each ch across. Ch 1, turn—12 sc.

Crochet Language

Plain English translation for Step 1: Make 13 chains. Make a single crochet in the second chain from the hook, and then make a single crochet in each of the chains across the Foundation Chain. You will have 12 single crochets in the row. Make one chain for the "turning chain" and turn the work, like turning the page of a book. If you need help remembering the abbreviations, use the guide on page 120.

### Working Single Crochet in "BLO"

**2** Begin the first stitch of Row 2 by inserting the hook BETWEEN the two arms of the top V of the first stitch, so that the hook goes under only the back loop. (See drawing of parts of a single crochet stitch, page 27. You did this for one round, without having turned the work, in Project 5. It looked a little different, but the motions are the same.)

Draw up a loop as usual, and complete the single crochet stitch as usual. The stitch of Row 1 that you're working into may stretch out a bit, but don't worry about that. It's normal, and will even out as the rest of the stitches in the row are made. Place a stitch marker in the completed stitch.

Continue to work across the row, making one sc in BLO in each stitch of Row 1. At the end of the row, chain 1 to turn, and turn the work.

Crochet Language

Pattern language for Row 2: Sc in BLO of each st across. Ch 1, turn.

Inserting the hook under only the back loop of the stitch.

First completed sc in BLO.

Row 2 is finished and the turning chain made, ready to turn and go on to Row 3.

**3** Keep going, using the stitch markers to help you find where the last stitch of each row belongs. As soon as you insert the hook to make that stitch, you may take out the marker so it will be handy to place in the first stitch of the following row. Keep repeating Row 2 until you have 4 ridges—a total of 9 rows of sc in BLO.

A completed swatch of ribbing.

You Will Need

_Yarn_

• worsted (medium) yarn, about 10 yds (9.1 m)

_Tools_

• hook size I (5.5 mm), J (6 mm), or K (6.5 mm), whichever is comfortable for your hand

• scissors

• 2 stitch markers

### Ribbie Mitts

  Now let's have some fun with stretchy projects! First, you can practice using ribbing to make a pair of fingerless mitts. They'll leave your fingers free while keeping your hands warm. Then try The "Howl"—a hat that instantly converts to a cowl. If the two projects are made in the same yarn, your head and hands will be all set for fall, winter, and spring. A yarn labeled "self-striping" or "long print" (LP) is ideal for this project.

You Will Need

_Yarn_

• worsted (medium) yarn, about 75 yds (68.6 m) (sample was made with Bernat Mosaic, color 1301)

_Tools_

• hook size G7 (4.5 mm), H (5 mm), or I (5.5 mm)

• scissors

• yarn needle

• tape measure

• 2 sewing pins

• 3 stitch markers

_Stitches and Abbreviations_

ch—chain

Sl st—slip stitch

sc—single crochet

BLO—back loop only (scBLO means, "make a single crochet in the back loop only")

st(s)—stitch(es)

RS—right side (the outside of the mitt)

WS—wrong side (the inside of the mitt)

PM—Place marker (put a stitch marker in the stitch)

_Gauge_

4 sc = 1"

Take time to measure gauge, and feel free to change hook size to make sure your stitches are the same size as stated. Sample was made with hook size H (5 mm).

**Directions**

**1 GAUGE SWATCH**

This is a good project to practice measuring gauge. The directions are based on measurements, so if your gauge is off by part of a stitch, your project will still work. But for your mitts, the important part is that the fabric being made is soft and dense—not so tightly worked (too small a hook for the yarn) that it feels stiff, and not so loosely worked that the ribbing stretches out right away. A common way to measure gauge is to make a small practice square, or swatch.

With your chosen yarn and size H (5 mm) hook, ch 13.

Row 1: Sc in 2nd ch from hook, and in each ch across. Ch 1, turn—12 sc.

Rows 2–5: ScBLO in each stitch across. Ch 1, turn.

At the end of Row 5, do not fasten off. Lay the piece down flat, and use a ruler to measure 2" (5 cm) in the middle of Rows 3 and 4. Place a pin at each end of the 2" (5 cm) sections. Count the number of stitches between the pins. If gauge is correct, there will be 8 stitches. If you have fewer stitches, it means your stitches are larger, and you should try again with a smaller hook. If you have more than 8 stitches, it means your stitches are smaller, and you should try again with a larger hook.

Gauge is too tight and there are 5 small stitches per inch (10 in the 2" area). A larger hook is needed.

Gauge is too loose and there are 3 large stitches per inch (6 in the 2" area). A smaller hook is needed.

Gauge is just right, and there are 4 stitches per inch. This is the right hook for this crocheter to use.

**2 MEASURE TWICE**

Write down this Length Measurement, too, but without adding anything to it or subtracting anything from it.

Have someone use the tape measure to measure around your hand, right at the knuckles. Subtract 1" (2.5 cm), and write down this Key Measurement.

Next measure from knuckles to the spot on your forearm where you want the mitts to end—some people like them longer or shorter than others.

**3 CROCHET A RIBBED RECTANGLE**

Foundation: Make a loose chain, long enough that when you lay it flat without stretching, it equals the Length Measurement. Add 1 extra ch st, for the turning chain.

Row 1: Sc in 2nd ch from hook and in each ch across. Ch 1, turn—12 sc.

Row 2: ScBLO in each st across. Ch 1, turn.

Repeat Row 2 until the whole piece, laid flat and unstretched, equals the Key Measurement. Do NOT Fasten off, but PM in the loop remaining on the hook. Remove the hook. This marker will hold the loop and keep it from pulling out and raveling the work until it's time to put the hook back in and start crocheting again. Count the number of rows (each "bump" or ridge of the ribbing is 2 rows) and write that number down.

Foundation Chain, made and measured, with 1 extra chain for starting the first row.

tip  Count the sc in Row 1 and write the number down. Then count the stitches in any row to make sure you aren't accidentally increasing or decreasing.

**4 ASSEMBLY**

With the rectangle laid flat and the marker holding the working loop at ending edge of the last row, go to the opposite, or beginning edge of the row—measure 1" (2.5 cm) from the starting edge and PM (place a marker in the stitch that is closest to the 1" measurement). From that marker, measure another 2" (5 cm) and PM. (Place a second marker in the stitch closest to 2" farther into the row from the first marker).

Fold the piece so that the final row and the Foundation Chain are together. Put the hook back into the working loop and remove that stitch marker. Matching up the stitches and inserting the hook under just one strand of yarn from each side, sc through both thicknesses from the edge until you come to a marked stitch (it will be the second marker you placed for the thumbhole). At the marked stitch, fasten off and remove that marker.

Place a fresh slip knot on the hook. Starting at the stitch with the remaining thumb hole marker, insert the hook under one strand of each thickness (the final row and the Foundation Chain) and complete a sc. Sc in this way through each of the remaining stitches to finish the seam. Ch 1.

Being careful to insert the hook under two strands of yarn in each, sc in the sides of the row-end stitches, all the way around top edge. Sl st to join the final st to the first st of this round. Fasten off.

Attach yarn with a sc in any st of the thumbhole edge. Sc in each st around thumbhole, sl st to join last st to first st. Fasten off.

Ready for Step 4.

The space between stitch markers will be the thumb hole of the mitt.

Inserting the hook under 1 strand from each side makes a nice, thin seam.

Joining new yarn with a single crochet in the marked stitch.

The number of stitches in this edging round should be the same as the number of rows you counted earlier, in the completed rectangle.

tip  If you're still getting used to the way the first and last stitches of each row look in ribbing, use a stitch marker in the top of the first stitch of each row as you finish that stitch. Then you'll know where to insert the hook for the final stitch of the next row.

**5 FINISHING**

Turn the mitt inside out. Use the yarn needle to securely weave in the yarn tails on the WS of the mitt. Remember to run a stitch in each of 3 directions—along a row, across several rows, and diagonally back toward where you started. Then trim off the extra yarn.

Repeat Steps 2–4 for second mitt, using the same measurements, number of stitches per row, and total number of rows. Careful counting will make sure that the two mitts are the same size!

A neat finished edge will help the thumbhole edge stay sturdy.

A contrasting yarn shows the path of the 3 "weaving in" stitches, which will actually be hidden inside, between the RS and WS of the crochet stitches.

### The "Howl" (Hat + Cowl)

  A neckwarmer that just goes around the neck without hanging down is called a cowl. The next project is a "two in one" special—a hat that converts to a cowl! So when it's cold outside, you can put the warmth wherever you need it most. You'll start by making a ribbed rectangle, similar to the rectangles you made for the Ribbie Mitts. But a seam will turn the rectangle into a tube, and a drawstring will turn it into a hat! Yarn can be any fiber, but a soft acrylic or wool blend will be most comfy and warm to wear. A "long print" or "self-striping" colorway will create stripes for you, but a plain or variegated yarn is also fine to use.

You Will Need

_Yarn_

• worsted (medium) yarn, 100 yds (91.4 m) [Samples were made using Universal Yarn Deluxe Worsted LP (100% self-striping wool) and Lion Brand Vanna's Choice (100% acrylic).]

_Tools_

• hook size I (5.5 mm) or size needed for accurate gauge.

• scissors

• yarn needle

• 2 sewing pins

• ruler for measuring gauge

• 2 stitch markers, optional

_Stitches and Abbreviations_

ch—chain

Sl st—slip stitch

sc—single crochet

BLO—back loop only (scBLO means, "make a single crochet in the back loop only")

st(s)—stitch(es)

_Gauge_

7 stitches = 2" (5 cm), 7 rows = 2" (5 cm).

Gauge is important for this project, so be sure to check and change hook size if needed.

**Directions**

**_Note:_** The number at the end of a line of instructions indicates the number of stitches in that row.

**1 GAUGE SWATCH**

With your chosen yarn and size I (5.5 mm) hook, ch 13.

Row 1: Sc in 2nd ch from hook, and in each ch across. Ch 1, turn—12 sc.

Rows 2–9: ScBLO in each stitch across. Ch 1, turn.

At the end of Row 9, do not fasten off. Lay the piece down flat, and use a ruler to measure 2" (5 cm) in the middle of Rows 3 and 4. Place pins and count the number of stitches in that 2" (5 cm) section. If gauge is correct, there will be 7 stitches. If you have fewer than 61/2 stitches, it means your stitches are larger, and you should try again with a smaller hook. If you have more than 71/2 stitches, it means your stitches are smaller, and you should try again with a larger hook.

When you have a swatch made with the right number of stitches per 2" (5 cm), double check by laying the ruler in the other direction, across rows 2–8. Don't stretch the ribs flat—don't stretch at all—just lay the ruler over the ridges of the ribbing. Rows 2–8 should measure 2". If your rows are too short, check as you crochet that you are pulling up the first loop of each stitch to the height of the row. If you've only been pulling just barely enough yarn though to the front, the stitches will be squashed and short... and the fabric will not be as soft and warm! If your rows 2–8 measure more than 21/4" (5.5 cm), then leave off rows 54 and 55 of the instructions.

Seven stitches measure 2" (5 cm) in this swatch, so gauge is correct.

**2 CROCHET A RIBBED RECTANGLE**

Foundation: Ch 26.

Row 1: Sc in 2nd ch from hook, and each ch across. Ch 1, turn—25 sc, 1 ch.

Row 2: ScBLO in each st across. Ch 3, turn—25 sc, 3 ch.

Row 3: Sc in both loops of first st. ScBLO in each st across. Ch 1, turn—25 sc, 1 ch.

Rows 4–55: Repeat Rows 2 and 3. At the end of Row 55, ch 1 and do NOT fasten off.

Rows 1–3 complete. The longer turning ch in Row 2 forms a loop at the end of the row.

tip  As you work from row to row, stop at the end of each row and count stitches to make sure you have not accidentally increased or skipped a stitch. Use stitch markers in the first stitch of each row if you need them. When you stop to count, you can also check that all the ch-3 loops are at the same edge of the rectangle. They will be needed in their correct place later on.

**3 SLIP STITCH THE SEAM**

In the Finishing step of the Eenie Meenie Easy Beanie, you worked a round of slip stitches. In assembling the Felted Phone Pocket and the Make Believe Monster, you learned to single crochet through two thicknesses of fabric to make a seam. For The Howl, you'll make a different kind of seam that uses both of these skills. This time you'll fold the rectangle, match up the stitches, and work through both thicknesses, as you did before, but with a couple of differences.

Fold the finished rectangle so that the stitches of Row 55 and the Foundation Chain match up. With yarn on the hook, insert the hook under just 1 strand of yarn in each of these two edge stitches. Yarn over and draw up a loop; immediately pull that loop through the loop on the hook to complete a slip stitch. Move the hook to the next stitch, and make another slip stitch using just one strand from Row 55 and 1 strand from the Foundation Chain. Continue across the paired edges. At the end, fasten off and weave in both ending and beginning yarn tails on the inside of the tube. This is now the wrong wide of the project. The ribbed fabric is the same on both sides, so there has not been a right side and wrong side until the seam is made.

Inserting the hook under just 1 thread of each piece of the crocheted fabric.

**4 THE TIE**

Ch 75, or enough ch sts to equal 24–25" (61–63.5 cm) unstretched. Fasten off, and weave both yarn tails into the chain in two directions (in and out up the chain, and then back down toward the end).

Lace the tie in and out through the chain-3 loops that are at one edge of your ribbed tube. When the tie is laced all the way around, tie an overhand knot (see Glossary, page 122) at each end of the tie to keep it from being pulled back out through the loops.

When the tie is fully loosened, the Howl is a neck-warming Cowl that you pull over your head and wear around your neck. When the tie is pulled tight like a drawstring and tied in a bow, the Howl becomes a hat.

Lacing the drawstring tie.

tip  Different kinds of seams are used in different projects. You'll notice that this seam is much flatter and does not make a ridge like the single crochet seams you made before through 2 strands of each fabric.

##   A TALLER STITCH

### Double Crochet in Rounds and Rows

The single crochet stitch you've been using is very useful, but with crochet you can do so much more! The taller stitches involve adding extra loops to the process, opening new doors for the crocheter to make softer fabric with more DRAPE (see glossary, page 122) and to create fabric much faster for larger projects. So grab your hooks and some yarn with which to practice, and let's get taller!

### Making the Double Crochet Stitch

In this chapter you'll learn how to make the most commonly used taller stitch: the double crochet, or dc. You'll work the stitch in both rounds and rows to create a soft and warm winter scarf, the Great Grannies Scarf. Find some yarn to practice—leftovers from earlier projects will be fine—and choose a hook large enough to allow you to easily make the stitches you already know with your practice yarn.

**1 GET READY**

Starting with a chain ring is familiar and works as well for double crochet as single crochet.

Foundation: Ch 6. Join with a sl st to form a ring. Ch 3.

A stitch marker in the top of the turning chain makes it easier to find later. The turning chain counts as the first stitch of the round.

### Taller Stitch = Longer Turning Chain

Remember that the purpose of the turning chain is to create the height of the stitches in the new row that is about to be crocheted. Since the double crochet stitch is as tall as 3 chains, every round or row of dc starts with 3 chains. The turning chain actually counts as a double crochet stitch—the first stitch of each round or row. However, it doesn't look exactly like a dc stitch, and it's easy to accidentally skip working into it in the following round or row. To help with this, place a stitch marker in the top (3rd) ch of the turning chain.

**2 BEGIN THE DC WITH A YARN OVER**

Before inserting the hook into the ring, yarn over, and use your pointer finger to hold the yarn over with the loop already on the hook.

Make sure the working yarn is held at the back of the work, under the hook.

**3 INSERT AND DRAW UP**

Stick the hook into the ring as you would to sc, still holding the yarn over and the original loop on the hook with your index finger. At the back of the work, yarn over as you would for sc, then draw that loop back through to the front of the work, just as you would for sc.

There are now 3 loops on the hook.

**4 WORK 2 LOOPS OFF THE HOOK**

Yarn over and pull through 2 loops, leaving 2 loops on the hook.

Dc stitch, halfway finished.

**5 WORK THE LAST 2 LOOPS OFF THE HOOK**

Yarn over again and pull through 2 loops.

Congratulations! You've made a double crochet! Repeat steps 2–5 ten more times. Join with a Sl st in the top (marked) ch of the beginning ch-3. Fasten off with a final locking chain, and pull the tail through that loop. Dc stitches can be counted by their top Vs (like sc) or by their vertical posts. The top V is slightly to the right of the post when looking at the right side of the work.

Completed double crochet stitch, standing next to the beginning ch-3.

There are now 12 dc in the ring—the marked ch-3 to start, the first stitch, and the 10 repeats.

You Will Need

_Yarn_

• worsted (medium) weight of any fiber, 2 colors

_Tools_

• hook size H (5 mm), I (5.5 mm), or J (6 mm)

• 1 stitch marker

### Going On with Rounds or Rows

### Attaching new yarn with a Double Crochet

In making many motifs (see glossary, page 122), the pattern depends on changing the color of yarn used for each round. One traditional way to attach the new color is to place a slip knot on the hook, slip stitch into the correct place and then ch 3 to start the dc round. But this method leaves a visible knot at the soft base of the stitches. Instead, attach the new yarn color with a double crochet!

**1 YARN OVER**

With a slip knot of the new color on the hook, yarn over, using your pointer finger to hold the yarn over and the starting loop together firmly. Make sure the working yarn passes beneath the hook and is held at the back of the piece to which you're attaching it.

It's not ideal to have a knot at the soft base of the next round of double crochet!

Ready to insert the hook into the top of a stitch.

**2 INSERT THE HOOK**

While still holding the two loops on the hook, find the correct place (according to pattern directions) to insert the hook. In this case, with RS facing, insert the hook into any of the dc stitches of the finished round, making sure to go under both loops of the top V.

**3 COMPLETE THE DC STITCH AS USUAL**

Yarn over, then draw the loop to the front of the work and up to the height of the new stitch. Yarn over and pull through 2 loops; yarn over and draw through the 2 remaining loops.

The slip knot is now in a position where it will be much easier to hide inside another stitch when weaving in the yarn tails.

### One More "Tricky Bit"—the Turning Chain, in Rows

### Starting a New Row

When working with double crochet stitches in rounds, a stitch marker helps to locate the top of the beginning ch-3. The joining slip stitch goes into that marked chain, and if the color isn't being changed, the next round begins with a new ch-3, with its top ch marked, which counts as the first dc of the round.

When working dc sts back and forth in rows, that "ch 3 to turn and start the new row" also counts as the first stitch in the row. Until you become comfortable with locating it, it's important to always mark the top of the turning chain AND to SKIP the first stitch of the row—the turning chain will not be standing exactly in the top of the end stitch, but you must count it as if it were. The turning chain counts as the stitch in that first space. If you also make a double crochet in that stitch, you will have increased, just as if you worked 2 stitches in the same place.

The left swatch shows the first stitch of each row correctly skipped. The center swatch shows an increase in each row caused by _not_ skipping the first stitch. And the right swatch shows the result of forgetting to work a row's last stitch into the top of the turning chain, losing 1 stitch per row.

### Great Grannies Scarf

  You'll get lots of practice with both rounds and rows of dc in this project, a scarf that uses both motifs and solid rows of double crochet. With a pair of Granny Square motifs at each end, this warm and soft scarf is also bright and colorful! The motifs are made separately, attached to each other in pairs, and then the rows of double crochet are worked to connect the two ends.

You Will Need

_Yarn_

• worsted (medium) any fiber type, in 4 colors: Color A, 10–15 yds (9.1–13.7 m); Color B, 20–30 yds (18.3–27.4 m); Color C, 40–50 yds (36.6–45.7 m); Color D, 80–100 yds (73.2–91.4 m)

_Tools_

• hook size J (6 mm) or K (6.5 mm)

• scissors

• tape measure

• yarn needle

• 2 stitch markers

_Stitches and Abbreviations_

ch—chain

Sl st—slip stitch

dc—double crochet

st(s)—stitch(es)

sp(s)—space(s)—the large hole created under a ch-1 or ch-2 in the pattern

rnd—round

RS—right side

WS—wrong side

PM—place marker

MM—move marker

( )—Parentheses enclose a group of stitches to be worked in the same stitch or space

_Gauge_

First round of motif = 2" (5 cm) across; in Scarf pattern, 8 sts and 6 rows = 3" (7.5 cm).

While exact gauge is not important for this project, you may want to experiment with hook size to make sure that the fabric you'll be making is soft and not stiff, but also not so loose that the scarf won't be warm.

**Directions**

**SUGGESTED GAUGE SWATCH**

Making a gauge swatch will help you decide if the size of hook is working well with the chosen yarn. It's also a great opportunity to practice making rows of double crochet. Here's how:

Foundation: Ch 17. Place first marker in last ch made (immediately below the hook).

Row 1: Dc in 4th ch from hook and each ch across. Ch 3, marking top of chain with 2nd marker, turn.

Row 2: Skip first st (turning ch counts as first st). Dc in next st and each st across, including the marked ch of the Foundation. Ch 3, and move the marker to the top of this turning chain. Turn—15 dc, counting turning ch.

Row 3: Repeat Row 2, working into the marked chain from Row 1. Do not fasten off, but pull the final loop out large enough so the work doesn't unravel. Take a look at the swatch. Does it have the thickness, softness, and desirable drape for your scarf? If it seems thick, lumpy, and stiff, use a larger hook for the project. If it seems too loose, droopy, and holey, use a smaller hook for the project.

**1 MAKE 4 GRANNY SQUARES**

Foundation: With A, ch 4 and join with a Sl st in first ch to form a ring.

Rnd 1: Ch 3 (counts as first dc here and throughout), 2 dc in ring, *ch 2, 3 dc in ring. Repeat from * twice. Ch 2, join with a Sl st in top ch of beginning ch-3. Fasten off—4 groups of 3 dc, 4 ch-2 spaces.

Rnd 2: With RS of Rnd 1 facing, attach B with a dc in any corner ch-2 space. (2 dc, ch 2, 3 dc, ch 1) in same ch-2 sp. * (3 dc, ch 2, 3 dc, ch 1) in next ch-2 sp. Repeat from * twice. Join with a Sl st in top of first dc. Fasten off—4 corners with 2 groups of 3 dc each, 1 ch-1 sp on each side of square.

Rnd 3: With RS facing, attach C with a dc in any corner ch-2 sp. (2 dc, ch 2, 3 dc, ch 1) in same sp. *(3 dc, ch 1) in next ch-1 sp; (3 dc, ch 2, 3 dc, ch 1) in next corner ch-2 sp. Repeat from * twice; join with a Sl st in first dc. Fasten off—4 corners with 2 groups of 3 dc each, 1 group of 3 dc and 2 ch 1 spaces on each side of square.

Rnd 4: With RS facing, attach D with a sc in any corner ch-2 sp. 2 sc in same space. *Sc in each dc and in each ch-1 sp across to next corner. 3 sc in corner ch-2 sp. Repeat from *twice, sc in each dc and in each ch-1 sp of final side. Join with a Sl st in first sc. Fasten off—3 sc in each corner, 15 sc per side including corner stitches in count.

Weave in yarn tails as soon as you've checked that the square is correct (4 equal sides and 4 equal corners). Make 3 more squares.

First round is finished and fastened off.

Joining with a slip stitch in the top of the attaching double crochet.

Working a round of single crochet around the square.

Finished granny square

tip  For any project with more than one color, use the same yarn for all the colors or make sure that the various yarns can be laundered the same way. For example, do not use acrylic yarn for one color and wool yarn for another color. When washed, the wool might shrink while the acrylic will not.

**2 PAIR THE SQUARES**

Hold 2 squares with WS of each facing. On top edge of both pieces held together, locate the center sc of each corner and pin the two squares together through these two stitches, using stitch markers as pins.

Use color D to single crochet through the edge sts of both granny squares together, from one marker to the other, making sure to match stitches on the two squares.

Attach the other two squares in the same manner, but leave the two pairs separate from each other, as one pair will form each end of the scarf.

Paired squares

**3 CROCHET THE SCARF IN DC AND SC ROWS**

In this step, you'll be alternating rows of dc and sc. This pairing of rows makes a strong and soft fabric, and gives you practice in making the correct turning chain for each height of stitch.

Row 1: Hold 1 pair of joined grannies with RS facing and one short side of the rectangle upward. Attach color D with a dc in the corner stitch. Dc in each st across to next corner st. Ch 1, turn—15 dc.

Row 2: Sc in each st across. Ch 3, turn. PM in top (3rd) ch of turning ch-3—15 sc.

Row 3: Skip first st, dc in each st across. Ch 1, turn—15 dc.

Row 4: Sc in each st across, including first st and marked ch at end of the row. Ch 3, MM to top of this new turning ch.

Repeat Rows 3 and 4 until the whole piece measures 36" (91.5 cm) or to desired length (remember that the scarf will be lengthened by the pair of grannies yet to be added). Stop after a Row 3 (dc row). Turn as if to start the next Row 4. WS of the first pair of grannies is now facing you. Do not fasten off.

Row 1 finished, with correct turning ch for the next row's height.

Row 2 finished, with correct turning chain for next row's height.

Second pair of Granny Squares being attached by slip stitch on the wrong side of the scarf. When the final yarn tails are woven in, the scarf will be ready to wear.

**4 ATTACH THE FINAL GRANNIES**

With WS of scarf facing and holding the hook at the right hand edge, prepare to start the joining row. Lay the remaining pair of grannies end to end with the scarf, WS of scarf facing up. Pick up the scarf and grannies together, with RS touching and WS facing you. Matching stitches of the two pieces and working through both thicknesses, sl st in each st across. Fasten off. Weave in remaining yarn tails.

Granny Square Projects

There are so many things you can make from Granny Squares. Here are a few ideas to get you started:

**1** Make a scarf entirely from squares. Make ten or twelve Granny Squares, and attach them to each other in a long line.

**2** Make a blanket from one gigantic Granny Square. Use up all your scrap yarn by continuing to make round after round of the double crochet repeat. Save Round 4 for the very end and use it as an edging. Whenever one color of yarn runs out, just add the next color and keep going.

**3** Make a blanket from lots of squares. Sixty-four squares made exactly like the ones in the scarf pattern and crocheted together in 8 rows of 8 squares with a final round of single crochet, will make a nice-size blanket. This will require about 36 oz (1020 g) of yarn. You can mix up the order in which you use the colors in each square to add visual interest.

**4** Make a bag by joining 4 Granny Squares to each other in a 2 × 2 square for each side. Make a strap by working rows of single crochet or double crochet as wide and long as you like.

**5** There are many other square motif patterns in various sizes available in magazines, books, and on the Internet. Any of them can be used in place of the Granny to make any of these items.

##   PATTERN STITCHES

### More Shapes and Textures

So far, you've made open, lacey fabric with chain arches or groups of double crochet separated by chain spaces. You've also made solid fabric of different textures with single crochet in rounds and rows, and with double crochet in rows. You've learned how to use increases to create shapes that grow larger as they are worked outward from a start at the center. In this chapter you will learn how to decrease by working two (or more) stitches together, and how to combine basic stitches into pattern stitches to create even more textures in the fabric. You will also begin to read crochet symbols, the other main type of crochet pattern. To practice these new skills, this chapter includes projects for a bright, decorative pillow and a fun belt.

### Decreasing in Single Crochet

One way to make each row narrower than the previous row is to simply skip some of the stitches without working a corresponding chain space above the skipped stitch. That's the method used in the flap of the Felted Phone Pocket on page 58. The one drawback of this method is that if the project is not felted, the skipped stitches leave holes in the fabric. That would pose a problem if the project contained stuffing, like the Monster toy on page 64. Another way to reduce the number of stitches in a row or round is to work two stitches together. That means that at their bases, there are stitches worked into each of the stitches in the previous row—but at the tops of those stitches, they are joined, and have only one top V. There is no hole, but every time two stitches are worked together, the total for the row or round is reduced by one stitch. The best part? You'll find that decreasing is very easy to do!

**1 A SOLID START**

Foundation: Ch 11.

Row 1: Sc in 2nd ch from hook and each ch across. Ch 1, turn—10 sc.

Row 2: Sc in each st, ch 1, turn.

Rows 3 & 4: Repeat Row 2. At the end of Row 4, ch 1 and turn, but do not fasten off.

**2 START 2 STITCHES**

Row 5: In the first stitch, insert the hook and draw up a loop, just as if you were going to make a single crochet. Don't finish the stitch, though! With 2 loops now on the hook, insert the hook into the next stitch and draw up a loop in it, as well. Now there are 3 loops on the hook.

Two stitches started.

**3 FINISH THE 2 STITCHES TOGETHER**

Yarn over and pull through all 3 loops on the hook.

Completed decrease (sc2tog).

Now there are 8 sc in the row, including a contrasting color decrease at each edge.

One decrease in center of row.

You Will Need

_Yarn_

• worsted (medium) yarn in a light color, 5–10 yds (4.6–9.1 m)

_Tools_

• hook size H (5 mm), I (5.5 mm), or J (6 mm), whichever feels comfortable with the chosen yarn

### Finish Row 5

Sc in each of next 6 sts, sc2tog (repeat steps 2 and 3 in the final 2 stitches of the row). Ch 1, turn.

### Decrease in the Middle of a Row

Row 6: Sc in each of the first 3 sts, sc2tog, sc in each of next 3 sts. (This time, work a regular sc in the first stitch. Work 2 more regular sc. Repeat steps 2 and 3 above, decreasing over the 4th and 5th stitches of the row. Work 3 regular sc to finish out the row.)

Sc2tog decreases can be used anywhere in a row or round, as often as the pattern directs. Practice until the decrease is familiar and as easy as a regular sc.

Crochet Language

The abbreviation for single crochet decrease is usually "sc2tog"—single crochet 2 together. Some older patterns refer to it as "dec 1 over next 2 sts"—decrease by 1 stitch over the next two stitches. Both mean the same thing.

### Decreasing in Double Crochet

Decreasing in dc is similar to decreasing in sc—two stitches are started, but they are finished together into one single top V. Either stitch can be decreased when working in either rows or rounds. The practice swatch for single crochet decrease used rows; you'll practice the dc decrease in rounds.

**1 A CIRCULAR START**

Foundation: Ch 4, join with a Sl st to form a ring.

Rnd 1: Ch 3 (counts as first dc of round; place a stitch marker in top of ch-3), 11 more dc in ring. Join with a Sl st in top of beginning ch-3.

Rnds 2 & 3: Ch 3, move marker to last ch made. Dc in each st around, join with a Sl st in top of beginning ch-3.

Rnd 4: Ch 3, move marker. Dc in next st.

You Will Need

_Yarn_
