## _Editors' Preface_

FIVE PREVIOUS VOLUMES in the New Naturalist Library (NNs 17, 31, 50, 51, 67) have dealt broadly with humans and their impact on the landscape, particularly through farming activities. The last of these (NN 67 Farming and Wildlife by Kenneth Mellanby) was published in 1981, which on current farming timescales is a very long time ago. Hence Farming and Birds by Ian Newton is a timely analysis and a most welcome addition to the Library.

Readers of his three previous New Naturalists on Finches, Bird Migration and Bird Populations will be familiar with Ian Newton's characteristic comprehensive and insightful analyses, fact-packed and readily assimilable. This approach he here applies to the development of farming and farmland over the millennia since our ancestors first laid their hands on the land at the start of the Neolithic Period, with an inevitable closer focus on the last century. Farming and Birds deals with a breadth of topics, which today probably comprise the biggest ecological problem ever to have threatened the British and Irish environment.

Ian Newton has an outstanding research career in ornithological ecology, with over 300 scientific papers and several landmark books to his credit. One component of this research involved assessing the adverse impact of agricultural pesticides on raptor populations that absorbed the various toxins involved through their prey and the associated food chains – highly relevant to this text. Overall, Dr Newton's national and international standing in avian ecology is impeccable. He has served not only as President of the British Ecological Society and the British Ornithologists' Union but also as Chairman of the RSPB and the British Trust for Ornithology, he has been elected to Fellowships of the Royal Societies of London and Edinburgh, and he has been appointed OBE.

The Editors' Preface to Ian Newton's Finches (NN 55) considered it a 'model of scientific writing for the general reader, balanced, lucid and absorbing'. Nothing has changed. This volume will be valued and fascinating reading for those interested in their countryside, with many 'so that's why...' explanations resolving problems that have puzzled readers. It should also be required reading for all those professionally involved in farming, from agricultural students and companies to relevant civil servants and, indeed, agriculture ministers.

## _Author's Foreword and Acknowledgements_

THE EFFECTS OF MODERN AGRICULTURAL practices on the countryside and its wildlife are strikingly evident to every naturalist. During the latter half of the 20th century, a revolution in farming occurred, bringing a heavy dependence on synthetic fertilisers and pesticides. At the same time, farming became much more mechanised, science-based and large scale. All together, these changes increased crop yields and livestock production to levels previously unattainable. However, these changes were achieved only at huge financial and environmental costs, one of which was a massive loss of wildlife, including birds.

This book describes what has happened to farmland birds in Britain over the centuries, as agriculture has changed, but deals especially with the changes of recent decades. After two introductory chapters on farmland birds, the book consists of six main sections: one is concerned with the history of agriculture in Britain and its main effects on birdlife; the second with the main plants and animals of farmland, including crops and livestock; the third with the recent changes that have occurred in the management of arable and grazing land; the fourth with woods, lakes and other semi-natural habitats within farmland; the fifth with upland grazing land; and the sixth with conservation farming and agri-environment schemes, followed by some general conclusions. All 22 chapters relate to the birds of farmland, and unless stated otherwise they refer to findings from Britain. Throughout, I have used common vernacular names for birds, other animals and plants, but added scientific names to the captions of diagrams and photographs and also to the index.

For most of my life, I have studied birds as a professional biologist. My knowledge of agriculture is naturally more limited, but I have lived through the major agricultural revolution of recent decades, witnessing at first hand its impacts on wildlife. I was raised in the Derbyshire countryside, and spent much of my boyhood on farms, learning how and why most farming operations were done. This was a time, in the 1950s, when local farmers got rid of their remaining work-horses as tractors took over; they acquired their first milking machines and combine harvesters, and started to use the new agrochemicals on a large scale. This early experience gave me an understanding of farming methods against which I could compare the subsequent changes.

Disappointingly, almost every aspect of agricultural change over recent decades has proved harmful to wild plants and animals in one way or another. In documenting these changes, it is easy to give the impression of criticising farmers. But this is not my intent. The nation's farmers did an excellent job of what was asked of them, in terms of food production, and were in no better position than anyone else to foresee the severe environmental consequences of post-war and recent agricultural policy. We now look again to farmers to restore some of the lost biodiversity: not by putting the clock back and reverting to old-style farming, but by using new scientific discoveries to integrate the need for food production with all the other essential products and services that the countryside is expected to provide.

Several books have already been written about farmland birds. Four that I found especially helpful were Farming and Birds (1986) by Ray O'Connor and Mike Shrubb, Birds, Scythes and Combines (2003) by Mike Shrubb, Bird Conservation and Agriculture (2009) by Jeremy Wilson, Andy Evans and Phil Grice, and the two-volume Wildlife Conservation on Farmland (2015), edited by David Macdonald and Ruth Feber. Over the period covered by these books, hundreds of studies of farmland birds have been published in scientific journals, most of which I have consulted in preparing this book.

With so much already written on farmland birds, you may well wonder whether another book is needed. My own book overlaps in coverage with these earlier volumes, and recycles the title of one of them. But I believe it offers something different. It is more up to date in its coverage of the ornithological science, and examines in greater depth than previous books the impacts of specific agricultural practices on the habitats and food supplies of birds, and hence on their numbers and distributions. It also discusses the wider environmental problems created by recent agricultural policy, and offers more historical context, giving a step-by-step account of the main changes in farming since the Neolithic period, insofar as this is possible.

In writing this book, I have benefited over the years from discussions with many friends and colleagues who studied birds in farmland, including some of the authors of the volumes mentioned above. Some of my own research has involved birds on farmland (especially seed-eaters and waterfowl) and pesticide impacts on birds, and for 20 years I was based at Monks Wood Research Station, near Huntingdon, where much of the Natural Environment Research Council's research on the effects of modern agriculture on wildlife was done.

I am grateful to the farmers who have given up their time to show me their farms and to answer my questions. Too numerous to mention individually, they are in no way responsible for any errors on agricultural matters they might find in the following pages. For advice on content and presentation, I thank Jeremy Minot and Kelly Gray. For use of photographic images I am grateful to many friends, among whom Richard Chandler, Edmund Fellowes, Chris Knights, Alan Martin, Frank Snykers, Richard and Barbara Mearns, and Bobby Smith together provided the majority. For comments on particular chapters, I thank Paul Bellamy (Chapter 17), Richard Carden (Chapters , , ), Rob Fuller (), Rhys Green (), Shelley Hinsley (), Jeremy Minot (–), Mike Newton (–), David Norman (), John Osmond (, , ), Rob Robinson () and Jeremy Wilson (, ). I also thank Dario Massimino and David Noble for help with diagrams from the BTO, and Tim Bernard for his expert drawings of insect larvae. For constructive review of the whole text in draft I am grateful to David Jenkins, Jim Flegg (in his role as editor) and Hugh Brazier (in his role as copy-editor). Finally, I thank my wife, Halina, for support throughout, and for commenting helpfully on the penultimate draft.

## CHAPTER 1

## Introduction

THIS BOOK IS INTENDED for anyone who wants to know more about how bird numbers and distributions are affected by human land use. Three-quarters of the land surface of Britain is cultivated or is grazed by domestic livestock. So it is mainly farming practices that influence the habitats and food supplies available to most birds, and thereby largely govern where different species can live and in what numbers. This has increasingly been the case since Neolithic times. But the 20th century saw unusually big changes in British agriculture that led to greatly increased crop yields, but also to major declines in wildlife, including birds. Never before in our history are we likely to have lost so many wild plants and animals in so short a time from so large an area. Most of this loss occurred within the space of 30 years, and many of the species involved are still declining.

Understanding why these declines occurred in different species tells us much about the impact of our activities on the natural world, and also about the factors that influence bird and other animal numbers – knowledge that is essential for effective conservation.

Agricultural changes over the last 60 years or so were driven by a general desire to increase home food production. To this end, farmers benefited from government grant aid, from regular subsidies, and in some years also from guaranteed market prices. They also benefited from improved machinery, and from fertiliser and pesticide development. To their credit, crop and livestock production increased greatly, but the resulting changes in landscape and wildlife fostered widespread public unease. Suddenly, a much-loved countryside had changed, becoming more uniform and less attractive, with fewer trees, hedgerows and other natural features. Many once familiar plant and animal species became scarce, some disappearing altogether from large parts of the country. Problems created by pesticides and other agricultural pollutants were constantly in the news, and soil erosion and floods became more frequent.

Agriculture affects wildlife in two main ways. The first is through the clearance of natural or semi-natural habitats to produce more farmland, and the second is through the more intensive use of existing farmland, aimed at increasing crop and livestock yields per unit area. In Britain, relatively little semi-natural habitat had survived through to the mid-20th century, and the more intensive use of existing farmland was the major factor raising agricultural production but also reducing wildlife populations. The main changes involved the greater use of agrochemicals and mechanisation, as mentioned above, together with improved husbandry and the development of higher-yielding crop cultivars and livestock breeds. These various changes are often lumped under the umbrella term of 'agricultural intensification', a process that can be measured either in terms of 'inputs' such as vehicle fuel, fertilisers, pesticides and veterinary drugs, or in 'outputs' such as crop and livestock yields.

DEVELOPMENT OF AGRICULTURE

But first let us take a big step back in time. Modern humans (Homo sapiens) are thought to have evolved as recently as around 200,000 years ago, and for the first nine-tenths of this time they lived as other animals, dependent on wild foods, and at low population densities. All this changed with the development of agriculture – the cultivation of food plants and the domestication of animals. These processes are thought to have originated independently in at least three different parts of the world (eastern Asia based on rice, the Middle East based on wheat and barley, and western South America based on maize), gradually spreading from each. 'Our type' arose in the fertile crescent of the Middle East around 12,000 years ago, and spread slowly across Europe to reach Britain around 6,500 years ago, marking the dawn of the Neolithic period. It then took another 1,500 years or more to spread through the whole country. Since its arrival, the people of Britain have depended less and less on a wide range of wild foods and increasingly on a much narrower range of cultivated plants and domesticated animals, a change which has sustained a huge increase in our numbers.

Nowadays, very few human communities in the world are as yet untouched by agriculture, still living as hunter–gatherers. Agriculture gave people food in abundance, enabling some to live in bigger and more fixed settlements, doing things other than just food acquisition. It gave rise to civilisation as we know it, and became our most widespread industry. As the world population grew on this new kind of food, the processes involved in producing it became ever more efficient and technological, allowing greater proportions of people to make a living in other ways. In Britain into the 16th century, more than 90% of adults worked on the land, but now the proportion is less than 1%. Yet over the same period the total human population of the country increased by more than tenfold. In their level of urbanisation, Britain and other highly developed nations are exceptional, however, and over the world as a whole, half of all people still work the land, many scraping a living by physical effort from a less-than-generous soil. In the last half of the 20th century, global human numbers almost tripled to reach seven billion individuals, half of whom now live in rapidly expanding cities (around 90% in Britain). The cost of this agriculture-based development of human numbers and lifestyle has been the loss of much of the natural world, with its diverse plant and animal life. In recent times it has also brought widespread pollution and climate change. Over the centuries, then, as agriculture became increasingly essential to humanity, it has also become a major threat to other resources we value, such as clean air and water, fertile soil, wild plant and animal life, and all the ecological services that the natural world provides.

This book is mainly about how agriculture has developed in one small part of the world, and the various ways in which it has affected one group of animals. It is the story of agricultural development in Britain as seen through the eyes of an ornithologist, and is as much about farming as it is about birds. Agriculture now influences practically all the land-bird species of Britain, including those found only in fairly natural habitats (if only because farming limits the extent of these other habitats). In addition, pesticides and fertilisers used on farmland, along with industrial pollutants, contaminate all habitats, affecting to some degree the whole land surface from sea coast to mountain top, whatever the vegetation. During the period of most recent change, developments in agriculture were well documented, and bird populations were monitored more thoroughly than ever before. We therefore have good information from which to explore recent changes in farming and bird populations, and the relationships between the two.

FARMLAND IN BRITAIN

For these purposes, farmland can be defined broadly as any land that is used for crop or livestock production, whether in lowland or upland. It amounts to all land that is not taken up by towns, villages and associated infrastructure, by woodland and forest, wetland and seashore. Throughout farmland, small fragments of semi-natural habitats, such as woods, hedges, ponds and streams, support most of the wild plants and animals of the countryside, and form focal points for many of the birds that feed in the fields. The occurrence of these non-cropped areas depends largely on the nature and intensity of farm management, and nearly all such fragments are affected by farmers to some extent. On this basis, farmland is highly variable, embracing a wide range of habitat types, which together form by far the largest chunk of wildlife habitat found in Britain.

To give some more precise figures based on recent Countryside Surveys (see later), some 12% of the total land area of Britain is occupied by towns, villages, roads and other infrastructure, and another 12% is under woodland or forest, while 23% is under arable crops and 24% under (mostly cultivated) lowland grassland. The remaining 28% is under rough grazing, moorland and bog in the uplands, and around 1% is open water. In other words, about 75% of the total area of Britain is under some form of farming, involving tillage or grazing, and is thereby influenced by national agricultural policy. Even grouse moors usually support some sheep, and some nature reserves support sheep, cattle or ponies as aids to management. On open land, only the highest rocky mountain tops and the lowest tidal mudflats remain free of tillage or livestock grazing. The arable (including horticultural) farms and improved grassland of the lowlands constitute the most intensively managed land in Britain, providing most of our agricultural produce.

These figures depend on how particular habitats are defined and measured, and different surveys have given somewhat different results. But they probably give a reasonably accurate picture of Britain in the early 21st century. They indicate why farmland wildlife is so important to conservation in Britain, why it is so loved by many people, and why it has been so well studied. It forms the bulk of what we have. But even the most casual observer will have noticed marked differences in farming activities in different parts of the country, with more arable in the south and east and more grassland in the north and west, mainly cattle on the low ground and mainly sheep in the hills. Specialist crops are grown in particular areas, such as fruit in Kent and Worcestershire, and wheat and vegetables in East Anglia. These regional variations result mainly from local conditions, but to some extent also from local traditions, all affecting regional bird populations.

The overwhelming prevalence of farmland in Britain contrasts with some other larger parts of the world, such as North America, Australia and Africa, which still have substantial areas of unspoiled natural habitats. In these regions, almost the entire natural flora and fauna can be conserved in abundance in these natural areas, without concern for farmland. In contrast to Britain, therefore, conservation efforts in these regions have focused on remaining natural habitats. Native birds are still referred to by their natural habitat associations, such as forest birds, grassland birds or wetland birds. It is chiefly in western Europe that large numbers of birds are referred to collectively as 'farmland birds'. Some such species have been associated with farmland for so long that it is no longer clear what their original natural habitats might have been, or indeed whether they occurred in primeval Britain at all. Nor is it clear when most of the current farmland bird species first occupied farmland. Some woodland species probably moved into hedges as soon as hedges became available, but others may have made this jump only centuries later. One reason for suspecting such a delay in colonisation is that several species, which in Britain are now widespread in hedgerows, parks and gardens, are in eastern Europe still restricted to natural habitats such as forest. They include such familiar species as the Blackbird, Mistle Thrush, Robin and Dunnock. This regional difference suggests that the step from natural to man-made habitats has not always been immediate.

FIG 1. Some extremes of agricultural land in Britain. Upper, the hilly well-wooded landscape of Galloway, with shallow unproductive soils and poor grassland devoted to livestock production (Keith Kirk). Lower, the flat drained fenland of Cambridgeshire, with deep productive soils devoted almost entirely to arable crops. In the centre is Woodwalton Fen Nature Reserve of uncultivated damp peatland, now mainly tree-covered (Shelley Hinsley).

FIG 2. Four species which in Britain nest commonly in farm hedgerows, parks and gardens, but in eastern Europe are still confined to natural forest habitats: upper left: Robin Erithacus rubecula (Stan Wilson); upper right, Dunnock Prunella modularis (Richard Chandler); lower left, Blackbird Turdus merula (Richard Chandler); lower right, Mistle Thrush Turdus viscivorus (Richard Chandler).

Another way in which farmland in Britain differs from farmland in many other parts of the world is that it does not serve merely to grow crops or produce livestock. For society at large, it has important cultural, heritage and recreational value. Some features of modern farmland are relicts which had some purpose in the past, but no longer do so, while others are there for reasons other than farming, such as game management. Many farm ponds, woods and hedgerows are in one or other of these categories. Such features add to the beauty and heritage value of the countryside, and at the same time are largely responsible for the presence of many bird and animal species in the farmed landscape.

For many years, nature conservation in Britain was preoccupied with the protection of small special areas – 'nature reserves' – patches of semi-natural habitat devoted to wildlife. Their primary aim was to preserve biodiversity. But after 65 years of land acquisition by public and private bodies for this purpose, nature reserves in Britain still total less than 2% of the overall land area, and cannot possibly protect viable populations of a wide range of species in the long term, at least not in a way that they are readily accessible to most interested people. If we add to the dedicated nature reserves other areas under conservation (as well as agricultural) influence, such as Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs), then another 9% of the land surface of Britain could be said to come (at least temporarily) under some form of conservation influence, according to an unpublished RSPB study. However, most of this land (7 of the 9%) is in a poor or deteriorating state, and is still subject to aspects of agricultural policy.

Overall, then, only about 4% of the land surface of Britain is currently managed primarily for wildlife on a consistent basis, unimpeded by other interests. Because of changes in farming practices over recent decades, if wildlife is to be conserved effectively into the future, its needs will have to be integrated with crop production and other land uses. This is by no means a new idea, and was accepted as a given by earlier conservationists. Without this acceptance by farmers and politicians, as well as by the general public, wildlife is unlikely to persist for much longer in Britain in its present variety and abundance.

This situation stands in marked contrast with earlier times. Even as late as the mid-20th century, farmland could still legitimately be called 'the country's largest nature reserve' (Murton 1971). Farmers produced biodiversity as effectively as they produced farm crops, the one as an incidental by-product of the other. But over recent decades the two products have become increasingly separated. Nowadays, farming and conservation are often viewed as conflicting, as an ever-rising proportion of the annual productivity of the land has been absorbed by crops and livestock, at the expense of wild plants and animals. Management for the one reduces the other; the one manages for monoculture, the other for diversity. With a continually increasing human population, this is the nub of a growing conflict: how much of our land should be devoted solely to human food production and how much to other assets that people value, such as appealing scenery, clean water and abundant wildlife? In the past, the best land has usually been taken for agriculture, and only the poorest 'sacrificed' to nature, so in general its value to wildlife has also been relatively low. Nevertheless, agriculture and wildlife conservation have much in common. They are both concerned with renewable living resources that can either be managed for sustained yield or squandered for short-term gain. Examples of these two extremes of treatment can be found among both farming and wildlife management in Britain, as shown in later chapters.

INFORMATION ON AGRICULTURE

Many early written accounts and landscape paintings yield useful information on past agriculture. However, the history of farming in Britain has been documented in detail only over the past few centuries, including all the major developments in the methods and practices used. Among early documents, much of England and parts of Wales had the Domesday Book of 1086, which provides useful insights into the countryside of the time, but Scotland had no equivalent until the Statistical Accounts of 1791–99 and 1845. From the 18th century on, many books described the prevailing agriculture, and provided advice to farmers on new techniques. In addition, since 1866, assessments of the different crops grown and different livestock kept in Britain have been made every year by government, based on annual questionnaire returns from the occupiers of agricultural land: the so-called June census statistics. In more recent times, we also have the Pesticide Usage Surveys, referring to the areas treated each year with different chemicals. These obligatory individual returns are consolidated each year into parish summaries, which are in turn grouped to give county and national totals. For purposes of survey, agricultural land is usually divided into the three broad categories of arable (tilled) land, cultivated grassland and rough grazing land, most of the latter now being in the uplands.

Another useful programme for assessing the vegetation cover of Britain, including agricultural crops, is the Countryside Survey (CS) of the Natural Environment Research Council. The first CS was made in 1978, followed by others in 1984, 1990, 1998 and 2007. At each survey, the British countryside was sampled using rigorous methodology, so that the results could be compared between different surveys, enabling assessments of change over the 30 years involved. Each survey was also accompanied by a land-cover map, based on satellite images. Urban areas were excluded.

INFORMATION ON BIRDS

For information on the birds of ancient Britain we have to rely on old bone remains, mostly from archaeological sites and in various degrees of fossilisation. This record is not good, because the light bones of birds do not fossilise readily. In more recent centuries, we also have lists of species that were commonly hunted and eaten, or mentioned in literature, and from the 18th century we have books specifically about birds and other wildlife, notably the 'county avifaunas'. These various sources give some idea of the relative abundance levels and distributions of different species at the time. However, from the mid-19th century, the documentation of 'game bags' and 'vermin lists' provided quantitative information on a limited number of species, and from the mid-20th century regular counts and surveys were extended to an ever-widening range of species seen live in the field.

From this time, most of the important bird survey and monitoring programmes in Britain have been conducted by volunteer observers working mainly under the auspices of the British Trust for Ornithology (BTO). The most relevant annual monitoring programmes relating to farmland birds include the Common Birds Census (CBC), which began in 1962 with annual counts of birds at consistent sites scattered around the country, and the Breeding Bird Survey (BBS), which began as its replacement in 1994 (Freeman et al. 2007, Baillie et al. 2013). The two schemes used different counting methods but overlapped by seven years, enabling them to be calibrated against one another, and ensuring a smooth transition between them. Based on counts during April–June each year, both schemes were designed to measure year-to-year changes in the abundance of breeding birds in farmland and other habitats. They have thereby revealed the extent and precise timing of population changes in many common bird species. In both schemes observers have made regular bird counts in particular places year after year, using standardised methods. The BBS employs a less time-consuming method than its predecessor, and is of more robust statistical design. It attracts more participants, enabling a wider range of randomly selected areas to be sampled in different habitats across the country, including upland grazing land, which was barely covered in the CBC. In general, some 300–400 observers contributed each year to the CBC, compared with several thousand to the BBS.

We also have the benefit of three Atlas projects, designed to map the breeding distributions of bird species in 10 km squares across Britain, conducted at roughly 20-year intervals – in 1968–72, 1989–92 and 2007–11 (Sharrock 1976, Gibbons et al. 1993, Balmer et al. 2013). Additional mapping of winter bird distributions was attempted in 1982–85 (Lack 1986), and again in association with the 2007–11 Atlas. These mapping projects have provided reliable wide-scale data on the changing distributions of almost all bird species in Britain, and hence on changes in community composition. To set against these national projects, local atlases organised by some county bird clubs have generally operated at finer scales, often mapping birds in tetrads (2 × 2 km squares), rather than in 10 × 10 km squares, and thus giving 25 times greater resolution. This extra detail has shown distributional changes not visible at the larger scale of the national atlases (Norman 2008).

Other long-running programmes, also organised mainly by the BTO, have revealed whether recorded population changes were due to changes in reproduction or survival. The bird-ringing scheme, started as long ago as 1908, has provided recovery data from which the annual survival/mortality rates of various common species have been calculated, while the Nest Record Scheme, which started back in 1939, has recorded the outcomes of their individual breeding attempts. In this scheme, individual nests cannot normally be attributed with certainty to particular known pairs (Crick et al. 2003). Especially in multi-brooded species, therefore, nest records give no measure of the total seasonal production of young per pair, which would be a more useful figure. In some species, such as Corn Bunting and Turtle Dove, nest record data indicate that there is an increase in individual nest success during a period of population decline, while more detailed data resulting from special field studies reveal a shortening of the breeding season, and hence a reduction in the total seasonal production of young (compare nest record data for Corn Bunting and Turtle Dove from Siriwardena et al. 2000 with seasonal data from Brickle & Harper 2002 and Browne & Aebischer 2003). Another scheme, involving constant netting efforts in particular sites year after year, gives information on the ratio of young to older birds in the population each year, thereby giving a measure of seasonal productivity.

Other regular BTO surveys, such as Garden BirdWatch, the Heronries Census, the Waterways Breeding Bird Survey and the Wetland Bird Survey (in the non-breeding season), are less relevant to farmland, but give some additional information used in this book. However, not all bird species can be readily sampled by these schemes, and some rarer, less accessible or nocturnal species are monitored instead by special surveys, designed to suit the species concerned, and conducted at intervals of one to many years, depending on species. These special surveys may entail a complete count of the British breeding population or a statistically selected sample, in some species enabling the long-term population trends to be assessed (for Woodlark see Conway et al. 2009, for Twite see Langston et al. 2006, for Cirl Bunting see Stanbury et al. 2010). In addition to these organised surveys, records of rare breeding birds submitted in confidence by individual observers are collated annually by the Rare Breeding Birds Panel (RBBP), from which summaries are published in the journal British Birds.

Inevitably, these schemes all have strengths and weaknesses, are more appropriate for some species than for others, and depend on some untested assumptions (Grice et al. 2004). One strong point is their nationwide coverage, which ensures that the findings are widely representative, even though in most schemes regional variations in human population density result in more data being collected from some regions than from others.

In addition to these large-scale monitoring schemes, many shorter-term studies have been made of particular species. Most have been done by individual scientists, based in universities or research institutes, working in specific localities. Such studies typically involve intensive fieldwork, such as the trapping and marking of individual birds, nest-finding, food analyses and behavioural observations, and may also involve experimental modifications of habitat or food supplies. They can often provide convincing evidence of the role of different factors in influencing population trends, and suggest how best to apply conservation measures. Results from wide-scale surveys and detailed local studies together provide a powerful and reassuring combination of evidence.

The net result is that the birds of Britain have been monitored more thoroughly over the past 60 years than at any previous time, and are now some of the most intensively studied in the world. Without effective population monitoring, the scale of declines in farmland birds over recent decades would stay unmeasured, and sceptics could remain unconvinced that anything had changed, or that any accepted changes had anything to do with farming. Birds are the best known of all our native wildlife. But it is nevertheless clear that the other animals and plants of farmland have suffered similar recent declines, as discussed in later chapters.

FARMLAND BIRDS

While many people talk loosely of 'farmland birds', it is not easy to come up with a good definition because almost any British terrestrial bird species can be seen on farmland at one time or another. Different authors have given different figures, depending on their criteria for inclusion. But on my reckoning, at least 90 bird species regularly obtain food from lowland pasture or tilled land in the breeding season, and at least 113 species in winter (Tables 1 and 2). These totals exclude all the other species which occupy hedgerows, wetlands or other semi-natural habitat patches within farmland, but get little or nothing from the farmed land itself. Adding in these species would give totals of 158 in the breeding season and 168 in winter. Numbers are greater in winter because, although some species leave Britain after breeding, a much greater number move in to the British lowlands then. They come from the nearby uplands or from other more distant regions where they breed. At both seasons, the figures include some species that are common and widespread, and others that are scarce or localised. They also refer to lowland alone, and for the unenclosed grazing land in the hills the figures are lower, especially in winter.

In the lowlands, most farms might hold some 20–40 breeding bird species per year, depending on the areas and diversity of habitats present. From surveys of 29 farms in different areas made in the 1960s, densities of birds on farmland (including any small woods, hedges and wetlands present) were mostly in the range of 100–400 pairs per km2, with extreme values of 55 and 505 pairs per km2 (Williamson 1967). The lowest densities were on extensive grassland farms with few hedges, and the highest were on mixed farms, with many hedges and other features. In order of abundance, the 15 most frequently recorded species were Blackbird, Chaffinch, Dunnock, Robin, Wren, Skylark, Blue Tit, Song Thrush, Yellowhammer, Willow Warbler, Great Tit, Linnet, Greenfinch, Starling and Whitethroat. The list excluded House Sparrow, Barn Swallow, House Martin and Swift because they were usually restricted to farmsteads for nesting, and Woodpigeon, Rook and Jackdaw because they bred only on a small proportion of farms, but ranged over a larger number to feed. These three larger species nevertheless together formed well over half of the total biomass of wild birds present. Species composition varied somewhat, according to region, farming regime and whether or not game rearing was prevalent.

FIG 3. Two of the most typical and widespread birds of farmland: right, Linnet Linaria cannabina (Frank Snykers); left, Yellowhammer Emberiza citrinella (Alan Martin). Both species nest in hedgerows and obtain their food mainly from arable land.

FIG 4. Two introduced gamebirds, now widespread on farmland in Britain as a result of artificial rearing and release: above, Red-legged Partridge Alectoris rufa (Richard Chandler); below, Pheasant Phasianus colchicus (Alan Martin).

One significant point about these figures is that most of the common species depend on woodland or scrub, at least for nesting, and only one widespread species (the Skylark) could be classed as a true open-country bird which shuns trees and buildings. Other open-country species, such as Lapwing, did not appear in the top 15. Moreover, since these counts were made, the overall wild bird populations on most farms in Britain are likely to have declined, and the species composition changed, with Skylark in particular becoming much less common and Willow Warbler much more restricted to northern Britain. Over much of the country, Grey Partridges have now disappeared, but released Pheasants and Red-legged Partridges are much more numerous than in the 1960s, owing to extensive rear-and-release activities (Chapter 10).

Within Britain, both species numbers and the overall bird abundance on lowland farms tend to decline from south to north. In addition, in both the north and the south of Britain, lowland farms hold more bird species on average in the east than in the west, but with little difference in overall bird abundance (O'Connor & Shrubb 1986). These geographical trends largely parallel regional variation in the types of farming and the crops grown, and in the numbers and types of non-cropped habitats present. Nevertheless, some species are found only in the southern or southeast parts of Britain, despite the presence of apparently suitable habitat elsewhere. As shown by successive atlas surveys, regional variations in bird populations are not wholly consistent through time, partly because the regional character of farmland can be altered by management, and partly because bird distributions and numbers change for other reasons, such as climate change.

Seasonal changes

The species composition and overall numbers of birds on particular farms may also change greatly between summer and winter, as indicated above. Summer visitors, such as hirundines and warblers, leave after breeding to winter elsewhere, while other species from higher latitudes or altitudes move in for the winter. The main winter visitors from afar include thrushes, such as the Fieldfare and Redwing, waterfowl (especially wild geese and swans) and waders (especially Lapwing, Golden Plover and Woodcock). These species also breed in Britain, but in most the winter visitors greatly outnumber the local residents. Again, however, it is those localities which offer the greatest diversity of habitats that have the greatest numbers of species and individuals. Wetlands seem to greatly increase winter bird abundance, owing mainly to the presence of large numbers of waterfowl and gulls.

FIG 5. Two of the commonest winter visitors to farmland in Britain, feeding on fruits from hedgerows and invertebrates from grass fields: left, Fieldfare Turdus pilaris (Alan Martin); right, Redwing Turdus iliacus (Richard Chandler).

FIG 6. Golden Plovers Pluvialis apricaria, Lapwing Vanellus vanellus and Black-headed Gull Chroicocephalus ridibundus on arable farmland in winter (Chris Knights).

Most species that forage on farmland in winter tend to be gregarious, roosting communally and feeding in flocks, concentrating wherever food is plentiful at the time. The same habitat features that influence their distributions in the breeding season are also important in winter, when they provide communal roost sites to which the birds can return each night. Rooks and Jackdaws often occur together in winter, both for roosting and for feeding, and the same is also sometimes true for Redwings and Fieldfares, for Lapwings and Golden Plovers, and for different species of geese. The number of birds on individual lowland farms in winter varies greatly with the resources available. Arable farms that offer abundant winter seeds can support flocks of hundreds or thousands of small seed-eaters, while pastoral farms may support few or none.

FIG 7. Barnacle Geese Branta leucopsis on grassland in winter at Mersehead, south Scotland (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

FIG 8. Flock of larks and finches over feeding area on farmland at Southerness, south Scotland (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Apart from exceptionally severe winters, farmland in Britain remains damp but unfrozen for most of the time. It is the mildness of our winters that attracts the large seasonal influx of immigrant Lapwings, Starlings, thrushes and other ground-feeding species which depend on accessible soil-dwelling worms and other invertebrates. Grass fields tend to be used more in winter than in summer, because in winter the grass is short, giving easy access for ground-feeding birds, along with all-round visibility. For grazing and seed-eating species, too, autumn harvesting can leave substantial crop residues such as stubble grain and waste potatoes, while autumn sowing creates young growth of cereals and grass that may be grazed in winter by geese and swans, and rape that may be grazed by pigeons and others.

IMPORTANCE OF SEMI-NATURAL AND NON-CROPPED AREAS

One feature of British farmland, as mentioned above, is that patches of different semi-natural habitats occur within a matrix of crops and grass, bringing many more birds into the farmed environment than would otherwise occur there. In addition, some species make use of more than one type of habitat at the same time of year, nesting mainly in one and foraging mainly in another. Species such as the Rook and Woodpigeon nest in trees but feed chiefly on the ground in open fields, while some upland species, such as Twite and Golden Plover, nest mainly on moorland but get much of their food from nearby hill pastures. The requirements of such species are perhaps better described in terms of landscapes or habitat mosaics than in terms of specific vegetation types, with individuals using different habitat components for different purposes. It would thus be inappropriate to describe Rooks, for example, as birds of tree clumps or as birds of fields, because they require both. Their habitat is best described in landscape terms, as tree clumps within a matrix of open farmland. Many species also use fields of different crop types at different times of year, depending on whether the field is bare or vegetated, or on the growth stage of the crop, pre-harvest or post-harvest, all of which influence food availability for different birds. Many species therefore rely on an appropriate mix of habitats close together, in order to breed successfully or to survive on farmland year-round.

FIG 9. Rooks Corvus frugilegus nest colonially in tall trees and forage mainly on open farmland: left, pair at nest in high tree, as photographed from a church steeple (Richard Chandler); right, nests can be readily counted from the ground before the trees leaf out (Ian Newton).

Some bird species would not occur in the farmed environment without the presence of woods, trees or hedgerows, others without the presence of wetlands (with static or flowing water), and yet others without cliffs, quarries or buildings (Tables 1 and 2). Certain species occur only within these restricted habitat areas, getting little or nothing from the open fields, while others use these habitat patches as bases from which to forage over the surrounding farmland. Species vary greatly in how far they are prepared to venture onto open farmland. Typically, House Sparrows forage at no more than a few metres from bushy cover, darting back whenever danger threatens, while other species, such as plovers, gulls and geese feed out in the open, away from any type of refuge.

Look at these variations in bird behaviour in more detail. Among 'farmland' species that depend on woods and hedgerows, some, such as tits and warblers, obtain practically all they need from within these habitats; others, such as Bullfinches and Song Thrushes, frequently venture out to feed up to several metres from woody cover; while others, such as Red Kites, Woodpigeons, Rooks and Linnets, use woody vegetation for nesting and roosting but obtain almost all their food from the open fields, travelling up to several kilometres on foraging trips (Table 1). The distribution and abundance of all these species on farmland is to some extent influenced by the distribution and amount of woodland and scrub, but the removal of some woods and hedges from a farmed landscape would affect the full-time occupants or short-distance foragers long before the long-distance foragers were affected, because, on the face of it, the latter could make do with fewer, more widely scattered focal habitat patches. But they all still require different types of habitat within their daily ranges.

Among species dependent on cliffs or buildings, some, such as the House Sparrow, feed close by, while others, such as the Stock Dove, travel up to several kilometres for food. Similar differences occur among wetland species: Little Grebes and Reed Warblers obtain practically all their needs from their main habitat; Moorhens and Coots venture short distances onto nearby farmland to feed; gulls and geese may feed nearby but may also fly up to many kilometres to feed in open farmland, commuting daily between their roosting and foraging sites.

Similar variation in bird behaviour with respect to base-points is apparent in both lowland and upland, summer and winter, even though some different bird species are involved. These statements on the habitat associations of different species hold as generalisations. The fact that species occasionally behave differently or turn up in unexpected places does not alter these basic patterns.

FIG 10. Requiring open water for security, the Moorhen Gallinula chloropus is the commonest wetland bird on farmland, nesting on any open water, from small ponds to large lakes, and foraging partly on open land nearby (Richard Chandler).

In the breeding season, some 77 species seen on lowland farmland can be said to depend on woody cover of one sort of another, 40 species depend on open waters and 23 species on cliffs or buildings (although some species occur in more than one category, Table 1). However, these features are not alone in influencing bird distributions on farmland, because some species are restricted to localities where other necessary conditions are found. For example, being mainly centred on sea cliffs or buildings in coastal towns, Herring Gulls are much more commonly seen in the breeding season within 20 km of the coast than further inland. Less than half the species listed in Table 1 can be considered as widespread across Britain. Many are found in restricted parts of the country or in a few scattered areas which offer suitable conditions. Some, such as Redshank, are seen in lowland farmland in the breeding season and are largely confined to the coast in winter, while others, such as Merlin, are present on lowland farmland chiefly in winter, nesting in the uplands in summer.

The same types of habitat features influence the distribution and abundance levels of birds in winter, through providing consistent rest and roost sites. On my reckoning, some 69 species on lowland farmland in winter depend on woods or hedgerows, 18 on cliffs or buildings and 52 on wetlands, while only about 19 occur in open areas independently of these features (Table 2). The main difference between seasons is that, without the need for frequent feeding of young in fixed-positioned nests, species often forage at greater distances from their roost sites in winter than from their nest sites in summer. For example, Starlings rarely feed more than 1 km from the nest in summer, when they have to return every 10–15 minutes with food for their chicks, but they sometimes fly up to 20 km from their roost sites in winter, when they do not have to return until evening. The communal roost sites of some species, such as Starling and Rook, tend to be fairly regularly spaced across landscapes, and some sites are used year after year, so long as they remain suitable and undisturbed (Wynne-Edwards 1929, Munro 1971). Individual birds also change base-location more frequently in winter than in summer, in response to changes in weather and food supplies, as revealed mainly by ringing.

Some species nest or roost in just one type of site (Rooks in trees, Little Grebes on water), while others use more than one. For example, Kestrels and Stock Doves regularly nest and roost on trees, cliffs or buildings (Stock Doves also occasionally nest in holes in the ground), while Starlings roost in trees, in wetlands (reed-beds) or on cliffs and town buildings. The important point is that all such features form foci of distribution for birds in open farmland, and influence the extent to which farmed land can be used for feeding by different species.

These various habitat features thus have major influence on the dispersion and numbers of many bird species on farmland, summer and winter. They act not only as safe nesting and roosting sites, but as access points to the food resources of the farmed land. Without them, many bird species may not occur on farmland at all. The removal of many of these features from the farmed environment, mainly between the 1950s and 1990s, can be expected to have caused declines in the species that depend on them.

FIG 11. In winter, Starlings Sturnus vulgaris assemble at night in huge communal roosts, with many thousands of birds gathering each evening and flying out to feed in the surrounding farmland by day. They perform spectacular mass flying displays, before descending into the roost in thickets or reed-beds (Edmund Fellowes).

Relatively few species in the lowlands of Britain live entirely in open farmland, nesting and feeding on the ground or in low vegetation. They include 'steppe-land' species such as the Skylark, Meadow Pipit, Yellow Wagtail, Whinchat, Corn Bunting, Montagu's Harrier, Grey Partridge, Red-legged Partridge and Great Bustard, and various waders, some of which nest on dry ground (Lapwing, Ringed Plover, Stone-curlew) and others on damp ground (Lapwing, Black-tailed Godwit, Curlew, Ruff, Redshank and Snipe). These are the only species which nest in areas of lowland farmland that lack the other features mentioned above, and some actively avoid nesting, feeding or roosting close to trees, bushes and buildings, relying on camouflage or on speed and agility to escape predators. Numbering about 25 in total during the breeding season (Table 1), these species are all vulnerable to farming operations that destroy ground-based nests and chicks. Most of the waders also make use of wetland shorelines where they are available nearby in farmland. The Corn Bunting and Whinchat need song perches, but these need not be trees or bushes; tall herbaceous plants or overhead wires serve just as well.

FIG 12. Two bird species of open farmland: left, Lapwing Vanellus vanellus (Richard Chandler); right, Skylark Alauda arvensis (Richard Chandler).

Although different bird species require habitats of different structure and foods of different types, they all live in farmland because it provides appropriate habitat in which food is abundant and accessible, at least for parts of each year. The main foods on farmland that are eaten by birds include not only the seeds, leaves and roots of the crop plants themselves, but also the seeds and leaves of weeds, and various invertebrates that live either on the crops and weeds or in the soil below. Birds of prey eat birds and mammals which themselves depend on these other foods.

ORIGINAL HABITATS OF FARMLAND BIRDS

While we can define fairly closely the current habitat needs of the various bird species found in modern farmland, it is much more difficult to imagine where they might have lived in pre-Neolithic Britain. We can suppose that all the species now associated with woodland and scrub, or various types of wetland, were present in natural habitats in Britain long before people had significant influence on the natural vegetation. For many years, though, uncertainty hung over the strictly open-land species, such as Grey Partridge and Great Bustard, or on those tree-nesting species that needed extensive open land for feeding, such as Rook and Starling, because it was assumed that little or no suitable habitat would have been available. However, although most of primeval Britain was tree-covered, sizeable areas of open grassland probably remained available in the lowlands throughout the Mesolithic Period, before people affected the vegetation in significant ways (Chapter 3). This conclusion has been drawn from studies of ancient plant pollen preserved in peat or lake beds. Moreover, bone remains of grassland bird species, including Grey Partridge and Great Bustard, dated from different times in the Mesolithic and Neolithic periods, have been found at various localities in southern Britain (Yalden & Alberella 2009). These finds imply that open grassland has almost certainly been available in Britain throughout the post-glacial period to the present, and that some open-land species occurred in Britain throughout this period.

Whatever the amount of open land available in pre-Neolithic Britain, it clearly expanded greatly as people began to clear the forest for agriculture, and their grazing livestock, perhaps together with fire, prevented tree regeneration. Obvious beneficiaries of this new and expanding open habitat would have included Kestrels and harriers, Red Kites, Great Bustards, Grey Partridges and Quail, Corncrakes, plovers and Stone-curlews, Short-eared Owls, larks, pipits, wagtails, chats and buntings. In wetter areas, birds such as Redshank and Common Snipe would have benefited. Furthermore, other essentially forest-dwelling species could have found sustenance away from trees on the open farmland, including pigeons, thrushes, finches and some corvids. Overall, it is likely that at least most of the bird species that now breed in Britain, plus others, could have done so in Mesolithic times, but with very different distributions and abundance levels from those of today. Some recent colonists, such as Collared Dove, may be exceptions to this generalisation.

Nevertheless, farmland is relatively recent in the evolutionary history of the birds that occupy it. All the species that now breed there must inevitably have moved in from various natural habitats, in which most species can still be found in other parts of their range, if not in Britain. Some of the species that now live side-by-side on farmland may not have occurred together in any natural habitat, so that the farmland community as a whole owes its origin to human activity. For example, the wader species which now breed together on wet grassland in Britain occur naturally on tundra, marshland, coastal shingle, saltmarsh and wet floodplain, different species in different habitats. Only on the wet grassland created by farming activities in western Europe do they come together as a distinct community, consisting mainly of Lapwing, Redshank and Common Snipe, and in some localities also Curlew, Black-tailed Godwit, Ruff, Dunlin and Oystercatcher (Chapter 13).

CONCLUDING REMARKS

The aims of this chapter have been to outline the scope and methodology that underpin the rest of this book, and to provide some baseline information on farmland and its bird populations. About three-quarters of all land in Britain is under some form of agricultural management, so farming practices have major effects on bird populations, even on some species that live mainly in other more natural habitats. Farmland birds are here defined as those that regularly obtain food from lowland pasture or tilled land, at least 80 species in the breeding season and at least 91 species in winter. Not all these species are widespread, however, as some are scarce or restricted to particular areas. In the breeding season, most lowland farms are likely to hold around 20–40 species at any one time. Some other species occur in the open grazing land of the uplands, but these are discussed in Chapter 19.

In general terms, like other animals, all bird species are restricted to the landscapes and habitats that suit them, these being the primary factors that influence their distributions and abundance levels. While the habitats of some bird species can be described in terms of a single vegetation type, such as deciduous woodland, heathland or reed-bed, many of the species that occur on farmland require a combination of vegetation types, perhaps using some for nesting and others for feeding. Various patches of semi-natural habitat act as bird distribution centres within farmed landscapes, and thus have a major influence on the dispersion and numbers of many species. They act not only as safe nesting and roosting sites, but as access points to the food resources of farmed land. The removal of many of these areas from the farmland environment in the second half of the 20th century is likely to have caused declines in the species that depended on them, especially those that fed almost entirely within them or at only short distances onto farmland. Typical farmland birds also move around from field to field during the course of a year, exploiting whatever appropriate foods are available there at different times.

## CHAPTER 2

## Population Trends in Farmland Birds

CHANGES IN THE BIRD POPULATIONS of Britain, due to human effects on their habitats, have presumably been occurring at least since the start of the Neolithic period, about 6,500 years ago, when agriculture began. Some of the known changes from earlier centuries are discussed in other chapters, but here we are concerned primarily with the changes of recent decades, coinciding with the period of agricultural intensification, when changes in both agriculture and bird populations were well monitored.

MEASURED CHANGES

Recent population changes in farmland birds are often assessed from 1970 because, although detailed counts started in the 1960s, exceptionally hard winters early in this decade had major effects on bird numbers. By 1970, populations had recovered from these weather effects, but had not yet been exposed to the full impacts of developing agriculture. Measured changes in numerical abundance over the period 1970–2013 are shown in Figure 13 for 24 widespread bird species which gain their food mainly or entirely from farmland. A decline of 100% would represent extinction in Britain, and four of the species shown declined in this time by 90% or more, namely the Grey Partridge, Turtle Dove, Tree Sparrow and Corn Bunting, while the Starling declined by an estimated 81%. More than half the species on the list decreased in this period by more than 50%. The seven species that increased included three corvid species whose numbers rose for reasons not fully understood (but see below), two pigeons that were declining but began to increase after the widespread introduction of oilseed rape, whose leaves provided them with winter food, and two finches which also benefited from new food sources. The Goldfinch was declining into the mid-1980s but was then provided with an alternative food source (mainly niger seed) at garden bird-feeders, and has since undergone a sustained increase, while the Chaffinch throughout the period concerned exploited the growing food sources provided by garden bird-feeders and game-bird feed sites.

Further details of population changes for a larger number of farmland bird species which have been counted annually are given in Table 3. In addition, the year-by-year population trends of all the main farmland birds can be viewed in graphical form on the BTO website, and some of them in Figure 16. These graphs reveal that several species (such as Song Thrush and Skylark) began to decline from the mid-1970s, while others (such as Yellowhammer and Little Owl) did not begin to decline until the mid-1980s. Such temporal differences would be expected if different species were affected by different aspects of agricultural change.

Among less widespread species, counted only at intervals of many years, Twite were estimated to have declined by 21% between 1999 and 2013, and Woodcock by 29% between 2003 and 2013 (Hayhow et al. 2014). Some of the estimates for uncommon species made at long intervals were within the range of expected annual variation, but interestingly they were all downward, except those for Corncrake, Stone-curlew and Cirl Bunting, which were subject to special conservation measures (Chapter 21).

In general, declines in farmland birds have occurred over practically the whole of Britain, but have been more marked in the southern half of the country than further north (Noble & Raven 2002). This may have been associated with less marked changes in farming practices further north. For example, mixed livestock/arable farms, which have gone from most of southern Britain, still prevail in much of the low ground in northern Scotland, and many more cereal stubbles are left unploughed through the winter, providing seeds and other foods for birds.

Species that have increased at a national scale over recent decades have included: (1) some birds of prey, mostly in process of recovery from past persecution or organochlorine pesticide use; (2) corvids, which may also be persecuted less than in the past, but in addition have broad diets and feed on foods which, through other human activity, have increased greatly over recent decades; and (3) pigeons, geese and swans, which feed largely or entirely on farm crops and do not require insects or other invertebrates to raise their young.

FIG 17. The Woodpigeon Columba palumbus is one of the small number of farmland birds which has increased greatly over recent decades. It feeds almost entirely on farm crops and, like other doves, requires no insects to raise its young (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Not only have more farmland bird species decreased than increased over recent decades, but most of the declining species occur at naturally higher densities than the increasing ones, so the overall loss of birdlife from farmland, all species together, is much greater than these figures suggest. Furthermore, in the years since 1970, birds of farmland have fallen more drastically than those of any other habitat (Fig. 18). Even in the same species which occur in other habitats as well as in farmland, declines have usually been more pronounced in farmland. For example, by 2000, the Bullfinch had declined by 65% on farmland, compared with 28% in woodland (Siriwardena et al. 2001). Because birds can move freely between different types of habitats, declines in farmland may be less marked than they would otherwise appear (because of net immigration); or they may be more marked in other habitats than they would otherwise appear (because of net emigration). In fact, with farmland drawing birds from other habitats, numbers in these other habitats may decline, even though their carrying capacity for birds remains unchanged.

FIG 18. Population trends for birds in different habitats in Britain over the period 1970–2014. Birds in most habitats have declined over this period, but those in farmland have declined most, by about 54% since 1970. These overall trend lines do not necessarily represent the trend for any individual species, but are based on the average trends for all the monitored species in each habitat, giving all species equal weight, whether increasing or decreasing. From Hayhow et al. (2015a).

Species also seem to have declined more severely in Britain than in other European countries (Donald et al. 2001). Across Europe as a whole, population declines and range contractions among farmland birds during the last quarter of the 20th century were significantly greater in countries with more intensive agriculture (as measured by several indices), and significantly greater in the European Union (EU) than in former communist countries. One measure of agricultural intensification, namely cereal yield, alone explained over 30% of the variation in bird population trends between countries: the greater the average yield per hectare, the greater the population declines. It was not that cereal yield itself was important, but that cereal yield was indicative of many other changes on farmland, such as greater agrochemical use. Overall, these findings implied that recent trends in agriculture have had deleterious and measurable impacts on bird populations on a continental scale. In the years since this analysis was made, several former communist countries have joined the EU and come under the influence of the Common Agricultural Policy. So far as I can establish, farmland birds are now declining in all these new member states.

According to a report published in 2012, an estimated 44 million breeding birds (all habitats included) were lost from the UK between 1966 and 2010, about 21% of those present in 1966, and equivalent to about 1 million birds per year on average (Eaton et al. 2012). This was a net loss, for the totals included some species which increased over that period. In fact, overall numbers increased from 1966 to 1975, in part through recovery from the hard winters of the early 1960s, and the subsequent decline resulted in the loss of 54 million birds between 1975 and 1987, the period of most rapid overall decline. Most of the declining species occurred on farmland, and their period of steepest decline corresponded with the period of greatest agricultural change (as reflected, for example, in agrochemical use, Chapter 8). Although no species disappeared totally from Britain during this period (except arguably the Red-backed Shrike and Wryneck, which are no longer recorded breeding every year), without targeted conservation measures other species such as the Corncrake and Cirl Bunting would almost certainly have gone.

The figures above refer to British breeding species, but changes in farming practices within Britain are likely also to have affected the many bird populations that come to winter in Britain from other parts of Europe and beyond. For these winter visitors, we have no annual monitoring, except for waders and waterfowl. In general, these two groups of birds increased to the 1990s and then levelled off (waterfowl) or declined slightly (waders) (Hayhow et al. 2014). Increases in waterfowl were associated with the increasing numbers of protected wetlands that became available over the years concerned, together with reductions in shooting pressure, owing partly to improved legislation. Increases were particularly marked in wintering geese, most of which feed primarily on farmland, eating either harvest waste or growing crops (Chapter 6). Various gull species increased during the latter half of the 20th century, reaching a peak in the 1990s, and subsequently declined, notably the Black-headed Gull which feeds widely on farmland (Banks et al. 2009). Among other wintering birds, the most noticeable decline was probably in Starlings, in which roosts exceeding a million individuals occurred in most counties into the 1960s, but now most of these roosts have dwindled to a few tens of thousands or fewer. The largest nocturnal gatherings are now found mainly in lowland western districts where extensive areas of pasture remain as foraging habitat. While some of these recent declines in wintering populations could be due to changes on British or continental farmland, there is another possible explanation. Winters have also become milder over this period, causing some of the migratory species to shorten their migrations and winter more in continental Europe, closer to their breeding areas. Counts and ring recoveries confirm that this has happened in at least some of the waterfowl and waders, but this does not mean that changes on British farmland have not also had some influence.

Birds and people

While many bird species have declined in Britain over recent decades, the human population has increased. In 1970, the number of people in the UK was estimated at 56 million, while the number of breeding birds in the UK – all species together – was estimated at 210 million, about 3.8 birds for every person (calculated from Eaton et al. 2012). By the year 2010, human numbers had risen to 62 million, while total breeding bird numbers had fallen to 166 million, about 2.7 birds to every person (Eaton et al. 2012). Many people find these ratios hard to believe. Driving through the countryside, you may see hundreds of birds on each journey as you speed by, gaining the impression that birds vastly outnumber people. But those same birds could be seen by hundreds or thousands of other motorists on the same day, vastly reducing the ratio of birds to people. Similarly, the birds you see at the feeders in your garden may greatly outnumber the number of people living in your house, but the birds may be drawn from a wide area of countryside, and visiting many other gardens on the same day. The estimates of human numbers are probably within a few percent of the real value, but no-one could claim anything like this level of accuracy for the bird counts. Nevertheless, they are sufficient to make the points that birds are now much scarcer in Britain in relation to people than most people might think, and that the ratio of birds to people has declined substantially over recent decades.

Farmland in relation to other habitats

For many bird species, typical breeding densities are much lower on farmland than in more natural habitats nearby, yet because of the vast extent of farmland, it can hold the bulk of their British populations. For example, Skylarks have nested at average densities on coastal marshland of 76 pairs per km2, in semi-natural grassland at 40 pairs per km2, and on lowland heaths at 56 pairs per km2. But on farmland their average densities were much lower, at 18 pairs per km2 on pastoral land, 28 pairs per km2 on arable land and 22 pairs per km2 on mixed farmland (Donald 2004). Nevertheless, a national survey in 1997 implied that 70% of all Skylarks in Britain occurred on lowland farmland, with 50% on arable land (Browne et al. 2000). Similar conclusions could be drawn for many other birds: modern farmland is a relatively poor habitat as reflected in nesting densities, but because of its extent it could still hold the bulk of their populations.

Other factors in the declines in farmland birds

While the declines in farmland birds can be attributed primarily to changes in agricultural practices, as discussed in detail later in this book, other causal factors may have been involved. In particular, over recent decades some predatory species have increased, notably various corvids, such as Carrion Crow and Magpie, and raptors such as Buzzard, along with Foxes, Badgers and Grey Squirrels (Box 1). The increases in raptors can be regarded as recoveries from past persecution or pesticide impacts, and those in other species are probably due to reduced persecution and increased food supplies resulting from various human activities. So can increased predation have contributed to the declines in farmland birds?

FIG 19. Some predatory bird species which have increased in Britain over the period of farmland bird declines. Upper left, Magpie Pica pica (Edmund Fellowes); upper right, Carrion Crow Corvus corone (Richard Chandler); lower left, Buzzard Buteo buteo (Andrew Everitt); lower right, Sparrowhawk Accipiter nisus (Keith Kirk).

BOX 1. Increases in the numbers of predators in the British countryside over recent decades

Since the 1960s, most common mammalian and avian predators in Britain have increased, especially those affecting ground-nesting birds. In the period 1961–2009, according to the National Game Bag Census of the Game & Wildlife Conservation Trust, the numbers of Foxes killed annually by gamekeepers on game-rearing estates in Britain increased by threefold but had changed little from the 1990s; the numbers of Rats and Grey Squirrels approximately doubled, and Stoat numbers increased less markedly, while Hedgehogs and Weasels declined by about one-half, and feral cats by about one-fourth. The number of Minks killed reached a peak during the mid-1970s to mid-1980s, and subsequently halved, possibly in association with the return of Otters as they recovered from the past impacts of organochlorine pesticides, and reoccupied many lakes and rivers which had meanwhile been colonised by Minks. Protected by law, Badgers do not figure in vermin records, but national surveys in 1985–88 and 1994–97 suggested a 24% increase in social groups and a 75% increase in numbers over this nine-year period (Wilson et al. 1998). Among avian predators, the numbers of Carrion/Hooded Crows that were killed by gamekeepers roughly doubled in numbers, while Magpies tripled, but both stabilised from the 1990s. It is assumed in this monitoring scheme that the numbers of each species killed reflect the numbers in the environment.

According to the BTO website, between 1970 and 2013, based on counts of breeding birds, Carrion Crows and Magpies approximately doubled in numbers, Sparrowhawks increased by around threefold, Buzzards and Red Kites increased by around tenfold, while Kestrels declined by about one-half. It is difficult to be sure why some species have increased, but there is clearly much more food available for them than in the past, resulting from large-scale Pheasant rearing, outdoor pig units, and the increasing amount of human waste, especially in towns and cities. Raptors are in a different category, for they are generally less common than corvids, and the increases of most species largely represent recoveries from past human impact, whether persecution or organochlorine pesticide use, depending on species. However, with such an abundance of released Pheasants in the countryside, Foxes, Buzzards and other predators may have achieved higher densities in recent years than at any time in the past two centuries. During the present century, some of these predators have declined (the Fox by about 40% and the Sparrowhawk by about 15%), while the numbers of Buzzards, Carrion Crows and Magpies have more or less stabilised (BTO website). The domestic cat population of Britain is estimated at more than 10 million, having doubled in numbers since the 1960s (Murray et al. 2010). In all these species, figures referred to the overall national trend, which nevertheless varied regionally.

FIG 20. The Fox Vulpes vulpes is a major predator of ground-nesting birds and their eggs; its numbers are thought to have doubled between the 1970s and 1990s, since which time they seem to have stabilised. This one is carrying a Grey Squirrel Sciurus carolinensis it has caught (Chris Knights).

Several studies designed to investigate this matter have provided little or no support for the view that predators have been a primary causal factor. Nevertheless, predation rates on the eggs and chicks of some ground-nesting birds, such as Lapwing, have seemed in recent years to be exceptionally high, a finding that could be attributed to increased predator numbers or to changed habitats making their eggs and chicks easier for predators to find (Chapter 13). Over much of Britain and western Europe, reproduction in several wader species is now so low as to account for the observed population declines (Chapter 13, MacDonald & Bolton 2008a, 2008b, Roodbergen et al. 2012). So while predation may not have caused the declines of many species observed into the 1980s, it may have contributed to subsequent continuing declines or prevented population recoveries, leaving much apparently suitable habitat unoccupied. At a national scale, the main predators involved are Foxes and Carrion/Hooded Crows, but many others have also been implicated (Chapter 13).

Among birds of prey, attention has so far focused on the Sparrowhawk and Buzzard, whose recoveries from previous low levels were especially obvious. Declines in most farmland birds began in the 1970s or 1980s, but at least in eastern Britain, recoveries in these two raptors did not become obvious until the 1990s or later. Another important bird predator, the Peregrine, has spread widely over the lowlands since the late 1990s, nesting on churches and other tall buildings in towns and cities. Although it nested in a few lowland quarries in earlier times, its widespread adoption of buildings has enabled it to occupy many areas formerly closed to it, so it is now in a position to hunt over lowland farmland as never before. Again, however, the main declines in farmland birds occurred well before Peregrines took to nesting widely on city buildings in Britain, and in addition, the small bird species which have most declined have always formed no more than a very small component of the Peregrine's diet, compared to larger species such as pigeons, which have increased (Ratcliffe 1993). In southern Britain, the Hobby has also increased in recent years, spreading gradually northward, but again its major increase post-dates the main decline in the small farmland birds which form part of its diet. So whatever effect these four raptors may now have on farmland birds, they are unlikely to have contributed significantly to the major declines of the 1970s–90s, especially in eastern districts. It is also worth noting that, while in farmland most bird species declined, in other habitats greater proportions of species remained more or less stable or increased over the same period, again pointing to a particular problem in farmland. Combining the data from all monitored species into an overall average, the birds of farmland show a steeper decline than those of other habitats (Fig. 18).

In addition to increased predator numbers, the climate is now changing, and in theory this may also have contributed to some bird population trends. Many species are known to respond to prevailing weather, decreasing during hard winters or severe summer droughts, and recovering subsequently (Newton 2013a).
