But in many species these annual fluctuations are superimposed on long-term trends due to some other factor, such as a progressive change in habitat or food supplies. Moreover, as the weather has become generally warmer over the past 50 years, many resident species affected by hard winters should have benefited and increased over this time rather than decreasing. Milder winters may even have lessened the impact of other limiting factors, such as reduced food supplies. The main documented changes attributed to long-term climate change include northward extensions in the breeding or wintering ranges of some species, allowing them to survive or breed in areas formerly too cold for them. Other species (such as Willow Warbler and Curlew) are now declining more severely in the south of Britain than in the north, and change in climate is one of the potential causal factors suggested. Other changes attributed to long-term climate change have included shifts in phenology, as many species now start breeding earlier than in the past, while some migrants also arrive earlier and depart later from their breeding areas than in the past (Newton 2010, 2013a, Pearce-Higgins & Green 2014).

In an attempt to assess the relative importance of land use and climate change to farmland birds, annual variation in the breeding season counts of 18 species in the UK were examined in relation to measures of land-use intensity and weather over 43 years, 1966–2008 (Eglington & Pearce-Higgins 2012). The year-to-year changes in bird numbers emerged as being much more closely related to changes in agricultural intensity than to changes in weather, although the latter had some effect. Despite more stable land-use intensity in recent years, climate change (inferred from weather trends) did not overtake land use as the dominant driver of population changes in these farmland birds. We will return to matters of predation and weather in later chapters.

Other agents capable of causing declines in bird populations are parasitic diseases. Most such diseases occur as sporadic outbreaks, causing temporary and local declines in selected species whose numbers usually recover within a year or two. However, at least one species in Britain has undergone a long sustained national decline which has now lasted more than a decade, namely the Greenfinch, as affected by a protozoan parasite, Trichomonas. This parasite normally affects pigeons and doves, in which virulent strains have occasionally caused heavy mortality. Such strains may have passed from Collared Doves to Greenfinches at garden feeders and drinking bowls. The doves seem fairly resistant to the strains involved, for they showed no obvious mortality, whereas sick Greenfinches have been seen at many garden feeders. As the disease is still running, and since 2006 has caused massive decline in national Greenfinch numbers, it remains to be seen what the final outcome will be. Some other species, such as Chaffinches, have been less affected, but the same organism was more recently found in 25 live Turtle Doves that were examined, though only seven showed clinical symptoms (Stockdale et al. 2014).

FIG 21. Two species which increased through feeding at garden feeders: Goldfinch Carduelis carduelis (Stan Wilson); right, Greenfinch Chloris chloris, the latter having now declined through the disease trichomoniasis (Stan Wilson).

CAUSES OF POPULATION CHANGE: SOME GENERALISATIONS

Recent declines in the distributions and numbers of many bird species in Britain can be attributed to the destruction and degradation of their habitats, and consequent reduction of living space (Newton 2013a). They include, for example, many species of marshland and wet meadows which, because of land drainage, now have far fewer places to live and breed than in the past. Conversely, other species have expanded as new habitat has been created. They include various waterfowl which in recent decades have benefited from the construction of additional reservoirs and gravel pits. So change in the amounts of different habitats – whether resulting from agriculture or some other influence – is one of the important factors that bring about changes in bird distributions and numbers.

The habitat tells us where we may find particular bird species, but it gives little indication of the numbers in which those species are likely to occur, or even whether they will be there at all. Densities of birds within habitats can be influenced by prevailing resources (such as food and nest sites) or natural enemies (such as competitors, predators and pathogens). Within suitable habitat, any one of these 'limiting factors' could cause a population to decline or prevent it from increasing. Particular populations may be affected by more than one, perhaps all, of these different factors, but often one factor emerges as overriding at any one time. In addition, different factors can interact with one another, and with the weather. Birds may be particularly short of food, for example, during periods of winter snow or summer drought, depending on the species. And the threat of predation may prevent birds from exploiting an exposed food supply as much as they might do in the absence of this threat (Newton 2013a). Owing to the varying effects of limiting factors, areas of similar-looking habitat can hold markedly different densities of birds. Although much farmland in Britain seems on a casual glance much the same today as it did in 1970, it now supports far fewer birds, largely as a result of changes in management and consequent reductions in bird food supplies, as explained in later chapters.

All the external limiting factors mentioned above can have immediate direct effects on bird breeding, mortality or movements, and hence on local numbers. However, knowledge of the changes in breeding or mortality rates alone can often help to pinpoint the external causal factor, or at least to indicate whether population change is associated with changed breeding success or changed survival. Where reproductive and survival rates have been studied in the same population during periods of population increase (or stability) and decline, the comparison has pointed to where the cause of the decline might lie. If, over a period of population decline, reproduction declined while survival stayed the same, the problem would probably lie in the breeding season, but if survival had decreased, the problem could lie in the breeding or non-breeding season, depending on when the extra deaths occurred.

In some bird populations studied in recent decades, changes in breeding numbers – either year-to-year or long-term – have been attributed primarily to conditions that affect reproductive rates, and in others primarily to conditions that affect mortality rates. For example, long-term declines in the numbers of Lapwings and Curlews in Britain were associated primarily with a reduction in reproductive success while survival rates remained high (Peach et al. 1994, Taylor & Dodd 2013). But changes in the numbers of Reed Buntings and other small seed-eating birds were attributed primarily to changes in survival (Peach et al. 1999, Siriwardena et al. 1999). In yet other species, such as Skylark and House Sparrow, population declines were associated with declines in both survival and reproduction (Wolfenden & Peach 2001, Donald 2004, Hole et al. 2002, Morrison et al. 2014). In theory, any species which normally feeds on seeds but rears its young on insects could be influenced by declines in both types of food, and hence by declines in both survival and reproduction. All larks, sparrows and buntings are in this category.

Most of the common birds of farmland are resident in Britain year-round, so there is no doubt that the factors causing population changes operate here within the country. But with migrants the situation differs, for in theory population changes of summer visitors might be driven by events in their migration or non-breeding areas further south, while for winter visitors population changes might be driven by events in their migration or breeding areas further north or east. In several summer visitors that are associated with farmland, such as the Swallow, Sand Martin and Whitethroat, annual fluctuations in breeding numbers in Britain have been linked to annual variations in rainfall in their African wintering areas. More rain gives greater vegetation growth, seed production and insect abundance, resulting in greater bird numbers as measured in their European breeding areas (Newton 2010, Ockenden et al. 2014). However, we have to distinguish between the long-term trends in populations and the annual fluctuations about these trends, and it seems that weather fluctuations, either in Europe or Africa, influence mainly the latter. Long-term population trends in migrants could also be due to changes occurring in breeding, migration or wintering areas, but could involve other factors besides trends in climate, such as trends in habitat, food supplies or human hunting.

FIG 22. The Turtle Dove Streptopelia turtur has been declining in Britain since 1970, but the decline seems to have been especially rapid since the 1990s. Because the species is a summer visitor to Britain, unknown factors acting on migration or wintering areas cannot be ruled out as contributing to the decline (Chris Knights).

EARLIER POPULATION DECLINES

While the declines of many farmland bird species may have started or greatly accelerated in recent decades, others began much earlier. Judging mainly from written records, some British breeding birds have been in decline at least since the early 19th century (Gibbons et al. 1996, Holloway 1996, Shrubb 2003). They include the Corn Bunting, Twite, Chough, Red-backed Shrike, Ring Ouzel, Wheatear, Stonechat, Whinchat, Yellow Wagtail, Woodlark, Wryneck, Stone-curlew, Dotterel, Red-necked Phalarope, Corncrake, Bittern, Ptarmigan, Quail, Black Grouse and Barn Owl. To these, we could add the Whooper Swan, Bittern, Avocet, Ruff, Black-tailed Godwit and Savi's Warbler, all of which apparently became extinct as breeders in Britain and later re-colonised, and also the Great Bustard, which died out and is now in process of reintroduction. Most of these species almost certainly declined primarily through changes in land use affecting their habitats. This holds even for the Dotterel and Ptarmigan, whose high montane breeding areas have been adversely affected by sheep grazing (Chapter 19). In addition to these species, most raptor species declined strikingly during the 19th and early 20th centuries, as a result of relentless persecution chiefly in the interests of game rearing. At least five raptor species seem to have been eliminated totally from Britain, but all have since re-colonised or have been reintroduced (Newton 2013a).

Other species have fluctuated through recent centuries, as the ratio of arable to grassland has changed, or as drainage systems have been installed and then deteriorated. For example, shooting bags (and presumably population levels) of Grey Partridges were much lower in periods of agricultural depression, when much arable land was allowed to revert to grassland, as in the 1830s–40s and again in the 1930s (Sotherton et al. 2014). On the other hand, in these same periods, Lapwing, Redshank and Snipe flourished, under the widespread neglect of drainage systems (Shrubb 2003). However, other factors also now influence the numbers of some of these species in Britain, as explained in later chapters.

FIG 23. The Great Bustard Otis tarda once bred widely across open farmland in southern and eastern Britain, but gradually declined and disappeared. It may have been the first major casualty of changing agriculture in Britain. The last nesting records date from the 1830s. Attempts are now under way to re-establish the species on Salisbury Plain (Chris Knights).

CONCLUDING REMARKS

At least since 1970, most farmland bird species have declined in Britain, some by more than 90%. Species that are largely restricted to farmland have declined more than those which also breed commonly in other habitats. Birds in woodland and wetlands have, with some exceptions, declined less markedly or increased over the same period. This strongly suggests that changes on farmland have been responsible for the declines in farmland birds, an inference explored in later chapters. In some species, however, other factors may also have been involved. Similar declines in farmland birds have occurred across Europe, the degree of decline in different countries being correlated with measures of agricultural intensification. In most declining species for which information is available, declines began from the 1970s or later, but in others slow declines began at least as far back as the 19th century and have continued to the present.

## CHAPTER 3

## Farming Through Time

FOR AT LEAST 6,500 YEARS, from Neolithic times on, the landscapes and vegetation cover of Britain have been progressively changed by crop and livestock farming. No meaningful record exists for most of this period, but inferences can be drawn from dated plant and animal remains, from human artefacts and other archaeological material. Pollen deposits from peat bogs and lake beds have proved particularly useful in documenting vegetation changes. The record from other sources is skimpy but improves from Roman times, starting around 2,000 years ago, and particularly over the last 1,000 years with the development of an increasingly sophisticated written record. Literary sources give much useful descriptive information, and in more recent centuries scientific and statistical data were also added. Based on this gradually improving information base, this chapter highlights the known changes in vegetation and farming practices that have occurred in Britain since Neolithic times, and are likely to have had major impacts on birds and other wildlife. The well-documented changes in farmland bird populations over the past half-century can then be viewed within this longer-term perspective.

THE PRIMEVAL LANDSCAPE

At the end of the last glaciation around 10,000 years ago, as the ice sheets retreated, plants and animals were able to spread northwards from their glacial refuges in southern Europe. As the expanses of tundra and ice disappeared, trees began to return, initially birch, followed by Scots Pine and then various other broad-leaved trees. At that time, Britain and Ireland were still joined to the rest of Europe. They became separated about 8,000 years ago when, through the melting of glaciers, sea levels rose and flooded the low-lying land between Britain and Ireland, and then between Britain and continental Europe. By this time, as ancient pollen and other plant remains testify, most of the lowlands of these newly formed islands had become covered with forest, mainly dominated by the oaks Quercus robur and Q. petraea (indistinguishable in pollen remains), but with abundant Wych Elm, Ash, Small-leaved Lime, Hazel and other species in drier areas, and Alder and willows on wetter ground. In mountainous areas, pine, juniper and birch were more common, although the highest mountain tops remained as open tundra and rock, much as they appear today. At this time, the climate became warmer and wetter than it is now, favouring the growth of bogs and marshes. Mesolithic people were still hunter–gatherers, probably having little impact on their environment. Their numbers are assumed to have been low – perhaps no more than a few tens of thousands in the whole country – but there is little or no useful evidence on this point.

Debate continues on how closed the canopy of British and Irish forest was in late Mesolithic times. The record is dominated by pollen produced in abundance by wind-pollinated trees – especially oaks, Hazel, birches, Scots Pine and Alder. Low wind-pollinated plants, such as grasses and sedges, and insect-pollinated trees and herbaceous plants, are likely to be greatly under-represented among ancient pollen remains. If allowance is made for this likely bias in the pollen record, then rather more extensive grasslands or open parkland-like areas could have occurred in the otherwise continuous forest (Vera 2000). Another argument for the existence of dry open areas in Mesolithic Britain is that, despite their abundance in the pollen record, oaks and Hazel do not regenerate well under a closed canopy. They need open ground to establish themselves, by whatever means and however sporadically those openings were created. In Mesolithic Britain, open areas may have occurred permanently in river valleys, rounded chalk hills and exposed coastal areas, or they may have been temporary and continually shifting, created by natural fires and seasonal flooding, or by Mesolithic hunters (burning the forest) and the large grazing mammals they were hunting, including deer and wild cattle (Aurochs). The existence of such open areas could have accounted for the occurrence in southern Britain of open-country bird species, such as Great Bustard and Grey Partridge, in the Mesolithic period, as confirmed by dated bone remains found chiefly in archaeological sites (Yalden & Albarella 2009). Persistence of open areas through the Mesolithic, but in fluctuating amounts, is also implied by fossil data from other animals, such as beetles (Whitehouse & Smith 2010). In other words, despite the popular notion that the British Isles in Mesolithic times were forested from coast to coast, there may in fact have been substantial areas of open habitat – grassland, sedge or heathland, in addition to extensive bogs and marshes, altogether giving a highly diverse avifauna. However, the extent of open grassland in Mesolithic Britain is still disputed, as is the extent to which wild herbivores (as opposed to fire and flood) were involved in its creation and maintenance (Mitchell 2005).

EARLY NEOLITHIC TIMES

Neolithic (Late Stone Age) culture, involving the cultivation of cereals, was already under way 12,000 years ago in the 'fertile crescent', the region now occupied by eastern Turkey, northern Iraq, and parts of Syria and Jordan. But this culture took several thousand years to spread across Europe. It reached Britain about 6,500 years ago, when Neolithic people (or their knowledge) spread in from the south, bringing arable agriculture and domesticated animals. It apparently took more than 1,500 years to spread over the whole of Britain. Its arrival in each region marked the start of increasing human impact on the natural environment, which has grown and expanded to the present. This is not an easy concept to grasp, that human impact on the natural vegetation of Britain has extended over 65 centuries, for most of which we have only the skimpiest notion of what was happening. Nevertheless, the first 2,000 years of the Neolithic period are marked in the pollen record by a huge shift from tree to grass pollen, implying a substantial transition from forested to open landscapes brought about by people. The grass pollen included cereals, the commonest in early Neolithic times, according to archaeological evidence, being emmer wheat and six-row barley, together with eincorn wheat and spelt wheat. Such a transition also suggests a considerable growth in human numbers, as well as a substantial shift from forest-dwelling to open-land bird species.

Historians speculate on how these early people lived, how numerous they were, and what they did to the land. The assumption is that early farmers would have settled first where relatively open ground or sparse woodland could be easily cleared, and where good natural grazing existed for their animals. In these early times, it has been conjectured, small areas were cleared from forest and cultivated. Pollen analyses suggest that the forest was often cleared in patches, with a crop grown for a few years, and then abandoned, allowing the forest to recover, but repeating the process elsewhere. Such a pattern would have been similar to the slash-and-burn agriculture still practised in parts of the tropics. After each clearance, cereals were grown, and sheep, goats and cattle were grazed, extending the areas of grass in well-drained chalk and limestone areas such as Salisbury Plain, the South Downs, the Cotswolds, the Mendips, the southern Pennines and the Yorkshire Wolds. In these areas, the loamy calcareous soils were sufficiently deep and fertile to support regular cropping, and they were naturally drained, easily cleared of trees and fairly readily cultivated.

It was in these relatively high areas, on downland or moorland, that the earliest signs of agricultural life were discovered, with ancient settlements, barrows and field systems still obvious in places from the air today. As a result of these findings, it was long held that Neolithic, Bronze Age and Iron Age people lived only or mostly on high ground, avoiding the largely impassable wildwood on heavy lowland soils. Roadways followed the populated ridges and avoided the inhospitable forest on what was often waterlogged land. However, this notion has been shaken by discoveries over the past 50 years showing that ancient settlements were probably also abundant on lower ground, although their remains are less well preserved. In effect, Neolithic people could have lived almost everywhere that was habitable: that is, where seasonal crops could be grown or livestock tended. Even in marshy areas, like the fens of East Anglia and Somerset, communities lived their lives, partly off the local fish and birdlife, and operated via wooden trackways through the wetter areas. Well before the end of the Neolithic, 2000 years ago, effective track systems were established across much of the country, facilitating trade between areas as far apart as East Anglia and the Lake District (as implied by remnant stone tools traded between the two).

It is uncertain how much the early Neolithic people actually cleared the forest with primitive stone implements, how much they burnt it, and to what extent forest was gradually turned into open land over the centuries by livestock preventing tree regeneration. Pigs turned out to eat acorns and beech-mast from the woods may also have played a role. Unlike dry heath and pine forest, deciduous forest is not very flammable, even in the driest of times. But whatever methods the early Neolithic people used, within 4,000 years of their arrival, around the start of the Iron Age, some 2,700 years ago, an estimated half of England had ceased to be wildwood (Rackham 1994).

These various developments, requiring long-term residence in fixed areas, are also believed to have encouraged the growth of settlements – in the form of small villages and hamlets – enabling the inhabitants to spend more time tending their livestock and protecting their crops. This trend continued into the Bronze Age, eventually giving rise to small towns, whose larger populations could be sustained by the increasing productivity from nearby cultivated land. From Neolithic times, however, these self-sustaining human communities would have needed access to clean water, woodland for timber and fuel, arable land for crop production and grazing land for domestic livestock. In mountain areas, livestock were probably moved to higher ground in summer to take advantage of the seasonal grazing there, while protecting the lower ground for winter use. This system of 'transhumance' continued for millennia in Britain, in some places into the 19th century.

Since the last glacial period, various large mammals – both herbivores and carnivores – have become extinct in Britain and elsewhere, due initially to climate change and then increasingly to human impact. Their loss probably facilitated the development of agriculture. Wild horses had gone from Britain long before domestic ones were brought in, and the imported domestic cattle were derived from the Aurochs of the Near East rather than those still found in Britain. Wild sheep and wild goats did not occur naturally in Britain, and domestic forms were derived originally from the wild Asian Mouflon and the Bezoar, again found in the Near East. Similarly, the pigs imported to Britain in Neolithic times were almost certainly derived from forms of the Wild Boar found in the Near East, although some interbreeding with native Wild Boar probably occurred later. Most of these long-suspected findings have been supported by recent DNA studies (Troy et al. 2001, O'Connor & Sykes 2010). The important point, however, is that domestic animals were not developed from native animals present in Britain, but were imported, already domesticated, ultimately from the Near East where Neolithic culture arose. Because Britain had long been separated from continental Europe by this time, domesticated forms of all these species could only have been brought in by boat. In the ensuing millennia, they had a great influence on the vegetation of Britain, the types of crops that were grown, and the wild bird populations that developed.

FIG 24. The Wild Boar Sus scrofa was one of the last large wild mammals to disappear from Britain, surviving locally into the 17th century, but it was reintroduced from the 1970s. There are now an estimated 500–1,000 individuals in Britain, the Forest of Dean being a major centre (Ian Newton).

BRONZE AGE TO ROMAN TIMES

To judge from archaeological remains, human numbers grew as agricultural food production increased. Farming methods became more extensive and sophisticated with successive invasions of people bringing Bronze Age culture (4,500 thousand years ago) and then Celtic Iron Age culture (from 2,700 years ago). The rate of woodland clearance accelerated with the advent of metal tools. Iron was more plentiful and stronger than bronze, and revolutionised many aspects of life. Iron axes could fell trees more efficiently, and iron-based ploughs could turn land more deeply than earlier wooden ones. This greatly extended the range of soils that could be effectively tilled, with further effects on flora and fauna.

By the time of the Roman occupation, from AD 43, there were probably still fewer than a million people in Britain, mainly of Celtic origin, and their farming in southern districts was so successful that some wheat could be exported. By then, there were substantial areas of open fields with cereal crops and open grasslands for grazing livestock, but forest still covered large parts of the country, and marshes remained undrained. New crop species were introduced, including Hemp, Flax and Rye during the Iron Age, and Opium Poppy, Lentil, Broad Bean, Pea and other vegetables during the Roman period. In addition, some species now regarded as weeds were grown as food, including Persicaria (Redshank), Fat-hen, Knotgrass, Rye Brome and Wild Oat. Some of these species became important food plants for a wide range of seed-eating birds.

ANGLO-SAXON TIMES

During the Iron Age and Romano-British period, arable farming was apparently carried out in small fields divided by hedges or walls, and arranged around single farmsteads or collections of dwellings. Such farms still survive in parts of Cornwall, where large field walls date from the Bronze Age. During the ensuing Anglo-Saxon period, from the 5th century on, existing woodland was managed more intensively, and further land was brought under cultivation. In the 8th and 9th centuries, the open field system was introduced to many areas. It mostly involved three large fields grouped around a village. The fields were divided into 200 × 10 m strips, so that each villager (or commoner) could tend several strips scattered through each field. The same crop was grown throughout a given field, so that one field might have had spring-sown barley (or oats, beans or peas), another wheat, while the third was fallow. Each year the crops were rotated, but details varied from place to place and time to time. Animals belonging to the participants were left free to graze the stubble and weeds after harvest on the cropped fields, and year-round on the fallow, but other areas, including damp meadowland or wasteland, also provided food for livestock. To a large extent, open fields were created out of previous smaller hedged fields. They persisted into the 18th century, or even later in a few places. In their heyday, around 1350, large open fields covered nearly one-third of England, especially in the Midlands and northeast, and extended north into mid Scotland (Rackham 1994, Pryor 2010). Stock were either tethered or attended by cowherds or shepherds, so there was little need for stock-proofed enclosure of the fields, and hedges were essentially absent in such areas. Open strip cultivation was also common in Europe, and large areas from Germany eastwards are still covered with strip-cultivated open fields today. Traditionally, open fields had an interesting bird fauna, with abundant Corn Buntings and Grey Partridges and in places also Great Bustards.

As their numbers grew, the Anglo-Saxons increasingly tackled the wet clay soils of low ground. This was possible because of their huge ploughs drawn by up to eight oxen. The plough had a coulter, which is a vertical knife to cut through the soil ahead of the share and mouldboard, improving the plough's efficiency. With so many oxen, frequent turning was difficult and time-consuming, so ploughing took place in long straight strips, replacing the small irregular fields of their predecessors. Fields were enlarged to accommodate the bigger equipment, a trend familiar in more recent times. To help with drainage, the plough was designed to throw up the soil into broad ridges, separated by shallow furrows which served to drain away the surplus water. Remains of such ridge-and-furrow systems can be seen today where they have not been ploughed out by later cultivations, the broad ridges giving the land-surface a waved appearance. In hilly areas, smaller-scale methods were used, like 'lazy beds' of the kind still seen in the Outer Hebrides and western Ireland. The cultivation of heavy clay soils led to the removal of more forest and the establishment of further hedges to divide fields and parishes.

FIG 25. Remains of ancient ridge-and-furrow cultivation are still apparent on fields that have remained as pasture for centuries. This one is near the village of Pickworth in Lincolnshire (Ian Newton).

Supported by an assured food supply, the human population continued to grow, and further changes occurred in crop production. Between the Roman Period and the 12th century, the spelt and emmer wheat of early farmers were replaced by club wheat and bread wheat; rye and oats became commonly grown, and barley was still frequent. Flax and hemp became common fibre crops, while peas, beans and other vegetable crops were probably grown mainly in garden plots.

NORMAN TIMES ON

The Domesday Book, published in 1086 as a result of a detailed countrywide survey, gave the first written description of the land of southern Britain as it was at the time. England was recorded as consisting of about 35% arable land, 30% pasture, 15% woodland and wood pasture, and less than 2% meadow. The remaining one-fifth of England was taken up with mountains, heaths, moorland and fen, houses and gardens, and hunting preserves. Major areas of woodland remained in Kent (the Weald), Worcestershire, Buckinghamshire and Derbyshire, while the fens and Brecks of East Anglia were largely treeless.

From the Norman invasion in 1066 until the Black Death in 1348–49, the human population of Britain is estimated to have grown rapidly, from about 1.5 million to 3.5 million, and farming expanded to feed the rising numbers. Woodland declined from covering 15% of England in 1086 to perhaps 7–10% by 1350, and was generally managed intensively to provide much-needed material for buildings and fences, as well as for ships. Woods supplied not only timber, but smaller wood for hurdles, wattle-and-daub building, posts and firewood, the under-wood being worth more than the big timber. Some of the areas that were coppiced were surrounded by earth banks topped with hedges to exclude browsing animals. Although the Norman kings sequestered substantial areas of 'forest' for hunting deer, by the middle of the 14th century the arable area was extensive, at nearly 4 million hectares (compared to 4.6 million hectares in 2015). Most arable agriculture was still practised on the open-field system, giving a prairie-like landscape almost devoid of trees and shrubs between the remaining patches of woodland and other semi-natural habitat. But small, enclosed fields remained common in some districts, notably in the west, including much of Wales. The huge area of arable land only barely fed the population. Only about two-thirds was cropped each year, with the rest left fallow to restore its fertility. Yields were low, reaching perhaps 600 kg of wheat per hectare, less than one-tenth of that achieved today, and about a fifth of the crop had to be saved for seed-corn. Little manure was available for use on arable land because livestock were kept mainly on the grassland and other semi-natural areas. The grazing was poor by modern standards. The limiting resource for all kinds of livestock was winter feed, and for this purpose hay from damp meadows was crucial.

The Normans introduced deer farming to Britain, based on the imported Fallow Deer, which was considered more attractive than native species and easier to keep confined. The species had probably been introduced earlier, in Roman times, but it is not known whether it remained in limited numbers or whether it died out and was reintroduced by the Normans. In any case, deer parks were established in existing grassy landscapes containing isolated trees or patches of woodland. The Domesday Book records 35 deer parks in England (Rackham 1994). But in little over a century these numbers multiplied to reach about 3,200 at their peak around AD 1300, covering some 2% of the country. They were less common in Wales and Scotland. Such parks were status symbols among the upper classes, and the venison was usually reserved for feasts or special guests. Deer parks gradually declined in popularity, but enjoyed some revival in the 1520s when Henry VIII developed royal parks as attractive landscapes for ceremonial hunts, and again in the 18th century in the hands of professional landscape designers such as 'Capability' Brown. Fewer deer parks survive today, but escaped deer of several introduced species have now spread over much of lowland Britain, finding cover in the remaining woodlands. Deer never did much to feed the wider human population, and their main legacies today are woodland without undergrowth, reduced numbers of shrub-nesting birds, and substantial crop damage (Chapter 7). Pheasants were apparently also introduced in Norman times, and with modern artificial rearing, have now achieved an unimagined abundance on British farmland, with up to 40 million released per year in recent years for recreational shooting (Larkman et al. 2015).

FIG 26. Fallow Deer Dama dama, introduced to Britain by the Normans, perhaps following an earlier attempt by the Romans (Ian Newton).

DISEASE, STARVATION AND POPULATION REDUCTION

The 14th century was a difficult time for people in Britain, as the climate became cooler and wetter. The years 1315–17 were exceptionally wet, creating the 'Great Famine' when thousands of people died from starvation or diseases associated with malnutrition. The years 1348–49 saw the arrival from the continent of an especially deadly form of bubonic plague. The so-called 'Black Death' is thought to have arisen in Mongolia, spreading rapidly across Europe and then much of Britain. It wiped out whole communities and reduced the overall population of Britain from around 3.5 million to around 2.25 million. More than 1,000 villages were deserted. Caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, this plague was essentially a disease of rats and other rodents, transmitted to people mainly by fleas. It struck most severely where rats thrived, in the slum districts of towns and in rural villages. The main carrier was the Black Rat, which had been brought here in ships in Roman times. Further waves of bubonic plague swept through the country in later years, causing further shrinkage in human numbers.

With most people in the 14th century working the land, the impact on agriculture of a sudden collapse in their numbers is not hard to imagine. Crops remained unharvested and livestock died. Many fields went out of cultivation, and were re-invaded by shrubs and trees. Others were allowed to revert to grass, supporting growing numbers of sheep, which were less labour-demanding than arable crops. Food for people was sometimes short even with a reduced population, which did not reach its former level until about AD 1600. The sheep soon numbered more than 12 million, contributing not only wool and meat but also dung, which helped to maintain the fertility of land on which they grazed. The labour shortage also gave respite to the woods which had been heavily exploited during the 13th and early 14th centuries. Another later outbreak of bubonic plague, known as the 'Great Plague', came in 1665, killing 60,000 of London's 450,000 citizens. However, this outbreak did not spread widely across the country, so its impact on rural people and agriculture was much less. It was also the last major outbreak of bubonic plague in Britain.

The 14th century also saw the last of the major famines affecting the people of Britain, but the Highland Clearances of the 18th century brought on further starvation, and in Ireland the famine induced by potato blight in 1845–52 caused a massive reduction in the Irish population by starvation and emigration (an estimated 1 million people starved and 3 million emigrated). The vanishingly small prospects of famine in later times resulted largely from an increasingly productive agriculture, and eventually from the importation of additional food (see later).

THE ENCLOSURES

For several hundred years, at least from the Iron Age through to late medieval times, the lowland landscape of Britain consisted mainly of three components: (1) enclosed land typified by small fields with hedges or walls, winding lanes and a scattering of hamlets and villages, (2) large open fields used mainly for arable agriculture and kept largely free of trees and shrubs, and (3) the range of habitats covered by the old manorial term 'waste', which included heaths, rough grassland, woods, marshes and mosses, together with vast tracts of upland grazing and moor. These wastes were mostly privately owned, and managed, as before, by a system of common rights which meant that everyone in the locality had access for grazing and other resources, but they remained in a semi-natural state. They provided many essential resources for rural communities, including grazing for livestock, wood, fuel (turf, peat, reeds, gorse and wood), bedding (sedge and bracken), thatch (heather, reeds and sedge), wild fruit, herbs and fungi, together with fish and wildfowl in wetlands. Large parts of them were created from the grazing pressure of domestic livestock. In the 18th century every lowland English county included large areas of woodland, heathland or marshland, the latter mainly in river valleys. Parishes were laid out to give access to the resources of such areas. Such wasteland was estimated to cover at least one-fifth of the area of England and Wales, before the Enclosure Acts led to the disappearance of most of it. The open treeless fields were large, sometimes covering 300–500 ha, but divided into strips with fallow areas; they may have looked from the air like giant treeless allotments, complete with tracks and paths (Rackham 1994).

This mixture of sizeable areas of enclosed pasture and meadow, open arable land, waste with woodland, and intact marshland could have provided the most diverse lowland landscape seen in lowland Britain during the last thousand years, and with it, the most diverse avifauna. There would not necessarily have been more bird species in total than are present today, but many species were much more widely distributed across the country, giving greater diversity in each district. Such species included Crane, Black Grouse, Quail, Great Bustard, Stone-curlew, harriers (probably all three species), Nightjar, Red-backed Shrike, Woodlark, Wheatear, Whinchat and Stonechat, as well as species which are still widespread, such as Skylark, Tree Pipit and Meadow Pipit. Some of these species nested in these semi-natural areas, but also gained food from the open fields. On the extensive croplands, the relatively undisturbed period of 3–4 months between germination and harvest of cereal crops could have allowed most bird species of modern arable land to breed successfully. Such fields were large and clearly also provided important feeding areas for birds, as depicted in many medieval and later paintings.

FIG 27. Some birds of the ancient 'wastes': upper left, Hen Harrier Circus cyaneus (Alan Martin); upper right, Raven Corvus corax (David Boyle); lower left, Great Bustard Otis tarda (Chris Knights); lower right, Stonechat Saxicola rubicola (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

From the 17th century on, major agricultural developments occurred which completely altered the appearance of much of Britain, and which greatly increased food production. In former centuries, winter keep for cattle was scarce, so only a small number could be retained. New crops such as turnips, which could be easily stored, and new crop rotations produced much more storable animal food, making it possible to keep more livestock through the winter. This in turn resulted in more manure, which could be used to improve soil structure and increase crop yields, particularly for cereals. To make this system work, the land had to be divided into convenient-sized plots with more stock-proof hedges and fences. Over time, the resulting 'enclosures' not only spelt the end of the large open-field system, but also led to the destruction of much remaining 'wasteland'. But these enclosures greatly extended the typical patchwork landscape of fields and hedgerows which for many people now characterises the British countryside.

FIG 28. The introduction of turnips as winter feed for livestock changed the countryside, allowing more animals to be kept over winter and providing additional weed-laden feeding areas for birds (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Enclosure thus involved dividing up large tracts of land into smaller units with fences or hedgerows, and the assertion of private property rights over land which had previously been held in common. Altogether, the process of enclosure spanned more than three centuries (17th–19th), but most was accomplished between 1761 and 1844. Enclosure of the open fields peaked in the late 18th century, and of the wastes in the early 19th century. The latter process brought much more land under cultivation, including large areas of light, warm and well-drained soils, the fertility of which was raised by various means. Enclosure was accomplished almost on a parish-by-parish basis, depending on the presence of landowners or others with enterprise and capital. Consequently, neighbouring parishes or commons might be enclosed at very different dates. Former extensive areas of semi-natural habitat thus tended to become increasingly fragmented, before disappearing altogether from particular regions.

After enclosure, each owner was obliged to fence his holding within a year of acquisition (Hoskins 1969). Roads, steadings and houses were usually constructed later, as were the additional fences necessary to separate livestock from crops within each holding. Hedges were planted 'quick'; that is, by using live cuttings, usually of Hawthorn, but also Blackthorn and others. Oak, Ash and Elm were planted in the hedges and left to grow to mature trees. As the fields were enclosed, attention was paid to drainage, and the ditch by the hedge became standard in many areas. Land owned by parishes was also broken into smaller units by means of hedges and fences. Similar changes occurred in Wales and Scotland. However, in Scotland the legal process was different because most of the land was already held privately as large estates, and most of the new field boundaries in Scotland were not hedges but walls (drystane dykes), many dating from 1770–1870. Then, from 1870 to 1945, over Britain as a whole, maps indicate very little change in the distributions of either hedges or walls (Rackham 1994).

The process of enclosure was piecemeal and protracted largely because of constant opposition. It brought hardship to many people, who thereby lost the living they had made from the common land. The peasant who had worked strips in a common field and grazed his livestock on common land became a wage-earner seeking employment on the newly created farms. The Enclosure Acts thus resulted in both a new landscape and a new social order, but apparently with no great change in the numbers of people working the land.

Even into the 19th century, many bird species such as the Black Grouse, Nightjar and Raven which now have restricted ranges, were widespread, breeding in almost every county in remaining patches of semi-natural habitat (Holloway 1996). And in the absence of game rearing, birds of prey were much more numerous and widespread than they later became. An abundance of raptors is well documented for the 18th century, as is their 19th century demise, when they were practically obliterated from one area after another as specialised game rearing took hold (Newton 1979, 2013a, Lovegrove 2007).

Most of the wasteland areas that were enclosed could not be used immediately for arable crops because the soil was unsuitable. Comprehensive drainage was sometimes necessary. Light sandy soils needed clay, marl or chalk added to improve their structure and fertility, and peatland often needed sand. This operation was not trivial, as it could require 250–750 cartloads of material per hectare to achieve a good agricultural soil. Soils were thus manufactured from whatever appropriate material was available locally. This was clearly a costly operation, achieved by human labour and horse-drawn carts, and as Shrubb (2003) concluded from assessment of 19th-century accounts, 'economic criteria were never considered when destroying natural landscapes and habitats for agriculture. It seemed always to be regarded as a necessary and desirable object of itself, irrespective of cost.' These man-made soils still support the farming of today. If these areas were now abandoned, they would not all revert to their original condition, because the soil (and hence the vegetation) would now differ.

The effects of these changes on the lowland landscape and its bird populations were evidently profound, for not only did semi-natural habitat progressively disappear, but large open areas suddenly grew up with hedgerows, providing new habitat for many 'woodland birds' and other creatures (as documented in some early parish and manorial records; Hoskins 1969). According to Rackham (1994), the hedges planted between 1750 and 1850 – probably exceeding 300,000 km – were at least equal to all those planted in the previous 500 years.

The enclosure of open land had another important consequence. For several centuries, from Anglo-Saxon times on, the whole organisation of farming had depended on cooperation centred on villages, with each participant working to the same rules and the same calendar. There was little or no scope for individualism. But once sizeable parcels of land came under the sole control of individuals, experiment and initiative became possible as never before. It led to rapid improvement in crop plants and livestock through selective breeding, and in time to a further increase in agricultural productivity. It also led to the construction of some fine farmsteads well spaced across the landscape, incidentally providing additional nesting places for Barn Owls, Swallows and other birds associated with farm buildings.

The 17th and 18th centuries were also a period of wholesale land drainage. This process included the drainage of large wetland areas, including the Fens of East Anglia and the Somerset Levels, through the digging of large arterial drains. It also involved the general lowering of water tables on existing farmland, through the digging of smaller ditches, which enabled former damp grassland areas to be converted to drier more productive grassland or arable. These changes led to the loss of several marshland bird species from Britain and to a substantial reduction in the numbers and distributions of others (Chapter 15).

OTHER CHANGES OF THE 18th CENTURY

The 18th century saw two other great changes that affected agriculture and its dependent birdlife. The first was the introduction of new implements, initially associated with the name of Jethro Tull, who in 1701 promoted a drill through which seed could be buried in rows. This not only reduced the amount available on the surface to birds, but permitted the subsequent weeding of crops, because people could walk and hoe between regular rows, a process which was not possible in the old broadcast sowing ('one for the Rook, one for the Crow, one to die and one to grow'). Later inventions included horse-drawn drills, hoes, harrows and much-improved ploughs. These ploughs allowed deeper cutting (more than 10 cm), bringing up nutrients from greater depths than previously. However, this new technology was adopted slowly, and traditional methods were still widely practised into the 19th and in places even into the early 20th century. As written accounts confirm, new seed-drills had a major effect in reducing weed populations, some of which were important food plants for birds and insects. Seed-eating birds may have suffered both from the introduction of seed-drills and from the associated hoeing.

By the early 19th century, oxen had largely given way to horses as draught animals, but oxen were still used in some areas as late as the early 1900s. Horses needed better food and were more expensive to keep than oxen, but were faster and more easily controlled. They became the main source of power on British farms until the 1940s. But whether horse or ox, draught animals could not live by grass alone, and needed fodder, particularly cereals (usually crushed oats) or beans for energy. This ensured a wider distribution of arable crops than has existed since their demise, because almost every farm grew oats for horses, even in hill country. The more recent loss of these crops has been an important contributory factor in the declining diversity of mainly pastoral farmland. Yellowhammers and other species of arable land have gradually disappeared from large parts of the north and west, where livestock farmers lost the need for arable crops (Chapter 10).

The second major innovation of the 18th century was the spread of root crops. The turnip had been grown as a vegetable for centuries, but it was not until the mid-18th century that it was advanced as a fodder crop, used as a root break in arable rotations, replacing the wasteful fallow year. From 1730, a Whig cabinet minister, Viscount Charles Townshend (known as 'Turnip Townshend'), revolutionised East Anglian farming by instituting on his own Norfolk estate the four-course rotation consisting of turnips folded with sheep, followed by barley or oats under-sown to produce a grass–clover ley for the third year, and then wheat in the fourth. The inclusion in the rotation of a nitrogen-fixing legume (such as clover, beans or peas) replenished the soil nitrogen depleted by earlier crops. And the use of turnips solved the age-old problem of winter feed, enabling more animals to be kept overwinter and to be slaughtered as needed. Turnips removed the need for a mass slaughtering of animals in the autumn, and the salting of meat for winter use, as they reduced the dependence on limited hay. Turnips and other fodder root crops can last through the winter, either in situ in the fields, or harvested and stored in piles or 'clamps' in the ground, covered and protected by a layer of surface straw and then soil, to be unearthed when needed. Turnip fields usually also support an abundance of weeds, such as Fat-hen and Persicaria, which form an important food source for finches and other seed-eating birds (Chapter 7).

FIG 29. Agriculture in the early 20th century on large estates: upper, ploughing teams on Tendring Estate in Suffolk; lower, horse-drawn reaper-binder machines on Westacre Estate in Norfolk, one of the last breeding sites of the Great Bustard Otis tarda in Norfolk (David Mason).

Through these various developments, including drainage, liming and enclosure, land was increasingly adapted from the mid-18th century to suit the needs of farming, as some earlier constraints to cultivation were removed. Although this period also saw a growth in food imports from British colonies, restrictions on these imports did much to further stimulate home production. Under the Corn Laws enacted between 1773 and 1815, the government paid a bonus on exported crops but taxed all imported grain, giving an advantage to local producers. These laws made the eviction of commoners and the enclosure of common fields even more advantageous to landowners. They also encouraged the expansion of arable land and the intensification of production. The associated peak in the arable acreage in the mid-19th century was not surpassed until the 1950s, but conflicts over the ownership and use of remaining common land continue to this day.

HIGH FARMING

Further impetus for change from the mid-18th century was provided by the industrial revolution and the rapid rise in the human population of Britain, which nearly doubled over the 18th century and quadrupled in the next century. The resulting rise in urban manufacturing created a need for commercial food production on a large scale, and new farming systems supplied this. Individual farms practised crop rotation, so that at any one time a variety of crop types was found on every farm. They also kept livestock of various kinds, so that in every sense the enterprise was 'mixed'. The classic rotation was the four-course system described above, but regional variations occurred, according to local conditions and needs. From the mid-18th to the mid-19th centuries, root crops included potatoes, sugar beet, swedes, turnips or mangolds, the two latter grown chiefly as livestock food. Other less common crops included rye, kale, beans, peas, lucerne (alfalfa) and linseed, slotted as appropriate into the rotation. This 'high' farming, with its integrated mixed livestock and crop rotations, persisted from the mid-18th century until beyond the mid-20th century, but with increasing mechanisation.

Steam-driven traction engines were introduced as a source of power on farms in the 19th century. They were too cumbersome for wide use in the fields, and were generally hired as needed to provide a stationary power source. They were used either to drive other machinery by use of a belt drive, or in pairs, to drag an implement on a cable from one side of a field to another. By the 1860s, most threshing teams used steam power, travelling from farm to farm across a district over the autumn and winter months, to thresh and extract the grain from cereals stored in ricks. This system of threshing continued into the 1960s when combine harvesters took over. Increasing power and mechanisation on farms, together with the amalgamation of holdings, was matched by a progressively declining labour force from the 1850s to the present. Machines in the fields largely replaced gangs of workers and, as far as birds were concerned, reduced manpower may have been tantamount to reduced disturbance.

FIG 30. Steam engines were introduced into agriculture in the mid-19th century, and mainly used as a stationary power source, for example for threshing cereals to extract the grain, as in this reconstruction of the process. Much grain was spilled, providing food for seed-eating birds which concentrated around the stack-yards at such times. Threshing teams travelled from farm to farm, but steam engines were eventually replaced by diesel-powered tractors (David Mason).

Another feature of high farming was the great increase in manure applications, derived both from folding increased numbers of sheep on winter arable land and from stalled and yarded animals. Dung application increased soil humus, and hence soil-dwelling invertebrate populations, providing additional food for soil-probing bird species, such as Rooks (Chapter 5). The value of inorganic fertilisers was established in the mid-19th century as a result of experiments conducted on a farm in Hertfordshire which later became Rothamsted Experimental Station. Nevertheless, animal manure remained the main source of plant nutrients on farmland until beyond the mid-20th century.

Improvements to grazing systems were promoted by Robert Bakewell (1725–95), a great agricultural improver and animal breeder. He advocated that grazing land should be divided (by hedgerows) into small units of around 4 hectares, to be used in turn. Animals should be kept in each field, he said, until the grass was grazed down so close that 'you could whip a mouse across it'. However, overgrazing to this degree later proved to be bad for the grass because the reduced leaf area lessened photosynthesis and growth; it was also bad for livestock (which could not then feed at maximum efficiency), and incidentally bad for mice (which lost their habitat).

Nevertheless, the high farming which developed across Britain, including on former wasteland, provided important resources for birds, including crops and crop residues (especially on cereal stubbles), stock feed and stored crops, and weed seeds and invertebrates associated with crops, or turned up by ploughing. This mixed system, combining livestock and arable on the same farm, provided a sequence of feeding opportunities for birds throughout the year, with grass and arable constantly available, cultivations in every season, varied crops, stubbles left in winter and stock both stalled and folded in fields. On individual farms, cultivation and harvesting were each spread over two or more months each year, taking much longer than today and making the associated food supplies for birds available over longer periods. The storage of cereals in ricks until they could be threshed provided a major winter food source to which seed-eaters were attracted, especially in severe winter weather. Some species, such as the Grey Partridge and Yellowhammer, may have survived in some upland areas solely because of the presence of a food source at winter ricks, disappearing with their food supply in the 1960s and 1970s. The adoption of crop rotations increased diversity within farms, even though the overall diversity in the countryside had declined with the disappearance on low ground of almost all the 'wasteland'. Farmland itself probably supported greater densities of birds in the mid-19th century than at any other time, offering food supplies which were both more abundant and more evenly spread through the year and across the landscape than they are now.

FIG 31. A thatcher at work, thatching ricks of cereal sheaves to protect them from rain until they could be threshed, up to several months later (Chris Knights).

The changes up to the 20th century mainly concerned arable cropping. Although much grazing land had been lost with the enclosure of commons, those parts of farmland that would be classed today as 'unimproved grassland' changed much less. They included permanent pastures, flood meadows and hay meadows, which remained throughout as prime habitat for a range of grassland birds.

The industrial revolution of the 18th and 19th centuries went hand in hand with the agricultural revolution of those times. Growing factory towns absorbed the population displaced from the country by enclosure and agricultural improvement, but at the same time provided a market for the expanding productivity of farmland. In a sense, this enabled lowland Britain to solve its population problems, while avoiding mass starvation or emigration. Apart from the localised construction of factories, mines and associated housing on former farmland, the industrial revolution had little direct effect on the countryside, although many rivers were polluted and the 'smoke' from industrial towns affected the vegetation, especially in neighbouring upland areas.

RECESSION

From a peak of high farming in the 1870s, with large home markets in the ever-expanding industrial towns, the influx of cheap food from overseas caused a downturn in British agriculture, destined to last until the Second World War. Although the Corn Laws had been repealed in 1846, after which grain from overseas came in duty-free, it was not until the late 1870s that the trickle became a torrent, sweeping cheap food into the country in such quantities that it threatened to extinguish the increasingly uneconomic home production. Official figures show a steady drop in the arable acreage of all crops, a rise in the acreage of permanent grass, the abandonment of marginal lands and the consequent rise of rough grazing acreages, which persisted until 1939. These changes were much more marked in the arable districts of the southeast than in the north and west. Another change over the same period was the spread of potato and vegetable growing to replace fodder crops in rotations. Production of sugar beet in eastern Britain was encouraged by the government from 1926, as a way of preserving the arable sector there (Chapter 6). Nevertheless, overall tillage declined by nearly 40% between the 1870s and 1930s. In this same period, many upland farms made the transition from mixed sheep–cattle enterprises to sheep alone, with associated reductions in the numbers of farm workers. Under prevailing practices, grassland and stock required less labour than arable cropping, and shedding staff was an easy way for farmers to save on costs. Over this 60-year period, according to official figures, the agricultural workforce in England and Wales dropped by around 43%.

One positive change for agriculture in the late 19th century was the development of the liquid milk industry. This perishable home-produced commodity had no competitor from overseas. By 1870, a new countrywide rail network enabled milk to be transported fresh from country to city within a few hours, a change which led to a big increase in the numbers of dairy cattle. The development of motor vehicles after the First World War enabled transport from ever remoter regions, and by 1949 milk accounted for one-third of all farm income. Milk production still looms large in British farming, but from the end of the Second World War its production became increasingly concentrated westwards, as tillage crops returned to dominate the south and east.

In the early years of the First World War, up to 1916, two-thirds of all food consumed in Britain was imported. Industrial success enabled the country to afford cheap imported grain and to rely less on home produce. Then in 1917, the submarine menace raised the importance of home food production. However, the 'plough-up' campaign of 1918 (the last year of the war, when rationing of food products was introduced briefly for the first time) proved only a minor interruption in the general decline of home agriculture, and crop production in particular. Little investment was made in British farming until the start of the Second World War. My grandparents remembered the 'between-war years' as a depression period in farming, when arable cultivation declined, weeds flourished, drains and hedgerows were neglected, and some fields were allowed to 'scrub over'. This downturn enabled the spread onto former improved farmland of rushes and reeds, coarse grasses, heather, bracken and gorse, to create a variety of 'rough grazings', generally beneficial to birds. This period therefore had a big impact on the appearance of the countryside, and also on bird and other wildlife populations, with birds dependent on arable land declining, and waders of damp grassland increasing along with scrub-dwelling passerines. Nevertheless, agricultural mechanisation continued to develop, the internal combustion engine being first employed in North America, with early tractors, reaper–binders and eventually combine harvesters. Their use was soon to spread widely through British agriculture.

FIG 32. At times of recession in the past, some farmland was abandoned or grazed less heavily, enabling hedges to spread outwards and fields to 'scrub over'. Photos from Wigtownshire (Richard & Barbara Mearns) and Sussex (Ian Newton).

WARTIME AGRICULTURE

The agricultural recession, which had lasted more than 50 years, ended abruptly with the start of the Second World War in 1939. Destruction of shipping by German submarines again stimulated home production of food crops. Livestock numbers were reduced and much permanent pasture was brought back into cultivation. Tilled land is not only more productive than grassland, it is also more flexible, enabling a range of crops to be grown which could then be eaten either by people or by livestock. The government set a target for home food production which, with much reduced imports, was destined to feed the nation. Throughout the land, County War Agricultural Executive Committees decreed what each farmer must do. These Committees had the power of compulsion, even dispossession, of any recalcitrant farmers. To combat the shortage of male farm workers, some 80,000 town-girls were recruited to form the Women's Land Army, distributed on farms across the nation. So it came about that, in the first four years of war, from 1939 to 1943, despite a reduced male labour force and shortages of all sorts, Britain became the most highly mechanised farming country in the world. Total home production increased from about 20% to 55% of total consumption. Imports of animal feedstuffs dropped to about one-tenth of the pre-war level and, broadly, each farm became a self-contained unit, producing what it needed to support its own reduced livestock numbers, as well as food for people. Much unsuitable land was pressed into crop production. There was more emphasis on milk, with priority supplies for mothers and children. School milk deliveries were started, with each child receiving a free daily allocation of one-third of a pint per school-day. Beef cattle, sheep and pigs were all reduced in numbers, and severe rationing of meat, cheese and butter was instituted. Not before or since, we are told, has the nation's health been better. Moreover, 'much of the land in Britain emerged from the war in better heart than ever' (Stamp 1969).

DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS

This chapter gives a brief history of changes in the methods and extent of farming in Britain up to the Second World War, weighted towards those aspects most likely to have affected bird populations. Significant factors have included not only the total amount of land under agriculture (as compared to the amount under more natural vegetation), but also the relative proportions of tilled and grazing land, the types of crops and livestock that were produced at different times, and the intensity of production methods. For their effects on bird populations, the most important events in farming history were: (1) the original change from forest to open farmland, representing the single most profound anthropogenic change to Britain's landscape and wildlife habitats; (2) the change from the medieval open-field system to enclosed farms; (3) the destruction of the wastes of semi-natural vegetation and the drainage of marshland to produce more tillable land; and (4) in the last two centuries, a huge reduction in the number of people working the land, in response to greater mechanisation, especially the change from horse power to tractor power.

As land was increasingly converted from its natural or semi-natural state to farmland, birds associated with the natural habitats declined in distribution and numbers, while those able to exploit the new farmland expanded. The last major stages in this conversion process came in the 17th–19th centuries, first with the Enclosure Acts when most semi-natural open areas remaining in lowland Britain were enclosed and converted to farmland; and secondly with more sophisticated land drainage, when many remaining wetlands were dried and water tables were generally lowered (Chapter 15). Over time, then, almost all the familiar landscapes of modern Britain were created. They have been continually modified as human needs and desires have changed, and as new developments in technology emerged. Each major change in land-use practices brought changes in vegetation, and hence in the distributions and abundance levels of particular plant and animal species. Eventually, over the centuries Britain became 'clothed with trees and plants of human choice, and tenanted by animals which humanity has either tended or tolerated' (Stamp 1969). The bird communities of most of Britain can thus be considered as no less man-made than are the landscapes in which they live.

In recent centuries, most farms have been mixed, relying on a balance of arable crops and livestock. On well-drained soils of the south and east, the emphasis was on arable farming, especially cereals. Further west, the emphasis swung towards livestock, with hill farms relying almost entirely on sheep and cattle. But even in predominantly arable areas some livestock were kept. Horses were needed to work the land and for transport. Cows and sometimes sheep, pigs and chickens were kept at least for domestic use, and surpluses could be sold locally. Conversely, on predominantly pastoral farms, some cereals and roots were grown as animal feed, together with vegetables for the family. In every area, some substantial part of the farm was grassland used for pasture or hay production. Greater specialisation was found only in the production of horticultural crops, while general farmland retained its diversity until beyond the mid-20th century. This is still the case in some regions, including northern Scotland.

During the 19th to mid-20th centuries, farmland in Britain was probably in the best state it has ever been for supporting the range of bird species which we now call 'farmland birds'. The main features of this regime were the integration of arable and livestock production on the same farm, and a system of crop rotation which ensured that diverse habitats and food sources were available to birds in the same small area throughout the year. The persistence of cereal stubbles into winter and the periodic threshing of cereal stacks provided a continuance of foods for seed-eating birds into early spring. The addition of organic manures to soils fostered an abundance of invertebrates in the surface layers, available to birds year-round. Furthermore, ploughing in early spring ensured that supplies of buried seeds and invertebrates were continually turned to the surface, making them accessible to birds at a time of natural scarcity.

People, trade and farming

The 14th–17th centuries, when sheep reigned supreme, were probably the only times in our history when agriculture contributed greatly to national wealth, such was the value of wool across Europe. It made the sand and limestone regions of the south and east some of the wealthiest in Britain, as reflected today in the beauty of their churches, manor houses and small market towns. It also maintained extensive areas under grass, providing nesting habitat for a wide range of open land birds, from pipits and larks to partridges and bustards.

All past periods of agricultural change led to changes in the arable/pasture balance, both locally and regionally. This remained true into the 20th century, when economics and centralised policy became increasingly important in driving the direction of farming in Britain. From about 1875 the doctrine of free trade and the increasing flood of cheap North American wheat into British markets made possible by improvements in transport initiated a long decline in farming, culminating in the depressions of the 1920s and 1930s. In all these changes, the south and east were affected more than the north and west. At times of depression in local farming, nature reasserted itself, with impacts on bird populations. Under reduced grazing pressure, scrub spread out from hedgerows or sprang up on grassland, on sandy areas grassland returned to heath, and in low-lying areas water levels rose as drains disintegrated and clogged. Some of the hedges in these times became enormous, reaching up to 10 m wide, producing a band of scrub around each field. These changes would be expected to have raised overall bird populations, but this was long before systematic bird counts began. With all the developments mentioned above, farmland and wildlife cannot have remained constant for long, but could only have been in continual flux in response to the ever-changing patterns of human land management.

For most of the period covered in this chapter – perhaps 55 out of 65 centuries – the human population of Britain is judged to have numbered less than 1 million. It then rose with increasing rapidity from around 1.5 million in AD 1000, to more than 5 million in 1500, 10 million in 1800, 40 million in 1900, and around 60 million in 2010. For much of historical time, people in Britain depended largely on food produced within the country, and numbers grew as farming developed, despite the periodic reductions caused by epidemics or by starvation resulting from crop failures. Only in the 20th century did improved medicine contribute greatly to population growth, mainly through its effect on longevity. During the course of this one century, the mean longevity of people in Britain increased from around 50 to around 80 years, and starvation as a mortality factor was effectively banished. Since the 18th century, the numbers of people in Britain have outstripped home food production, a situation possible only because of massive food importation. By the end of the 20th century, with a human population approaching 60 million and an all-time high in agricultural production, 45% of food consumed was imported. No longer could Britain support its human population.

The next chapter is concerned with the changes in farming that have occurred since the end of the Second World War to the present. This period covered another agricultural revolution, exceeding all others in the scale of its environmental impacts, including its effects on birds and other indigenous life.

## CHAPTER 4

## Post-War Farming: the New Revolution

IN THE YEARS DURING AND AFTER the Second World War, the political and economic status of farming was transformed. This change came initially from the pressing need to increase home food production to offset wartime shortages. Imports were reduced because of the German U-boat assault on shipping. The same need continued for several years beyond the war when the nation was too impoverished to pay for much imported food. The public mind-set at the time was thus well disposed to the notion of raising home-based food production. Food had been short during the war, and food rationing was still in place, on some products up to 1954. Such deprivation should never occur again. Nor were people aware, any more than the farmers themselves, of the effects that this process would have on the natural world. It led to big changes in the appearance of the countryside, to loss of semi-natural habitats, to pollution of waterways, and to massive declines in wild plant and animal populations.

To begin with, agricultural production was encouraged by the provision for farmers of guaranteed markets and assured prices for crops and livestock, as embodied in the Agriculture Act of 1947, arguably the most significant piece of agricultural legislation of the century. Price levels for all farm products were set in an annual price review, which took account of changes in policy and perceived needs. The system encouraged home food production and ensured a more intensive use of farmed land, while reducing food prices in the shops. The same Act also set up a system of grant aid for many capital improvements on the farm, such as land drainage, ploughing old grassland, fencing, liming and erecting new buildings. All aspects of farming practice were intensified, and all were helped by huge technological advances. From this time on, political intervention in agriculture became the norm, and the momentum to increase food production grew unchecked.

Twenty-six years later, following Britain's accession to the European Common Market in 1973, the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) came into play, superseding previous measures. The CAP became the centrepiece of European unity, providing additional support for farmers and leading to further intensification of agricultural practice. Markets were guaranteed for all production (any surplus being put into storage and sold at a loss on world markets), subsidies were paid to producers and exporters, and tariffs were placed on imports. The aim was to maintain a threshold below which prices paid to farmers would not be allowed to fall, and particularly high subsidies were paid on cereal crops. Areas where farming was difficult received 'Less Favoured Area' status, involving substantial extra funds, paid largely as social subsidies. In the uplands, this led in time to large increases in the densities of sheep, with serious effects on soil erosion, vegetation and wildlife (Chapter 19).

State subsidies were not alone in causing a new agricultural revolution. They merely allowed it to proceed more rapidly than would otherwise have been possible. It was underpinned by technological developments in farm machinery and in manufactured fertilisers and pesticides. These twin developments – involving the mechanisation and 'chemicalisation' of farming – greatly increased the speed and efficiency of agricultural operations, as well as the general productivity of farmed land (Fig. 33). The use of agrochemicals enabled the same crop to be grown year after year on the same ground, making crop rotation less necessary. It encouraged specialisation at the level of the individual farm, and within a few decades had produced a greater concentration of arable farming in the south and east and of livestock farming in the north and west, as befitted the regional variation in climate and soils.

Large increases in annual crop and meat production accompanied these changes. Comparing British agriculture in 1936 and 1986, wheat output rose by more than 9-fold, barley by 13-fold, oats (in 1936 the most widely grown cereal) dropped to a quarter of its former level, but grain crops overall rose by about 6-fold. Potato production more than doubled. Among meat products, chicken production rose to eight times its 1936 level, lamb/mutton production doubled, pork production trebled, beef production rose by 60%, egg production by 90%, and milk production tripled (www.statistics.gov.uk). These increases occurred despite reduction in the area of land available for agriculture, as land was increasingly taken for other purposes, such as building and infrastructure development in the lowlands and forestry in the uplands. Since the Second World War, the arable area of Britain has decreased by some 300,000 ha, mainly owing to housing and allied development.
