But productivity in the remaining arable land has increased so much that total food production today is several times higher than it was in the late 1940s.

By 2012, UK agriculture was subsidised and grant-aided to the tune of £3.4 billion per year, and additional funding was available for farmers living in 'less favoured', 'environmentally sensitive' or other special areas. In the same year, another £450 million was spent in Britain on research and development for the food and farming industries. The average annual cost per household – in terms of taxes for agriculture – was calculated at £398. In the same year, British farmers were producing about 55% of home food consumption, but also exporting a range of products. In addition to the financial costs, the environmental costs were great, for the measures that delivered greater agricultural productivity had huge effects on landscapes and wildlife, and also brought increasing pollution of land, air and water, aspects discussed in detail later. The situation for agriculture in the UK as measured in 2015 in summarised in Box 2.

BOX 2. Summary statistics for agriculture in the United Kingdom during 2015

In 2015, the total agricultural land area of the UK was estimated at 17.1 million ha, forming around 70% of the total land surface; some 6.1 million ha (33%) was regarded as 'croppable', but only about 4.7 million ha grew arable or horticultural crops at the time. Cereals were grown on 3.1 million ha and oilseeds on 0.67 million ha, potatoes on 0.13 million ha, other crops on 0.61 million ha, and fruit and vegetables on 0.17 million ha. In addition, nearly 1.2 million ha of croppable land were covered with temporary (ley, < 5-year-old) grass and nearly 9.9 million ha of other land were classed as 'permanent' (> 5-year-old) grass, giving more than 11 million ha of potential grazing land. Some 214,000 ha were recorded as 'uncropped' arable land, including some voluntary set-aside, game crops and wild-bird seed crops.

For Britain alone (excluding Northern Ireland) the figures were: total agricultural land 16.1 million ha; total croppable land 5.9 million ha, with 4.6 million ha down to arable or horticultural crops; temporary (ley) grass more than 1.1 million ha and permanent grass 9.1 million ha, giving a total grazing area of around 10.2 million ha.

The June 2015 census also revealed an estimated overall UK population of nearly 10 million cattle, 33 million sheep, 4.7 million pigs, and 168 million poultry, but for various reasons livestock numbers fluctuated greatly during the year. The total milk production for the year was given as 15 billion litres, total table chicken production at around 975 million, and the total egg production for human consumption at more than 10 billion.

The gross 'added value' of UK agriculture in 2015 was estimated at £8.5 billion. Some 476,000 people (1.5% of the UK workforce, and less than 1% of the total population) worked in the industry, on a total of 214,500 holdings. The total annual payment to farmers in the form of grants and subsidies (less levies) was around £3.2 billion, plus another £25 million linked to production. This works out at an average of nearly £15,000 per holding, but in practice the funding was very unevenly distributed, favouring the largest and wealthiest land owners. The food produced was about 60% of the total consumed in Britain, but some additional food was exported. The value of exported food and drink was estimated at £18.0 billion, compared to imported food and drink at £38.5 billion, leaving a 'trade gap' of £20.5 billion.

(Defra 2016)

MECHANISATION

The levels of mechanisation achieved for British agriculture in the 18th and 19th centuries, as described in the previous chapter, were revolutionary, but small compared to what was to come in the 20th century. Nowhere was this process more evident than in the change from horse to tractor power. In 1936, there were around a million working horses on British farms; in 1946 there were 436,000, and by 1960 only 46,000. Thereafter, the numbers fell so rapidly that no further records at the national level were kept. Their decline had a marked effect on the countryside, because fields of oats and hay were no longer needed to feed them, and both crops were important as sources of wild bird food. Each working horse required one hectare of land to sustain it, so the loss of a million horses in little over 25 years would have released a million hectares for other livestock and crop production.

Tractors became available from the 1920s, but they caught on slowly, and fewer than 50,000 were in use by 1936. Their numbers then increased rapidly to more than 400,000 by the mid-1950s, after which their numbers remained relatively stable. A major advance in tractor design came in 1946, with the development of the three-point linkage and hydraulic lift on Ferguson tractors, which made it possible to hang a range of implements on the back of the tractor, making almost every operation easier and safer (Fraser 1972). This innovation was quickly taken up by other tractor manufacturers. The ensuing greater size and power of tractors enabled all cultivation and harvesting work to be accomplished much more quickly than before, thereby enabling each farm worker to tend a greater acreage. Some tractors now working British farmland weigh more than 20 tonnes, and are powered by engines of more than 500 horsepower. In association with these changes, the farm labour force fell by two-thirds over the same 50-year period, a trend which has continued to the present.

Parallel increases occurred in other farm machinery. There were only 50 combine harvesters in Britain in 1938, but by 1970 this number had increased to 56,670, used on almost every mainland farm (Fig. 33). The mechanisation of potato and other root-crop harvesting also progressed apace; in 1946, there were 183 complete root harvesters, and by 1970 some 14,920. Numbers of milking machines also rose rapidly, appearing on almost every dairy farm by 1970, while there were 1,002 grain driers in England and Wales in 1946, rising to 29,370 in 1970. By this time, saturation point had been reached in most kinds of farm machinery and the majority of purchases became replacements rather than novelties. Nevertheless, the size and power of tractors and other machines continued to rise, increasing the width of ground that could be processed at each pass, and hence the speed with which all cultivation and harvesting procedures could be accomplished.

Ploughing, seed-bed preparation and harvesting came to take a fraction of the time they had taken with horses. For example, one man with a pair of horses could plough an acre in an eight-hour day, but nowadays one man with a large tractor and a five-furrow reversible plough can turn over to greater depth 40 acres (16 ha) in an eight-hour day, a rate 40 times higher (Fig. 34). Men and horses get tired, but tractors can work non-stop day and night, so the whole process of cultivation and sowing on an entire farm or landscape can be accomplished in a much shorter time. This change was important to farmland birds because it reduced the period over which freshly turned-up seeds and invertebrates were available to them. Outside my window now, I can see a tractor working in the neighbouring field. It has one piece of equipment (a fertiliser spreader) hung on the front, and three other pieces on the back, designed respectively to break up the soil, create a tilth and sow the seeds (Fig. 35). Operations that would once have required four passes over a field are now accomplished in one, in less than one-fourth of the time.

Consider also how mechanisation affected the cereal harvest, and the consequences for grain-eating birds. For centuries, the harvesting of cereals was a slow process, heavily dependent on weather. It involved several steps: first the hand-cutting and binding of the stems to form sheaves, then the arranging of these sheaves into stooks, each consisting of eight standing sheaves, then the loading and carting of the dried sheaves into the stack-yard, and their unloading to form stacks, and then later in the winter the dismantling of the stacks and threshing of the sheaves to separate grain from straw, and then baling and stacking the straw. At each of these time-consuming, labour-intensive operations grain was spilled, and the continual wastage provided a rich food source for opportunist birds and mammals from late summer to the following spring.

FIG 34. The mechanisation of ploughing: one man working with two horses and a single-furrow plough could turn over about an acre (0.4 ha) per day (left, Chris Knights); whereas one man with a tractor and a five-furrow plough can turn over 40 times this area in the same time (right, Ian Newton).

FIG 35. Modern tractors can carry several implements at once, designed to break up the soil, prepare a seed-bed, and sow treated seed and fertiliser in a single pass, rather than the 3–4 separate operations needed previously (Ian Newton).

Following various prototypes, effective binder–reaper machines came in rapidly after the mid-19th century, mechanising the first two operations of cutting and sheaving. Today, the whole process from cutting to threshing is accomplished quickly in one operation by combine harvesters, greatly reducing the amount of grain that is spilled and the period over which it is available to wildlife. The self-propelled combine harvester copes with most seed crops at speed, a single machine processing more than 20 ha per day. The plants are cut and threshed, the grain is separated, and the straw is excluded and the chaff blown across the field; moreover, the grain is usually downloaded to a trailer driven alongside the combine without interrupting the harvesting process. Combine harvesters were imported into Britain from North America in the 1930s, and by the mid-1960s they were used on almost every mainland farm. The earliest models were towed by tractors, but they soon became self-powered and larger, with cutter bars extending from 2 m on the early models up to 12 m or more on some modern ones (Fig. 36). As these machines increased in numbers and size, the grain harvest was accomplished ever more rapidly and efficiently, harvest waste declined, and the grain could be sold immediately or stored in rodent-proof silos for later sale. Rick-yards and winter threshing thereby disappeared, taking with them a major winter food source for seed-eating birds. In addition, over much of Britain cultivation became concentrated into the autumn, so that any grain and weed seeds on the surface of stubble fields were ploughed under, becoming unavailable to birds. An estimated two-thirds of all arable land in Britain is now ploughed and sown in autumn, and only one-third in spring as in the past.

The mechanisation of other operations also affected birds badly. In the past, 'hedging and ditching' were the usual winter jobs for farm labourers, when nothing else could be done on the land. Both processes are essential to maintain the functions of hedges and ditches, but both can now be accomplished mechanically within days, and if they are inappropriately timed they can destroy bird nests, nesting cover and food supplies. The ease of modern hedge trimming has increased its frequency, resulting in a general lowering and narrowing of hedges (Fig. 37). This reduces the range of bird species which nest in many hedges, and the amount of fruit and insects that hedges produce (Chapter 18). The flailing of ditch sides can similarly remove bird nesting cover and food supplies, and is also done more often than in the past, and not necessarily in winter. Other equipment used in fields destroys the nests of many ground-nesting birds. This was always the case, but nowadays more operations take place within bird breeding seasons. In consequence, most ground nests of birds on cropland are destroyed before they can produce young (Chapters 10, ).

FIG 36. The increasing mechanisation of the cereal harvest as reflected in (top) an old binder–reaper machine pulled by two or three horses which would cut the cereals and bind the stems into sheaves for later collection (David Mason); lower left, an early self-propelled combine harvester with a 2 m cutter bar, which in one operation could cut and thresh the stems to extract the grain, but with substantial spillage (Bobby Smith); lower right, a modern large combine harvester with an 8 m cutter bar, with little spillage (Ian Newton).

FIG 37. Left, modern hedge trimming; right, after trimming, shorter, narrower and less good for birds (Ian Newton).

One of the latest technological developments is 'precision farming', giving more highly targeted placement of seeds, fertiliser and pesticide. Through the use of GPS, the application rates of seeds or chemicals can be varied across a field according to need, as assessed from previous measures of crop yield across the same field, from analyses of soil nutrients or from camera measures of the 'greenness' of growing vegetation as the tractor passes over. The resulting information is stored in an on-board computer, and is used to adjust treatments. The method also prevents the accidental double spraying of the same ground, as spray bands overlap. The advantage is that no more chemicals are applied to farmland than are judged necessary to achieve the desired crop yield, with minimum drift, spillage and wastage. For these reasons, precision farming can be considered as environmentally beneficial. However, similar technology is currently being developed for selective weed control by laser or mechanical means, which will further reduce the need for pesticides but also the food supplies for birds.

CHEMICALISATION

No change was more significant, though, than the almost complete chemicalisation of both soil nutrient inputs and pest and weed control. All the new wonder compounds could be bought in bags and bottles from the specialist giants of agrochemicals, such as Fisons, ICI and later Monsanto, and their various subsidiaries. Some artificial fertilisers and pesticides were in small-scale use before the Second World War, but afterwards their use mushroomed, following massive growth in the petrochemical industry that marked the start of the modern 'Oil Age'. For centuries, plant nutrients had been replenished mainly by use of manure, but the new synthetic fertilisers were able to supply all important plant nutrients with much less effort. In the half-century to 1980, there was a 20-fold increase in inorganic nitrogen use on British farms, a 2.5-fold increase in phosphorus and a 6-fold increase in potassium (until 1974 both nitrogen and phosphorus fertilisers were subsidised). In the mid-1980s, the average nitrogen input to tilled land stood at around 160 kg/ha per year, and to intensive grassland about 150 kg/ha per year, figures which then stabilised until declining subsequently. Over the same period, scientific plant breeding produced new crop varieties able to respond to increased fertiliser input and give higher yields, while animal breeding produced higher-performing livestock better able to process the richer food provided (Chapter 6).

Factory fertilisers can be added annually to the whole farm, with much less time and effort than manure. But one consequence is that relatively little humus is now added to arable soil over much of Britain, changing its structure and making it more prone to erosion and compaction than in the past. Erosion results in the loss of productive topsoil and the silting of rivers and reservoirs, creating problems for many people at times of flood (Chapter 15). The loss of soil organic matter has reduced the capacity of the soil to store water (at times reducing plant growth) and carbon (increasing carbon dioxide input to the atmosphere). At the same time, loss of organic matter reduces the invertebrate content of soil, thereby reducing the food supply of some soil-probing birds (Chapter 5). Another consequence of inorganic fertiliser is that, if not quickly absorbed by plants, it can be washed from soils by rain. This leads to the pollution of ground water, and in turn to the eutrophication of streams and rivers, ponds, lakes and ultimately coastal sea water (Fig. 38). These wider pollution problems affect plants and animals and sometimes (via drinking water) human health. They can be reduced to some extent by leaving a strip of uncultivated land between the crop and a waterway, and by applying the fertiliser in spring, rather than in autumn, in order to maximise its uptake by growing plants. In addition, high nitrogen applications give rise to dense, fast-growing crops of grass and cereals that are good for the farmer, but no longer offer suitable nesting habitat for ground-nesting birds such as Lapwing and Skylark, thereby rendering large areas of former habitat unusable by these birds (Chapters 10, ). Moreover, although crop plants benefit from nitrogen application, some 60–70% of wild plants in Britain decline in the presence of excess nitrogen, partly because they can then be out-competed by grass (Smith 1987, Stevens et al. 2006, Carey et al. 2008, Defra 2012).

FIG 38. Eutrophication of drainage ditch, caused by fertiliser use and marked by algal growth on the water surface, Lincolnshire (Ian Newton).

FIG 39. Pesticide spraying (Ian Newton).

The development of pesticides enabled weeds, insect pests and fungal pathogens to be swiftly eliminated by a spray (Fig. 39). Previously, they would have been ignored or controlled by hand. In 1940, there were 1,100 tractor-mounted sprayers in England and Wales, but by 1981 there were over 74,000 (O'Connor & Shrubb 1986). This was a time of growth for machine makers, as well as for agrochemical makers. In 1944, only 63 products were approved for use by farmers as pesticides; in 1997 there were 344. The tonnage of active ingredients in insecticides used on farms in England and Wales more than doubled during the 1970s alone, and had increased ninefold by the end of the century (Fig. 33). For 30 years, most farmers operated on the 'drench-and-be-sure' principle, but with renewed recession from the late 1980s, the terms 'targeted inputs' and 'precision spraying' came into vogue, followed by 'as much as necessary, as little as possible', an aspiration largely met by use of GPS in precision spraying.

Although some pesticides kill birds directly or reduce their reproductive rates, most affect birds indirectly by reducing their food supplies (Chapter 8). Insecticides diminish the numbers of invertebrates available to birds on farmland, while herbicides reduce the numbers of weeds (and hence the insects that feed on them). By killing the plants during their growth, herbicides also reduce the quantities of seeds available for seed-eating birds, and over long periods of years progressively deplete the seed-bank in the soil.

Another major impact of agrochemicals, however, was that they spelt the end of the kind of farming which for more than a century had supported huge bird populations in Britain. By removing the need for mixed farming, with stock and arable rotations, agrochemicals altered farmland habitats fundamentally. With the advent of inorganic fertilisers, livestock were no longer needed as a source of manure, enabling farmers on good ground to specialise in arable crops. In traditional farming, one main purpose of crop rotation was to prevent the weeds, pests and diseases associated with particular crops from getting out of hand. But with the advent of pesticides, weed and pest control became easier, and crop rotation less necessary. Fodder root crops had always been the cleaning crop in arable rotations, but the development of herbicides rendered them increasingly unnecessary for this purpose and, where no longer required as stock feed, they steadily declined.

Measured by the use of inorganic fertilisers and pesticides, the period 1970–88 saw the biggest degree of intensification in British farming. At the same time, land was being drained more actively than before, and the area under autumn-sown cereals and rape was rapidly increasing, while the area under spring-sown cereals, winter stubbles, bare fallow and root fodder crops declined. Not surprisingly, this was also the major period of farmland bird declines, as discussed in later chapters.

Together with orchards, market gardening and commercial flower production, arable land now covers about 6.1 million hectares in the UK, and almost all of it can be considered subject to regular fertiliser and pesticide use. Most of the grassland on low ground is now dominated by fast-growing species such as rye grass, and usually also receives heavy fertiliser applications. Such grassland covers 1.2 million hectares in the UK, so that more than two-fifths of the UK's 17.1 million hectares of crop and livestock land can be regarded as under intensive year-on-year chemical-based husbandry. Pesticides and fertilisers are used more sparingly or not at all on the remaining three-fifths, consisting largely of upland grazing land.

SPECIALISATION

Given the developments described above, economies of scale meant that it was more efficient for individual farmers to concentrate on either arable or livestock farming. Farming therefore became specialised, not just at the level of the individual holding but also at the landscape scale. As a result of variation in soil type, topography and climate, arable farming came even more to dominate in the east of Britain and grassland and livestock in the west. Landscapes became less diverse, as most farms came to consist of almost entirely arable or almost entirely grass. The main ecological impact of this change was a reduction in the diversity of habitats available to birds in any one locality, causing declines in many species. For example, small seed-eating birds declined markedly in pastoral landscapes from a lack of winter food, previously provided largely by arable land; and in more recent years the addition of even a small acreage of arable land was found to raise their numbers (Robinson et al. 2001).

In pastoral regions, the same process of specialisation occurred, as in much of Wales, northwestern England and Scotland, where fodder crops for cattle were replaced by grass silage. Over much of Britain, field sizes increased, further reducing the patchwork effect as crops came to be grown in bigger blocks. The consequent loss of hedges and other field boundaries reduced the remaining semi-natural habitats on farmland. With increasing farm size, larger areas have become devoted to a particular form of management.

Advances in crop husbandry and pest control sustained the swing away from mixed farming to specialisation, which became the most profitable way forward. The high cost of large, complex equipment such as combine harvesters further encouraged specialisation, because these costs were worthwhile only for farmers with a substantial acreage under cereals. Part of the specialisation process is that many farmers contract out certain types of cultivation and harvesting work to specialist companies who invest in the expensive equipment required, using it on demand on a range of farms through the season. At the same time, guaranteed prices removed any advantage of diversification: farmers could specialise without risk, selling everything they produced. Over much of Britain, therefore, the mixed farm, combining crop and livestock production, declined from usual to rare within the space of three decades.

Old-style rotations, involving livestock, virtually disappeared from most arable areas. Wheat, barley and oilseed rape came to occupy 75% of all tillage, and arable fodder crops less than 4%. Furthermore, more than 67% of all tillage crops in Britain came to be sown in autumn. The number of holdings with cattle declined from 76% in 1958 to 50% in 1997, but to only 29% in the arable regions of the east and southeast. Sheep became increasingly concentrated in the uplands, and no longer figured in the crop rotations of lower ground. These changes were less marked in Scotland, where mixed farms (predominantly producing meat) are still the rule on low ground in the north.

The agricultural support system also favours the amalgamation of smaller holdings by its support for ever-increasing production: larger farms make better use of larger machinery and in turn generate greater profits from fixed overheads. The Second World War saw the development of a National Agriculture Advisory Service (NAAS) and its successor body, the Agricultural Development and Advisory Service (ADAS). Through these organisations, all farmers had access to advice on how best to manage their land to raise its productivity, and on the grants available to help them achieve the necessary changes. The effect of this advice and financial encouragement was not only to raise the general efficiency of farming in Britain, but also to make it regionally more uniform. This all resulted in a less varied countryside, and produced further declines in biodiversity.

These changes occurred over a few decades to the present, in a process of steadily encroaching uniformity. It took less than 20 years for the recent agricultural revolution to spread right through farming in Britain, much quicker than any other major change in the past.

Specialisation, coupled with intensification, had another effect on rural diversity. It led to the replacement of a great variety of breeds of domestic livestock by a narrower range of highly productive ones. Regional cattle breeds have declined so much since the 1940s that more than 95% of all dairy cows now belong to a single breed, the familiar black-and-white Holstein. No fewer than 26 breeds of livestock became extinct in Britain in the years 1970–73, but since the formation of the Rare Breeds Survival Trust in 1973 no other breeds have disappeared, because rarities are maintained by enthusiasts. Their preservation ensures the survival of a wide gene-pool for possible use in future breeding programmes, and also enables some of the old breeds to stage a comeback when conditions permit. For example, English Longhorn cattle were almost extinct in 1970, but by 2014 the numbers stood at more than 7,000 individuals, scattered in herds around the country (Fig. 40). But the general process of concentration on a few highly productive breeds requires the growth of productive vegetation to feed them, a further factor leading to greater fertiliser use and reduced landscape diversity, with repercussions on wildlife populations.

FIG 40. Longhorn cattle, an old breed which was almost extinct in 1970, but now numbers more than 7,000 animals, scattered on farms across Britain (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

SURPLUS PRODUCTION

So effective was this whole agricultural support system that it soon led to huge food surpluses, in the form of 'milk lakes', 'wine lakes', 'butter mountains', 'grain mountains' and 'sugar mountains'. The production and storage costs of these surpluses – which for some commodities in the 1980s reached 20–30% of total production – became so great that eventually measures were needed to curtail production. With some products, such as milk, quotas operating at the level of the individual farm were introduced from 1984. Later, more widespread schemes such as 'set-aside' came in, optionally from 1988 and compulsorily from 1992 to 2007 (see Chapter 9). This was a scheme by which farmers were paid not to crop a proportion of their land. The aim was to reduce overall production, but the general public were unsympathetic, seeing farmers as being 'paid for doing nothing'. From the 1980s, as the CAP came to absorb more than 70% of the entire EU budget, the system was revised somewhat, and farm support throughout Europe moved to a system closer to that set up in Britain under the 1947 Act. Total expenditure was reduced from its peak of more than 70% of the total EU budget in the 1980s to around 40% in more recent years (2008–14), with more emphasis placed on pollution control, soil conservation, biodiversity and landscape values. Nevertheless, the basic principle that farming should be subsidised by the state has not altered, and policies aimed at reducing production (as well as those aimed at increasing production) remain subsidised. However, in the 1990s, tariffs on imported foodstuffs were relaxed, giving more competition to home producers.

INDOOR FARMING

The way in which farm animals are kept on British farms has also changed greatly over the past 60 years. Not only are such animals kept in greater numbers and less variety than in the 1950s, but far greater proportions are kept indoors. This is especially true for pigs and poultry, which are now housed in large specialised units – 'factory farms' – and fed chiefly on processed food produced on other farms, and even in other parts of the world. The largest intensive pig units now house more than 1,000 animals, and the largest poultry units more than 100,000 birds. Similar systems are increasingly being used for dairy cattle, and the biggest automated milk-producing units now house more than 1,000 milking cows. Meanwhile, the number of traditional milk-producing farms fell by more than 90% between 1950 and 2015, from 196,000 to fewer than 14,000. At the same time, increasing numbers of beef cattle have been housed in sheds or yards overwinter, and the same is true for some hill sheep, especially in northern Scotland.

FIG 41. Modern cattle yard, in which beef cattle are fattened for slaughter (Ian Newton).

Large-scale indoor farming systems have always been controversial because of animal welfare concerns, and because of the huge amounts of waste they typically produce. While farmyard manure has traditionally been a major means of maintaining farm fertility, slurry from animals in intensive farms has often proved difficult to dispose of, forming a serious pollutant of air and water. Its total has been estimated at around 170 million tonnes per year. Ammonia released from intensive pig, dairy and poultry units is said to account for nearly half of all nitrogenous pollutants added to the atmosphere, affecting vegetation when it is washed to earth. Pig and poultry farms, feeding their animals on bought-in food, often have no land on which to spread their manure. Smells from such units are also a source of public complaint, but all these problems are less severe than they were a few decades ago. However, a continuing problem of intensive livestock production is the routine use of antibiotics and other drugs. Some 40% of all antibiotics in Britain are used on farm animals, and 85% of this usage is for preventative reasons. This can only promote the development of resistance by infective agents, and in recent years dangerous strains of Listeria, Salmonella and other pathogens have been associated with intensive meat, milk and egg production. Not surprisingly, antibiotic resistance has become a major problem in human health worldwide.

The keeping of animals indoors is of no benefit to wildlife, because it goes along with the more intensive use of feed-producing land. Unlike old traditional buildings, modern ones also offer no access to wild birds such as House Sparrows and Starlings, which formerly thrived on animal feed. Moreover, with the moving of livestock indoors, fewer feeding sites are maintained out in the fields, where some of the foods provided are available to birds.

Despite the advances in the methods of crop production described above, the most technically advanced growing techniques now concern plants traditionally grown in market gardens, but which are now produced mainly in polythene tunnels or glasshouses. Growers can thereby provide perfect nutrition, geared to particular crop types, and almost perfect pest and disease control. But more importantly, such methods enable growers to control the greatest uncertainty of all – the weather – by providing ideal conditions of light, temperature and humidity throughout the life of a crop. These are the controlled conditions in which most of our tomatoes are now grown, together with a large proportion of strawberries and salad crops. Birds are normally excluded from glasshouses and poly-tunnels, so their construction effectively removes habitat for all species, as with other modern buildings. However, when not in use they are sometimes used by roosting birds, such as Pied Wagtails, attracted by warmth and shelter. In the years ahead, this form of production is likely to extend to an ever-widening range of human food crops.

TRANSPORT AND MARKETING OF PRODUCE

The mechanisation of transport profoundly affected farming markets, as it became possible to move perishable products quickly over long distances. This process began with the establishment of a rail network from the mid-19th century, but more locally almost all road transport was still horse-drawn at the start of the 20th century, declining to about 5% in the early 1930s. Improved transport, first by rail and then by road, greatly assisted the trend to specialisation on farms, because bulk production needs rapid bulk-transport to distribute perishables, whether milk, vegetables or meat. The subsequent development of refrigerated transport further helped this process, as it further lengthened the journeys possible.

Associated changes also occurred in the marketing of produce, most of which came to be distributed, not through local merchants, but through large regional centres, initially subsidised by government: for example, the Egg Marketing Board (1956–71, with its 'Packing Stations') and the Milk Marketing Board (1933–94, with its 'Dairies'). Milk became pasteurised by law, with a proportion turned into butter, cream, cheese, yoghurt, ice cream and condensed milk. Such marketing boards did much to control prices for farmers and promote their products, becoming known to the general public from their advertising slogans, such as 'go to work on an egg', or 'drinka pinta milka day'. Their roles were later taken over by non-governmental marketing bodies without price controls.

Horticultural crops were also increasingly sold directly to packing stations and markets, or canned or frozen, depending on the crop. Many of these products now pass through huge supermarket distribution centres, so that it has become possible for people dwelling almost anywhere in Britain to live entirely on foods produced away from their home regions. The supermarkets now dominate the acquisition, distribution and sales of all major foodstuffs in Britain, as they provide more than 90% of all we eat. An efficient transport system enables fresh produce to travel from farm to supermarket to table within a few days. The ability to import fresh produce by air or refrigerated sea freight greatly increased the range of fresh foods available, practically eliminating the traditional seasonality in particular products when they were entirely home-produced. In the countryside, these parallel developments in transport and marketing both favoured specialisation, and acted to reduce local landscape diversity, for no longer did all the staple foods of a community, not even the fresh perishables, need to be produced locally. Food waste and 'food-miles' have become legitimate targets of concern.

Changes also occurred in the marketing of raw products for processing, such as grain, which are not normally handled directly by consumers. Into the 1970s, almost every town had its Corn Exchange where cereals were sold in man-to-man deals at prevailing prices. Now most grain goes to big milling companies, who produce the flour or animal feed, depending on the quality of the grain. As in other foods, health and hygiene became paramount. Consignments of grain contaminated in some way, for example by bird or mammal droppings, are now generally rejected, at least for human consumption, a practice which gives farmers further incentive to exclude rodents and birds from storage facilities.

So into the 1950s, people in Britain mostly ate seasonally available foods produced locally. For the most part the money they spent stayed within the local community. But within three decades people could eat a much wider range of foods from around the world, with almost all items available year-round, but the money they spent was distributed worldwide. In 2015, the British public spent an estimated £100 billion on food, mostly in supermarkets. Through these changes, and increasing urbanisation, people became gradually more separated from the land that produced their food, and increasingly oblivious of the environmental consequences of the changed methods used in its production and distribution. More than 80% of the people in Britain now live in towns and cities, which means that more than 80% of children are now raised with little or no contact with the natural world or with the farming on which their existence largely depends.

HOLDINGS, JOBS AND WAGES

Owing largely to mechanisation, agriculture is no longer a significant contributor to rural jobs and livelihoods. In recent decades, the overall number of holdings has declined as their average size has increased. Between 1945 and 1997, according to official figures, the numbers of farm holdings fell by 35%, the numbers of individual farmers by 55%, and the number of labourers by 77%. The trend towards fewer but larger farms has continued to the present day. In 2015, there were an estimated 214,000 farm holdings in the UK, ranging in size from under 20 to several thousand hectares, although most large estates remained as several separate holdings. Some 70% of farms were owner-occupied, and the remainder tenanted. In total, agriculture employed around 476,000 people, about 1.5% of the nation's workforce.

In general, though, farm size is still related to the kind of enterprise: extensive operations, such as upland livestock rearing, need large acreages to provide an adequate income; highly mechanised cereal farms tend to be large because of economies of scale; intensive pig and poultry units can be housed within one or two hectares, with all the foods bought in. But within all these different categories of holdings, mean sizes have risen over the years, largely because the minimum size for a viable business has itself increased. The associated reduction in farm holdings, and the conversion or demolition of associated buildings, has also affected some birds, such as Barn Swallow and Barn Owl, by reducing the numbers of dispersed nesting places available to them (Chapter 17).

Another major change has concerned the nature of farm work. On the mixed farms of the past, farm labourers were expected to undertake all the jobs of the farm, from cultivation and harvesting to animal husbandry, together with maintenance of hedges and ditches. Most of the work was outside year-round. Nowadays, most jobs are more specialised, and largely or entirely inside. An individual worker might spend most of his career in an air-conditioned tractor cab, a milking parlour or an indoor pig unit. In theory, fewer people actually on the land implies less disturbance to wildlife, but most of the land now holds much less wildlife to disturb.

The income of farmers in real terms doubled between 1936 and 1976, but was dropping back by 1986 and has since fallen lower. However, these national averages conceal big regional variations, with the cereal farmers of some eastern districts earning much more than the hill farmers of the north and west. Into the 1950s, at least half the money spent on food found its way back to the farmer and his rural community. The rest was spread among suppliers of various inputs (feeds, pesticides, fertilisers, seeds, machinery, labour and so on) and manufacturers, processors and retailers. Since then, the balance has shifted increasingly away from farmers, with money concentrated on the input side in the agrochemical, seed and feed companies, and on the output side in those who move, process and sell the food. For the average family, the amount spent on food declined from more than 40% of the annual income at the start of the 20th century to less than 10% by the end.

FIG 42. Typical nesting birds of traditional farm buildings. Upper left, Swallow Hirundo rustica (Chris Knights), upper right, House Martin Delichon urbicum (Bobby Smith); lower left, House Sparrow Passer domesticus (Stan Wilson); lower right, Barn Owl Tyto alba (Andrew Everitt).

SOME RETHINKING AND CHANGE

From the late 1980s, a recession in farming again emerged, with a fall in cereal prices, and later in milk prices. Farmers were no longer 'feeding the nation', but operating in a global market and, no longer protected by the state, their earnings from crop and livestock sales became vulnerable to world prices, especially of wheat, declining in years of global surpluses. In the ensuing years, the British meat industry fell into disarray, as a result of two major animal epidemics, bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) and foot-and-mouth disease (FMD). Both resulted at least partly from husbandry practices in vogue at the time, and proved extremely costly. The then Prime Minister, Tony Blair, remarked that the foot-and-mouth outbreak of 2001 and its ramifications cost the British taxpayer more than the Gulf War. Together these disease outbreaks provided the impetus and opportunity for government to restructure the industry, but still within the constraints of the CAP.

In a report published in 2002, the UK government's Policy Commission on the Future of Farming and Food considered that the agricultural industry had become dysfunctional – unsustainable in every sense, detached from the rest of the economy, and also from the environment, which it continued to degrade. The report laid much of the blame at the door of the CAP and its subsidies, and recommended that direct subsidy payments should be decoupled from production and ultimately be phased out, with subsidies paid only under the principle of 'public money for public goods'.

A step-change in thinking emerged at government level. In the wake of the foot-and-mouth outbreak, the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food (MAFF) was abolished in 2001 and incorporated into a new Ministry called the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra). This new department was to be concerned not only with food production but with its environmental consequences and the rural economy more generally. At present, the farming industry still contributes less than 1% of GDP, and receives at least one-third of its income from explicit subsidies and other payments (Helm 2015). The total annual CAP budget for Britain in 2015 stood at £3.2 billion, but to this sum must be added the external costs of agriculture, such as those consequent on water pollution, greenhouse gas emissions, effects of soil erosion and flooding, and public health issues resulting from agrochemical use. These extra costs were earlier estimated at more than £2.3 billion per year, and were again met by society at large, through taxes and other expenses (Pretty et al. 2000). In other words, it was costing two-thirds as much to deal with the environmental consequences of modern agriculture as to support it, and some of the environmental damage looked 'permanent' or at least not reparable on normal time scales. Moreover, for much of the CAP period, farmers received much more than the world market price for cereals and milk, which in turn led to inflated land prices. This system did nothing to encourage farmers to adopt less intensive practices, and became a barrier to change.

Attempts to lessen the damage

As early as 1988 the European Commission openly acknowledged that its agricultural policies were causing serious environmental damage. It started on the long road to reform, with changes soon felt in Britain. Because of the various pollution problems arising from inorganic nitrogen, from the 1990s steps were taken to reduce its use (Defra 2012). As a result, the quantity of nitrogen fertiliser used on British farmland decreased by 37% between 1990 and 2012, mainly due to a reduction of application rates on grassland. Over the same period, the use of phosphate fertiliser declined by 55%, due to reductions in application rates on both grass and tillage crops. These were desirable trends, but more fertiliser was still being applied than was necessary for efficient crop production, as revealed by soil analyses.

Together with other changes, reductions in fertiliser use led to substantial decline in the output of various pollutants. Among greenhouse gas emissions from agriculture, nitrous oxide (derived mainly from chemical fertilisers) was reduced by 19% between 1990 and 2011, and methane (derived largely from livestock and slurry/manure) by 20%. In addition, ammonia emissions (mainly from 'factory farms') fell by 24% over the same period. Despite these welcome reductions, in 2012 fertilisers were estimated still to contribute 61% of the nitrogen and 28% of the phosphorus in river water (although the latter figure may have also included phosphorus from septic tanks). Agriculture also accounted for 86% of all ammonia emissions to the atmosphere, 84% of nitrous oxide and 43% of all methane (Defra 2012). Half of all the nitrogenous compounds emitted in Britain came from intensive pig and poultry units, and most of the rest from fertilisers, industrial sources, and vehicular emissions. Overall, this still left agriculture as a major source of aquatic and atmospheric pollutants in Britain.

For all their problems, pesticides are often the most convenient and efficient method of pest suppression, and for these reasons they are likely to remain central to human food production. On a world scale, however, it has been estimated that losses of crops to pests would increase by an average of only 10% if all pesticide use was stopped – although in particular fields, crop losses could range from zero to total (Pimentel et al. 1992). Despite a tenfold increase in insecticide use in the United States between 1945 and 1989, total crop losses from insect damage nearly doubled in this time, from an estimated 7% to 13%. This rise in damage was attributed partly to a reduction in crop rotation, and partly to the killing by pesticides of the predators of crop pests. Most assessments of the effects of pesticide use are based only on crop yields, and exclude the associated environmental and economic costs (Pimentel et al. 1992, Pretty 1998, Pretty et al. 2000). These extra costs include: (1) health problems and poisonings of people and domestic animals; (2) increasing pest control costs resulting from the destruction of natural predators of crop pests and the development of resistance in pest species; (3) pollination deficiencies resulting from poisonings of pollinating insects; (4) crop losses through accidental destruction or contamination of the crop; (5) contamination of water, fish and wildlife; and (6) governmental expenditure on regulations and other measures to reduce these social and environmental problems. Taking all these factors into account, pesticide use emerges as profitable for farmers and agrochemical manufacturers, but as a financial drain on society at large (Pretty 1998, Pretty et al. 2000). It does, however, give nice-looking food on supermarket shelves. Increasing recognition of these societal costs of pesticide use have led to measures to reduce the quantities used, notably the development of more targeted and less wasteful methods of application.

Pollution of drinking water with agrochemicals had come to represent a major cost to water companies, and ultimately to the general public. Some of the contaminants involved, such as nitrates and some pesticides, were known to harm human health. By the end of the 20th century, water companies in Britain were spending about £168–250 million per year to reduce these compounds in drinking water to acceptable levels, a cost reflected in our water bills (Environment Agency 2002, Boardman 2013). Conscious of these costs, some water companies bought up land in reservoir catchments, so they could reduce or eliminate the use of agrochemicals. This was cheaper than treating the water once it had been contaminated.

Ecosystem services

Through the changes of recent decades, it has been increasingly recognised that the countryside provides much more than food, and that it was largely these other aspects that were being destroyed or degraded by agricultural practices. We can split these 'ecological services' into three categories: (1) essentials directly produced by the environment, such as fresh clean water, fresh clean air, fuel wood, foods from wild plants and animals, pollination, and biodiversity in all its forms; (2) essentials resulting from natural environmental processes, such as climate regulation, carbon storage, watershed protection, flood alleviation, nitrogen fixation, nutrient cycling, soil formation and protection; and (3) social and cultural aspects, such as recreational, aesthetic, educational and spiritual benefits, all adding to human wellbeing. While they are considered essential to humanity, these latter benefits cannot be valued in monetary terms, so they tend to get ignored or undervalued in a cash-driven economy. Farmland offers many of these services (or could do), and can itself only function effectively because of some of them, such as nutrient cycling and crop pollination. Decisions on the management of the countryside are made all the more difficult because different people put different values on these products. Individual farmers generally prioritise the commodities on which their wealth depends, whereas they and the rest of society also benefit from other ecosystem services.

One major form of damage limitation came from the 1990s with the development of 'agri-environment schemes' through which farmers were paid to farm in a less damaging way, and were compensated for any loss in crop production or extra work incurred. Limited funds were made available for farmers to restore or create habitats and food supplies for birds and other wildlife, and to protect cherished landscapes and heritage features for the benefit of future generations. In later years, funds also became available to reduce pollution and soil erosion. These various agri-environment measures, and their effects on birds, are discussed in Chapters 20 and .

CONCLUDING REMARKS

Without question, the developments and measures described in this chapter greatly increased agricultural productivity in Britain from the 1950s onwards: the figures are there to prove it. But this increased productivity was achieved only at huge financial and environmental costs, the latter including less diverse and less attractive landscapes, less wildlife, and massively increased pollution, soil loss and degradation. A high level of nitrogen and phosphorus in agricultural soils, resulting from the use of inorganic fertilisers, increased the pollution of water bodies through drain-flow, soil erosion and leaching. Serious nutrient enrichment (eutrophication) led to excessive growth of aquatic plants and algae, resulting in poor water quality, including low dissolved oxygen at night which led to widespread fish deaths. For reasons of human health, excessive levels of plant nutrients and pesticides had to be removed from drinking water, which meant significant costs for water companies. High levels of atmospheric pollutants resulting from agricultural practices added substantially to greenhouse gases and to the nitrification and acidification of soils, especially in the uplands (Chapter 19).

So the costs to the general public of modern agriculture result not only from the subsidies and grants that are provided directly to farmers, but from the general pollution and other problems that modern agriculture creates. These problems have accelerated in recent decades, mainly though agrochemical use. Few of them are confined to the farms on which they arise, and most are 'externalised' to become a cost to society as a whole.

Agricultural policies in the latter half of the 20th century have emphasised external inputs as the means to raise food production. Within the space of 50 years, throughout the developed world, the entire agricultural industry became dependent on oil, on energy captured over many millions of years by plants, condensed and buried safely in the earth's crust. The petrochemical industry of the 20th century came to provide not only the fuel which powered the machines, but also the agrochemicals on which high farm productivity came to depend. Without oil, it is not only transport, heating and lighting that would grind to a halt in Britain, but agriculture too. It is ironic that the earth's plant productivity over billions of years, condensed mostly into oil, is now fuelling current energy needs and crop growth, dangerously returning to the atmosphere the carbon which it removed over millennia.

The changes in agriculture since the Second World War can justifiably be called a revolution, because of the new political and technical elements involved. To my mind, the three most important are: (1) the political–economic acceptance by government that a prosperous and productive agriculture is desirable; (2) the general replacement of muscle power by machine power in agriculture and transport; and (3) the increasing development and use of agrochemicals. It is these features, and the speed with which they were introduced countrywide, that brought agriculture and conservation into conflict in Britain from the 1960s on.

Not all the events of recent decades were unprecedented. In previous centuries, periods of major agricultural change seem always to have altered the appearance of the countryside, and the wildlife dependent on it. They have also often affected the number of people employed on the land, and the social structure of rural communities. Over the past two centuries, the prosperity of arable farming in Britain has invariably depended on protected markets in one form or another, or on direct government subsidy (Shrubb 2003).

Much of the land lost to agriculture during the 20th century (about one-tenth of that present in 1900) was taken for urban development, but since 1919 the Forestry Commission and others have been planting trees on a growing area of open hill land. These losses have been more than offset by an increase in productivity of the remaining farmland, which more than doubled within the space of 30 years. Later chapters discuss the effects of agricultural changes on the birds and other wildlife of farmland. Almost the entire budgets of the governmental and non-governmental conservation bodies in Britain since the 1960s have been spent on trying to understand, moderate and mitigate the impacts of official agricultural and forestry policy.

## CHAPTER 5

## Soils, Invertebrates and Birds

DESPITE POLITICAL AND ECONOMIC pressures, agriculture is ultimately limited by physical factors, such as topography, soil and climate, and by biological factors, such as the crops and livestock able to thrive locally. This chapter is concerned with climate and soil, the organisms that live in the soil and the birds they support.

Physical factors impose a strong regional character on agriculture in Britain. Topography affects the climate, with greater severity and shorter growing seasons at higher elevations. It also affects the ease with which the ground can be worked. Most land above 240 m in southern Britain cannot be cultivated profitably, and is used mainly as rough grazing land. This critical altitude declines northwards, and in some northern areas uncultivable moorlands descend almost to sea level. Regardless of latitude and altitude, steep slopes are also uncultivable, and are usually either wooded or grazed.

Across Britain, soils are generally deeper and more fertile in the lowlands, but most can be divided into heavy moisture-retaining clays, and lighter and drier sandy or calcareous soils. For agriculture, different soil types offer different constraints, require different treatments, and are suited to different crops. Light soils warm up quickly in spring, drain readily and are easily worked at most times, but they are generally poor in plant nutrients and prone to dry out, limiting plant growth in summer. Heavy clay soils are often more fertile, but are slow to warm in spring, and can owe their productivity largely to man-made drainage. When wet, they expand and become soft and sticky, and when dry they contract, crack and harden. They are therefore more costly to cultivate, and can usually be worked for only limited periods of the year.

Most high-quality farmland in Britain is found in the east, where rainfall is lower, land less hilly and soils less acid. This promotes the most striking division in British farming, namely the easterly distribution of cultivation and the westerly distribution of grass-and-livestock. Local variations occur, and some areas of fertile soil in the far west use their mild frost-free climate to specialise in early vegetables and flowers, while damp coastal or floodplain grasslands in the east are used for grazing cattle and sheep.

Broad though these patterns are, they are also reflected in regional bird faunas. For example, farmland seed-eaters are much more numerous in the arable east than in the grassy west, while pipits and other grassland species show the opposite pattern. On a smaller scale, any county shows similar variations for the same reasons, giving great overall spatial diversity to British farmland and its bird populations. Physical factors that influence agriculture also affect birds, and not only through their effects on vegetation. The severity of winter weather clearly limits the latitudinal distribution of many bird species in Britain, and also their altitudinal distribution, some having extended northward and upward in recent decades as climate has warmed. Examples include the Barn Owl, Nuthatch and Green Woodpecker (Balmer et al. 2013). Many birds occur on a wide range of soils, but in equivalent habitat are typically more numerous on more fertile ground. Some species are found primarily on neutral or alkaline soils and are absent from acid soils. Some occur primarily on well-drained soil, and others on wet soil, as described in more detail later.

CLIMATE

Climate influences agriculture in a number of ways. In Britain, temperature is the main constraint on plant growth, which in our seasonal climate is chiefly restricted to the warmer months. This means that, through most of history in the absence of imports, enough food had to be produced in the warm period to support people and livestock year-round. Food storage was paramount, whether as dried seeds, root crops or fruits, or meat that had been dried or salted.

The high year-round rainfall of Britain means that lack of water is seldom a constraint on plant growth except in rare summer droughts. It also means that heavy soils are sometimes hard to work for much of the winter, and that crop harvesting can be difficult in damp autumns. In the past, weather at harvest time affected the proportion of cereal crops that could be successfully harvested, and in wet summers wheat was sometimes left so long that it began to germinate in the head. Some kinds of livestock, notably pigs and dairy cows, need sheltered accommodation in winter, and in some years snow and cold are sufficient to cause substantial mortality among sheep on high ground. Most animals kept outside need supplementary food in late winter, and especially at times of snow.

FIG 43. Feeding supplementary food to livestock kept outside is often necessary in winter when most of the fresh vegetation produced in summer has been eaten (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

These same weather conditions affect wild birds in similar ways. Most species have abundant food in summer, but few species store food, so most face a depleting amount through winter. Severe weather, coupled with food shortage, can lead to heavy mortality among resident birds, thus limiting their numbers, but other species migrate to warmer climes for the cold season. In summer, food production for wild birds depends partly on rainfall and, as rain occurs in every month, the soil tends to remain damp in most years. Soil-dwelling invertebrates therefore generally live near the surface, within reach of probing birds such as Rooks and Starlings, for large parts of the year. In most years, though, summer drought makes these invertebrates less accessible during July–September. On the other hand, prolonged and heavy summer rain often reduces other food supplies and impedes bird foraging, so that in some years growing young can die through chilling or starvation (Newton 2013a).

Over most of eastern Britain, an annual rainfall of less than 75 cm is sufficient for arable crops, and more dry days improve the chance of successful harvests. However, light shallow soils in the east are too dry in most years for grass to grow without check through the summer, unless they are irrigated. In northern and western districts, most of which receive more than 100 cm of rain per year, frequent downpours make conditions for harvesting crops difficult, especially cereals. And the damp acid grassland of many such areas is poor unless repeatedly restored by liming and reseeding. Rainfall affects livestock mainly through its influence on grass and crop growth, but some soils become too soft and muddy for cattle in winter.

Particularly for livestock, the length of the annual growing season is crucial. Most grass starts to grow at a mean air temperature of 6 °C, and thus has a much longer growing season on low ground in the southwest than in the mountains of the north. In northern England, its growing season shortens by about 10 days for every 80 m rise in altitude (Coppock 1976). Light values also influence plant growth, and are lower under rain and cloud. Owing to climate change, average growing seasons in Britain have lengthened by about one month since 1990.

SOIL

Sitting as a friable layer on the underlying bedrock, soil supplies nutrients and water needed by plants, and forms the natural capital on which all terrestrial life depends. It varies with the underlying rock type, and can be changed through natural processes and human use. It is made of a combination of tiny rock particles, divided by size into sand, silt or clay, and organic matter (humus) consisting of the decaying remains of plants and animals. It also contains huge numbers of living organisms from bacteria to earthworms and Moles. The rock types from which the soil is derived largely influence its chemical composition and fertility, and the proportions of different particle sizes affect soil behaviour: too much clay (tiny particles) and the soil can become waterlogged, too much sand (big particles) and the soil drains and dries too rapidly. The perfect soil for crop growth is loam, intermediate in structure between clay and sand, rich in humus, well drained, well aerated, and naturally fertile.

Apart from loam, clay soils are generally the most productive, but only if they are sufficiently drained and aerated. They naturally hold plant nutrients and moisture, but for much of the year they are often difficult to work. Sandy soils are almost entirely composed of inert silica, and have no naturally retained water or plant nutrients. Plant growth depends entirely on other substances within the sand, especially humus. Sandy soils in Britain were traditionally grazed by sheep or rabbits, giving a grassy sward, mixed with heather where the grazing was light. Throughout history, the poverty of sandy soils caused great stretches to be left uncultivated, including the various heathlands of southern England.

Calcareous soils over the chalk and limestone downs and wolds tend to be shallow, perhaps largely through centuries of use and erosion. Because the underlying rock is soft and porous, the hills tend to be rounded and lack surface streams. Rain soaks through and seeps out at the base of the hills. Under centuries of sheep grazing, these areas supported soft springy turf; but now most of this land has been converted to arable, growing cereal crops, and suffering in places from severe erosion.

On waterlogged areas with anaerobic conditions, plant material does not fully rot, but accumulates as peat, mostly neutral in pH on low ground and acidic on the hills. On low ground, most of the marshland that gave rise to peat has now been drained, allowing vegetables and other demanding crops to be grown on the fertile peat remaining, as in the 'fens' of East Anglia. This soil lacks any rock-derived particles or stones typical of other soils, and consists entirely of decomposing organic matter, ideal for growing root vegetables which elsewhere can become misshapen in stony soils. Over time, however, this humus rots away, shrinking and exposing the underlying mineral soil present when the marsh began to form.

With the varied geology of Britain, soil type and fertility can change over short distances, even at a local level. In the past, soil properties were often changed by ferrying material from one place to another. For example, some soils that were too acid for crop growth were neutralised by applying lime or chalk, while marl (a clay–lime mixture) was added to counteract both acidity and lightness of soil. On peaty land, the surface was sometimes pared off and burnt and the ashes then distributed. The deficiencies of sandy soils, poor in nutrients and in water retention, could be rectified by adding manure and other organic matter, or calcareous material such as lime or marl.

The main ways in which farmers of the past could replenish nitrogen and other nutrients in the soil was by spreading manure and compost, a good dressing of which would support cropping for a further 2–3 years. In effect, the use of manure often involved taking nutrients from one part of the farm and adding them to another, where the most demanding crops were grown. This process changed the soil for better or worse in different places. Many other off-farm materials were added to soil to improve its fertility, including various suitable waste products from industry, ash and soot from fires, grassy turf and peat from hill ground, sewage, horse dung from cities, the ground-up bones, hooves, horns and other unwanted body parts from dead livestock, old wool, seaweed and fish guts, and any other appropriate material available locally.

In the 19th century, phosphates and nitrates were dug from the ground in various parts of the world and imported for use on British farmland, as was guano from Peruvian seabird colonies, and waste organic matter from various countries. In these ways, over the centuries, farmers built up, as well as fertilised, their land to produce a deeper layer of productive topsoil. Some of the better soils of British farmland can thus be regarded as largely man-made, not merely as man-modified. The farmers of today benefit from the efforts of their predecessors. One consequence of these activities is that soils of modern farmland are not only more productive than in the past, but they vary much less in fertility than they would have done under the natural conditions. They also vary much less in fertility than the present soils of the hills and mountains which have not been modified in these ways.

Much use was made of leguminous crops, such as peas, beans, lucerne, sainfoin and later clover. With the help of bacteria housed in nodules on their roots, all these plants can convert nitrogen from the atmosphere into a more useable form. Ploughed in after cropping, these plants substantially raise the nitrogen content of the soil. All these procedures were presumably learnt by early farmers through trial and error, and the mechanisms involved were not understood until they were investigated scientifically in the 19th and 20th centuries.

Another aspect of soil, important to its function, is the life it contains, mostly bacteria and other microorganisms, fungi and various kinds of invertebrates. These soil organisms ultimately depend on humus in the soil which they consume and break down, releasing nutrients for further plant growth. They thereby influence the ability of the soil to support vegetation, and to retain and circulate nutrients. The organic matter in the soil also acts as a carbon store, helps to retain and purify water, and makes the soil more resistant to erosion.

In natural habitats where soil is undisturbed, it develops a layered structure, with distinct horizons and most of the humus and its animal life in the surface layer. Ploughing breaks up this structure, and also has other effects, including the creation of a hard pan at plough depth. This can inhibit drainage, causing waterlogging of crop plants on some soils and creating a physical barrier to root penetration. Pan-busting equipment can be used periodically to break this pan and make it more permeable.

BIRDS AND SOIL

The relationships between birds and soil features have been little studied. But it is clear that soil type and fertility, humus content, pH and wetness all influence birds in various ways, largely through their effects on food availability.

Soil productivity

Many bird species occur on a wide range of soils, but in equivalent habitat they usually live at higher densities on more fertile ground (von Haartman 1971). Plant growth is generally better here, so insects are more abundant and diverse, and soil-dwelling organisms are more plentiful, affecting the whole food chain up to predators.

FIG 44. Red Grouse Lagopus l. scoticus (left) and Golden Plover Pluvialis apricaria (right), two upland species which nest at greater density on more fertile ground than on poorer ground (Edmund Fellowes).

Most of the uplands of Britain overlie acid rocks of low productivity, but in some areas they overlie basic (calcareous) rocks, which are much more productive. This difference is reflected in the densities of sheep they can support, and also in the native plants, insects and birdlife. Red Grouse usually reach their highest densities of 50–60 pairs per km2 over base-rich rocks (such as diorite and epidiorite), which offer more fertile soils and food plants of higher nutrient content (Picozzi 1968). Ptarmigan achieve higher densities on the richer schist mountains Cairnwell and Meall Odhar than on the sterile granite of the high Cairngorms (Watson & Moss 2008).

The effect of soil fertility also extends to invertebrate feeders. The highest breeding density of Golden Plovers recorded in Britain in recent times exceeded 16 pairs per km2 on close-grazed, hummocky limestone turf in the Pennines (Ratcliffe 1976). In other upland areas, densities of 5–8 pairs per km2 are usual, down to less than one pair per km2 on the poorest ground in the western Highlands (Ratcliffe 1990). In addition, Dotterels settle at greater nesting densities and breed more productively on areas over schist than on areas over granite. Soils over schist tend to be deeper and more fertile, and are presumed to support greater densities of crane-flies and other invertebrate prey (Watson 1989). Dunlins are sparsely distributed over wet flows and high peaty watersheds, where typical densities might be 1–5 pairs per km2, sometimes reaching 10–15 pairs per km2. But they reach quite spectacular breeding densities on some of the rich calcareous machair marshes of the Hebrides (27 pairs per km2 in 1984–85, reaching an incredible 307 pairs per km2 in one area of South Uist in 1984, Ratcliffe 1990).

The same effects are evident in the predators. The mean distances between neighbouring Sparrowhawk nesting territories in continuous forest habitat varied in different parts of Britain from 0.6 km on the most productive soils to 2.5 km on the least productive, equivalent to a tenfold difference in nesting densities in similar-looking forest (Newton et al. 1986). Many other woodland bird species also occur at higher densities on more fertile soils, as do water-birds in the more productive wetlands (Chapter 16; von Haartman 1971, Newton 2013a). The nutrient content of soils and water is clearly a major factor underlying variations in bird and other animal densities, but it is particularly evident in the uplands, where the range of land fertility is great, and where fertiliser is not generally applied.

However, there are exceptions to the general trend, in that carrion-feeding Ravens and Golden Eagles currently reach their highest nesting densities in geologically poor western areas, where sheep mortality is highest (Marquiss et al. 1978, Watson 2010). Like many other birds, they are reacting to food supply, which in their case is greater on poorer ground.

Slope and altitude

For most birds, given appropriate habitat, slope makes no difference to their presence. However, most waders occur on flat or gently sloping ground, and are absent from steep slopes, while most birds dependent on open water are necessarily restricted to flat areas. Altitude limits the distribution of many birds. This is partly because habitat tends to change with altitude, but in our highest mountain areas it is also noticeable how different species drop out successively at different altitudes, often before their habitat disappears. This holds in the breeding season as well as in winter, and the severity of montane weather is clearly one factor involved.

Soil pH

Soil pH is important because it has a major influence on soil fertility, on the organisms that live within the soil, and on the plants that grow upon it. In general, acid (low pH) soils are much less productive, and support a much lower range of plants and animals than neutral or alkaline soils, with effects on bird populations. While some bird species, such as Redshank among terrestrial species and Shoveler among aquatic ones, are found chiefly on alkaline or neutral soils or their associated wetlands, others, such as Greenshank among terrestrial birds and divers among aquatic ones, are found in the breeding season on their acid equivalents. But apart from these obvious associations, few studies have been made of the effect of soil pH on more widespread species. However, in the Outer Hebrides, wader densities proved to be associated with soil fertility, pH, salinity and moisture content, as well as with vegetation height and density, and extent of cultivation (Calladine et al. 2014). Elsewhere in Scotland, Lapwings on farmland were found mainly in open landscapes with short vegetation; but in a study of 89 farmland sites, Lapwing densities were also related to soil depth, pH and organic content (McCallum et al. 2015). Breeding densities were greatest at sites with less peaty and less acidic soils. The subsidy on lime was removed in 1977, after which applications fell by more than one-half (Dawson 2011). Some upland soils may therefore have deteriorated as Lapwing habitat in recent decades because of the reduction in earthworms and other invertebrates expected as soil acidifies. Re-liming pastures could improve conditions for earthworms, and in turn for Lapwings and other birds that feed on them.

FIG 45. Two closely related species, the Redshank Tringa totanus (left) nesting mainly on fertile low ground (Richard Chandler), and the Greenshank Tringa nebularia (right) on poorer, acid hill ground (Frank Snykers).

Soil wetness and organic content

Some bird species in Britain are found chiefly on drier, freely draining soils on sand or chalk. Examples include the Stone-curlew, Ringed Plover, Woodlark, and to a large extent the Corn Bunting, Grey Partridge and Red-legged Partridge (except where released). The reasons are unknown, but none of these species seems to thrive on heavy clay or wet peaty soils. Any ground-nesting bird is likely to benefit from a well-drained soil which reduces the chance that the nest becomes waterlogged or flooded. However, many ground-nesters, such as Snipe and Redshank, nest on wet soils, building a thicker nest of grasses to raise the eggs above the ground surface.

For waders and other species which probe into the soil to obtain prey items, wetness and penetrability are important. The Black-tailed Godwit is more or less restricted to damp and neutral peaty soils in Britain, and other waders, such as Snipe and Redshank, also occur at relatively high densities on such soils. The capillary action of the peat may be important, because it brings a continual supply of water to the soil surface, keeping the soil profile damp through the breeding season and soil-dwelling prey items accessible.

FIG 46. Four ground-nesting species that thrive on dry, well-drained soils: upper left, Stone-curlew Burhinus oedicnemus (Chris Knights); upper right, Ringed Plover Charadrius hiaticula (Chris Knights); lower left, Woodlark Lullula arborea (Frank Snykers); lower right, Red-legged Partridge Alectoris rufa (Richard Chandler).

Yellow Wagtails are also more abundant on soil types with a high organic content, and in southeast England they nest at higher densities in fields with more penetrable soils, even though they do not probe in the soil for food (Gilroy et al. 2008). Their brood sizes also tend to be larger on soil types with higher organic content. Monitoring of invertebrate abundance across 20 cereal fields revealed that both soil penetrability and organic content significantly influenced the rates at which Yellow Wagtails caught aerial insects. This relationship was strongest during the latter part of the breeding season. Presumably, land drainage and its effects on soil played a role in the widespread decline of Yellow Wagtail populations in Britain during the 1960s–80s. Among woodland birds, Nightingales also show higher densities on soils with high organic content, which may again be associated with more invertebrate prey items in the soil or on the surface (Wilson et al. 2005a).

FIG 47. Snipe Gallinago gallinago, which probes in soggy ground for worms and other invertebrate prey (Alan Martin).

Other birds such as Rooks and Starlings which probe into soil to obtain prey items require soil which is damp enough to allow this, and often have to resort to alternative feeding areas and foods during dry periods in summer, when the surface soil of drained farmland is often hard and dry.

SOIL INVERTEBRATES

The soil contains an amazing variety of invertebrates. In pre-pesticide times their average densities were estimated at 15 million individuals per acre (about 37 million/ha) in a wheat plot receiving annual dressings of manure, down to 5 million per acre (about 12 million/ha) in an un-manured plot (Russell 1957). Most of the species involved were too small for birds, but the larger species represented a huge potential food source for any birds able to access them. These large invertebrates feed on living or dead plant material, animal dung and carcasses, fungi or other soil organisms, depending on species. Some spend their whole lives in the soil, but most of the insects live there as larvae and emerge above ground as adults, while others simply pupate there as they transform from larval to adult stages. Both below and above ground, then, soil-dependent invertebrates provide an important food supply for birds.

Earthworms

The largest soil-dwelling invertebrates are earthworms, of which at least 26 species occur in Britain. Their abundance is strongly influenced by soil moisture, organic content and pH (Edwards & Bohlen 1996, Edwards 2004).
