They remain available to birds year-round, except when the ground is frozen or too dry, when they retreat to greater depths. They are most available near the surface during March–May, when other food items for birds are often scarce, and again in October–December. Earthworms are major foods of Rooks and other corvids, Blackbirds and other thrushes, Lapwings and Golden Plovers, Woodcock, Snipe and various other longer-billed waders, Black-headed and Common Gulls, Tawny and Little Owls, Buzzards and Red Kites, and minor foods for many other species. Almost all the invertebrate-eating bird species listed in Tables 1 and  eat earthworms at some time. Some of these species rely on finding worms on the soil surface, while others can extract them from various depths. Without earthworms, most of these birds would probably be much less abundant on farmland than they are now. Among mammal species, Badgers, Hedgehogs and Moles are earthworm specialists, and many other species eat them in smaller quantities (Macdonald & Tattersall 2001). So, given the importance of earthworms to so many birds and mammals, what influences their densities and availability?

FIG 48. Four species that feed largely on earthworms: upper left, Song Thrush Turdus philomelos (Edmund Fellowes); upper right, Rook Corvus frugilegus (Richard Chandler); lower left, Woodcock Scolopax rusticola (Peter Harris); lower right, Lapwing Vanellus vanellus (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

FIG 49. Two species of owls which at times feed largely on earthworms: left, Little Owl Athene noctua (Andrew Everitt); right, Tawny Owl Strix aluco (Chris Knights).

Earthworms are often divided into two groups, surface-dwelling species that produce no burrows or casts, and soil-dwelling ones that live within defined burrow systems. Most species concentrate in the surface litter-layer or in the top 8 cm of the soil for most of the year, but tend to have quiescent periods in summer (June–September) and midwinter (January–February), when they retreat deeper in the soil and become less available to birds (Gerard 1967). Common Earthworms Lumbricus terrestris can burrow deeply but emerge at night. They usually remain attached by their tails to the entrances of their burrows, into which they retreat rapidly when disturbed. They browse on plants within reach, and also pull down dead and living leaves on which they continue to feed underground. But on wet nights they may travel for several metres over ground. In line with this nocturnal behaviour, many of their predators feed at night, including Tawny and Little Owls, Woodcock and Snipe, and Lapwing and Golden Plover among birds, and Badgers and Hedgehogs among mammals. Common Earthworms do not escape predation during the daytime, however, for they spend much of their time resting just below the mouths of their burrows, where they may be caught by various thrush species, for example, which seem particularly adept at this form of hunting (witness Blackbirds on lawns).

Although different earthworm species have somewhat different needs, and feed in different ways, they generally reach their greatest densities in medium-textured soils, as opposed to heavy clay or dry sandy soils. Terrestrial species prefer moist but not waterlogged or compacted soils. Most require a soil pH in the range 5.0–7.0, and with increasing acidity one species after another drops out. In Britain, earthworms of any kind are almost absent from soils and litter below pH 4.2, as in much of the acid ground of the north and west (Satchell 1955, Edwards & Lofty 1977). Otherwise their abundance levels are influenced largely by their food supply, whether residues of plants on the surface or humus in the soil (Satchell 1955, Edwards & Bohlen 1996). Additions of animal manure or other organic material enhance their numbers, which can double or triple within a year (Curry 1976, Edwards et al. 1995). Some inorganic fertilisers can also lead to increased worm densities, but chiefly as an indirect effect of increased crop biomass and residue production (Edwards & Bohlen 1996). However, nitrogen fertilisers used year after year tend to acidify soils, which acts against earthworms.

Comparing different locations in Britain, earthworm densities can vary from a few individuals to more than 1,000 per square metre, with their numbers and vertical distributions changing seasonally. Long-term grassland generally holds the highest densities (typically 300–500 individuals per m2), arable land much lower densities (50–250/m2), and fallow land lower still (20–30/m2). Despite much variation, both the densities and biomass of earthworms are typically around five times greater in old grassland than in arable land (Edwards & Bohlen 1996). Deciduous woodland (typically 100–150/m2) holds fewer than old grassland, and numbers are much lower in conifer forests (< 50/m2) and almost zero in acid moorland soils (where they are found mainly in the litter-layer). Within the soil, earthworms usually outweigh all other invertebrates put together, and in old grassland their total biomass per unit area can exceed that of the livestock grazing above (Edwards 2004). They clearly represent a huge potential food source for birds and mammals. A rough idea of their relative densities in different pastures can often be gauged by the number of molehills present (Edwards et al. 1999).

Following the conversion of grassland to arable, earthworms decline swiftly. At Rothamsted Research Station, after five years of annual ploughing of previously undisturbed soil, earthworm populations were reduced to 30% of their initial numbers, and after 25 years to only 11–16% (Edwards & Bohlen 1996). While this decline was mainly associated with the progressive reduction of humus in the soil, there was also a loss of sheltering surface vegetation and litter, as well as periodic physical disturbance caused by cultivation. The act of ploughing kills many worms, and turns both dead and living specimens to the surface where they are quickly consumed by birds which accompany the plough, most commonly Rooks and gulls. Nowadays, cultivation often also involves the use of a rotavator whose spinning blades rapidly slice through the soil repeatedly to a depth of 15 cm or more, making it practically impossible for any sizeable invertebrate to survive there. The important point is that, despite the short-term feast provided by ploughing, arable land normally contains less humus and provides far fewer invertebrates for birds than long-term grassland.

Two of the most important factors affecting the availability of worms and other invertebrates in agricultural soils are therefore the amount of organic matter near the soil surface and the time since last cultivation (Edwards & Bohlen 1996). Compared to the 12% of organic matter typically present in old grassland, in arable land under annual cultivation using only chemical fertilisers, organic matter eventually falls to around 2%, a level maintained largely by the rotting of plant roots, while the soil fauna is reduced accordingly (Russell 1957). However, organic matter can rise again under direct drilling, a process in which seed is sown without prior ploughing (Edwards & Bohlen 1996, Chapter 10).

In other experiments at Rothamsted, grassland plots to which dung was added annually contained three times as many earthworms as similar untreated plots, and on arable land sometimes up to 15 times as many (Satchell 1955, Edwards & Lofty 1977). In the absence of manure, earthworm numbers in arable land depend largely on the amount of crop residue ploughed back after harvest, a residue which varies from one crop type to another (Edwards 1983). Some species of earthworms are naturally attracted to animal droppings and dung on the soil surface, although with the recent use of anthelmintic drugs on livestock, fewer worms occur under their dung now than in the past (Chapter 8).

Over the period 1932–84, the overall area of permanent pasture and rough grassland in lowland England and Wales declined by 92%, from 7.2 to 0.6 million hectares, through conversion to improved grassland or arable land (Fuller 1987). This was tantamount to a 92% change from high-density to lower-density earthworm habitat, an average 80% reduction in earthworm biomass on every hectare involved. If this converted grassland had then been left, earthworm populations could have recovered within a few years, but modern practices require that improved grassland is ploughed and reseeded every few years. So we can surmise that at least most converted grassland in England and Wales now holds worm densities much lower than in the 1930s, a situation presumably replicated through much of lowland Scotland.

Besides the conversion of old pasture to short-term grass or arable, three other changes of recent decades are likely to have reduced the availability of earthworms to birds. The first is the more limited production and use of farmyard manure. Into the 1960s, manure was produced on almost every farm, and after being left to rot for six or more months, it was spread on the fields. But nowadays about 85% of farms in Britain no longer keep cattle, and even more have lost their pigs and poultry, so regular manure applications to fields are much rarer than in the past. While well-rotted manure can greatly benefit worm populations, the same is not true of fresh slurry obtained from intensive dairy units. Because of its high content of ammonia, various salts and anthelmintic drugs, slurry tends to reduce worm populations. Secondly, recent land drainage, while reducing the likelihood of waterlogging, may also have reduced the period each year when earthworms and other soil-dwelling invertebrates are available to birds, not only because the land is too dry in some summers for birds to probe, but also because the worms themselves retreat too deeply. The third adverse impact of recent decades is the use of pesticides, some of which can devastate earthworm populations. Particularly lethal pesticides include carbamates such as carbofuran, aldicarb, carbaryl, methiocarb and methomyl, and fungicides such as carbendazim and benomyl, some organophosphate insecticides such as chlorpyrifos, and some pyrethroids such as cypermethrin. In addition, most fumigant nematocides and fungicides, which permeate the soil as vapours, kill most of the earthworms, even those in deep burrows (Edwards & Bohlen 1996). It seems, then, that many chemicals used on arable land can adversely affect worm populations as an unintended side effect, over and above the impacts of reduced organic input and frequent soil disturbance. Only on golf greens and other sports turf are earthworms killed deliberately using pesticides (such as chlorpyrifos), most of which are toxic to a large part of the soil fauna.

In addition to all these impacts, earthworms in the British Isles have gained a new and potentially devastating predator. The New Zealand flatworm Arthurdendyus triangulatus is thought to have been imported in pot plants. Since 1961, it has spread throughout Northern Ireland, parts of central Scotland and parts of England. In some areas, it reduced earthworm densities to undetectable levels within a year. It could therefore have severe long-term ecological impacts, both on soil structure and fertility and on the numbers of the many bird and mammal species that feed heavily on earthworms (Blackshaw 1991, Boag et al. 1997). Only time will tell how this threat unfolds.

Earthworms and birds

Apart from specialist herbivores, virtually all bird species found on farmland eat earthworms given the chance, and the various probing species mentioned above depend on them for large parts of each year. Such birds tend to concentrate on fields where earthworm densities are high or where they have been turned up by ploughing. In one study in southern England, worm-eating birds fed most frequently in those fields that had received regular applications of farmyard manure and that held the greatest densities of earthworms (Tucker 1992). After autumn ploughing of fields in Switzerland, Black-headed Gulls consumed nearly 30–100 kg of earthworms per hectare, but this represented only 1–5% of the total annual production of earthworm biomass in these fields (Cuendet 1977). However, bird predation can sometimes markedly reduce worm numbers, as shown by studies of Golden Plovers and Black-headed Gulls (Bengston et al. 1976, Barnard & Thompson 1985).

Other soil-dwelling invertebrates

Most other invertebrates that live in the soil – including many fly and beetle larvae, slugs and nematodes – depend on living or rotting plant material. These animals are likely to have been affected by cultivation and cropping in a similar way to earthworms, with their numbers greatly reduced at least on arable land. Over many years, some have also been specifically targeted by pesticide use.

Particularly important prey species for birds include tipulids, whether as larvae (leatherjackets) in the soil or as adults (crane-flies or daddy-longlegs) after they emerge above ground in late summer or early autumn. Crane-flies generally favour damp soils, and different species occur in a range of habitats from lowland grassland to high-elevation moorland, feeding on decaying plant matter or living roots in the soil. One of the commonest species is Tipula paludosa, which is widely distributed and numerous on grassland. The adult crane-flies emerge in July–September, and live for around 10 days, during which time they mate. The females then lay their eggs in the surface soil of short grassland. The eggs hatch after 2–3 weeks to produce greyish-brown larvae ('leatherjackets') which feed largely on plant roots, and grow in size through winter and spring. As they occur just below the soil surface, they are easily reached by birds such as Starlings, various thrushes, Rooks and Jackdaws, Lapwings and Golden Plovers. The combination of numbers and size results in a peak biomass in May–June, an occurrence to which the breeding of Starlings seems well timed, leatherjackets forming the main food of chicks (Dunnet 1955). Small round holes in the turf of lawns and pastures mark the sites where Starlings have inserted their beaks. The larvae grow up to 3 cm long and pupate in June–July, and a few weeks later the adults emerge, becoming available to a variety of additional birds, from pipits and wagtails to corvids and gulls, which pick them from the vegetation or catch them in flight.

FIG 50. The Starling Sturnus vulgaris gets much of its food by probing in soft ground in search of invertebrates, in this case a leatherjacket (Richard Chandler).

Leatherjackets can reach densities in grassland of up to several hundred per square metre, but are usually much more thinly spread. At more than 100 per square metre, they can damage grass and cereal roots and stem bases, killing the plants and causing obvious bare patches in fields. For this reason, they have for several decades been controlled by pesticides sprayed onto the field surface. Crane-flies are now much less common than in the past, perhaps partly because of continuing pesticide use, but also because land drainage makes the surface soil too dry for the larvae to survive in dry weather. In general, tipulid larvae represent another important and widespread food source for certain birds that on lowland has greatly declined in recent decades, although I know of no assessments of the extent.

Some other animals living in the soil feed on plant roots and are therefore also classed as pests. Two beetle larvae are worth special mention because they are (or were) important as food for many birds, namely wireworms and white grubs. Wireworms are the larvae of click beetles (Elateridae: Agriotes and Athous), and white grubs are the larvae of cockchafers (Scarabeidae: Melolontha). Adult click beetles lay their eggs in soil close to the larval food plants in May and June. The newly hatched larvae are small and white, but as they grow over the next 2–4 years they develop a tough, golden brown skin, and reach up to 3 cm in length. They are mainly associated with old grassland, but they also feed on other crops, including potato tubers. Larvae move up and down in the soil according to moisture levels, and pupate about 30 cm below the soil surface in a small chamber, well beyond the reach of probing birds. In ideal habitat, wireworms typically occur at less than 50 per square metre, but occasionally in old grassland they exceed 200 per metre square, representing a massive food source for birds able to access them. They are often eaten by Rooks, Starlings, game birds, plovers and gulls. Controlled by pesticides, wireworms are now much less numerous and widespread than in the past. Rooks often pulled out young crop plants to obtain the wireworms and other insects on the roots.

FIG 51. Three common soil-dwelling invertebrate prey species of soil-probing birds on farmland: upper, white grub, larva of cockchafer Melolontha; mid, wireworm, larva of click beetle Agriotes/Athous; lower, leatherjacket, larva of Cranefly Tipula paludosa (drawn by Tim Bernhard).

The cockchafer Melolontha melolontha was almost eliminated from much of western Europe (including Britain) in the 1950s, when organochlorine pesticides were widely used against soil-dwelling insect pests. The species has recovered slightly since the organochlorines were banned, but it is still rare partly because it is also vulnerable to other soil pesticides. However, the large white larvae (called 'white grubs') were eaten by some soil-probing birds, and the adult beetles were relished by many others, such as shrikes and corvids. The larvae live in the soil, feeding on plant roots for 3–4 years and reaching a length of 4–5 cm before pupating, again usually more than 30 cm deep. Although mainly associated with old grassland, the larvae also feed on roots of crop plants, including potatoes. In the past, white grubs were eaten by all the common soil-probing birds on farmland. These grubs were sometimes called 'rook worms' because both larvae and adults were known to be relished by Rooks. So in addition to earthworms, we have three main types of large soil-dwelling insect larvae eaten by birds which have declined greatly over the last 60 years or more. Apart from pesticide use, the long multi-year larval periods of wireworms and white grubs probably made them especially vulnerable to frequent soil disturbance.

Other invertebrates associated with soil are eaten by a wide range of birds, but do not normally form major parts of their diets. Earwigs (Dermaptera: Forficula auricularia) are nocturnal as adults, staying in crevices by day, where they are most readily available to probing birds such as Choughs. They feed on tender plant foliage and flowers, and have short life cycles, with eggs laid in the soil in spring and emerging as adults a few months later. Centipedes and millipedes are also nocturnal, hiding under leaves or stones in the daytime. Centipedes are carnivorous and feed on small insects and other animals, while millipedes are mainly vegetarian, attacking roots, bulbs or tubers.

Most species of slugs eat rotting or living plant material, including the fresh leaves, roots and soft fruits of crop plants. They can cause serious damage to seedlings and leaf crops such as young cabbages, soft fruits such as strawberries, and potato tubers. Some other slug species feed on fungi, and yet others on animal carcasses. Total densities, all species together, sometimes exceed 100 per square metre. Their soft slimy bodies are prone to desiccation, so land-living species are confined to moist places and may perish in times of drought. They benefit from abundant humus in the soil, which provides food and maintains dampness. They spend the day in the soil or other dark and damp places, and emerge to feed mainly at night. Despite their unpleasant slime, they are eaten by a wide range of birds, including Blackbirds and other thrushes, Starlings, Rooks, Jackdaws, Tawny Owls, some game birds and waders. All these birds get slugs mainly from the soil, especially in summer as most species hibernate or die off in winter. On farm crops, they are controlled by pelleted baits containing a pesticide (such as metaldehyde or methiocarb). These lethal baits are sometimes eaten directly by birds, with thrushes being the main recorded casualties. Snails are less common than slugs, and survive winter cold and summer drought by closing off their shell entrances with a layer of hard mucus. Their shells give protection against many birds – but not Song Thrushes, which bash them against a hard surface to break them open. They therefore provide a food source for Song Thrushes at times of drought when most soil invertebrates are less available.

Important groups of surface-dwelling invertebrates taken by birds are the carabid, staphylinid and scarabeid beetles, some weevils and araneid spiders. Unlike the soil-dwelling earthworms and leatherjackets, these various invertebrates remain available through the summer, and in some habitats they increase substantially at this time, as their pupae hatch and emerge from the soil. Birds such as the Lapwing can use such food items throughout the summer, switching to them increasingly as worms become less accessible. Birds such as the Rook and Starling also tend to switch foods in summer from soil-dwelling to surface-dwelling species, and eventually to plant material such as grain or fruit.

The full effects of pesticides on soil organisms are difficult to judge, especially in non-pest species such as earthworms, partly because most of the losses occur underground, and partly because there has apparently been no long-term monitoring of their numbers. From indirect evidence, however, we can infer substantial declines in most of the species important to birds, with some species killed by pesticides directed against them (as with leatherjackets and wireworms), and others killed by pesticides directed against their soil-dwelling neighbours. Insecticides used as seed treatments are placed within the soil, coating the seeds themselves, and are thereby able to kill not only the seed-eating and shoot-eating insect pests, but also other invertebrates that come within range. Some pesticides, such as aldicarb, can be drilled in granular form directly into the soil, to give a slow and prolonged release of chemical. They are used mainly to control nematodes and other invertebrate pests of growing plants. Fungicides sprayed on crops also reach the soil, affecting soil fungi, and indirectly the invertebrates that feed on them. Other more localised impacts result from the anthelmintic drugs (avermectins) that are fed to cattle and other livestock to control internal parasitic worms (Chapter 8). These drugs are excreted, killing insects which feed on the dung plus others in the soil below. In consequence, dung flies and dung beetles – favourite foods of wagtails and corvids respectively – have now become scarce in much of lowland Britain. By killing larval flies in cow dung, these chemicals also reduce the number of adult flies in the airspace, and hence the number available to hirundines and bats.

Because the soil-dwelling larvae of many insects depend on rotting plant matter, reduction in soil humus is likely also to have reduced the numbers of these larvae, and hence of adult insects that emerge to mate in summer. In several of these insects, the larvae live in the soil for some years, making them even more vulnerable to frequent ploughing. Changes in soil management are thus likely to have contributed substantially to the general decline of insect populations in Britain. Those species whose larvae remain in the soil for more than one year are especially vulnerable. Annual ploughing gives too little time for individual larvae to develop, or for their populations to recover, whereas the occasional missed year (as where grass leys form part of the rotation) can help to sustain populations. It may be for this reason that Lapwings on arable land seem to prefer to nest in fields that have not been ploughed for more than a year, as some farmers maintain.

SOIL-PROBING BIRDS

With so many small creatures living in the topsoil, it is not surprising that various birds have evolved to exploit them, being able to dig or probe to various depths to reach them, or grabbing them when they emerge onto the soil surface. Finches, larks and thrushes flick or sweep aside surface particles or leaves; game birds dig and scrape away the soil with their feet or bill; cranes, waders, Starlings, Rooks and other corvids probe into the soil with the bill. Choughs are adept at poking under stones and into nooks and crannies, gaining prey that other species cannot reach; they also use their curved pickaxe bills for digging into harder soil and ant-hills to access insect prey. For other probing birds, the softness of the soil is especially important, and waders and other long-billed birds can access food from deeper in soft or waterlogged ground than most other birds. In marshland, or in flooded pastures in winter, swans and geese can probe for roots and rhizomes that would be hard to extract from drier ground. The length of the bill limits the depth to which each species can probe, although birds seldom probe to the full length of the bill except in very soft ground: typically to around 2 cm in the Jackdaw, Lapwing and Golden Plover, 3 cm in the Starling, 5–6 cm in the Rook and Carrion Crow, and up to 7 cm in the Chough (Cramp & Perrins 1994). Given softer soil, some long-billed waders can probe even more deeply, up to 3.5 cm in the Ruff, 4 cm in the Redshank, 6–7 cm in the Snipe, 7 cm in the Woodcock, 7–8 cm in the Oystercatcher, 9–11 cm in the Black-tailed Godwit, and a remarkable 12–14 cm in the Curlew. In some waders, the larger sex has a longer bill and can probe more deeply than the smaller (Cramp & Simmons 1983).

FIG 52. With its long curved bill, the Chough Pyrrhocorax pyrrhocorax specialises on invertebrates that live in the soil and in livestock dung, and can dig into ant-hills to access the occupants (David Boyle).

The Starling is specially adapted for probing and prying, taking much of its food from just below the surface of the soil or among grass roots. Typically, it pushes its closed bill up to 3 cm into soil, litter or grass roots, and then opens it to create a hole; during which process the eyes rotate forward to see into the hole. The skull and musculature are modified to allow this behaviour; the protractor muscles which open the bill are better developed than in most other similar-sized birds, enabling the bill to be opened forcefully; also the front of the skull is narrow, enabling the eyes to rotate forward to give forward binocular vision (Beecher 1978). Most other birds hold their head on one side and use one eye to look into a hole.

FIG 53. Gulls following the plough to feed on invertebrates turned to the surface (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Besides picking prey items off the soil surface, some ground-feeding birds also use other behaviour when hunting invertebrates: for example, waders and some others use foot-trembling to disturb prey to make it visible; Starlings, Rooks and Jackdaws often jump into the air to catch flying insects flushed from the vegetation; while corvids and others often flip over dried dung, leaves or stones to reveal prey on the damp ground underneath. Some bird species which feed on soil-dwelling prey habitually follow the plough, seizing any invertebrates turned to the surface. These are mainly Rooks and Jackdaws, Black-headed, Common and Mediterranean Gulls, but also Starlings and Lapwings, and less commonly, pairs or singletons of other opportunists, such as Magpie, Carrion Crow, Raven, Stone-curlew, Ruff, Redshank, Kestrel, Red Kite and Buzzard. Elsewhere in Europe, White Storks and Cattle Egrets are regular plough-followers, but much depends on the kinds of animals exposed.

CURRENT THREATS TO SOIL AND SOIL-DWELLING ORGANISMS

Almost all terrestrial life and crop production ultimately depend on the soil. However, the methods of modern agriculture can cause the loss and degradation of topsoil, with potentially serious effects not only on crop yields, but on soil organisms and their dependent predators, including birds.

Soil erosion

In most natural situations, soil is bound in position by living plant roots, making its removal by water and wind difficult. Land tillage has long been known to increase soil erosion, because the surface is bare and vulnerable for part of the year, and the plant roots that normally bind it are dead and broken. Slope, soil type and rainfall all influence erosion, but during recent decades its rate has increased, as a result of changes in agricultural practices.

Soil erosion is usually a slow process, hardly noticeable to most people. In wind-blows, most of the eroded soil, apparent as dust in the air, is presumably deposited some distance away, on other farmland or other habitats, but it can also settle on cities or out at sea, effectively ending its agricultural life. Erosion caused by water is evident not only from the small rain gullies that appear in bare fields, but on a grander scale by the muddy waters of swollen rivers after periods of heavy rain, and in the longer term by the gradual silting of rivers, reservoirs and harbours. Except locally, soil loss through water erosion is a much bigger problem than that caused by wind, especially in the south and east of Britain, where most rivers flow through arable land. Some once-busy sea ports on eastern coasts can now take only small boats or have closed altogether because of silt deposition. Examples include Boston and Wisbech near the Wash, Cley in Norfolk, and Rye Harbour in Kent. Where old harbours remain open, they usually need continual dredging.

FIG 54. Examples of soil erosion: above, a wind-blow on the sandy soils of East Anglia (Chris Knights); below, water-borne erosion of a bare field after heavy rain (unattributed copyright-free web-sourced image).

One consequence of river-borne erosion is the seaward expansion of estuarine mudflats, providing more habitat for wintering shorebirds. However, over the centuries, some areas of coastal mud have been 'reclaimed' for agriculture, thereby bringing eroded soil back into agricultural use, although in due course this new farmland may disappear under rising seas.

Currently, an estimated 2.2 million tonnes of topsoil are lost by erosion every year in the UK (Environment Agency 2004, Defra 2009). Erosion is not distributed evenly over the country, and in some arable areas soil loss can exceed 5.3 tonnes/ha in some years. Nearly half of all arable land in Britain is considered prone to erosion, and 17% is currently in process of serious erosion, as is about 20% of upland soils and peat. Agricultural practices are the main causes: ploughing and long periods without plant-cover in the lowlands, and overgrazing and ditch-digging in the uplands (Chapter 19). Climate change gives rise to further concerns, in that drier winters are likely to bring more wind-caused erosion, and wetter winters more water-caused erosion. The total cost of this erosion has been estimated at £45 million per year, including £9 million in lost food production (Defra 2009). Included in this cost is the annual dredging of ports and harbours, through which an estimated 40–50 million cubic metres of material are removed each year, much being re-dumped far away in deep water (Ausden et al. 2016).

Erosion is associated with several routine farming practices: the removal or lowering of hedgerows, especially on slopes; the switch from grass to maize silage; the use of tramlines in crop spraying; outdoor feeding of livestock at fixed sites which become churned to mud; outdoor pig units on unsuitable sites; ploughing of grassland on slopes (especially when up and down rather than along the contours); and damage to river banks by grazing livestock (Chambers et al. 1992, Evans 1996). Perhaps the most widespread problem, however, results from the switch from spring to autumn sowing. In the past, cereal fields were left as stubble over winter, so the soil was bound by roots from the previous crop. Nowadays, despite autumn ploughing, the new crop is usually sufficiently well rooted by winter to serve the same function. Nevertheless, some fields are ploughed after harvest (destroying the old root system) and left unplanted until the following spring. This is often the case when the intention is to plant maize, and it is in these situations on sloping ground that the risks of soil erosion during periods of heavy rain are greatest. In addition, the greater weight of tractors and other equipment enhances soil compaction, encouraging water to flow over the surface (rather than percolating downward), conveying topsoil with its fertilisers and pesticides into nearby waterways.

Arable soils are vulnerable to erosion from the time the ground is ploughed to the time when new vegetation develops sufficient roots to protect against runoff, a period which differs between crop types. Oilseed rape is sown densely and covers the ground quickly, giving a short-term risk of erosion. In contrast, maize is planted in widely spaced rows and takes up to three months to provide adequate crop cover. Winter cereals take on average about two months to reach a 30% crop cover, which generally provides enough protection for the soil (Boardman 2013). However, this two-month growth period coincides with the wettest period of the year in southern England, raising the vulnerability of land under winter cereals to erosion by water. Over time, as the finer material is eroded away from farmland, the heavier stones are left behind, so that the soil becomes progressively stonier (Boardman 2013).

Apart from the loss of productive topsoil, other problems have concerned the gradual filling of reservoirs with silt, the flooding of buildings with muddy water, and the damage to fish spawning areas caused by silt deposition on gravelly river beds (Boardman 2013). The famous trout streams of southern England, such as the western Rother, Wiltshire Avon, Test, Kennet, Itchen and Allen, have all suffered from silting (Evans 1996), as have the salmon rivers of northeast Scotland. The removal of soil-binding trees and shrubs from river banks and the removal of fences to give access to rivers by cattle only accentuate the problems of silting. Off-farm costs of erosion thus include damage to property, roads and communications, pollution of waterways and drinking water, damage to fisheries, and sedimentation of reservoirs, harbours and ports.

Problems of soil erosion may seem far removed from bird populations, but like all other organisms, most bird species depend ultimately on productive soils and, in some hill districts, the extreme loss of topsoil by water erosion over centuries has greatly reduced the carrying capacity of the land for most plants and animals (Chapter 19).

Reduced organic content

The reduced input of manure and other organic matter to arable land, especially in eastern Britain, leads to loss of soil structure and stability, which results in erosion, soil crusting and leaching. Much of any added fertiliser can then be lost before it can be used by plants. Many key soil functions are underpinned by its organic content and associated soil organisms, including water and gas flows (Benckiser 1997). The more humus a soil contains, the greater its capacity to retain water, lessening the impact of drought on vegetation and animal life, and lowering the risk of downstream floods at times of heavy rain. Paradoxically, a high humus level also improves drainage, probably because it supports more earthworms, whose vertical burrows act as drainage channels and help to maintain a well-aerated and well-watered soil structure.

Because of its organic content, the soil is also a great carbon store, holding on a world scale some 2–3 times as much carbon as the atmosphere, according to some estimates. However, with its reduced humus content, arable land contains far less carbon than natural habitats, especially forests, wetlands, peatlands and other waterlogged land. This is because, through drainage and tillage, the humus in arable soils is continually turned to the surface where its carbon is more readily oxidised to carbon dioxide, adding more greenhouse gas to the atmosphere. The soil is thus less effective as a carbon store under arable agriculture than it would be under more natural conditions.

Organic matter within the soil also reduces the leaching of pesticides to water through adsorption and higher microbial activity. Pesticides and inorganic fertilisers can influence soil structure directly, and through their impact on the soil fauna. The total costs of the loss of organic matter from the soil in the UK has been estimated at £82 million per year (Environment Agency 2004). Measures to protect and enhance soil organic matter include: returning straw and other crop residues to the soil after harvest; including grasses in crop rotations; applying animal manure, compost or sewage sludge; planting bare soil that would otherwise remain bare over winter with a temporary cover crop (Chapter 6); and using reduced cultivation to slow the loss of organic matter by oxidation. Apart from the last, these measures were standard practice among earlier generations of farmers.

In wide river valleys, the conversion of humus-rich permanent grassland to arable can also have serious environmental consequences. For example, in West Germany mostly over the period 1965–85, some 1.5 million hectares of wet meadowland, amounting to 6% of the country's total area, was drained and converted to arable. This process was calculated to have led to the release of about 10 tonnes of nitrogen per hectare (as nitrate) and 100 tonnes of carbon per hectare (as carbon dioxide). In addition, enhanced water runoff from the sealed and compacted surface of winter arable land is thought to have contributed to the increased frequency of winter flooding along major German rivers, evident from the 1980s (van der Ploeg et al. 1999). There is no reason to think that the situation may have differed in Britain, with the drainage of former grassy floodplains (Chapter 13).

CONCLUDING REMARKS

Almost all terrestrial life depends on soil, and its ability to support plant growth. Soils vary greatly in their fertility, and in their ability to produce farm crops and to support wildlife. Given suitable habitat, birds are generally found at greatest densities on the most fertile soils, and some are associated only with particular soil types, neutral or acid, wet or dry. With the most fertile areas in Britain being taken for intensive agriculture, many native plants and animals are generally confined to less fertile areas. This is another factor reducing the potential of the countryside to support wildlife in Britain and elsewhere.

In the past, soils were continually improved by farmers adding other materials in order to achieve a particular structure, pH and fertility. Manure was applied and leguminous crops were grown to enhance fertility. Over recent decades, these processes have lessened, especially in arable areas, increasing the erosion and degradation of topsoil, and lowering its humus content and ability to support soil-dwelling organisms. The implications of soil degradation for farmland biodiversity have received little attention. However, the reduced organic content of the soil clearly reduces the invertebrate content, especially the densities of earthworms and other creatures that form major prey items of many bird species. Land drainage clearly reduces soil penetrability, and hence the ability of waders and other probing birds to access any suitable prey animals that are present.

The decline of soil-dwelling invertebrates in arable land over recent decades, though not properly quantified, could have accounted for some of the decline in bird populations (notably Starlings), although to my knowledge this possibility has not been examined. In addition, the larval stages of many insects feed on plant material in the soil, so the decline in soil humus may also have contributed to the general decline of insects in Britain, with further repercussions on bird populations.

Some ecologists have expressed concern about the whole system of modern intensive arable farming. It is accepted that soil deterioration and erosion lead to reduced crop yields, and the costs of reduced yields have already been quantified (Defra 2009). Some loss of plant nutrients is made good by the natural processes of soil weathering, nitrogen fixation, and the addition of nutrients from the atmosphere (especially from 'smoke' and other gaseous pollutants), but most of the loss is now offset by continual applications of inorganic fertilisers. Others have warned about the potential effects of farm chemicals on soil structure: 'The notion that the soil is an inert mass which needs only a constant plastering with chemicals to give increasing yields is one of the tragic follies of the twentieth century' (Powell 1971). Light soils with low organic content become liable to erosion from wind blow and winter floods, especially in large fields devoid of windbreaks (the height to which most hedges are now cut on arable land greatly reduces their ability to resist wind). Some farmers still plough fields in autumn but sow them in spring, leaving them bare and prone to erosion over the winter months. This may be accidental if bad weather strikes before the field can be sown, or it may be deliberate to save time in spring or to expose the soil to winter frosts, which can break down lumpy soil to a fine tilth. Worldwide, concern for soil degradation is growing, and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) designated 2015 the 'International Year of Soils' to draw attention to the problems, created on a global scale by a combination of deforestation and agriculture as currently practised.

## CHAPTER 6

## Crops, Livestock and Birds

CROPS AND LIVESTOCK LARGELY determine the vegetation over most of Britain, and thus the habitats and foods of birds. Neolithic people who entered Britain from continental Europe brought with them a range of different crops, mostly cereals, and various domesticated animals. These plants and animals had all been derived from wild ancestors, but had been gradually changed over millennia to give man-made forms with more desirable characteristics. This could have been achieved simply by breeding from whichever individual plants and animals had in most extreme form the desired attributes. Cereals were evidently selected for features such as larger and more numerous seeds, rapid growth and uniform ripening, while animals were selected for features such as docility, rapid growth, and milk or meat yield. Although people had no understanding of the mechanisms of inheritance, they could see for themselves the consequences of selective breeding.

In the 20th century, selective breeding became more scientifically based than in the past, and now – in the case of plants – it can entail genetic engineering. This process involves deliberately altering the molecular structure of the DNA so as to obtain the desired characteristics. During the course of the 20th century, crop plants and livestock changed markedly.

Crop-plant breeding is now mainly in the hands of specialised research stations, mostly funded by government or commercial seed producers. One major aim is to achieve greater productivity per unit of input, and in this respect major gains have been made in recent decades. For example, in the 1950s, wheat crops in Britain averaged about 3.4 tonnes/ha, but productivity increased gradually over the decades to reach 4.8 tonnes/ha in the 1970s and 8.6 tonnes by 2001–10. In 2015 one Lincolnshire farmer achieved the all-time record for Britain of 16.5 tonnes of grain per hectare. Over the same period, as more farmers specialised on arable and no longer needed straw for livestock bedding, modern wheat plants were bred to have shorter stems than their predecessors. More of the plant's nutrient could then go into producing grain, and less into unwanted straw. Shorter stems also made harvesting easier, because they were more resistant to flattening by rain. The medieval crop, which in Britain yielded only about 0.6 tonnes/ha, was closer to its wild ancestor and taller than today, but it also grew in competition with more weeds, and probably also in less fertile fields. Partly owing to the development of new crop varieties and partly to improved and higher-input husbandry, the yield of most crops has increased greatly over the decades. Perhaps the most striking result of modern plant breeding is provided by commercial tomatoes, whose yields increased 40-fold in just 50 years.

Disease resistance has been another objective of selective plant breeding. Most fungal diseases can now be addressed with chemical fungicides, but this expense is unnecessary for resistant plants. Many wild plants contain toxic compounds through which the plant defends itself against potential predators. Such chemicals may be distasteful, interfere with digestion, or affect herbivores in other ways, sometimes causing nausea or diarrhoea, and under prolonged exposure even death. Another major aim of selective plant breeding, therefore, is to reduce the levels of these toxins so that particular plant types become more nutritious or palatable to people or livestock. In recent decades, owing to selective breeding, Brussels sprouts and other brassicas have become less bitter than they once were, and one of the most significant changes of recent years has involved oilseed rape. The leaves and seeds of this plant contain erucic acid and bitter glucosinolates, making the leaves and seeds unpalatable, but through selective breeding these compounds were eventually reduced to a level at which the seeds and leaves became acceptable to a wide range of animals, including humans. This led to a huge increase in the acreage grown, and rape is now one of the commonest crops in Britain and elsewhere, and a major source of cooking oil. Some toxic chemicals in plants, including some found in certain beans, can be destroyed by cooking, but this option is not easily applied to livestock feeding. Modifying crop plants in these ways also makes them more nutritious and palatable for wildlife, so it is not surprising that throughout history farmers have fought a never-ending battle with 'pests'.

In the past, selective breeding of farm animals was associated with the name of Robert Bakewell (1725–95), a farmer who introduced several new farming techniques, and also selectively bred animals for particular characteristics, such as the quality of wool in sheep, producing the Leicester breed. He was the first to breed cattle specifically for meat (rather than draught purposes), producing the English Longhorn, and horses for their strength, producing what eventually became the Shire horse, widely acknowledged as the most powerful horse in the world. Bakewell's work on 'artificial selection' was cited by Charles Darwin in support of his theory of evolution. In the recent past, most regions had their characteristic breeds of cattle and sheep, and sometimes also of pigs and poultry, developed to fit the conditions and needs of the region. Different types of sheep and cattle were required for upland and lowland, different types of cattle for beef and milk production, and different types of poultry for meat and eggs. Some of these breeds were also selected for their beauty, as well as their performance in local conditions. During the latter half of the 20th century, these regional breeds were largely replaced by a smaller number of more productive breeds. Among cattle and pigs, in particular, public preference for less fatty meat from the 1950s led to a major change in the types of animals favoured. Nevertheless, regional breeds are still kept by a minority of enthusiasts, and their products supply a niche market. Many of the older breeds possess characteristics, such as hardiness or disease resistance, that could be useful in future breeding programmes. They generally have slower growth rates than modern ones, but can survive on less nutritious vegetation, all that was available in the past. Modern breeds are more productive, but only because more nutritious vegetation is available to feed them.

Except for poultry, selective breeding of farm animals is still largely in the hands of individual farmers intent on improving their stock. Nevertheless, government agencies have fostered the use of artificial insemination, introduced in the 1930s. In theory, this practice gives every farmer the chance to improve his animals rapidly by use of a small number of the most desirable males, whose semen can be used to inseminate thousands of females. Artificial insemination is also used frequently on pigs and occasionally on other livestock. Selective breeding of farm animals has gone hand-in-hand with the selective breeding of grass and other crops because, as mentioned above, today's farm animals can only perform at the level they do because of nutritious foods.

CROP PLANTS

The leaves, seeds or roots of all farm crops are eaten by birds, and some form substantial components of the diets of some species for at least part of each year (Table 4). Different birds exploit different crops, but the numbers of species seen on any particular crop type may depend partly on its distribution across Britain, with more species recorded as eating the most common and widespread crops than the rarer and most localised ones. Typically, a particular crop type may be a major food source for a small number of bird species, but an incidental food for many more. For example, sugar beet roots form a major food source for Pink-footed Geese, especially in East Anglia, but various other geese feed on them from time to time, along with game birds and others.

Grasses and cereals are the crops most commonly eaten by birds, either the leaves or the seeds (Table 4). Other frequently eaten crops include clover (leaves and stolons) and potato (tubers). Crops are exploited not just by herbivorous species, such as geese and pigeons, but by a wide range of omnivores, such as corvids and Starlings. The importance of particular crops in the diets of birds depends largely on their availability, and many that were eaten commonly in the past are now only locally available (for example, rye and oats). Some widespread crops, such as cereals and rape, greatly influence the population sizes of those bird species that make most use of them. These birds have greatly changed in numbers over recent decades, as their crop foods have become more or less available (see Box 3 for Woodpigeon). Birds exploit some crops at the time of sowing and during growth of the plants pre-harvest, and are therefore classed as 'pests', while these and others glean the waste and spillage from the fields after harvest, causing no further loss to the farmer. Farm crops often bring together in the same field several bird species that otherwise live apart: for example waterfowl, pigeons, corvids, buntings and others on harvested cereal fields. Some kinds of birds may have started feeding on agricultural crops only in relatively recent centuries, or switched progressively from natural to farmed foods during the 20th century, as exemplified by some species of geese and other waterfowl in Britain (Box 4).

TABLE 4. Crop-plants eaten by birds in Britain. B = bud, F = fruit, L = leaf, R = root, S = seed.

BOX 3. Farm crops and Woodpigeon populations

Although originally a woodland species, the Woodpigeon has long sought much of its food from farmland, and its population levels now largely depend on cropping patterns. Its feeding behaviour and population levels have altered over the years in response to the food available. Throughout the period 1960–2000, Woodpigeons were studied in a 1,070 ha area of mainly arable land in Cambridgeshire. In the 1960s, the main food from July to December was cereal grains, obtained first from the plant (in response to lodging) and then picked from the surface of stubble fields which then lasted into winter. Once the grain was consumed, the birds shifted to clover in pastures and under-sown leys, which formed their main food in January–February. During these months, some pigeons died of starvation, reducing the population level for the next breeding season (Murton et al. 1966). Then in the 1970s, with the shift from spring-sown to autumn-sown cereal crops, and the associated reduction in winter stubble fields and in the amount of clover available (through decline of under-sown leys), Woodpigeon numbers began to decline (Isaacson et al. 2002). Some years later, the situation changed again when from 1973 oilseed rape was promoted as a break-crop in cereal rotations, becoming increasingly widely grown. Its young leaves provided an alternative winter food for Woodpigeons and Stock Doves, and over Britain as a whole rape increased in area from less than 1,000 ha in 1970 to more than 750,000 ha in 2012. Over the same period, Woodpigeon numbers in Britain approximately trebled and Stock Dove numbers doubled. As rape became widespread, the average weight loss of Woodpigeons over winter months was less, overwinter mortality from starvation declined, and the number of young produced each summer took over as the main demographic factor influencing population change. Rape leaves are as nutritious as clover leaves but can be plucked more rapidly (Inglis et al. 1997). Time will tell how long pigeon numbers will continue to rise, but it is clear that far more young rape is now available in the winter countryside than could ever be consumed by pigeons in their present numbers. Bird scaring devices deter pigeons up to a point, but in any case the plants usually recover quickly from heavy grazing, and seed yield is not reduced. Nevertheless, many farmers still class Woodpigeons as major agricultural pests.

Cereals

From an agricultural viewpoint, the main advantage of cereal grains is that they are nutritious and can be dried and stored long term, providing a dietary staple year-round. Cereals have short growth periods and can self-pollinate, with the aid of air currents rather than insects. Wheat and barley have been grown in Britain since the Neolithic. Rye is a later introduction, probably dating from Anglo-Saxon times, while modern oats are thought to have been derived from a wild species brought in as a weed with wheat and barley, but more tolerant of damp conditions. Maize from the Americas was brought to Europe in the 16th century, but not commonly grown in Britain until the late 20th century, following the development of hardier varieties.

Cereal grains provide food for people and livestock, while the straw also provides bedding. They lend themselves to mechanisation, requiring little attention between sowing and harvest, and are less demanding in their soil requirements than root crops. In recent decades, the acreage of cereals has increased in Britain at the expense of grass and fodder crops.

Wheat is more particular in its needs than barley and oats, being intolerant of soil acidity, and more susceptible to fungal diseases such as mildew and yellow rust. The British climate is good for wheat only in the east where sunshine levels are sufficient in most years to ripen the grain properly. Between 1900 and 1970, some 0.5–1 million hectares of wheat were grown each year in Britain, but in the early 1980s, within the space of five years, the area under wheat doubled to around 2 million hectares, with little change since then (Defra 2016). Modern milling wheat, with high gluten content, is used for bread-making and commands the highest price, while the poorest wheat is used mainly for animal feed. In the 1930s, owing to low gluten content, hardly any of the wheat grown in Britain was suitable for making modern breads, but now – thanks mainly to selective breeding – the country is almost self-sufficient in this respect. The weather at harvest time is crucial, for the gluten content is highest in freshly ripened grain, and deteriorates progressively the longer it remains in the field.

FIG 55. Wheat is the main cereal crop in Britain, whose yield per hectare has trebled in the last half-century through a combination of selective breeding and changed cultural practices. Owing partly to its improved gluten content making it more suitable for bread production, wheat is also now grown over twice the area that it covered into the 1970s. Wheat grains are eaten by at least 44 species of birds in Britain, and form major components of the diets of at least 28, especially pigeons, game birds, corvids and waterfowl (Ian Newton).

For most of the 20th century, barley was grown over a larger area than wheat. It is hardier and less demanding, with a lower gluten content, so it is used mainly for animal feed, with smaller amounts for malting, in beer and whisky making. It is grown mainly in the south and east of Britain, and from around 1960 the area under barley more than doubled within five years, reaching nearly 2.5 million hectares, from which it declined to its recent level of around 1 million hectares (Defra 2016). Current yields are similar to those of wheat, averaging around 8 tonnes/ha but reaching more than 10 tonnes/ha on the best land. The crops tend to be more open and weedier than wheat, so more birds feed on the stubble after harvest.

In the past, oats were grown mainly for feeding livestock and for high-quality straw, with much smaller amounts for human consumption. Fields of oats could be found scattered through most of the country, but especially in the north and west. Compared to wheat and barley, oats are more tolerant of acid soils, grow well under cooler and wetter conditions and ripen with less sunshine; but they are liable to fail in dry seasons in the east. Until the mid-1950s, more than 1 million hectares were grown each year in Britain, after which the area rapidly declined to around 100,000 ha by 1980, increasing again to 131,000 ha in 2015 (Defra 2016). The crop has fluctuated around this level to the present. Its demise was associated with the decline in the numbers of working horses, for which oats were a staple food. Average productivity has remained less than that of other cereals at around 5.8 tonnes/ha during 2001–10.

Rye has long ceased to be a major crop in Britain. In recent times, less than 12,000 ha have been grown, with a mean yield of around 6.0 tonnes/ha. It is used mainly in specialised products for human consumption, such as rye breads, and also in biogas production. Maize is a recent introduction as a field crop, but with the development of hardier and earlier-maturing varieties, it has expanded, covering 187,000 ha in 2015 (Defra 2016). Most maize goes for animal feed, and is harvested either green (for silage) or when ripe (for the seed-heads). One recent practice is to harvest the whole crop in October or later, by which time the seeds have ripened but remain in situ, while the supporting plants are dead and brown. Everything is then cut and pulverised to a whitish powder and used as cattle feed. Only small amounts are grown as 'sweetcorn' for human consumption.

Cereal grains form a substantial part of the diet in some months for at least 28 bird species on British farmland, and are taken occasionally by at least 16 others (Table 4). These birds seem to take any cereals that are available, in Britain now mainly wheat and barley. The smaller-billed species, such as Cirl Bunting and Reed Bunting, include fewer grains in their diets than the larger-billed Corn Bunting and Yellowhammer, and seem to prefer them soft; in other words, unripe or rain-soaked. Some birds take the grain directly from the plant before harvest. House Sparrows and sometimes Corn Buntings and Yellowhammers can cling to the stems to pick off the ripening grain, geese reach up to pluck the ripening seed-heads, while Rooks, Crows and Woodpigeons feed from mature plants battered down by wind or rain, putting the grain within reach from the ground. Rooks have been seen to jump into an unripe crop from nearby fence wires, flattening it with their spread wings. After harvest, these and many other species glean the spilled grain from stubble fields, or pick it from freshly sown fields. Corn Buntings have been seen to pull up cereal seedlings, squeeze out the milky endosperm, and discard the remainder (Goodbody 1955). Of the cereals sown in autumn, barley is the first to mature, and the forming grains can be present from around mid-May in southern England. In areas where insects are scarce because of pesticide use, soft unripe barley grain forms an alternative food for nestling Corn Buntings, and also for nestling Yellowhammers, Reed and Cirl Buntings, House and Tree Sparrows, although all these species need insects too and may grow less well on diets containing cereal grains (Douglas et al. 2012). On farms where Corn Buntings still persist, they often concentrate to nest around fields of autumn-sown barley, despite their shorter breeding seasons there. Their love of barley fields is of long standing, as suggested by the old names of 'barley bird' or 'fat bird of the barley'. Corvids, Starlings and House Sparrows also feed heavily on cereal-based animal feeds available within farm buildings or at open feeding sites.

FIG 56. Corn Bunting Emberiza calandra feeding on the soft unripe seeds of barley (Nicholas Watts). When insects are scarce, Corn Buntings often feed unripe cereal grains to their young, whether wheat, barley or oats. Autumn-sown varieties are preferred because the grains are ready earlier. At the stage the grain is eaten, it has a higher protein but lower starch content than mature grain, and more closely approximates the high-protein food available as insects. In southern Britain, winter barley provides such grains from mid-May to late June, winter wheat from early June to late August, and spring barley from mid-June to August. Other seed-eaters that feed unripe grain (along with some insects) to their chicks include House Sparrow Passer domesticus, Tree Sparrow P. montanus, Chaffinch Fringilla coelebs, Greenfinch Chloris chloris and Yellowhammer Emberiza citrinella.

FIG 57. The Whooper Swan Cygnus cygnus is one of several large waterfowl species which feed on spilled grain from cereal stubbles in autumn (Chris Knights).

Maize seeds are too big to be eaten comfortably by small seed-eaters. However, soft grains within maize silage are sometimes taken by sparrows and other birds, and the more fully formed seeds are eaten by Jackdaws and Woodpigeons. Greylags have been seen to fly into the edges of maize fields in late summer, knocking down the crop with their wings to access the cobs from the ground, but this behaviour appears uncommon. At harvest, some maize grains may be spilled but these are soon consumed, leaving nothing but bare ground for the winter. Towards the end of summer, roosts of Swallows sometimes form in maize fields, presumably attracted by the cover and secure perches that the full-grown plants provide.

In their wintering areas, some wader species, notably Black-tailed Godwits and Ruffs, feed partly on wild grass and cereal grains, mainly rice and millet (Moreau 1972). Many thousands of waders, as well as waterfowl, exploit these crops in parts of West Africa where from the 1960s their original marshland habitats were gradually converted to rice fields. In recent years, since barley has been grown in Iceland, returning godwits have fed on the grain remaining in poorly harvested fields. This provides another example of a crop having to be available in the right place at the right time before particular bird species start to feed on it, in this case adjacent to other longer-used habitat.

In earlier centuries, grain was broadcast by hand, and then harrowed to cover it over. Nevertheless, much remained on the soil surface, and a substantial proportion was eaten by birds. Protecting newly sown fields using various scaring devices was a major occupation, and the importance of Rooks and other corvids is reflected in the name 'scarecrow'. These losses were much reduced from the late 18th century when newly introduced seed-drills enabled grain to be sown below the surface. Some birds learnt to dig up the buried seeds. Rooks probed for it, while Pheasants and partridges scratched the soil away. Nevertheless, the introduction and progressive improvement of seed-drills greatly reduced the losses of newly sown grain to birds, enabling more of it to grow and seed. Moreover, since the 1950s, cereal grains have usually been coated with pesticides to protect them against soil-dwelling insects and fungi, a treatment which also makes them to some degree toxic to birds.

Traditionally, cereals were planted in spring to avoid the risk of crop loss in severe winter weather. Plant breeders produced hardier varieties which could survive well over winter, and at the same time new machinery enabled the crops to be harvested more quickly than before, while the weather was still mild. In little over 20 years from the 1960s, cereal production over most of Britain switched from predominantly spring-sown to predominantly autumn-sown (strictly late summer). One effect of this change was the loss of most of the winter stubble fields that had previously provided spilled grain and weed seeds for a variety of seed-eating birds in winter. In addition, the short and sparse vegetation of spring-sown cereal crops provided ideal habitat for some ground-nesting birds such as Lapwing, Stone-curlew and Skylark. Autumn-sown cereals have usually grown too tall and dense by spring, which makes them less suitable for these ground-nesting birds (Chapter 10).

Nevertheless, the young leaves of autumn-sown cereals provide nutrient-rich food for some birds and mammals in winter. The growing leaves are important to at least nine species of swans and geese in Britain, and leaves from freshly germinated plants are also taken by Skylarks, game birds and others. Wintering Skylarks have been reported as causing substantial damage by eating the tender shoots of sprouting cereals, but mostly during hard weather when thousands ended up in limited snow-free areas (Donald 2004). Hares, rabbits and deer also feed on growing cereals in winter. In the past, livestock were sometimes grazed on young cereals to encourage the plants to tiller, thickening the stand and increasing the grain yield. Nowadays, grazing by wild animals is considered undesirable, especially in spring, because it can delay growth and seed formation, and lead to uneven ripening across a field.

In contrast to most wheat and barley, maize seeds are not normally sown until May, usually by precision sowing, which means that the field surface remains bare for several weeks in spring. The seedlings do not compete well with weeds, so the crop requires good pre-emergence weed control, which results in few invertebrates and seeds being present within the growing crop. Some farmers place polythene strips on the soil surface, each strip covering two rows of maize. In the warmth, the seeds germinate and grow quickly, pushing their way through the polythene. Some birds still nest and feed in these fields, using the bare ground between each polythene strip, but the total field area available for nesting and feeding is much reduced.

FIG 58. Polythene strips used to cover rows of newly planted maize seeds. The seeds germinate quickly under the warmed soil, but the practice makes large parts of the ground surface inaccessible to birds (Ian Newton).

Legumes

Before the days of inorganic fertilisers, leguminous nitrogen-fixing crops were more important than they are now, the total of all kinds having been reduced to about 213,000 ha in 2015 (Defra 2016). Most of this area consisted of beans, which do best in dry climates and on heavy soil rich in lime, so their main growing area is southeast England. Peas grow better on lighter land, but are now seldom used for feeding livestock. Both peas and beans are rich in protein, and can be harvested in summer, earlier than cereals.

Lucerne (alfalfa) is a perennial crop, being left in place for 4–7 years, but each year cut for animal food. It was often sown with grass in a ley, fulfilling a role similar to clover in fixing atmospheric nitrogen. When cut for silage just before flowering, it yields 2–3 crops per growing season in southern Britain, and after a winter rest, the same again. It grows up to 1 m tall, and because of its deep rooting habit, lucerne does well in areas with porous soils, where the water table lies deep below the surface, as in the Breckland of East Anglia. It likes a fairly warm and sunny climate, with neutral or alkaline soils, but little has been grown in recent years. Lucerne is extremely rich in insects, and hence provides good foraging habitat for birds. In France, Skylarks were found to nest in young lucerne (less than 50 cm tall) at greater densities than in any other crop (Eraud & Boutin 2002).

The leaves of cultivated legumes, including peas, beans, lucerne and clover, are eaten frequently by pigeons and doves, game birds and bustards, and some waterfowl, and most of these species and corvids also eat the seeds of peas and beans (Table 4). Until the 1970s, when cereal crops were often under-sown with grass–clover mixes, clover leaves formed a major winter food of Woodpigeons on lowland farmland (Box 3). Some ground-nesting birds of arable land, such as Skylark and Yellow Wagtail, frequently nest in pea crops because they provide open ground for foraging and thick plant growth in which to hide the nest.

FIG 59. Legumes and birds. Above, pea crops are usually grown on well-drained sandy soils, and at an early growth stage are favoured nesting sites for Skylarks Alauda arvensis, Lapwings Vanellus vanellus and other ground-nesting birds (Richard & Barbara Mearns). Right, the Bean Goose Anser fabalis got its name from its habit of gleaning harvested bean fields in the autumn, but now the small areas of beans grown in Britain are harvested and ploughed long before any wintering geese arrive here (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Root crops

Root crops include turnips and swedes (Swedish turnips), mangolds, fodder beet, sugar beet and potatoes. The harvested parts of these plants grow in the soil or partly protruding above it, and are all bulky. In the past when they had to be tended and lifted by hand, they were generally grown in small fields, but nowadays they are all planted, hoed and harvested mechanically, so they can be grown over larger areas. Most root crops do best in deep, well-drained soils of light to medium texture, free from the stones which make for ill-formed roots and difficult harvesting. Different root crops predominate in different parts of Britain, with sugar beet grown mainly on light soils in the southeast and turnips and swedes in the north and west. All root crops are sown in spring, lifted in autumn, and (apart from sugar beet which is processed) are stored in clamps or sheds until needed in winter or the following spring. Alternatively, all except potatoes can be left in situ in the fields, with livestock allowed piecemeal access controlled by temporary fencing. Over recent decades, all fodder root crops have greatly declined in popularity, their place as winter animal feed being taken first by kale and latterly by silage. Sugar beet for human use is also grown in more limited areas than in the 20th century, covering about 90,000 ha in 2015 (Defra 2016).

As with other crops, it is not only the distribution of root crops which impinges on bird populations, but also the way the crop is sown and harvested and the amount of waste left in the fields. In the early stages of their growth in spring, beet fields in East Anglia are attractive to Stone-curlews, which may succeed in rearing a brood before the crop becomes too tall for them, when they move on to seek other nesting areas. Recently planted crops also attract nesting Lapwings and Skylarks, but again only for a few weeks. Until they are harvested, well-grown crops provide cover for many animals, including Grey Partridges and Dunnocks, and any weeds among the crops provide food for seed-eating birds.

While in the past the seeds of root crops were eaten by several bird species and rodents, they are now sown in pelleted form and are normally left untouched, but young growing plants are eaten by various birds. In fields with little else to eat, Skylarks consume the cotyledons of emerging beet plants, as do Grey Partridges, Woodpigeons and mice. In one study, over 60% of the diet of Skylarks feeding in beet fields was crop leaves and cotyledons (Green 1978). However, crop damage declined greatly as more nutritious weed seeds and invertebrates became available in the same fields. But through plant breeding, the sugar content of beet has increased substantially since the 1970s, making both leaves and roots a more valued food source for birds. Perhaps for this reason, some farmers claim, Woodpigeons started to feed more heavily on unharvested beet leaves in recent years.

Until mechanisation, sugar beet was pulled by hand, topped and tailed, thrown into carts, and transported to the factories. The earliest mechanical harvesters cut off and discarded the leafy tops and then lifted the roots, knocking off pieces from some. For Pink-footed Geese, the leaves were the most attractive part, and the hard root remnants were taken mainly later, after they had been softened by frost. However, the most modern harvesters flail off the tops before lifting the roots, and shred the leaves, which can get mud-covered and unattractive to geese. After harvest, the root remnants left in the fields may be consumed by geese and game birds (Table 4). For years, sugar beet remains have formed a major food of Pink-footed Geese in East Anglia, and in the past turnips/swedes were important for Greylag in parts of Scotland (Newton & Campbell 1973, Gill et al. 1996). Discarded carrot roots are eaten after harvest by Whooper Swans and by at least two goose species, Pink-footed and Greylag (Table 4).

FIG 60. Pink-footed Geese Anser brachyrhynchus in a harvested sugar beet field, feeding on waste from the crop (Chris Knights).

Into the 1970s, sugar beet, turnip and swede crops were especially important for small seed-eating birds, because of the broad-leaved weeds they usually contained. This situation arose because these crops could be killed by herbicides used to control broad-leaved weeds, so the crops were left unsprayed. Weeds such as Fat-hen and Persicaria are still abundant in some turnip fields, and attract large numbers of Linnets, Tree Sparrows and other small seed-eaters. Weed seeds are taken from within the crop, but become more accessible when the crop is grazed, with strip grazing opening up new feeding areas through the winter.

Grown primarily for human consumption, the potato is the most widely planted of all root crops in Britain. Stored in cold dark conditions, the tubers can last up to 10–12 months, depending on variety. In recent years, about 129,000–149,000 ha were grown in the UK, with an average yield in most years exceeding 40 tonnes/ha (Defra 2016).

Waste potatoes, left on the field after the autumn harvest, form an important food source for Greylag and Pink-footed Geese in autumn, and in some areas are also eaten by Whooper and Bewick's Swans, Mallard, Pintail and other ducks, as well as by game birds, corvids and others (Table 4). The smaller species take the remnants mainly after they have been softened by frost; the most unexpected species seen 'very often' feeding on rotting potatoes in a harvested field was Reed Bunting, described as slowly chewing pieces before swallowing (King 1985). Some species, such as Greylag, Pheasant and various corvids can dig out the tubers or pull at the haulms to expose them before harvest, although to my knowledge this is not a major feeding method by any species. Further north in Europe, Cranes have been seen to pick newly planted tubers from the ground, walking along the rows and somehow recognising where each tuber was buried. Between planting and harvest, potatoes offer little for birds except cover, and some species, notably Yellow Wagtails, sometimes nest in potato fields, under the foliage (Chapter 10). Nowadays, weeds are rare in potato crops, but any present could provide food for seed-eating birds.

Other brassicas

Oilseed rape (canola) is one of the recent triumphs of plant breeding, as explained above, and has now become the third highest source of vegetable oil in the world. Until the 1970s, it was grown in small amounts in Britain mainly as livestock feed (the leaves), and the distasteful oil was used primarily as a lubricant or for biodiesel. But new more palatable varieties produced oil fit for human consumption. This in turn led to a rapid expansion of rape cultivation from the 1970s, colouring large parts of the countryside yellow when the plant flowers in May and June. The total area of rape grown in Britain in 1970 was 19,240 ha, or less than 0.5% of the tilled acreage. After its promotion as a break-crop for cereals, and use of its seed oil for human consumption, the area grown increased rapidly, reaching a peak of 756,000 ha in 2012, some 18% of the total tilled area, reducing to 652,000 ha in 2015 (Defra 2016). The average yield is around 3.4 tonnes of seed per hectare. Besides the oil, the seeds are moderately high in protein, and when the oil has been extracted the residue can be turned into animal feed, popular for cattle.

The leaves of autumn-sown rape plants now form a crucial winter food source for pigeons and other birds, but the plants usually recover from grazing and the seed yield is little affected. In addition, rape seeds now form an important summer food for various finches, especially Linnet, Goldfinch and Greenfinch (Table 4). Birds start to eat these seeds while they are still green within the pod, usually in June in southern Britain, and continue to pick them from the ground after harvest, until they are ploughed under. Autumn-sown and spring-sown rape varieties provide this seed successively through the breeding season. They thus provide food for more than three months each year, depending on when the fallen seed is ploughed under, in preparation for the next crop. Well-grown rape crops also provide secure foraging habitat for ground-feeding birds such as Dunnock, Blackbird and Song Thrush which seek invertebrates on the damp soil below the canopy, while other birds, including various warblers, seek insects from the canopy itself. Reed Buntings can occur throughout rape fields and are not restricted to the edges; they forage among the leaves and pods, but also nest within the crop, either on the ground or in the canopy if it is bent over and able to support a nest. Nowadays more Reed Buntings probably nest in rape than in any other lowland habitat (Gruar et al. 2005). They are able to raise one or two broods before the crop is harvested, usually in July in southern Britain. However, before harvest the plants are killed either by spraying or swathing (cutting), and then left to dry for harvesting. Active nests usually escape if spraying is used because it delays cutting for a week or so, but swathing can destroy many of the later broods (Burton et al. 1999).
