Later in the scheme, however, farmers were allowed to grow industrial crops (such as fuel or biomass crops) or non-commercial crops (such as game-cover or wild-bird seed crops) on set-aside land, and to spread it in patches or strips around the farm rather than taking whole fields out of production. They could also put low-yielding areas and field margins under grass and keep them out of production for more than one year. These various amendments to the set-aside scheme greatly increased its value for birds in the further time that payments under the scheme remained available.

CONCLUDING REMARKS

As a habitat for birds, arable land differs from more natural habitats in several ways. First, with the annual need for the preparation of a seed-bed, ploughing usually leaves the soil bare for some weeks or months each year. In the absence of manure applications, repeated cropping tends to reduce the humus content of the soil, and hence the abundance of soil-dwelling invertebrates on which many birds feed. The vegetation of arable land usually consists of a single short-lived monoculture crop, changed from year to year, but each year subjected to pesticide applications which restrict its weed and invertebrate populations, and hence the food it offers for birds. Farmland bird species that nest on the ground within crops often have their eggs or chicks destroyed by agricultural operations.

Over recent decades, the numbers of mixed arable/livestock farms in Britain have greatly declined, crop rotations have become less rigid, and many hedgerows and other semi-natural habitat patches have been removed, so that landscapes have become generally less diverse. Many bird species depended on a local mixture of crop types and semi-natural areas on farmland to maintain themselves year-round, and as farmland has become less diverse, many species have declined and contracted in distribution.

Organic and other farms with low chemical inputs generally hold greater numbers and diversity of plant, invertebrate and bird species than farms with high chemical inputs. In some studies, these differences were striking, in others less so. But farms differ in many other ways than agrochemical use. On a national scale, organic farms are generally found in more diverse landscapes, have more and bigger hedgerows than conventional farms, more spring-sown crops and winter stubbles, and more often support livestock, thus more closely resembling mixed farms of the past. All these features benefit bird and other wildlife populations, in addition to the lack of pesticide use.

A 'set-aside' scheme ran in Britain from 1992 to 2007, in which farmers were paid to leave some of their land uncropped for one or more years. Management of set-aside was not designed to benefit wildlife, and in this respect it was an opportunity missed. On average, however, rotational (one-year) set-aside proved able to support greater densities of birds, summer and winter, than other agricultural land under conventional management. Its value increased over the years, as more bird-friendly management was permitted.

The net impact of all these various changes in farms, crops and rotations was a great reduction in the diversity of habitats available to birds within districts, a big reduction in the food supplies of many species, and a less suitable environment for ground-nesting species. Other major changes affecting birds on arable land are discussed in the next chapter.

## CHAPTER 10

## Arable Land: Crop Growth, Harvest and Birds

THE REVOLUTION IN ARABLE FARMING that occurred mainly during the latter half of the 20th century involved the development of higher-yielding crop varieties, massively increased use of chemical fertilisers and pesticides, and greater mechanisation of almost every operation, from ploughing to crop management and harvest. It also involved a large-scale transition from spring-sown to autumn-sown cereals, which in turn brought a big decline of winter stubble fields. These were additional to the changes in landscape, farm structure and cropping discussed in the previous chapter. All these changes led to greatly increased crop yields, but also to big reductions in wild plant and animal populations, including birds. The period of most intensive change, as judged by various agricultural and biodiversity measures, occurred during the 1970s–90s (Chamberlain et al. 2000b). This chapter examines these changes in more detail, together with their effects on bird populations.

AGRICULTURAL OPERATIONS

Mechanisation means that jobs around the farm are now done by machines powered by fossil-fuel derivatives, rather than by horse-power and man-power as in the past. This makes jobs easier, less sensitive to weather, and faster, so that all the major operations can be compressed into shorter periods with reduced labour needs. This is advantageous for the farmer but not for birds, because most operations make food accessible to birds, whether seeds and invertebrates exposed by ploughing, or grain and other edible products left after harvest. It is better for birds to have these foods spread over a longer period of the year than provided in short bursts, separated by long periods of scarcity. Modern harvesting procedures also produce much less spillage and waste than in the past, further reducing the amount available to birds.

Ploughing and seed-bed creation

The main purpose of ploughing is to turn over the upper layer of soil, bringing fresh nutrients to the surface as bare ground while burying weeds and remains from the previous crop. In the past, before planting the new crop, each arable field was subjected to several operations – some combination of ploughing, disc-harrowing, harrowing and rolling – at each of which buried food was revealed, whether weed seeds or earthworms and other invertebrates. Only after a suitable seed-bed had been created could seed be sown or plants planted. The whole process extended from field to field over several weeks in late winter and spring, a time when alternative foods for birds were scarce. Flocks of hundreds of birds took advantage, invertebrate-feeders following the plough and seed-eaters remaining on freshly turned ground for up to several weeks, feasting on the seeds exposed. Another opportunity for birds to obtain cereal grains came with sowing, when some seeds were spilled on the surface or were not properly buried. Nowadays, the several operations from ploughing to sowing can be accomplished in one or two passes by tractors that carry several implements at once. With improvements in seed-drills, the spillage is also much less than it was, and because most sowing over much of Britain now takes place in late summer rather than spring, it comes at a less useful time for birds. In addition, foods suitable for birds in the soil, whether seeds or invertebrates, are much reduced, as explained below.

Root crops are now often planted using precision drilling, in which treated seeds are placed individually at appropriate depth and spacing in the rows. This procedure reduces the seed and thinning costs, and gives more uniform crop growth and higher yields, because each plant has the space for optimum development. However, good preparation of the seed-bed is crucial, and more careful management is needed. As far as birds are concerned, the pesticide-coated seeds are effectively unavailable, and probably at too low a density to be worth digging for.

Another change that has occurred on a smaller scale is the introduction of 'minimum cultivation' methods (MIN-TILL, or non-inversion tillage, NIT). These methods involve sowing seeds directly into unploughed ground such as cereal stubble, using specialised drills. This can be achieved without any prior cultivation (direct drilling), or by first working the surface soil with a disc harrow or cultivator (chisel plough) to create a seed-bed and incorporate trash from the previous crop. The three alternative processes of conventional mould-board ploughing, chisel ploughing and direct drilling result in progressively decreasing degrees of soil disturbance, and progressively decreasing exposure and mortality of soil-dwelling organisms.

Minimum cultivation methods have several advantages for the farmer. Besides saving time and cultivation costs, they also reduce the loss of soil moisture, leaching of soil nitrogen and risk of erosion. If there is any reduction in crop yield, it is more than offset by reduced diesel costs. Such methods are also good for birds because they reduce the oxidation and breakdown of the soil organic matter, leaving more food for soil invertebrates; they also leave some grain and weed seeds on the surface, and kill fewer soil-dwelling organisms than conventional ploughing (Cunningham et al. 2002). In winter, various birds more often use fields under non-inversion tillage than fields under conventional tillage (Cunningham et al. 2005). However, non-inversion methods cannot be applied universally, for in some places they encourage soil compaction and weed-grasses, rather than the broad-leaved weeds favoured by ploughing (Higginbotham et al. 2000).

In the long term, earthworm numbers can increase under minimum cultivation. In one study, after eight years of direct drilling, the deep-burrowing earthworms Lumbricus terrestris and Aporrectodea longa were 17.5 and 37.3 times more numerous than in ploughed fields, while numbers in chisel-ploughed plots were intermediate. Over the same period, the shallower-burrowing A. caliginosa and A. chlorotica increased in direct-drilled over ploughed plots by at most 3.4 times (Edwards & Lofty 1982). On another farm, a comparison of seven cereal fields that had been direct-drilled for several years with seven other cereal fields that had been ploughed conventionally again revealed significantly more earthworms in direct-drilled fields: L. terrestris was six times more numerous, and A. longa and A. chlorotica were both three times more numerous, with no difference in A. caliginosa (Edwards & Lofty 1982). Other studies showed that this difference in worm populations between direct-drilled and ploughed fields increased through time, and that direct drilling had no adverse effect on crop yields. In general, the deep-burrowing earthworm species (which nevertheless come to the surface) benefited most from minimal cultivation and thereby provided a big increase in potential food for worm-eating bird species (Edwards & Lofty 1982).

Operations during crop growth

Until the mid-20th century, cereal fields were often left undisturbed for several months between sowing and harvest, which was about a month later than now. This left ample time for birds to breed undisturbed within the crop. Skylarks could raise 2–3 broods in that time, and Corn Buntings 1–2. Nowadays, cereal crops are often sprayed several times during the growing season, and although tractors stick to the same tracks each time, these operations are disturbing, and any nests on the trackways are destroyed (Donald 2004). Spraying may not harm birds directly, but it can greatly reduce the insects on which they might otherwise feed.

Look at a modern cereal or rape field and you will see a pattern of parallel tracks running through the crop (Fig. 99). These so-called tramlines, each 30–50 cm wide, accommodate the wheels of the tractor and guide it through the crop in such a way that no parts are missed during fertilising and spraying operations, and none receives a double dose. The distance between parallel tramlines is calculated according to the width of the boom on the sprayer (current maximum 36 m). Tramline spraying began around 1970 and soon became the norm. It is aimed to give modern cereal fields a uniform dense sward and a uniform absence of weeds and insect pests. Using GPS technology, the most modern equipment will also adjust the amount of fertiliser to what is needed in different parts of the field, according to measures of the greenness of the vegetation as the tractor passes over, or to measures of the yield of the previous crop on the same ground, all information which can be stored in an on-board computer.

For root crops, the type and timing of disturbance has changed. In the past, hand hoeing of surplus plants and weeds was a time-consuming operation occurring well within the bird breeding season. Gangs of men hoeing every row have now been replaced by tractor-drawn hoes or chemical sprays. Whether by hand or mechanical means, hoeing can destroy nests, but other potential effects on birds result from the removal of weeds and their associated insects, which can now be achieved more efficiently than in the past, with longer-lasting results.

FIG 99. Tramlines in cereal crops, made by the tractor wheels and used consistently through the summer for spraying operations (Ian Newton).

FIG 100. A scene from the past: thinning and weeding of young turnips by hand (Bobby Smith).

Harvesting

In the past, the harvesting of cereals involved several steps, as described in Chapter 4, at each of which grain was spilled, providing a food source for birds and mammals over more than half of each year. Some birds still feed on the grain before harvest, with House Sparrows and other small birds clinging to the stems to access the seeds, and larger birds such as Rooks and Woodpigeons gaining access to the seed-heads mainly when the plants are 'lodged' (flattened by wind or rain). But in the past, after the crop had been cut and sheaved, these and other birds also perched on the stooks (typically formed of eight standing sheaves) to access the grain. And after harvest on the stubble fields, many species picked the spilled grain or weed seeds from the ground, as long as they lasted into winter. This stubble seed thus provided a major autumn–winter food source for game birds, pigeons and doves, some waterfowl, corvids, finches, buntings and sparrows (Chapter 6). Further grain and weed seeds were made available at intervals through the winter into the next spring, as stacks were dismantled for threshing, attracting many different seed-eating species to stack-yards. On some farms, sheaves were withdrawn every week to provide oats for cattle and horses, again creating spillage available to wild birds. Grain was also stored in barns to which birds often had access, so one way or another grain was available to wild birds almost year-round.

FIG 101. House Sparrows Passer domesticus feeding on ripening wheat gain (Chris Knights).

Today, cutting and threshing are accomplished quickly in one operation by combine harvesters, greatly reducing the amount of grain that is spilled and the period over which it is available to birds. As combine harvesters increased in numbers and efficiency, harvest waste declined, and rick-yards dwindled, taking with them a major winter food source for a variety of wildlife. For the most part, grain is now stored in bins and silos to which neither rodents nor birds have access; and the presence of rat or bird droppings in grain intended for human consumption usually leads to rejection of the whole load by milling companies.

PESTICIDES ON ARABLE LAND

As discussed in Chapter 8, the use of pesticides in Britain increased more than tenfold during the latter half of the 20th century. This resulted from increases in the land area treated, the number of applications per year, and the variety of chemicals available. Several hundred toxic compounds in various formulations are now sold in Britain each year for use as pesticides. The numbers of birds dying from direct pesticide poisoning has apparently declined over the years, as most of the more toxic chemicals have been phased out, but the indirect effects of pesticides on bird populations, via depression of their food supplies, have probably worsened.

Herbicides and weed control

The use of herbicides to control the weeds of arable land removes a huge food source for seed-eating birds. Seeds may be taken directly from the plants or picked from the ground, while others are turned to the surface each time the soil is ploughed (Chapter 7). Herbicide use thus not only destroys the food-base of these birds in the year of spraying, it also prevents replenishment of the seed-bank in the soil, leading to its progressive depletion over time. Each year, seeds turned up by ploughing may germinate and grow, but are then killed by herbicide sprays before they can produce more seeds. As a result of this process, arable land in Britain seems now to have almost lost most of its former wild plants, with declines widely documented, both in local studies and in the Countryside Surveys conducted at intervals since 1978 (Smart et al. 2000, Firbank & Smart 2002, Carey et al. 2008, Potts et al. 2010). There are more critically endangered plant species on arable land than in any other habitat in Britain (Dines 2016).

Common arable weeds which into the 1970s provided food for large numbers of seed-eating birds include Persicaria, Fat-hen, Knotgrass, Charlock and Chickweed (Newton 1967, Wilson et al. 1999). These and other broad-leaved weeds have to some extent been replaced by a small group of other crop weeds, including Black-grass, Barren Brome and Cleavers, which are inadequately controlled by the herbicides in current use, but are of little or no value to seed-eating birds. The impact of herbicides on the wild plants of arable land could increase further in the years ahead if more herbicide-resistant crop varieties come into use, encouraging chemical weed control on an even wider range of crop types than at present.

Herbicide use also leads to decline in the insects that depend on 'weeds'. The dramatic decline of the Grey Partridge from the 1960s was attributed largely to poor production of young, in turn due mainly to lack of insect food for chicks (Potts 1986, 2012, Potts & Aebischer 1995). Broad-leaved weed species, which form the food plants of the relevant insects (notably sawfly larvae), became scarce in modern cereal fields as a result of herbicide use, and many other insects were affected directly or indirectly by fungicides or directly by insecticides. The survival of young Grey Partridges (up to three weeks old) was found to be directly correlated with the abundance of insects in cereal fields. In experimental field trials, reduced herbicide use resulted in improved weed and insect populations, better chick survival, and greater Partridge densities (Rands 1985). The finger pointed unequivocally to herbicides as the primary cause of decline in Grey Partridges during the 1960s–80s, but in later years other factors also became involved (Potts 2012).

FIG 102. The Grey Partridge Perdix perdix was once widespread on arable land throughout Britain, but has now disappeared from most of its former range (Frank Snykers).

The collapse in Grey Partridge numbers was not restricted to Britain, where this research was done, but was general throughout the agricultural range of the species, with an estimated decline in the world population from around 120 million in 1950 to around 4.3 million in 1990 (Potts 2012), with further reduction since then. Research findings in Britain led to the recommendation that landowners keen to conserve Grey Partridges for hunting purposes should leave an unsprayed strip around the edges of cereal fields, so-called 'conservation headlands' (Chapter 20). This procedure enabled broad-leaved weeds to grow, which in turn supported the necessary insects. It led to increased local densities of Partridges and several other bird species (Potts 2012). However, not enough farmers adopted this measure, and the overall Grey Partridge population in Britain continued to decline, with a net loss of around 92% between 1970 and 2013 (Table 3, Fig. 16). In other studies, chick survival in Red-legged Partridges and Pheasants was also correlated with the abundance of preferred insects (Green 1984, Hill 1985). Were it not for the fact that both these species can easily be reared artificially and released, they would almost certainly have also declined greatly over recent decades.

Insecticides, molluscicides and fungicides

Together, these various chemicals can destroy a large part of the invertebrate fauna of arable land, mainly those species that live in the crop vegetation but also some that live on or below the soil surface (Chapter 5). Fungicides are used to control the fungal diseases of plants, but in so doing they reduce the fungal food supplies of many insects and other small organisms. The net result is a substantial reduction in the invertebrate food supplies of many farmland birds, particularly in late spring and summer when these chemicals are mainly used. This is a time when many birds are feeding young. Some species which feed primarily on seeds, such as buntings, sparrows, Skylarks and partridges, also rely on insects to feed their chicks.

Some fungicides and insecticides are applied in powdered form to cereal and other seeds intended for sowing, protecting them against fungal or insect attack. During sowing, some seeds are usually spilled on the soil surface, so are available to birds which can then be poisoned by eating the treated seeds (Chapter 8). Some birds (such as partridges) can scratch up shallowly buried seeds, while other species (such as Rooks) can obtain them by probing into the soil. In the past, the newly sown seeds of beet, turnips and swedes were sometimes eaten by birds, but the pelleting of the seed with a pesticide-infused coating has now reduced the availability and attractiveness of this source of food.

FIG 103. Skylark Alauda arvensis at nest in arable field (Chris Knights). Skylarks prefer to nest in the shorter, sparse growth of spring-sown cereals, but when they nest in autumn-sown cereals most pairs abandon their territories by late May, when the vegetation is too tall for them, and any remaining pairs nest near the open tramlines where they are vulnerable to predation.

In modern farmland, most insects are now much scarcer than in pre-pesticide days, apart perhaps from the aphids against which much of the spraying is directed. This is not because aphids are resistant to the chemicals used against them, but because their insect predators are even more vulnerable, so after spraying, aphids can re-colonise and recover more rapidly in almost predator-free conditions. Comparing insect populations in different crops subject to a standard spraying regime in 1999–2000, rape and beans often supported more insects than cereals, and cereals more than root crops such as potatoes and sugar beet (Holland et al. 2002). Because of the dependence of rape, beans and peas on insect pollinators, farmers normally avoided spraying insecticide on these crops during the flowering period. With wind-pollinated crops, such as cereals, the destruction of insect pollinators was not an issue. Regardless of crop, insects were generally more abundant near the edges of fields than nearer the centre.

The Grey Partridge is not the only species to suffer from shortage of insects. Several studies have shown how scarcity of insects, resulting mainly from insecticide use, reduces the productivity of nesting songbirds, such as the Yellowhammer, Corn Bunting and Skylark (Brickle et al. 2000, Boatman et al. 2004, Morris et al. 2005, Hart et al. 2006). In all three species, relationships were apparent between insecticide use, arthropod abundance, adult foraging behaviour and chick condition and, in at least the two buntings, between chick condition and chick survival. Minimising pesticide applications during March–June, and the provision of unsprayed foraging habitat, were found to benefit Yellowhammers and others (Morris et al. 2005). On the basis of their diets and ecology, at least 18 bird species are likely to have been affected indirectly by pesticide use in Britain (Campbell et al. 1997, Boatman et al. 2004). Such species have declined substantially, but in the absence of more detailed studies, it is hard to say how much these declines were due to pesticide use, and how much to other agricultural changes that occurred at the same time.

For decades, many pesticides have been applied directly to the soil, either as seed-dressings or as nematocides or molluscicides, all affecting soil-dwelling invertebrates. Decline of these soil organisms has not been documented as fully as that of some above-ground insects. But if underground invertebrates have been affected as much as above-ground ones, the depletion of the soil-based food supplies of birds may have been similarly great, with many species largely eliminated from many arable areas. Besides the obvious declines in pest species such as wireworms and leatherjackets, and the vulnerability of earthworms and other organisms to toxic seed-dressings, little quantitative information is available.

TIMING OF SOWING AND HARVESTING

Several developments underpinned a change in the timing of crop-sowing from mainly spring to mainly autumn. One was the selective breeding of hardier cereal varieties which could withstand the conditions of winter. A second was newer herbicides which facilitated the greater weed control involved. This was important, because cereals sown in the autumn would usually become smothered with weeds, such as Chickweed and Cleavers, which at this time of year could outgrow the cereals, reducing their subsequent yield. But post-harvest spraying with herbicide before the new crop was sown prevented this from happening. A third development was the combine harvester, which greatly speeded up the cereal harvest, as mentioned above. The land could then be ploughed and re-sown before it became too wet under autumn rains. This change in timing of ploughing and sowing greatly reduced the numbers of winter stubble fields, which had previously supported large numbers of seed-eating birds through much of the winter. Cereal stubbles are still the main feeding habitat for Skylarks wintering inland in Britain, and also for Yellowhammers, Cirl Buntings and Corn Buntings.

Spring-sown cereals, stubbles and leys

In traditional spring sowing, cereal crops were planted sometime between January and April in the south, and mainly in March or April in the north. There was little growth before April at the earliest, and harvest was fairly late, mostly in August–September. The stubble was then left for ploughing whenever conditions allowed during the winter or spring. But until they were ploughed, stubble fields provided important feeding places for seed-eating birds, which ate any spilled grain or weed seeds remaining on the field surface.

In the southern half of Britain, most stubbles had been ploughed by Christmas, with a few remaining into March, with considerable year-to-year variation depending on weather. The advantages of early ploughing were the better tilth that resulted from subsequent frosts and the security against poor weather that could prevent ploughing later in winter. Spring sowings needed to be started as soon as the land had dried sufficiently to prepare a seed-bed. Despite regional differences, seed-eating birds would have faced a progressive decline in the area of stubble available during each winter, as well as a progressive depletion in the food they contained (Potts 2003). Some fields were 'under-sown' with a grass–clover mix soon after planting the cereal crop. Wheat can germinate in 2–3 days, while the grass and clover take longer. The grass and clover remained short until after the cereal harvest and then grew up through the cereal stubble to produce by early spring fresh grazing suitable for sheep or cattle. It was chiefly these under-sown stubbles, which formed up to a fifth of the total, that survived the winter and beyond without ploughing.

In the past, three main alternative seed sources were available to seed-eating birds in late winter, namely the seeds spilled at livestock feeding sites in the fields, those spilled at threshing and other operations around farmyards, and the weed seeds turned up by ploughing and subsequent cultivations. For different reasons, all three sources are now almost gone. And with the demise of under-sowing, most of the winter stubble fields seen in the countryside since 1988 resulted from set-aside (ended in 2007) or from agri-environment schemes (still ongoing). However, these modern stubbles differ from their predecessors in containing much reduced quantities of seeds, as a result of herbicide use and more efficient harvesting.

In modern autumn-sown cereals, ploughing and sowing take place in late summer, soon after harvest, with the new crops emerging days later. In some years in southern England, large areas of landscape have been harvested and re-sown before the end of August. Late-summer sowing is not a wholly new phenomenon: cereal varieties developed for this purpose began to appear in the 1930s, but it was not until the 1960s and 1970s that they came into general use. To farmers, such crops are known as 'winter cereals' and as 'autumn sown' even though they are usually planted in late summer.

In England and Wales, spring-sown cereals declined from nearly 80% of the total in the 1960s to around 10% of the total in the 1990s, with a slight increase to the present. In Scotland, the proportion declined from more than 95% to less than 60% over the same period. The change affected Scotland less than England and Wales because harvests are later in Scotland and autumn sowing less certain. In the north of Scotland, conditions are generally considered too cold and wet to plant cereals until April, and spring planting is still the norm, although – weather permitting – the fields may be ploughed in autumn or winter in preparation for sowing in spring. In southern Britain, most rape is also sown soon after the previous harvest, before autumn sets in. In most years, the net consequence is that more than two-thirds of all arable land in Britain is now planted in late summer or autumn.

Farmers gain several advantages from this change in timing. Autumn sowing gives the grain an early start, so the plants are well rooted before winter sets in. By the following spring, they are tall enough 'to hide a hare', and are thus better able to exploit the greater hours of sunshine in spring and early summer, which ensures a higher yield. The harvest is usually about a month earlier than for spring-sown crops, beginning about mid-July in southern Britain, and giving plenty of time for the field to be cleared, ploughed and sown with the next crop. Seed germination failures are much less frequent in autumn than in spring, when wet weather can sometimes lead to poor and patchy establishment. Given these advantages, farmers over much of Britain are unlikely to shift back on a large scale to spring-sown crops, except perhaps as a result of some pest or weed problem that they cannot resolve in other ways.

This simple change in the timing of ploughing and grain planting became within a few years the norm over most of arable Britain. It had three main consequences for birds: (1) it removed a huge winter food supply for seed-eating species, burying it out of reach within a short time after harvest; (2) it removed much optimal breeding habitat for Lapwing and other ground-nesting birds that favoured the short and sparse vegetation provided by spring sowing; and (3) the earlier harvest could destroy the late nests of other bird species still nesting within the crop. The sections below examine these matters in more detail.

The decline in winter stubble fields and their seed supplies

Earlier ornithologists recognised the importance of stubble fields, and older texts mention flocks of hundreds or thousands of seed-eating birds commonly seen feeding there in autumn and winter. Although some stubbles are still left over winter, for reasons already mentioned, they provide much less food than in the past. Moreover, varieties of grain intended for autumn sowing have little dormancy, so what little is spilled germinates soon after harvest. Only if spring-sown varieties are used does grain last on the stubble into winter without starting to grow.

Studies have shown that birds still use cereal stubbles much more often than expected from their proportion in the landscape (Wilson et al. 1996, Perkins et al. 2008). As well as various seeds, stubbles that are left into winter provide habitat for further weed growth, and protection from cultivation for some invertebrates. Some weeds that germinate after harvest, such as Chickweed and Groundsel, can produce seeds within a few weeks (Butler et al. 2010). Together with any spilled grain and weed seeds already on the soil surface, they provide food for seed-eating birds. Pigeons, game birds and Skylarks also eat the leaves of various weeds. Barley stubbles generally attract more birds than wheat stubbles. This may be because barley crops tend to be grown on lighter soils and receive fewer chemical inputs, resulting in more weed seeds in the stubble, and also because the slightly sparser sward gives birds easier access to the ground. If left unploughed, fields of harvested broad-leaved crops, such as oilseed rape, also provide winter seeds for many small bird species, but are less useful for Yellowhammers and Corn Buntings, which mainly eat cereal grains and seemingly avoid oily seeds.

Cereals grains weigh, on average, about 0.45 g each, which is about 45 times heavier than the average small weed seed, at around 0.01 g (Larkman et al. 2015). Cereal grains are therefore much more suitable for large birds, such as pigeons, game birds, corvids and waterfowl. But they are also eaten in quantity by Corn Buntings, Yellowhammers and Skylarks. In the past, grains from stubble fields were a major food source for the larger species from late summer into December, by which time remaining grain densities had declined to such a level that they no longer provided an adequate food source for these birds. However, they were still sufficient for smaller birds such as Corn Buntings and Yellowhammers. Past studies of the feeding habits of various species confirm that the four groups of larger birds took stubble grain into December but little beyond this date, whereas Yellowhammers and Corn Buntings took stubble grains commonly into late January, and in smaller amounts beyond (see Newton et al 1974 for Greylag and Pink-footed Geese; Colquhoun 1951, Murton 1964 for Woodpigeon; Holyoak 1968 for Rook and other corvids; Evans 1969, Prys-Jones 1977 for buntings). In all of these species, cereal grains increased again in the diet at the time of spring sowings, which were normal at the time.

FIG 104. In autumn and spring, Goldfinches Carduelis carduelis, Linnets Linaria cannabina and Chaffinches Fringilla coelebs feed on the seeds of early-growing Chickweed Stellaria media which springs up on stubble fields (Chris Knights).

In 1970, grain loss from combine harvesters was calculated at 2–3% of the crop, amounting to around 250 cereal grains per square metre left on fields (Robinson 1997, Robinson & Sutherland 2002). Despite increasing crop yields, this figure had fallen to around 60 grains/m2 by 1990, and losses as low as 20 grains/m2 were reported in the late 1990s (Robinson & Sutherland 2002). So over the period 1970–2000, the average grain spillage on cereal fields could have declined from 250 to 20 seeds/m2, a 92% reduction. Now if 67% of cereal fields were ploughed soon after harvest, this would reduce the 8% of seeds remaining to 2.7% of their former abundance. Allowing for the slight increase in the area of cereals grown over this period, these figures still imply a roughly 97% reduction in the amount of grain available on unploughed stubble. In fact, the reduction could be even greater because, unless they were quickly consumed, many of these grains would have germinated within a few weeks after harvest. Early germination is less likely to have happened in the past when spring-sown varieties prevailed. However approximate these calculations may be, the amount of available grain on stubble fields has clearly decreased massively over recent decades. Only in years of bad weather, with a delayed or unachieved harvest, is a substantial amount of grain now likely to be left.

Now consider the loss over the years of weed seeds from overwinter stubble fields. Being such small seeds, they are most important for smaller seed-eaters, such as finches, Tree Sparrows, Reed Buntings and Skylarks. But when present at high densities, they are also eaten by pigeons and game birds. The densities of weed seeds in arable soil have been calculated in various studies spanning more than a century. Most estimates lie in the range 300–1,200 seeds per square metre present on the surface and in the top centimetre of soil (Robinson & Sutherland 1999; Moorcroft et al. 2002; Robinson et al. 2004; Bohan et al. 2005; Butler et al. 2010). An analysis of time trends indicated a reduction in mean seed density of approximately 17 seeds/m2 per year, from some 1,400 seeds/m2 in 1920 to 1,000 in 1945, 500 in 1975 and 170 in 1995 (Fig. 105; Robinson & Sutherland 2002, Larkman et al. 2015). This represents an 88% reduction in available weed seeds on stubble fields over this 75-year period, and an 83% reduction within the last 50 years of this period. Accepting that about two-thirds of all stubble fields were lost to late summer ploughing over this same period, this brings the total reduction in stubble weed seeds to about 95%. So taking cereal and weed seeds together, this represents an enormous decline in bird food supplies over recent decades. It is not surprising that those small seed-eating species that fed mainly in winter stubble fields have declined so markedly in Britain in the years since 1970 (see Table 3). They include the Corn Bunting (declined by 90%), Yellowhammer (55%), Tree Sparrow (90%), Linnet (60%) and Skylark (60%). Larger seed-eating species had alternative foods, some of which increased over recent decades, and most of these species did not decline (see later).

Whether a given bird species can survive on stubble seeds alone depends not only on the types of seeds present, but also on whether the seeds occur at densities high enough for individual birds to find and eat enough in the daylight hours available (Larkman et al. 2015). Birds normally pick seeds from the ground individually, and smaller species (such as finches, buntings and sparrows) usually have to de-husk them before swallowing, a process that takes time. Larger birds, such as pigeons and partridges, swallow seeds without de-husking them, but have much greater daily food needs than smaller birds, so they require greater densities of seeds. In autumn, Grey Partridges and Yellowhammers rarely fed on fields with grain densities less than 50/m2, and in autumn and winter Linnets and Reed Buntings rarely fed on fields with small weed-seed densities less than 250/m2 (Moorcroft et al. 2002), and Skylarks rarely below 450/m2 (Robinson 2001, Stephens et al. 2003). At lower seed densities, it was calculated that individual birds could not find and process seeds sufficiently quickly to maintain themselves. So it was not just the presence of appropriate seeds that mattered, but also their densities and availabilities on the ground.

FIG 105. Published estimates of seed densities in arable soils. Points represent densities of dicotyledonous seeds in the top 1 cm of soil in arable fields in Britain and Denmark. Studies were included only if they sampled the entire seed-bank between September and November and the fields had been part of a cereal-based rotation for at least five years; results from adjacent fields and years were averaged. Slope of regression through British data: −17 seeds m−2 year−1, R2 = 0·35. From Robinson & Sutherland (2002).

Because cereal grains are so much bigger than weed seeds, the same bird species can survive on lower densities of cereal grains than of weed seeds. With cereal grains down to 20/m2 on stubble fields, Skylarks would need to spend almost all of a nine-hour winter day foraging, still risking starvation on cold days (Robinson 2001). As well as picking up cereal grains from the surface, they can dig out grains from just below the surface, although this slows their intake rates. In experimental trials, Skylarks removed more than 90% of grains on the surface, about 23% of those down to 3 mm below the surface, and less than 5% of those down to 6 mm (Robinson 2001). They presumably found the buried seeds by raking the soil aside with the bill, an action also used by finches, but not possible where the soil surface has hardened. In another study, Skylarks took mainly cereal grains whenever they were available at sufficient density, but otherwise turned to weed seeds from bare ploughed land or young cereal leaves, providing one-tenth as much energy per unit time as cereal grains (Green 1978). With such a heavy dependence on cereal or weed seeds from winter stubble fields or bare ploughed land, it is little wonder that numbers of Skylarks in Britain have been in decline for nearly 50 years. And because Skylarks nesting in the uplands also move to low ground for the winter, they also experience the massively reduced food supplies on winter arable land.

Before around 1975, weedy stubbles in autumn could provide small seed food (that is, excluding cereal grains) at average densities adequate for all small species, but at least since 1945 (and possibly well before that) not at sufficient average densities for large species (Larkman et al. 2015). For much of the winter, weed seeds in cereal stubbles therefore represented a widespread low-density food resource that could be exploited by small species relatively free from competition from large seed-eating species. However, at some point prior to 1995, the average weed-seed density in autumn fell below the level required to support even the smallest species, such as Linnet and Tree Sparrow. Thus, not only did the area of overwintered stubbles decrease dramatically with the switch to autumn-sown grain, but most of the remaining areas became inadequate as food sources for even small birds. However, these statements are based on average seed-values, and throughout the period concerned, individual fields would have varied greatly in their seed-contents. Even in recent years, some have supported small flocks of finches and buntings, at least into early winter. Moreover, during each winter, the progressive depletion of the whole seed resource, consisting of both cereal and weed seeds, would have made arable stubbles steadily less suitable, first for the largest species and then for the smaller ones.

On cereal stubbles and other arable fields, most birds are found on those offering the greatest densities of surface seeds, either cereal grains or weed seeds (Fig. 106). In different studies, relationships between seed and bird densities were evident in Grey Partridges, Red-legged Partridges, Skylarks, Chaffinches, Linnets, Tree Sparrows, Yellowhammers, Reed Buntings and Corn Buntings (Robinson & Sutherland 1999, Robinson 2001, Moorcroft et al. 2002).

As well as seed densities, stubble height can affect its use by birds. Many flocking seed-eaters, which rely on flight to escape predators, prefer to feed in areas of short stubble and much bare ground, thus reducing visual obstruction (Butler et al. 2005, Whittingham et al. 2006). For example, the likelihood of Linnets, Reed Buntings and Corn Buntings occurring on stubble fields increased from less than 10% to over 50% as bare ground increased from zero to 70% of the field surface (Moorcroft et al. 2002). Skylarks and partridges are more reliant on crypsis, and favoured denser and taller stubble. In an experimental study, two heights of stubble were provided in different halves of the same fields. Again, tall stubble (over 12 cm) was preferred by cryptic species seeking cover, such as partridges and Skylarks, while shorter stubble (6 cm) was preferred by species that depended more on vigilance and fleeing to escape predators, such as finches, sparrows and buntings (Butler et al. 2005). The taller corvids and pigeons showed no clear preference for either height of stubble.

FIG 106. Use of fields during November–March by four seed-eating birds in relation to the densities of seeds available. Each point is a mean density across several counts from each field. Yellowhammer figures are for cereal grains alone, other species for total edible seeds. All relationships statistically significant. Modified from Robinson & Sutherland (1999).

FIG 107. Buntings feed on grain and weed seeds available on stubble fields, but on most fields the density of seeds has declined to the point where the birds are often unable to find enough food. Left, Reed Bunting Emberiza schoeniclus; right, Yellowhammer Emberiza citrinella (Alan Martin).

Many small birds that search for seeds in fields feed for preference on the field edges, escaping into the hedgerow when danger threatens. This is obvious in the behaviour of Tree Sparrows and Yellowhammers, for example. But species with a different escape response, such as Skylarks, prefer to feed in the middles of fields, working towards the edges in late winter as food in the middle becomes depleted (Robinson & Sutherland 1999). Not surprisingly, periods of snow can prevent small birds from getting seeds from the surface of stubble fields, an effect especially important for Skylarks, which have few alternative food sources in winter. The amount of field surface covered by snow was found to affect the numbers of Skylarks seen feeding there (Robinson 2001), and at times of widespread deep snow Skylarks are among the most conspicuous 'weather migrants' which travel southward to areas still free of snow, with thousands per hour seen passing particular observation points (Newton 2010).

Importance of under-sown cereals

In the past, as mentioned above, it was common practice to under-sow growing cereals with a mixture of grass and clover to provide the next crop in a rotation (a ley). Under-sown stubbles were major winter feeding areas for various seed-eating birds into the winter, and as seed stocks dwindled, Woodpigeons and Grey Partridges switched increasingly to the developing clover leaves, which became a major food in January–February until spring-sown grain became available (Murton et al. 1966). Under-sown fields also provided undisturbed wintering habitat for various invertebrates, including the pupae of many insect groups important to farmland birds in the subsequent breeding season. Cultivations drastically reduced their numbers, but where stubble fields were left into spring, adult insects emerged and produced the next generation of larvae. For example, sawflies overwinter successfully in leys established under cereals. After emergence, the adults move into growing cereal crops, where their larvae form an important summer food for Skylark, bunting and partridge chicks (Barker et al. 1999, Ewald & Aebischer 1999, Potts 2003). In Sussex, the distribution of Grey Partridges and Corn Buntings into the 1990s was closely related to the distribution of under-sown arable leys (Aebischer & Ward 1997, Potts 1997). On one large farm where grass–clover leys were still grown, Corn Buntings maintained good numbers at a time when they were fast disappearing from most of southern England (Potts 2012). Over much of Britain, under-sown stubble fields are now quite rare.

Stubbles under-sown with clover also provided favoured nesting sites for Corn Buntings and Skylarks, as well as for Reed Buntings in some areas (O'Connor & Shrubb 1986). Clover also suppresses broad-leaved weeds less than grass does, so it allows larger numbers of weeds to develop and seed (Green 1978). This advantage is lost, however, if the cereal crop under which the ley is established was sprayed with herbicide. In the early 20th century, when every farm had livestock, one field in five was under-sown stubble in winter, reducing to one in ten in the three-year ley system which became fashionable for a time in the immediate post-war period (Shrubb 2003). The existence of under-sown cereals in arable systems thus guaranteed overwinter stubbles with food for various species, and provided an element of stability for invertebrate populations in arable land. The loss of this habitat over most of the country, along with the use of insecticides, has probably contributed to big reductions in crucial insect populations, as well as winter seeds.

Implications for birds

From the 1970s then, seed-eating birds in Britain have faced major reductions in food on farmland both from the increased use of herbicides and from the loss of winter stubbles. These two changes could have largely accounted for the declines in small seed-eating species. Starting in the early to mid-1970s, declines continued at least into the mid-1980s, and in some species at a slower rate to well beyond this date. The main species involved included the Greenfinch and Goldfinch (increasing from about the mid-1980s, coinciding with their growing use of garden feeders), Linnet, Redpoll, Twite, Bullfinch, Yellowhammer (declined from the mid-1980s), Reed Bunting, Corn Bunting, House Sparrow, Tree Sparrow, Skylark, Turtle Dove (present in summer only) and Grey Partridge (Fig. 16, Table 3). Not all these species regularly feed from the ground in stubble fields, but they all take the seeds of farmland weeds, so could have been affected by herbicide use. Exceptions to these downward trends among seed-eaters were the Woodpigeon and Stock Dove, which increased from the 1970s, in association with the spread of autumn-sown oilseed rape, whose leaves have since provided an important winter food (Chapter 6). Other exceptions included various corvids, which eat a much wider range of foods and found alternative supplies of cereal grains at the increasing numbers of feed sites established for released game birds (see later). Chaffinches also increased over much of this period, and they increasingly exploited both garden feeders and game-bird feed sites, while in summer they feed largely on insects from trees, immune from the shortages on sprayed farm crops (Whittingham et al. 2001). We can come up with plausible explanations for the increases in most of these species, but only for the pigeons has the situation been researched in depth (Inglis et al. 1997, Box 3).

Habitat problems resulting from early crop growth

Spring-sown cereal crops, with their short sparse vegetation in April–May, have long provided breeding habitat for several bird species that nest on the ground, especially Skylark, Corn Bunting and Lapwing, and more locally for Yellow Wagtail, Oystercatcher and Stone-curlew, and even more locally for Ringed Plover. Birds which nest early in spring-sown crops can suffer high rates of nest failure from farming operations, such as rolling and harrowing, and also from predation. But they benefit from being able to make one or more repeat nesting attempts after early failures. In spring-sown cereals, single-brooded species such as the Lapwing have time after a previous nest failure for two or more further attempts, while multi-brooded Skylarks have time to raise one or two broods before the crop becomes too tall for them (Donald 2004). Lapwings begin breeding earlier than the other species, producing their first clutches in March or April, while Skylarks begin mainly in April. However, most farm work concerned with crop establishment has finished by the end of April, so repeat clutches laid after this date are more likely to hatch successfully (Shrubb 1990). Stone-curlews begin later than Lapwings, in late April or early May, so miss some of the spring activity, but not all.

In contrast to spring-sown cereals, autumn-sown cereals have grown quite tall by spring, and attract fewer nesting birds, which then have time for fewer nesting attempts before the vegetation is too tall for them (see Box 10 for Skylark). Lapwings and Stone-curlews have been found to desert their nesting habitat early in the season, apparently in response to rapid crop growth (Galbraith 1989, Wilson et al. 2005b). Compared to these waders, Skylarks, Yellow Wagtails and Corn Buntings tend to move out at a later stage of crop growth, but some pairs continue to nest there until harvest time, mainly on or near bare patches or tramlines. In effect, the switch in emphasis from spring-sown to autumn-sown cereal crops has reduced the amount of good nesting habitat for all these species, and reduced the number of nesting attempts that can be made each year by a substantial proportion of pairs.

FIG 108. Lapwing Vanellus vanellus at nest on spring-sown barley (Bobby Smith).

For all these open-land birds, the habitat is in an ideal state when the crop is at an early stage, and as it continues to grow it becomes progressively less suitable. The birds find themselves more and more enclosed by the growing crop, and have increasing difficulty in moving around as the vegetation becomes taller and denser. The Corn Bunting and Yellow Wagtail begin laying mainly after mid-May, later than the other species, so they miss the main period of spring cultivations altogether. But they are also more likely to attempt a second nest in spring-sown than in autumn-sown cereals. In a study in eastern Scotland, Corn Buntings that used spring-sown crops for first nesting attempts were almost four times more likely to re-nest than females that nested in autumn-sown crops (Setchfield et al. 2012). The latter females rarely produced a second nest and, when they did, they usually switched nesting habitat.

FIG 109. Left, spring-sown wheat in late May, still attractive to Skylarks Alauda arvensis and other ground-nesting species; right, autumn-sown wheat on the same date, beyond the stage it is attractive to Skylarks (Ian Newton).

For the smaller species, tramlines offer easy access to the ground in an otherwise dense crop, providing both foraging and nesting opportunities for Skylarks, Corn Buntings and Yellow Wagtails. Of almost 1,000 Skylark nests found in cereal crops during 1996–98, nearly half were built near tramlines (Donald 2004). These nests suffered from heavy predation, apparently because predators such as Foxes used the tramlines as walkways through the crop, thereby finding the nests. In autumn-sown cereal crops, Yellow Wagtails also nested mainly on the edges of tramlines, and again suffered high predation rates, but the few nests placed more than 75 cm into the crop produced fledglings (Gilroy et al. 2011). The area covered by tramlines typically amounts to around 5% of the whole field surface, so it is little wonder that, as autumn-sown crops grow, they support much lower densities of birds than spring-sown crops at the same date, and that nests are concentrated in a small part of the overall field area where predation rates are high (for further discussion, see Box 10).

FIG 110. Yellow Wagtails Motacilla flava nest on arable land in some areas, having their first nests in cereal crops, and later nests in potato or bean crops. With the loss of most wet grassland from Britain, arable land has now become the main nesting habitat of this species (Chris Knights).

Because large areas of autumn-sown cereals offer few alternative nesting places for small ground-nesting birds, the breeding season of most pairs in these crops is shortened, reducing their seasonal production of young. But where opportunities are available, some pairs move out of cereal crops part way through the breeding season and settle in different crops nearby, providing they offer easy access to the ground. In one study, Yellow Wagtails were found to shift from partly grown cereals into potato crops, and start another nest there (Gilroy et al. 2010). Autumn-sown wheat was their preferred nesting habitat in May-June, followed by potatoes in July–August, although some pairs nested in field beans where they again suffered high predation rates. Yellow Wagtails nested and fed within the crops, but also foraged on grassy tracks and wet ditch sides. Where no alternative crops were available, it was assumed that the birds made no further nesting attempts, and produced fewer young per season (Gilroy et al. 2009, 2010). They clearly gained from having a diversity of different crop types available close together on the same farm, generally preferring bare ground or short grass for feeding. However, a later study in different areas revealed that Yellow Wagtails could raise two broods in autumn-sown wheat, producing on average more than enough young to maintain the population (Kirby et al. 2012). Clearly, the situation may differ between areas, depending on weather, crops, predation rates and other factors.

Problems of an earlier harvest

Another problem with autumn-sown cereals, compared with spring-sown ones, is the earlier harvest, which often falls within bird breeding seasons. Montagu's Harriers were first documented nesting in cereal fields in Britain in 1968 (with two nests in Norfolk), and by around 1980 cereal crops provided the main nesting habitat. It is practically impossible now for Montagu's Harriers to complete their single-brood nesting cycle in cereal fields before the crop is harvested, a process which kills the young. The risk increased in Britain as the harvest got earlier. Before the 1980s, harvest dates in southern England were around mid-August and very few Montagu's Harrier broods were destroyed at cutting (less than 2%; Underhill-Day 1990). But as harvest became up to a month earlier, almost every brood would have been destroyed if measures had not been taken to protect them. In parts of Europe, where cereal fields are now the main nesting habitat for Montagu's Harriers, the species survives only because ornithologists find and mark the nests, which, with cooperation from farmers, can then be protected at harvest time (Arroyo et al. 2002). Without this intervention, the species would almost certainly disappear from cereal-growing regions, and possibly from most of western Europe. After harvest, fencing the unharvested patch around each nest can protect the brood against mammalian predators (Santangeli et al. 2015).

In large parts of western Europe (including Britain), Montagu's Harriers Circus pygargus frequently nest in cereal fields, but can rear young only if the nests are protected from combine harvesters, which usually operate before the chicks can fly. BOX 10. Effects of the change from spring-sown to autumn-sown cereals on breeding Skylarks

When nesting in growing cereals, Skylarks prefer stands that are less than 30 cm tall, with easy walking between the rows. As the crop grows, it also becomes denser, covering more of the ground. Autumn-sown cereals reach this critical stage a month earlier than spring-sown ones, almost enough time for a whole nesting attempt. Research in various European countries has consistently shown that spring-sown cereals support higher densities of Skylark territories than autumn-sown cereals, but in both types territory densities decline through the season as the crop grows. Skylarks build their nests in the gaps between the rows of plants. Modern cereal fields, and particularly autumn-sown ones, are too densely sown and fertilised for this to be possible once the crop becomes well established. Indeed, birds may even have difficulty in penetrating a growing crop to get at the ground. So as the crop develops, Skylarks run out of usable ground space, and have to seek out patches of retarded growth (if there are any) or tramlines in which to nest and feed.

Radio-tracking studies in Denmark showed that, as cereal crops developed, the Skylarks in them were forced out of the crop and on to the tramlines, despite the fact that food was more available within the crop (Odderskaer et al. 1997). By the end of the breeding season, birds were spending around 70% of their time in tramlines, which occupied around 5% of the field area. Correspondingly, the proportion of nests built on or adjacent to tramlines in autumn-sown cereals increased from zero in April, when birds were clearly avoiding tramlines, to around half of all nests in July. In spring cereals, there was a smaller seasonal rise in the proportion of nests on tramlines. By the middle of the breeding season, around 95% of the area of autumn-sown cereal crops was effectively useless to Skylarks.

As Skylarks can nest on tramlines, it may seem strange that many pairs abandon cereal fields through the summer. However, as more and more of a field is closed to them, remaining pairs may have to claim ever greater lengths of tramline in order to gain enough food, in which case growing competition for shrinking space may force ever more birds out of the field altogether. Increasing nest failures may also play a role. Nests on tramlines are exposed both to tractor wheels and to mammalian predators that evidently use tramlines as walkways through the crop. In consequence, nests built on or adjacent to tramlines are more likely to fail than nests built further into the crop (78% vs. 54%). In addition, because autumn-sown cereals are harvested earlier than spring-sown ones, higher proportions of Skylark nests in autumn-sown cereals are lost to harvesting, although most pairs have ceased nesting by then. Whatever the reason, autumn-sown cereals curtail the Skylarks' breeding season, and their overall seasonal productivity is less in autumn-sown cereals than in spring-sown ones (Eraud & Boutin 2002). If a territory overlaps two or more fields with different crops, pairs may move from one crop to another shorter one during the season. But some pairs in autumn-sown cereals seem to finish breeding early for that year. So a shortened breeding season (with reduced production of young) may be one factor contributing to population decline. Despite a much curtailed breeding season, individual nest success still emerged as better in cereals, at 1.26 chicks per nest on average, compared with 0.78 in set-aside and 0.63 in grass.

(Mainly from Donald 2004)

In parts of western Europe, Hen Harriers also nest in cereal fields, but because they lay, on average, about a fortnight earlier than Montagu's Harriers, most of their young fledge before harvest. In Britain, Marsh Harriers occasionally nest in cereal fields, with the first documented nest in this habitat in 1982, but they too lay earlier than Montagu's Harriers, and mostly escape (Underhill-Day 1990). In any case, Marsh Harriers in Britain still nest mainly in reed-beds, where they are free of disturbance throughout the season. Other species affected by the earlier harvest, such as the Corn Bunting, may manage to raise some young, but not necessarily enough to offset the usual annual mortality, so that they too would be expected to decline. Corn Buntings which lay eggs in late July or early August can still be feeding nestlings into late August or beyond, which takes them through the harvest season for autumn-sown cereal crops, making nest failures almost inevitable.

While the above are the main species affected by harvesting operations, they are not the only ones. There are records of Grey Partridge broods being killed during the cutting of green cereals and lucerne, and later in year of roosting Partridge coveys killed by combines operating at night (Potts 2012). The latter can occur regardless of whether the harvest is early or late. Overall, however, the effect on nesting habitat of the wide-scale change from spring-sown to autumn-sown cereals has been taken as one factor contributing to the decline of Skylarks, Lapwings and other ground-nesting species in Britain over recent decades.

MORE HABITAT ISSUES

Species declines have not been uniform across the country, enabling the population changes of some species to be examined in relation to local farming practices. Over a 10-year period, population trends of Skylarks and Yellowhammers in different 1 km squares across Britain were related to the amount of winter cereal stubble in the local landscape. The average density of this stubble, at 3 ha/km2, was associated with declining populations of both species. But where stubble covered 10–20 ha/km2 both species showed local increases, the Skylark more than the Yellowhammer (Gillings et al. 2005a). Stubble fields provided winter food for both species, and for Skylarks also better nesting habitat in the associated spring-sown crops. This dual advantage for Skylarks may have explained why they showed a stronger relationship to winter stubble than Yellowhammers (which nest in hedges rather than crops). A population model based on these data revealed that, for each additional 5 ha of winter stubble in each km2, the 10-year decline in breeding Skylarks was lessened by four percentage points. So winter stubble availability could explain some of the geographical variation in population trends for these species, and may have been instrumental in their national declines.

Arable fields in pastoral areas

As many farmers in western Britain have increasingly concentrated on grass-based beef and milk production over recent decades, the proportion of arable in these areas has dwindled. This change was accompanied by particularly striking declines in seed-eating birds, including the Grey Partridge, Tree Sparrow, Yellowhammer, Reed Bunting and Corn Bunting, all of which have now gone altogether from many western districts. Moreover, most of the cereal crops that were planted in recent years in pastoral areas were mown for silage before they could seed, and local declines of some species, such as Corn Bunting, have been associated with the change from cereal grain to cereal silage (J. D. Wilson et al. 2007). Studies revealed that the most useful cereal silage crop for birds was spring-sown barley, which, compared to other cereals, provided more invertebrates and weed seeds during its growth and, after cutting for silage, through the ensuing months on the stubble fields (Peach et al. 2011, Westburg et al. 2011). The least useful crop was spring-sown maize, in which the requirement for weed control during the establishment phase limited the quantities of weed seeds produced in the growing season and also after harvest in the stubble.

One proposed way to counter this shortage of seeds in pastoral areas is to grow arable crops in among the grassland. These crops could produce seeds themselves or enable the growth of broad-leaved weeds to provide seeds, a practice supported by agri-environment schemes. Suitable crops include cereals that are allowed to seed, especially when sown in spring. Others include fodder root crops which can be fed to cattle or sheep, while any associated broad-leaved weeds provide the seeds needed by birds. Unripe grain is also a valuable chick food for buntings and sparrows in cold wet summer weather when insects are scarce. Even a small amount of arable land in a pastoral landscape was found to increase the numbers of six seed-eating bird species, an effect that was stronger where arable habitat was scarcer (Robinson et al. 2001).

In any area, fodder root and brassica crops, such as turnips, swedes, fodder beet, rape and kale, can be especially beneficial in providing winter food for seed-eating birds (Chapter 6). At this time of year, it is the broad-leaved weeds within these crops, rather than the crops themselves, that provide the seed food. However, invertebrate prey species are also numerous and accessible in the relatively warm damp microclimate under the canopy, attracting thrushes, pipits, wagtails and Dunnocks to feed there. In spring, the bare ground following brassica and root crops can also provide nesting habitat for Lapwings if cultivation is sufficiently late. All these crops have declined greatly in area over recent decades, because far fewer farms hold livestock, and silage has come to prevail on those that do.

Maize crops

Maize differs from the other cereals produced in Britain, not only because it grows taller and has much larger seeds than the others, but also because it can only be sown in the warm soil of spring. Before the crop grows, maize fields can attract nesting Lapwings and in some localities also Oystercatchers, Ringed Plovers and Little Ringed Plovers, as well as Skylarks, but as in other cereals, the nests of all these species can be destroyed at cultivation and sowing. However, most of these species are now so patchily distributed in Britain that nesting on maize fields is by no means widespread. In the three waders, it occurs mainly near coasts or shingle-bedded rivers which form their main feeding areas. In association with each crop, the land remains bare for several weeks or months each year, which in some districts makes it especially prone to erosion.

NEW FOOD SUPPLIES

Autumn-sown cereals are not a complete loss as far as birds are concerned. One benefit is that the young green plants provide nutritious food for some bird and mammal species in winter. Geese and sometimes swans graze growing cereals, as do Brown Hares, Rabbits and deer. In the past, livestock were sometimes deliberately grazed on young cereals to encourage the plants to tiller, thickening the sward and increasing the yield of grain. Nowadays, any form of grazing is considered undesirable, especially in spring, because it can delay growth and seed formation, and lead to puddling and to uneven ripening across a field. As stressed already, the leaves of autumn-sown rape plants now form a new but important winter food source for pigeons and other birds, and rape seeds (grown for human and livestock consumption) form an important summer food for various seed-eating birds, especially Linnet, Goldfinch and Greenfinch. Rape has thus become a major new food source for birds on farmland, providing seeds in summer and, when sown in autumn, green food through the winter. And if rape fields are left unploughed in autumn, they continue to feed seed-eating birds into winter.

Over the period when winter stubble grain became progressively reduced in Britain, alternative sources of grain and other foods became available at game-bird feed sites. In recent years, thousands of tonnes of seeds have been provided in the countryside each year for released Pheasants and partridges. Although not compensating entirely for the loss of other grain, this huge food source has been exploited not only by game birds, but also by other species, including corvids (Sánchez-García et al. 2015). Its use is likely to have increased over the years in parallel with the numbers of game birds released. According to a survey by the Game & Wildlife Conservation Trust, 89% of shoot managers in Britain provided supplementary food for game birds: the majority (93%) used feed-hoppers and 72% also provided food by hand-scattering. The most commonly provided food was wheat (87%), but barley, maize, triticale and proprietary pellets were also used. In total, some 566,000 tonnes of grain per year could now be provided for game birds (Larkman et al. 2015). This provision is drastically reduced each year after the end of January when the shooting season ends, but leading into the period of greatest food shortage for small seed-eating birds (Siriwardena et al. 2008; Siriwardena 2010; Sánchez-García et al. 2015). Also, some of the seed is distributed in woodland, and so is unlikely to attract open-land species, such as buntings and larks.

The proportion of grain provided in hopper feeders taken by different species was studied in detail using motion-sensing cameras at various sites in southern England (Sánchez-García et al. 2015). In total, some 33 bird species and 14 mammal species were seen to feed at these sites, and hoppers placed near hedgerows attracted more species than those placed in the open. Game birds consumed only 39–48% of this food, depending on the analysis; non-target bird species (predominantly pigeons and corvids) consumed 29–45% of the food provided, while rats consumed 8–33% (the study feeders were caged to exclude deer). Surprisingly, small bird species made little use of the food during the shooting season when supplementary feeding typically occurs, but increased their use of feeders after the end of the shooting season (during the 'hungry gap'), even though only a proportion of hoppers were re-filled then. If the findings from this scattered sample of sites were typical, such sources of grain food may have contributed to increases over recent decades in the numbers of large seed-eaters, such as pigeons and corvids, but can be expected to have been of limited value to small seed-eaters.

Grain feeding is influential in other ways. While on most game-rearing estates, food provision ends with the shooting season (1 February), on some it is continued into spring (usually 30 April). Alternative foods are scarce in the early spring, and in some species this latter practice could influence body condition in preparation for breeding. Analyses revealed that hen Pheasants from 15 estates where supplementary feeding was continued until 30 April had significantly larger fat reserves than hens from 20 other estates where feeding ceased around 1 February. The fat reserves of birds provided with grain in spring were maintained at their winter levels, whereas those of hens foraging on solely natural foods were reduced by up to 50%. This difference was associated with breeding success, for on the two types of estate, the mean numbers of young per hen in late summer were 0.9 and 0.6 respectively, and the mean numbers of young produced per km2 were 13.3 and 6.1 respectively, with both differences statistically significant (Draycott 2002). This study thus indicated the importance of food in late winter to the subsequent breeding success of Pheasants. The main losses of eggs and young were due to predators, and the reduced losses shown by well-fed hens were attributed to their better parental behaviour.

FIG 112. Rook Corvus frugilegus, one of the incidental beneficiaries of widespread Pheasant Phasianus colchicus feeding (Stan Wilson).

In addition to grain provision, game-bird shoots countrywide maintained an overall 93,000 ha of game-cover crops, as assessed in 2006 (PACEC 2006). The most commonly planted cover crop was maize or maize mix, with cereals, linseed, oilseed rape, millet and quinoa as additional ingredients. These crops provided food for many seed-eaters, in addition to game birds (Chapter 20). Seed yields of more than 2 tonnes/ha from such crops could reasonably be assumed (Larkman et al. 2015). On this basis, more than 180,000 tonnes of seed overall may be produced each year by game-cover crops, giving an energy density probably more than eightfold higher than a weedy stubble field. However, game-cover crops shed most of their seed before the end of December, and are typically ploughed at the end of the shooting season in early February, so again provide little or nothing for seed-eaters after this date, which is the most critical time of winter (Siriwardena et al. 2008, Gillings et al. 2010). The value of game-cover crops for wild seed-eaters is therefore uncertain.

In these ways, however, the shooting industry now dispenses very large quantities of seeds into the British countryside, perhaps amounting to more than 700,000 tonnes per year overall (Larkman et al. 2015). This may be compared with a concurrent estimate of 595,000 tonnes of wheat or its equivalent as the total combined winter food need of 14 species of resident farmland seed-eating birds, including reared game birds (Larkman et al. 2015). This food is provided in the form of large (very large in the case of maize) and medium-sized (such as millet) seeds, presented at very high densities. Much of it is taken by non-target species, and it seems inevitable that such a huge amount of food will have benefited some types of wildlife in the wider countryside, large seed-eaters if not small ones.

In addition to game-cover crops, agri-environment schemes have in recent years promoted the growing of wild-bird seed crops (Chapter 20). They are similar to game crops, but contain fewer cereals and a wider range of other seeds, commonly including kale, quinoa, sunflower and fodder radish. In 2009, approximately 12,000 ha were planted with wild-bird seed mixes in England alone (Natural England 2009), and the area has probably increased since then. In most cases, these plots are farmed using fertiliser to achieve high seed yields. Most of the seed produced is in the form of large and medium-sized agricultural seeds, provided at high seed densities. The crops are left unharvested, and both small and large seed-eating species utilise them (Chapter 20). However, like game-cover crops, wild-bird seed plots as currently implemented fail to deliver food resources from February, due to seed depletion, die-back and ploughing-in of the seed-bearing plants. Like game plots, therefore, they can normally be of little or no help to small birds through their period of greatest food shortage during February–April (Siriwardena et al. 2008; Siriwardena 2010). Measures are now being taken to address this issue.

The existence of these extra seed sources in the countryside, especially the seed-hoppers intended for game birds, may help to explain why small and large species of seed-eaters have shown contrasting population trends in recent decades (Larkman et al. 2015). Small species, notably Linnet, Reed Bunting, Yellowhammer, Corn Bunting, Tree Sparrow and Skylark, which in the past fed largely on seeds from winter stubble fields, have all declined; while large species, such as Woodpigeon, Stock Dove, Magpie, Jackdaw, Rook and Carrion Crow, which formerly fed partly on grain from autumn stubble fields, all increased greatly, at least until the end of the 20th century. Not only have these large species had the benefit of large seeds provided for game birds, they also have alternative winter foods which feed them through the lean period of late winter. Woodpigeons and Stock Doves feed largely on rape leaves, as mentioned earlier, while the corvids turn to road-kills and other carrion or to earthworms and other invertebrates found in pastures and newly ploughed fields. The Collared Dove, like the smaller Chaffinch and Greenfinch, has benefited increasingly over the years from garden feeders, so has largely avoided the shortages in the countryside.

CONCLUDING REMARKS

Because of changes in management and more efficient harvesting, arable farmland in Britain now provides much less food for birds and other wild animals than in the recent past. The main bird foods affected are the seeds of weeds, cereals or other crops, and soil-dwelling and plant-feeding invertebrates – most of the foods that birds gain from arable land.

Use of herbicides has greatly reduced the quantities of broad-leaved weed seeds available for seed-eating birds, and led to progressive depletion of the seed-bank in the soil. During the latter half of the 20th century, this seed supply on stubble fields declined by an estimated 83%. Similarly, the more efficient harvesting of cereal grains reduced the quantities spilled on stubble fields by about 92%. Allowing for the decline in area of winter stubble fields over recent decades brings the overall decline in these types of seeds to 95% and 97% respectively. Change in the main season of cultivation, from spring to autumn, led not only to the loss of winter stubbles with their once-abundant seed supplies, but also to the loss of most spring cultivation which turned up buried seeds and invertebrates for many birds at a time of seasonal shortage.
