In addition, the earlier growth of cereal crops resulting from autumn sowing made cereal fields less suitable than in the past for some ground-nesting birds, reducing their nesting habitat, shortening their breeding seasons, and limiting their annual production of young. Among species which continue to nest in tall cereal crops, an earlier harvest destroys more broods than in the past.

Almost all operations on farmland are now accomplished more quickly and efficiently than before. The combination of several operations in spring into one or two tractor passes speeds up the preparation of seed-beds. It thereby reduces the number of occasions when food items are turned to the soil surface, and hence the period over which they are available to birds. At the end of the growing season, the combine harvester has reduced the amount of food available to wild birds, first by spilling less grain than formerly and shortening the overall harvesting period, and secondly by removing the need for threshing in winter, with its associated grain spillage in stack-yards. So despite a trebling in grain production in Britain since the mid-20th century, much less grain is now available in the fields and farmyards in winter.

The change of emphasis from spring-sown to autumn-sown cereals has affected some species in both summer and winter. In the breeding season, compared to the past, Skylarks now suffer from shortage of good nesting habitat and shortening of the breeding season, and in winter they have less cereal stubble as habitat, and that which remains offers many fewer seeds as food. The same holds for Corn Buntings, which nest generally later than Skylarks, and lose more of their nests to harvesting. In winter they are affected in the same way as Skylarks, but perhaps more seriously because they depend more heavily on seeds then. Corn Buntings declined more markedly than Skylarks (90% versus 60% during 1970–2013).

Despite the massive declines in bird foods on arable land, some new sources of food increased in recent decades. Some grazing species now feed extensively on the nutritious leaves of oilseed rape and cereals sown in autumn, both providing important winter foods, rape mainly for pigeons and cereals mainly for geese and swans. Another new food is rape seeds which feed finches in summer, compensating to some extent for the various summer weed seeds largely lost since pre-herbicide times. Moreover, in recent years shortage of stubble grain has been offset to some extent by the localised provision of grain to feed released game birds, a food source which some other large bird species also exploit. Game crops producing smaller seeds could benefit smaller seed-eaters, but little remains by the end of January when the fields are often ploughed, leaving a time of shortage in late winter and spring.

It is easy to appreciate how most of the agricultural changes that have occurred over recent decades have made arable land less suitable for birds, through greatly reducing the amounts of habitat or food available. However, it is not yet possible to assess for most species the relative importance of different changes in causing population declines.

## CHAPTER 11

## Traditional Lowland Grasslands

GRASSES CAN THRIVE ALMOST anywhere in Britain, largely creating our 'green and pleasant land'. The climate is sufficiently wet and warm that they can remain green and growing for a large part of the year. Summer droughts and winter chills can check their growth, but are not normally long or severe enough to kill them. Grasses are also better adapted than most other plants to withstand grazing or mowing, continuing to grow again and again after being eaten or cut down. It is not surprising therefore that grassland covers more than half the land surface of Britain and is the mainstay of the British livestock industry.

Over 100 grass species are recognised as native to Britain, but only about a dozen are important agriculturally. Two of the most significant include Perennial Rye-grass, usually found on the best and most carefully managed pastures, and Common Bent, which predominates in the less valuable pastures. Other widespread and valued fodder species include Cock's-foot, Rough Meadow-grass, Crested Dog's-tail, Meadow Fescue, Meadow Foxtail and Timothy. On chalk downs and limestone hills, Sheep's Fescue and Red Fescue give fine matted and springy turf, interspersed with other grasses and herbs. Most meadow grass species are perennials, but species vary in their longevity and ability to compete with other plants. In the Countryside Survey 2007 (CS2007), Rye-grass emerged as the commonest of all British plant species, followed by Yorkshire-fog and False Oat-grass (Carey et al. 2008)

FIG 113. Pastoral landscape with mixture of improved and unimproved grassland, Monreith, Wigtownshire (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Most grassland in Britain today is found on land that was once under forest, to which it could revert within decades if left ungrazed and unmown. It is uncertain how extensive were natural grasslands in Mesolithic times before the advent of agriculture (Chapter 3), and grassland conservation today is aimed mainly at encouraging species and associations that are valued not so much for their 'naturalness' as for their scientific or heritage value, including their wildlife content. In these respects, the most valued grasslands are generally those that have developed slowly over long periods and consist of indigenous species, including flowering plants. In lowland Britain, long-term grassland is very much richer in plant species than short-lived grassland or arable land. It also supports more earthworms and other invertebrates in the soil below, and greater numbers of above-ground insects, some of which depend on broad-leaved plants among the grasses. It is these small creatures, and the seeds produced by various plants, that sustain the majority of grassland birds. Only some waterfowl species obtain a large proportion of their food by grazing the grass itself.

BIRDS OF GRASSLAND

Many bird species in Britain use grassland at some time of year, and some species show obvious preferences for particular types. However, few can be termed grassland specialists, as most also make use of arable or other open land. Different species prefer different sward structures to feed or nest in, depending on where they place their nests, where and how they feed, and how they protect themselves against predation. Some have other requirements, such as a certain level of soil wetness or wide open areas lacking trees and hedges. From an ornithological viewpoint, the most valuable pastures for nesting birds are structurally varied, containing patches of short and long grass intermixed. Short grass provides good all-round visibility and easy access to food, while tufts of grass and larger tussocks provide shelter from weather and cover for some species to nest or hide in. Patches of tall grass also harbour more arthropods than short grass and may produce more edible seeds.

FIG 114. Some grassland birds: upper left, Grasshopper Warbler Locustella naevia (Frank Snykers); upper right, Whinchat Saxicola rubetra (Richard Chandler); lower left, Meadow Pipit Anthus pratensis (Chris Knights); lower right, Yellow Wagtail Motacilla flava (Rebecca Nason).

During the breeding season, species that are regularly seen on lowland grassland of one sort or another include waders, such as Oystercatcher*, Curlew*, Lapwing*, Snipe* and Redshank*, waterfowl such as Greylag and Canada Geese, corvids such as Rook, Carrion Crow, Jackdaw and Magpie, and smaller songbirds such as Grasshopper Warbler*, Whinchat*, Skylark*, Meadow Pipit*, Pied and Yellow Wagtails*, Starling, Yellowhammer and Reed Bunting*. In a few more restricted areas, other grassland species occur, such as Chough, Black-tailed Godwit*, Ruff*, Dunlin* and Corncrake*, while the Green Woodpecker frequently ventures from trees to short-grass pastures to seek invertebrates, especially ants. Those species that are marked with an asterisk* nest on or near the ground within grassland, whereas the others nest elsewhere but obtain much of their food from grassland. In winter, grassland is used by flocks of foraging waterfowl (especially geese and swans), waders (especially Lapwing and Golden Plover), gulls (especially Black-headed and Common Gulls), and passerines, such as Rooks and other corvids, Starling, Skylark, Meadow Pipit, Redwing, Fieldfare and other thrushes. Locally, small parties of Woodlarks also occur on pasture land in winter, on fields often used year after year, and in past times of agricultural recession when shrubs were allowed to establish on old grassland, Woodlarks may have also bred on farmland over parts of southern Britain. Other bird species are found on coastal grasslands, as described below.

With the exception of corvids and waterfowl, all the breeding bird species characteristic of lowland grassland have declined in recent decades: some because the underlying soil is now too dry for them to probe for food, others because the vegetation is now structurally unsuitable (too dense, too tall or too uniform), and yet others because too many of their nests or young are destroyed by mowing or trampled by increased densities of livestock. These various causal factors are discussed in more detail in Chapters 12 and .

Declines in some of these species started in the 19th century or earlier, but have continued into the modern era. One such species is the Chough, which requires very short vegetation resulting from hard grazing or wind exposure; it feeds mainly by digging and probing into soil and livestock dung for invertebrates (Bignal & Curtis 1988). The species is now restricted to a few western districts, mostly coastal, where cave-like nest sites are available and where livestock are routinely grazed. It occurs in suitable lowland areas, near sea cliffs where it nests, and also in some montane areas, such as Snowdonia. Its need for caves or cave-substitutes such as deserted buildings or mine-shafts also limits its distribution, but its disappearance from some places during the 20th century can be attributed to reduced grazing pressure and greater grass growth. Where intense grazing was reinstated, the species has re-colonised some areas previously abandoned. Sheep or Rabbits are usually needed to get the grass short enough, as longer vegetation prevents Choughs from using their curved bills to best effect.

FIG 115. White-fronted Geese Anser albifrons and Greylag Geese A. anser on old pasture, Islay (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Turning to more recent times, some of the bird species most closely associated with grassland have shown big declines. On the basis of BTO counts from 1970–2103, the Starling decreased by around 81%, Snipe by 92%, Yellow Wagtail by 67%, and Meadow Pipit by 39% (Table 3, Fig. 16). All these species are found mainly on different types of grassland, but many other species that have declined also occur commonly in other habitats (including arable land).

Many grassland bird species prefer to forage in short grass, in which soil-probing is easier and surface prey are more readily seen and caught. Short grass also offers a clear view of the surrounding area so that approaching predators can be spotted at a distance, giving time for escape. Tall grass can conceal or obstruct access to prey items, even though they may be abundant there. Feeding in tall grass also requires more vigilance on the part of the birds, which can in turn reduce their feeding rate (Devereux et al. 2004, Whittingham & Evans 2004). Predation avoidance behaviours, and therefore sward preferences, differ among species, with taller birds (such as Curlew) feeding more successfully in tall vegetation than smaller birds, such as Skylarks. Only Corncrakes feed effectively while hidden beneath a canopy of dense grass, practically immune from avian predators searching from above.

TRADITIONAL GRASSLAND TYPES

Under traditional management, semi-natural grasslands consist of pasture and meadow, the one for grazing and the other for hay production (followed by grazing later in the year). Nowadays, together with lowland heathlands, they often provide species-rich areas for wildlife in otherwise intensive farmland, and are home to many rare and threatened plant and insect species. Thousands of invertebrate species and hundreds of colourful wild flowers can still be found in the remaining fragments of these habitats (Fig. 116). But the amount of traditional semi-natural grassland in the lowlands of Britain which has not been 'improved' in any way declined massively during the 20th century (Fuller 1987). Over the period 1932–84, the overall area of lowland permanent pasture and rough grassland in England and Wales declined by 92%, from 7.2 to 0.6 million hectares, through conversion to improved grassland or arable land (Fuller 1987). The process continued, and by 1996 only 1–2% of permanent grassland in lowland England and Wales remained in an 'unimproved' state; it comprised some 27,500–40,000 ha of calcareous grassland, 7,500–15,000 ha of unimproved neutral pasture and hay meadow, 8,000–15,000 ha of acidic grassland and 9,000–17,500 ha of wet grassland (Blackstock et al. 1999). Similar trends occurred in Scotland, although on average they may have been a few years behind. The total remaining in Britain as a whole could now be well below 200,000 ha. Major periods of destruction by ploughing occurred during the Second World War and during the 1960s–80s, when most traditional grasslands were converted to arable or intensively managed grass crops. The diversity of traditional grasslands was created largely by variation in physical features such as altitude and aspect, underlying soil type (whether neutral, alkaline or acid), soil depth and dampness, grazing or mowing regime and variability of sward height, and the presence or absence of tussocks and bare ground. All these features influence the variety of their plant and animal life, including birds.

FIG 116. Old-style hay meadows, with abundant wild flowers, supporting insects and providing seeds for finches (Ian Newton).

Neutral grasslands

Most of the lowland grasslands in Britain lie on neutral soils (pH 5.0–6.5), usually clays and loams, and are now subject to intense agricultural pressure. More natural areas, less intensively managed, include the floodplains of many lowland rivers, such as the 'washes' of East Anglia. These traditional damp meadows, consisting of a mixture of grasses and flowering plants, once occupied parts of every low-lying river valley, but they are now rare and localised. In the past, many birds nested in these hay meadows, including Corncrake, Grey Partridge, Quail and various waders, Whinchat and Corn Bunting, while other species, such as Linnet and other finches, came in to seek the seeds of flowering plants. Such damp meadows were mown once per year, usually in July, providing a major source of hay for livestock in winter. By the time they were cut, hay meadows had achieved a brownish-yellow tinge, coloured by seed. Earlier in the year, they had displayed a succession of floral highlights, as one group of plants after another had flowered and seeded, producing a succession of food-crops for nectar-eating and seed-eating species through the summer. For several weeks, these meadows were alive with the sound of 'meadow music' – grasshoppers, bees and larks – and with the colour of butterflies flitting over the vegetation. Swallows fed low over the meadows by day and bats at night. These delights can still be seen on the few remaining meadows that are managed in the traditional way.

Nutrients were removed each year in the hay crop, and traditionally their return was ensured by the recycling of farmyard manure, usually no more than once per three years on individual fields. In recent times, after ploughing and reseeding with more productive grass strains, and annual applications of inorganic fertilisers, 'wild flowers' have gone almost totally from many fields (Smith 1987). It was for this reason in the 1980s that 13,000 ha of the north Pennines were declared an Environmentally Sensitive Area, in which farmers were paid to farm in the traditional way to retain the beauty of the landscape, avoiding all use of chemicals, adding farmyard manure no more than once every three years, cutting hay no earlier than mid-July, and avoiding silage altogether (Smith 1987).

Dry neutral grasslands under modern management now contain few if any flowering plants, and far fewer animals of any kind during the growing season, but in winter they can hold good numbers of corvids and other birds which move in to exploit mainly earthworms and other soil-dwelling invertebrates (Chapter 12). In CS2007, neutral grasslands – mostly under intensive management – were estimated to cover about 2.2 million hectares of Britain, about one-tenth of the total land area, but their extent has fluctuated over the years, depending on the amount of land under arable crops.

Alkaline grasslands

The rolling downs and the wolds of southern and eastern England overlie limestone or chalk, giving rise to shallow well-drained alkaline soils (pH > 6.5). For hundreds of years, these areas were grazed by sheep, and became known for their short springy turf full of low-growing flowers and supporting a diversity of insect life. In some areas, it was common practice to graze the animals by day and then to enclose them overnight on nearby arable fields, which they improved with their dung and urine. From the 18th century, however, these areas of chalk grassland began to decline, as they were converted to arable, especially barley. Eastern areas, from Yorkshire south to Hertfordshire, were lost to the plough mainly in the 19th century, and the southern downs from Sussex to Wiltshire mainly from the 1950s. Nowadays, only about 3% of former downland is still covered by native grasses and forbs, and some of this area has been changed by the removal of sheep or the use of fertilisers. Some steep slopes that escaped the plough grew up with scrub in the 1950s–60s when sheep were absent and Rabbit populations had crashed through myxomatosis. Chalk is porous, and in many downland areas the valleys lack permanent streams, and no surface water exists other than in artificially created dewponds (whose main source of water is rain), often constructed on hilltops or ridges.

In the past, southern downland and similar sheep-grazed areas had a limited avifauna, consisting in the breeding season largely of open-country passerines, mainly Skylarks, and more locally Corn Buntings, Meadow Pipits and Wheatears. In places with short-cropped turf, there were also Lapwings and Stone-curlews, and, in places with taller vegetation, Whinchats, Grey Partridges, Quails, Great Bustards and Montagu's Harriers. Some of these species depended more on the patches of arable on the downland than on the short sheep-grazed turf itself. In winter, the open downs were rather desolate, and their bird populations even sparser. Hen Harriers and Short-eared Owls were often present as immigrants from elsewhere. Nowadays, with most of the original downland under arable crops, all these species are much rarer. Wheatears and Montagu's Harriers have virtually disappeared as breeding species, and Great Bustards totally so (except where attempts are being made to reintroduce them). The largest area of semi-natural calcareous grassland remaining in Europe is on Salisbury Plain, in a 390 km2 area protected for military use, and it is only here that a sizeable grassland bird community still survives. Over the decade 1987–96, the numbers of Stone-curlews nesting on the semi-natural grassland of Porton Down were found to fluctuate between 9 to 19 pairs in parallel with the number of Rabbits present in spring (Beasley et al. 1999). The breeding success of Stone-curlews was also better in good Rabbit years. Grazing by Rabbits presumably affected the amount of ground under short grass, and an abundance of Rabbits as prey may have lessened predation on the eggs and chicks of Stone-curlews. Rabbit burrowing also brings stones to the surface, which increases the attractiveness of an area to Stone-curlews.

The rolling limestone hills of southern Britain do not hold our only alkaline soils. The machair is a flat fertile plain of calcarious shell-sand beside the sea, rich in grasses and flowering plants, which is found locally on the coastlines of northwest Scotland, including the Hebrides, Orkney and Shetland. It could equally be classed as 'coastal grassland', as discussed below. It reaches its greatest extent on the west side of the Outer Hebrides, where it is usually cultivated on a strip rotation to give patches of flower-rich grass and patches of cereals. The land is naturally fairly wet and its continuity is broken by occasional shallow lochs. Ground-nesters include Skylarks, Corn Buntings and Corncrakes, with waders such as Lapwing, Ringed Plover and Oystercatcher on the drier areas of spring-sown cereals, and Redshank, Snipe and Dunlin in the damper areas of lusher grass (Fuller et al. 1986). These machair areas hold some of the highest densities of waders in Britain, sometimes exceeding 300 pairs per km2, and the densities of Dunlin and Ringed Plover are the highest recorded anywhere in the world. The machair is the only remaining lowland habitat in Britain where the Dunlin still breeds at high density, while elsewhere it has become restricted to high upland areas for breeding.

FIG 117. Barnacle Geese Branta leucopsis and Brown Hares Lepus europaeus on old pasture in April on which almost all green growth has been grazed off over winter, Islay (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

All the waders nesting on the machair of the Outer Hebrides have suffered declines in recent decades as a result of predation on their eggs by Hedgehogs, introduced around 1974 (Chapter 13, Jackson & Green 2000). Modern agriculture is also having an impact, with improved drainage leading to lower water tables, and much of the cereal now grown for silage. There is little grain to support Corn Buntings through the winter, which therefore declined in recent decades from being widespread and abundant to local and rare. Seed-eating Twite nest in taller shrubby vegetation nearby, but obtain much of their seed-food from the machair; Greylag Geese based on the lochs graze on the machair year-round; while Hooded Crows and various birds of prey hunt there. Most of the same species are present in winter, with the addition in less disturbed areas of immigrant Greenland and Barnacle Geese.

The CS2007 estimated that semi-natural alkaline grasslands covered in all nearly 44,500 ha in the lowlands, and another 18,900 in the uplands, representing about 0.3% of Britain's total land area. Upland areas of calcareous soils are found mainly in the Pennines of northern England, which also support relatively high densities of breeding birds.

Acid grasslands

Acid soils (< pH 5.5) are found chiefly in the uplands of Britain, and support large areas of semi-natural grassland, consisting of indigenous grass species kept in their present state mainly by grazing livestock. On the enclosed fields of hill farms, acidification is often countered, at least in the short term, by periodic dressings of lime, making these fields more agriculturally productive than they would otherwise be. In the lowlands, acid soils are more restricted, found mainly in areas of heathland and coastal sand dunes. In the past, heathlands were used for low-density livestock grazing, but they are now left mainly to Rabbits, maintaining the short turf favoured by Stone-curlews and Wheatears. However, their area has contracted greatly over recent decades, partly through afforestation and partly through conversion to farmland. When Rabbit numbers collapsed in the 1950s as a result of myxomatosis, the vegetation on many heaths and downlands grew too tall for Stone-curlews, Lapwings, Woodlarks and Wheatears (Green & Griffiths 1994, Green & Taylor 1995, Sitters et al. 1996), and as the years passed farmers became more reluctant to graze livestock on heathland because of the poor quality of the grazing. However, most remaining heathland in Britain is now under conservation management, and most of the characteristic bird species are on the rise (Chapter 17).

FIG 118. Tightly grazed acid grassland is suitable for Stone-curlews Burhinus oedicnemus, here defending a nest (Chris Knights).

The CS2007 estimated that semi-natural acid grasslands in Britain cover around 1.6 million hectares, mostly in the uplands and representing 7.3% of the total land area.

Coastal grasslands

On gently sloping shorelines, mainly in the south and east, saltmarshes form a zone between land and sea, periodically flooded by high tides, and containing vascular plants able to tolerate the salinity and temperature fluctuations. Saltmarshes are among the most productive places in Britain, receiving nutrient from the sea at each inundation, and also from rivers which flood them from time to time. They support a limited number of animal species, but some are present in great abundance. The wide open landscape devoid of trees and shrubs is attractive to many open-land birds. The upper parts of saltmarshes afford good grazing, and many such areas have been claimed from the sea by building embankments to keep out the tide, allowing their conversion to agricultural grass or arable land. This process of reclamation has gone on for centuries, including in the 1960s–90s, and the lower courses of many eastern rivers now flow through tracts of flat farmland that were formerly saltmarsh. Typically, the river is now confined to a narrow channel, a fraction of its original width. Coastal grazing marshes created years ago from upper saltmarshes could now also be classed as neutral grassland. Many have been subject in recent decades to further agricultural improvement, including levelling, ploughing and conversion to arable, leading to the loss of virtually all their birds. Some remaining coastal saltmarshes are now narrower than ever (sometimes less than 50 m), having been lost from the land side by reclamation and from the sea side by rising sea levels. On eastern coasts, many such claimed areas are likely to disappear in due course under further sea-level rise.

Only those parts of remaining saltmarshes that are seldom flooded are suitable for ground-nesting birds. The breeding community is dominated by passerines (especially Skylark and Meadow Pipit), but waders and ducks feature strongly, as in some places do gulls and terns. On a national scale, eight species are widespread on saltmarsh, namely Skylark, Meadow Pipit, Reed Bunting, Shelduck, Mallard, Lapwing, Redshank and Oystercatcher (Fuller 1982). In some areas, breeding densities of waders can exceed 50 or even 100 pairs per km2, higher than on neighbouring areas of non-tidal wet grassland (Davidson 1991). As on other grassland, grazing pressures influence bird densities. On the Dee Estuary in northwest England, Skylarks alone reached the exceptional density of 120 pairs per km2 on ungrazed and moderately grazed marshes, but fell to 50 pairs per km2 on heavily grazed marshes (C. E. Wells, in Donald 2004). In winter, saltmarshes host thousands of waterfowl and waders, many species of which are specialised in their feeding and hence localised in their distributions. The main grazing species include Brent Geese, Barnacle Geese and Wigeon. Saltmarshes in southeast England, especially around the Wash, provide the main wintering habitat for Twite drawn from nesting areas in northern England. As the total area of saltmarsh in southeast England was halved through reclamation schemes in the 1970s–80s, the numbers of wintering Twite counted during surveys on the Wash declined from more than 6,000 in the early 1970s to a few hundred in more recent years (Brown & Grice 2010). Similar or greater declines were recorded on other saltmarsh areas.

FIG 119. Coastal marsh grazed by sheep, northwest Scotland (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

FIG 120. Some breeding birds of saltmarsh: left, Avocet Recurvirostra avocetta (Frank Snykers); above, Shelduck Tadorna tadorna (Edmund Fellowes).

In the late 1980s, the total area of saltmarsh remaining in Britain was estimated at 45,000 ha, of which 72% was in England (Brown & Grice 2010). But since then, numerous coastal habitat creation and enhancement schemes have been undertaken, as at Wallasea Island in Essex, Frieston Shore in Lincolnshire, Hesketh Out Marsh in Lancashire, and Nigg Bay in Highland. These areas provide further coastal grassland and saltmarsh for birds, but they do not come near to compensating for the total lost over the previous half-century.

FIG 121. Twite Linaria flavirostris migrate from their upland breeding areas to winter in coastal saltmarshes, where they feed on various seeds (Chris Knights).

Roadside verges, sports turf and lawns

Other grasslands include road and railway verges, lawns and playing fields, and churchyards, all with their own management regimes. Collectively, road verges are now thought to contain more semi-natural grassland than remains on all lowland farmland. In most districts, they are now some of the best places for wild flowers, and are major sources of nectar for bees, and on quieter roads of seeds and insects for birds. With risks from motorised road traffic, they are no longer grazed as in the past and, being cut once per year, larger herbaceous plants can grow and seed there, including some, such as Meadowsweet and Knapweed, that are favoured by seed-eating finches. However, their management usually falls to local councils, and often leaves much to be desired. In the 1960s, many verges were treated with herbicides to remove broad-leaved plants, leaving grass which was then cut to look more lawn-like. This process was eventually ended, but the problem remains that most verges are cut too early, in June–July, while many broad-leaved plants are still in flower, thereby preventing them from seeding (the best time for cutting being September). In consequence, most verges are becoming progressively less diverse. It is often desirable, for reasons of road safety, to cut a short distance in from the road, but the rest of the verge can be spared.

In addition, Britain has substantial areas of golf courses and other sports turf, and at least 100,000 ha of mown grass in private gardens. In churchyards, management varies from frequent cutting to create a lawn-like sward to almost total neglect, creating a haven for wild plants and animals. As a rule, hard mowing or grazing to produce a short sward discourages many types of animals, particularly insects, breeding birds and small rodents. However, the short well-watered turf of garden lawns can provide valuable foraging substrate for some species, such as Blackbird and Starling, and on larger areas, such as golf courses, also for species such as Lapwing, Golden Plover and Black-headed Gull. Flocks of other gull species sometimes roost on golf courses and playing fields, attracted by their openness and (at times) lack of disturbance. All these species feed primarily on soil-dwelling organisms, such as earthworms and leatherjackets where these are not destroyed by pesticide use. In some areas golf courses are grazed by feral Greylag and Canada Geese, and in a few localities by wintering Brent Geese.

There is thus no shortage in Britain of grassland of one sort or another, but the wildlife value of different types varies greatly, and some of the older types, richest in native plants and animals, are now scarce.

GRASSLAND MANAGEMENT

The traditional division of grassland into hay meadow and pasture was based on the need for livestock food year-round. Animals could feed on pasture for much of the year, but in November–April growth was poor to non-existent, hence the need for hay. Good meadow land was scarce, but valuable. In the Domesday Book of 1086, meadow amounted to only 1.2% of the recorded land area, but was widely scattered across the country, occurring wherever the land retained its moisture year-round (Rackham 1994). Some of the best was liable to winter flooding, during which additional silt was often deposited, re-fertilising the land. By the 13th century, most floodplains could be classed as hay meadows (Rackham 1994). In parts of Europe, farmers still prefer to feed their cattle on hay made from flower-rich meadows as opposed to uniform cultivated grass swards. They say that the cattle stay healthier on old-style meadow grass, and that the milk and meat taste better.

Grazing and mowing have quite different effects on a grass sward. Grazing can occur at any time of year, with animals selecting what they want, trampling the vegetation and depositing dung and urine. In contrast, mowing occurs at a specific growth-stage; it is non-selective and sudden, cutting everything in one sweep. Like grazing, it results in defoliation, but it lacks the treading, dung and urine. Among other effects, the two processes encourage different plants. For example, Meadowsweet, Oxeye Daisy and Salad Burnet are easily destroyed by grazing but withstand annual mowing; while Yarrow, Dwarf Thistle and some buttercups tolerate grazing but not mowing (Rackham 1994). Mowing at specific times of year can also favour one set of plants over another. Because mown grass is removed from the land, it causes a bigger reduction than grazing in the amount of organic matter that is returned to the local soil.

The effect of grazing on any sward depends on its intensity – the density of animals and how long they are kept there in one session. Intensive grazing by any livestock reduces botanical diversity, leaving just those species that can tolerate repeated defoliation, such as some grasses and clovers. The few non-crop species that resist grazing have strong defences, such as distasteful or spiky leaves. Seasonal, rather than continuous, grazing is likely to promote sward heterogeneity, and hence invertebrate diversity (Morris 2000, Vickery et al. 2001). Grazing in autumn is less deleterious than grazing in spring in terms of its effects on insects.

Continued sheep grazing favours low-growing plants and their associated insects, together with birds that require short swards for nesting or feeding (such as Lapwing and Stone-curlew). Taller plants, such as thistles, docks and Ragwort, survive in places because they have some physical or chemical protection against grazing animals. Insects associated with dung degradation, such as flies and beetles, provide food for Lapwings and other waders, as well as for Swallows, wagtails, Starlings, Rooks and other corvids and many species of bats. Some bird species dig into the dung for prey items, while others pick them off the vegetation or catch flies in the airspace above. Earthworm densities are also generally high on grassland with regular inputs of animal dung (Chapter 5). However, for above-ground invertebrate life, tall swards offer more vertical structure and generally support more species and more individuals than short swards (Morris 2000). Nevertheless, some arthropod and bird species are characteristic of short swards.

Livestock effects

Different species of livestock create different sward structures and plant composition. Sheep are fairly selective grazers, concentrating on the most nutritious and palatable vegetation, and usually nibbling it down almost to ground level. At low or moderate densities, they produce a mosaic of closely cropped areas interspersed with patches of taller and tougher vegetation. Under high sheep densities, grasses produce more shoots, and low-growing plants are favoured at the expense of plants that cannot tolerate heavy grazing. This results in very short, dense and structurally uniform swards, as on the former downs (Kiehl et al. 1996, Vickery et al. 2001). Sheep also like flower heads, thereby reducing nectar sources and seed production.

Cattle are less selective, eating a wider range of vegetation, so that their grazing pressure is more evenly spread. Using their wrap-around tongues, they tear at vegetation further up the stem rather than biting it, creating a patchy but generally more open, less dense sward, and encouraging greater invertebrate diversity. Coupled with dunging and trampling, their grazing also creates more bare patches, offering opportunities for seed germination and new growth. For these reasons, cattle-grazed areas are favoured for foraging by several bird species, especially Starlings, Rooks and Black-headed Gulls and others which feed on soil-dwelling invertebrates. The natural tendency for cattle to avoid grazing near cowpats adds to the heterogeneity, and provides secluded and undisturbed tussocks where some ground-nesting birds (such as Skylark) can place their nests. The size and extent of patches of heavily grazed and lightly grazed swards depends upon stocking densities but, generally, any decline in cattle numbers coupled with high sheep numbers results in a shorter, more uniform sward. Because of their need for longer grass, cattle are frequently moved around from field to field and, unless they are given supplementary food, they are seldom kept on the same ground for more than a week or two at a time, whereas sheep may be in the same field for longer periods, sometimes for the whole bird breeding season.

Horses graze some areas very tightly while completely leaving others. Their habit of resting and dunging in the same areas day after day leads to local nutrient enrichment, and their heavy trampling leads to soil compaction. This tends to favour a generally short sward with patches of coarse unpalatable plants, such as docks, nettles and Ragwort. Horses also eat the fresh growth of shrubs, including Hawthorn, and the bark of other species, such as willows and birches. Wild herbivores – deer, Rabbits, hares and geese – also graze by shearing and biting, feeding selectively and biting down the vegetation almost to ground level. Deer also browse woody vegetation more effectively than sheep or cattle, removing any new growth within reach from trees and shrubs.

Wherever animals congregate, as at gateways and drinking points, the vegetation becomes short with bare areas that offer niches for plants and invertebrates that are scarce or absent over the rest of a field. Many birds are attracted to such bare areas, where they find easily accessible foods, such as beetles or grass seeds.

Because of the differing grazing habits of cattle and sheep, grass fields require careful management if they are to be used effectively and maintain their agricultural value. Until the Second World War, most livestock on British farms lived outside on permanent grass for most of the year. The grass was seldom used efficiently, as the animals were given access to whole fields and much grass was damaged before it could be consumed. It tended to be grazed unevenly, with patches around dung piles being left, trodden areas incompletely eaten, and wet areas puddled. This was good for birds and other wildlife. Little fertiliser or herbicide was used, so floristic diversity was high, and cowpats provided food for dung beetles and other insects, and enriched the soil below. Large numbers of flies were produced.

Rotational grazing helped to improve livestock nutrition and ensured more efficient use of grass, while reducing damage to the land. Stock management became easier with the advent of barbed wire (from the 1870s) and more flexible with the use of moveable electric fences (from the 1950s). Such fences enabled pastures to be subdivided temporarily, and grazed one narrow strip at a time, while the rest was protected until required.

Linked with the type of nest site they choose, different species of ground-nesting birds are often associated with different types of livestock, owing to their differing effects on vegetation. Breeding Lapwings, for example, are more closely associated with sheep than with cattle (Shrubb 1990), while breeding Redshank and Snipe are more often associated with cattle (Herbert et al. 1990). During the course of a year, some bird species require specific temporal patterns of grazing in order to get the best of a food supply. For example, Choughs often feed on leatherjackets obtained by probing and digging in the ground. On the island of Islay, off western Scotland, relatively tall grass swards in autumn encouraged egg-laying by crane-flies, which gave rise to large numbers of larvae in the soil during the following winter and spring. However, Choughs required short swards (ideally < 5 cm) in late winter and early spring to gain access to these larvae, a situation created only when tall autumn swards were grazed down over winter (Bignal et al 1997, McCracken & Bignal 1998). In some places, leatherjackets may have been abundant in the soil but the sward too tall for Choughs to get at them; in other places, the sward may have been short enough but leatherjackets scarce. Only by an appropriate seasonal pattern of grazing were the needs of both flies and birds met.

FIG 122. The Chough Pyrrhocorax pyrrhocorax is found in some cliffy coastal areas, with short grass tightly grazed by Rabbits or livestock, obtaining much of its food by probing for invertebrates in the soil or in animal dung (David Boyle).

Permanent and ley grass

So-called 'permanent grass' is old grassland which has not been ploughed for many years, and is mostly used for grazing livestock. It consists of various indigenous grass species with varying proportions of broad-leaved forbs. It can also be defined as grassland not in rotation, and is mostly used for grazing livestock. Under heavy grazing, permanent grass can be kept low and green year-round. Such short-grass areas provide favoured foraging habitat for many birds, including Little Owl and Chough, as well as various other corvids, thrushes and Starlings. Areas near trees are also visited by Green Woodpeckers and (in the past) Wrynecks seeking ants. But under reduced grazing, grass becomes taller with more tussocks, and often develops an under-layer of dead material below the living stems. In this state, it is often known as 'rough grassland', and provides good habitat for Field Voles, which live in the matted layer of dead vegetation, creating labyrinths of tunnels and feeding on the young green shoots. These animals in turn act as major prey for Kestrels, owls and other predators (Chapter 7).

The Short-eared Owl is more exclusively associated with rough grassland in Britain than any other bird of prey, but in the breeding season only in years when Field Voles are abundant. This owl seems to settle and breed only in places and years when the local voles are at peak numbers in their 3–5-year cycles. It seems to require extensive areas of rough grassland, and is not normally seen hunting over road verges and other grassy strips that are used routinely by vole-eating Barn Owls and Kestrels. Large undisturbed areas of rough grassland are now so scarce in lowland Britain that Short-eared Owls have become mainly confined to the uplands in the breeding season. Only small numbers of pairs were found breeding in lowland areas during the most recent Atlas project, mostly in coastal or other extensive stretches of rough grasslands (Balmer et al. 2013). To judge from old county bird books, it bred more widely in the lowlands in the 19th century, especially in the fens and heaths of East Anglia, and could still be found in these areas into the 1970s.

Rushes are a feature of old damp pastures, whether on neutral or acid soils, with Juncus effusus predominating in the north and west and J. inflexus in the south and east. They are important to some birds in providing cover and nest sites in otherwise short swards. Reed Buntings often nest within rush clumps, as do Snipe and Redshank, while Curlew nest on the ground between the clumps. Cattle farmers usually dislike rushes and take steps to get rid of them, but some hill sheep farmers value the shelter they provide for young lambs.

Nowadays, the term 'unimproved' is often applied to grassland that has not been ploughed or fertilised at least since the mid-20th century. In neglected or under-grazed grassland, shrubs and trees soon establish themselves, as in past agricultural recessions. This happened on a large scale in the 1930s, with the consequence that birds such as Tree Pipit and Woodlark started breeding on lowland grassland, only to disappear again when the scrub was cleared and the land brought back into agricultural use.

Other grassland may never have been ploughed, or at least not for several centuries. This occurs mainly on intractable hilly terrain and on low-lying land liable to flooding. The most extensive areas of 'permanent' pasture or 'rough grazing' occur in the open uplands. In this hilly terrain, ploughing is generally impossible, and grazing is provided mainly by self-sown wild grass and sedge species interspersed with many other plants, including dwarf shrubs such as heather (Chapter 19).

FIG 123. Left, rough grassland, an ideal habitat for Field Voles Microtus agrestis, a major prey for Kestrels Falco tinnunculus, Barn Owls Tyto alba, Short-eared Owls Asio flammeus and others (Ian Newton); right, Short-eared Owls are found mainly in extensive areas of rough grassland (Rebecca Nason).

FIG 124. Rushy pastures of the type favoured by waders and other ground-nesting birds (Ian Newton).

In contrast to permanent pasture, a temporary ley is essentially an arable crop which, when planted, may contain entirely cultivated grasses used for grazing or silage production. The planted grasses may be cultivars of native or foreign species (such as Italian Rye-grass) which have been improved and developed to feed livestock. The aim is to quickly establish a dense sward of highly productive grasses which respond strongly to fertilisers, and which recover rapidly from cutting or heavy grazing. However, within a year or two, such swards have usually been invaded by some wild grasses, such as Yorkshire-fog and bents, as well as by various broad-leaved 'weeds'. Because management is aimed at curtailing invasion by wild plants, leys are usually ploughed and replaced by cereals or other crops after 2–4 years, after which they are again reseeded to grass. They thereby provide a break in arable cropping, when soil fertility can be restored to some extent. In their short life, modern leys offer little of value to wildlife, as poor plant diversity, heavy grazing or frequent mowing limit the number of plant and animal species that can live there. Nevertheless, they are second only to permanent grassland in the quantities of soil-dwelling invertebrates they hold, and can attract large numbers of thrushes and corvids in winter. Short-term leys have been part of farming in Britain since the end of the 18th century, but in recent decades they have achieved much greater agricultural significance, especially in dairy farming. In 2012, the total area of ley grass in Britain was estimated at around 1.4 million hectares, about half as much as lowland permanent pasture.

Dividing grass into permanent and ley is a convenience for use in agricultural surveys. The division is to some extent artificial, because grassland exists at any one time at varying ages, depending on the time since last ploughing. Also, the number of years for which leys are left unploughed varies regionally, and in the lowlands, even so-called 'permanent' grassland is occasionally ploughed and reseeded. Into the 1970s, leys were often made by under-sowing cereal crops with grass and clover, cutting the cereals when they were ripe to leave the grass and clover below to provide some future grazing (Chapter 10). Mixed grass/clover leys were of much greater value to wildlife than modern grass-only leys.

According to Rackham (1994), traditional lowland grassland now survives mainly in three sizeable areas protected from modern agriculture by the military, namely Salisbury Plain and Porton Down in Wiltshire and the Stanford Battle Area in Norfolk. There are other smaller scattered fragments elsewhere, and the total area has been estimated at less than 200,000 ha (Crofts & Jefferson 1999). All areas that have escaped modern treatment are now of high conservation value, and most are preserved as nature reserves. They are ranked according to their botanical diversity, and kept close to their original state through old-style management, avoiding any drainage or chemical input. A visit to any of these areas reminds us how rich in plant and animal life grassland used to be. But some of these remnants are now so isolated that if any of their plant or invertebrate species die out, the chance of re-colonisation is probably small.

CONCLUDING REMARKS

Historically, the diversity of plants on grassland in Britain was determined by a combination of climate, soil type, topography, hydrology and management. Variation in these features produced a wide variety of short or tall grassland communities across the country, none of which was used intensively by current standards. If left alone for long enough, grasslands can develop an extraordinary diversity of life, being one of the most flower-rich habitats of Britain. However, in the second half of the 20th century most lowland grassland was changed dramatically, in the interests of greater agricultural productivity. Grassland communities are now much more uniform across the country than in the past, and individually less diverse. Their wildlife value is much reduced.

Sadly, old-style grasslands have no part in modern farming, and like most of the richest wildlife sites in Britain, they survive on philanthropy, whether from individuals, conservation bodies or the government. The next chapter examines some of the agricultural changes which have combined to destroy these traditional grasslands, and their dependent bird populations.

## CHAPTER 12

## Modern Grassland Management and Birds

IT IS NOT ONLY BIRDS OF arable land that have declined over recent decades, but those of lowland grassland too. Many grass-growing areas now seem totally devoid of some once-common species. Their declines have occurred over a period of increasing mechanisation and intensity in grassland management, beginning for some species in the late 19th century, but spreading to others from the 1970s on (Pain et al. 1997, Chamberlain & Fuller 2000, 2001, Vickery et al. 2001, Shrubb 2003). Declines have been more pronounced among species that breed entirely or mainly in grassland than among others that also breed commonly in other habitats. This chapter explores the various drivers of bird population declines on dry lowland grassland, while matters pertaining to lowland wet grassland and upland grassland are discussed in Chapters 13 and .

LOSS OF OLD GRASSLAND FROM THE LOWLANDS

The loss of old grassland from the lowlands was one of the most significant changes of 20th-century agriculture. It was ploughed up mainly in two periods, one during the Second World War (1939–45) and the other during the 1970s–80s, both in attempts to boost agricultural production. The process of intensification involved draining (or re-draining) if necessary, and then ploughing, harrowing and reseeding, liming if necessary and, from the 1970s, also heavy fertiliser use. Some of these newly reclaimed areas were seeded with more productive grass strains, producing short-duration grass leys, while others were converted to arable, mainly cereals. Old grass meadows could contain some 50–150 different plant species, with much regional variation, but modern intensive grass fields aim at only one or two (Dines 2016). These transformations amounted to massive habitat loss for many grassland birds, and turned good habitat into poor for others. Dense fast-growing rye-grass swards make poor nesting habitat for birds, and now contain fewer breeding birds than almost any other agricultural habitat in Britain. Overall, more than 98% of all long-term grassland present in the lowlands in the 1930s had been ploughed or otherwise modified by the end of the century, with less than 200,000 ha in total left (Chapter 11). In contrast, agriculturally improved grassland now covers around 4.5 million hectares, nearly one-fifth of the land area of Britain. This excludes the open uplands where much semi-natural (unimproved) grassland remains (Chapter 19), giving an estimated total of unimproved grassland for Britain of more than 1.6 million hectares (Chapter 19, Box 18).

Much of the old grassland that was lost in the 20th century (about 1.3 million hectares) was classed as 'rough grassland', having a layer of dead vegetation beneath the fresh growth, making it ideal habitat for Field Voles. The loss of rough grassland (three-quarters of the 1930s total) therefore led to widespread reductions in these small rodents (Harris 1995), along with their predators such as Kestrels, Barn Owls and Short-eared Owls. The Kestrel has continued downward to the present day. In the lowlands, Kestrels and Barn Owls now feed chiefly over remaining areas of rough grassland, including road and field verges and felled forest-areas which are outside agricultural management. Other types of old grassland that have been largely lost include the soft, calcareous, sheep-grazed turf of the downs and wolds, particularly favoured by Wheatears and other birds of short turf, and the damp flower-rich meadowland formerly used for hay production, and favoured by Corncrakes, Quails and Whinchats.

FIG 125. Intensive silage fields, south Scotland. Grassland covering more than a quarter of the land surface of Britain has been reseeded and 'improved' during recent decades (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

FIG 126. The Corncrake Crex crex was once a common inhabitant of damp hay meadows across Britain (Edmund Fellowes).

In the past, farmers preferred a high water table in grassland used for cattle, because it supported grass growth through the driest part of summer. The land was often too wet for grazing in winter, when cattle moved to drier ground and fed instead on hay and arable fodder crops. The fashion now is for intensive grass production for silage on drier land in summer, using irrigation when required, and using the resulting silage to feed cattle for the rest of the year.

MECHANISATION OF GRASS CUTTING

For centuries, hay was cut by lines of men wielding scythes. It could take up to several days to cut a field, and up to several weeks to cut all the hay fields on a farm. A good man could cut only an acre in a day. With hand-cutting, any birds in the crop that could fly or run could normally escape, but many nests were probably destroyed (Shrubb 2003). Mechanical mowing machines, initially drawn by horses, came in from the 1840s (Fig. 127). They speeded up the process of grass cutting, but destroyed adult and young Corncrakes, as well as nests (Norris 1947). They caught on slowly, however, and by 1890 40% of the hay in Britain was still cut by hand. In northwest Britain, including the islands, where the ground was often uneven, much hay was still cut by scythe into the 1950s.

To judge by comments in 19th-century bird books, mechanical mowing was judged highly destructive, not just to Corncrakes, but also to Quails, Whinchats, Corn Buntings and occasionally Spotted Crakes, which also nested in hay crops. Quail were regarded as just as vulnerable as Corncrakes. By the 1960s, Quails and Corn Buntings were not only much rarer than previously, but were found mainly in cereal crops, perhaps because growing grass had become too thick for them. All these species have naturally high mortality rates, so are unable to support much additional mortality or much reduced reproduction. It is not surprising that their population declines were rapid.

FIG 127. Horse-drawn mowing machine, the beginning of the end for the Corncrake Crex crex over most of Britain (David Mason).

The Corncrake was once widespread and familiar to country folk through its monotonous nocturnal calls. In good habitat, singing males could occur at 10 per km2, all with females and young. These figures give some idea of the numbers that were present in Britain in times past, and of the number that could have been killed at each mowing. Corncrakes were the most obvious casualties of mechanised grass cutting, as nests, young and sometimes adults were destroyed by the new machines, their bodies remaining for all to see. In southern England, practically the whole period when young were present coincided with the main hay harvest, so that 'whole broods were slaughtered' year after year (Norris 1947). But further north, in the Highlands and Islands, not only was less of the hay cut by machine, but mowing was around 2–3 weeks later, when the young were older. Fitting these patterns, the collapse of Corncrake populations began in southern districts in the 19th century, and then spread gradually northwards (Norris 1947). Where the species still persists, mainly on the islands off north and west Scotland, targeted funding has enabled fields to be cut late in the season and in a Corncrake-friendly manner (see here). This has helped to boost remnant populations considerably since the 1990s, and at the same time confirmed the assumed cause of the decline (Green et al. 1997, Green 2002).

FIG 128. Three other early victims of mechanised grass-mowing: upper left, Corn Bunting Emberiza calandra (Alan Martin); upper right, Whinchat Saxicola rubetra (Richard Chandler); lower left, Quail Coturnix coturnix, (Derbyshire Ornithological Society).

It was not just the speed of horse-drawn (and later tractor-drawn) mowers that killed more birds than scythes, but also the pattern of cutting. Using scythes, a line of men would work slowly across a field from one side to the other, driving birds ahead, and enabling them to escape through the hedge from one field to the next. They escaped by running rather than by flight. The mechanical mowing machine is instead towed round the outside of the field, continuing in an ever-decreasing spiral, gradually concentrating birds in the middle. Corncrakes and Quails are reluctant to break cover and cross the short grass, so most are killed by the last few cuts, or by dogs brought along to kill any fleeing Rabbits. So both the date and pattern of mowing affected the productivity of Corncrakes (Green et al. 1997, Tyler et al. 1998).

From the 1940s, further detrimental changes occurred. Firstly, horse-drawn machines were replaced by tractor-drawn ones. This change had little effect on the starting date for haymaking, but tractors were faster than horses and the whole process was accomplished more rapidly, advancing the average date of cutting and thereby putting more Corncrake broods at risk (Smith & Jones 1991, Green 1995). Secondly, from the 1950s, the use of fertiliser on improved grass varieties brought forward the optimal cutting dates. The increasing proportion of grass harvested as silage in subsequent decades would have put further pressure on any remaining Corncrakes, because most silage is harvested earlier than hay and more than once per season (see here).

The life-history features of Corncrakes added to their vulnerability, for even in ideal conditions few reach more than two years of age. The natural annual adult mortality in Britain has been calculated at around 75% (Green 1999, 2004). However, nest success is high, and most females can produce two clutches in a season, each averaging around 10 eggs. With such naturally high adult mortality, population trends are greatly influenced by breeding success, and a poor breeding year from any cause can result in a big decline in breeding numbers the next year. Museum skins indicate that, during the early 20th century, coinciding with the main period of population decline, the proportion of first-year adults in breeding populations was much depressed compared to earlier years, reflecting the poor reproductive success that prevailed over this period (Green 2008).

By the 1990s, more than 90% of the Corncrakes remaining in Britain were found on the Hebrides (Green 1995). From 1992, crofters were paid to manage their hay and silage fields in a way more sympathetic to Corncrakes. It entailed harvesting hay and silage as late in the year as possible, preferably August, and cutting from the middle of the field outwards (Tyler et al. 1998). In effect, the field is cut as two separate plots, with each being mown from the central long axis of the field towards the edge. This pattern of mowing entails driving a longer distance overall, and in places over uncut grass, which was not something farmers would normally do, but it allows most Corncrakes to escape from one field to the next or into tall vegetation at the field edges. The money to pay crofters for doing this came initially from the RSPB and later also from Scottish Natural Heritage and then government-funded agri-environment schemes (Chapter 21).

After these measures were introduced, the population trend of Corncrakes in northwest Scotland changed from a mean decline of 3.4% per year to an increase of 5.6% per year. This change was roughly as expected from the proportion of breeding attempts that benefited from the modified mowing. Effects on numbers were striking, as counts of singing males increased steadily from 480 in 1993 to nearly 1,274 in 2014 (Wotton et al. 2015).

While the Corncrake and Quail have precocious young that leave the nest within a day after hatching and then walk around in the grass, the Corn Bunting and Whinchat raise their young in nests placed on or just above the ground within the grass. All are vulnerable to mechanical mowing. The Skylark builds its nests in a depression in the ground and was apparently much less affected by scythe mowing or by the reciprocating cutter blades of the early mowing machines (which operated like a garden hedge-clipper). It is only in recent decades, following the introduction of mowers with rotating cutters that run at high speed under a cover (like a garden rotary mower) that all nests (including Skylarks) are likely to be 'sucked up' and destroyed (Shrubb 2003). The way in which mowing machines operate may thus have affected the number of birds and nests destroyed. In all these species that inhabit grass fields, declines in population levels are known or assumed to have occurred primarily because the birds are unable to produce enough young to offset the prevailing adult mortality. Their nests or young are destroyed by the physical process of mowing.

As intensive grass-growing methods have spread to the mountains of central Europe in recent years, mowing dates have advanced. Whinchat nests in the fields have been destroyed, and populations have swung into decline, repeating what happened in the lowlands of Britain in earlier decades (Muller et al. 2005, Strebel et al. 2015). However, a study in France showed that delaying mowing of 25% of meadow land, so as to allow more nests to produce young, soon led to a turnaround in the numbers of Whinchats and other small birds nesting in the fields (Broyer 2011).

Other operations that are carried out in spring on short grassland, such as muck and slurry spreading, rolling, topping and harrowing, can also destroy the nests of ground-nesting birds, although these spring losses may in part be compensated by re-laying. Topping (the cutting of taller vegetation such as rush clumps) can also affect invertebrate numbers and bird species composition through reducing sward patchiness and removing potential nest sites or by destroying ant-hills, a source of food for many birds.

CHANGE FROM HAY TO SILAGE

Into the 1960s, much of the hay in Britain was grown on poorly drained land. Soil warmed and grass began to grow relatively late in the year, and in the absence of fertiliser its growth was relatively slow. Even in the south, it was not ready for cutting until mid-June or July, when some plants had already seeded but while most stems and leaves were still green and nutritious. Many broad-leaved plants were present among the grasses, and were able to flower and seed, giving nectar, pollen and other foods for insects and seeds for birds such as Linnets and Goldfinches. After cutting, the hay lay in the fields for some days to dry before being gathered in. During this time, it may have been turned once or twice using a swath-turner to help the drying, but the process was weather-dependent, and could be delayed for days at a time by rain. There was one crop (entailing one cut) per year. Nearly a week of dry and sunny weather was needed to make good hay, and in western areas, timing the mowing to hit the gaps between rains was a gamble at best. A bad summer could ruin a winter's fodder. The old adage 'make hay while the sun shines' still retains its original significance, despite its wider modern usage.

The process of silage making first came to Britain in about 1880, but for decades production remained low and fluctuating, reaching less than 1 million tonnes per year in the 1940s, then increasing rapidly to more than 50 million tonnes per year in the 1990s (Brassley 1996). Silage is made from grass, cereals, or other leafy vegetation which is cut green, usually as seeds begin to form, when the nutrient content is near its peak. While still fresh, it is compressed in a pit or silo, or pressed into tight bales and wrapped in plastic. Under compression, it undergoes anaerobic fermentation either naturally or through the addition of specific bacteria, which ensure better quality of the final product. Silage can be conserved with a moisture content as high as 75%, compared with the need for less than 18% for hay, which is convenient given the vagaries of the British climate. Haylage is intermediate between hay and silage. It is dried in the field until the moisure content has been reduced to 30–50%, which takes about one-fourth of the time taken to produce hay. It is then gathered up, compressed into round bales and wrapped in plastic to exclude air.

Green grass cutting is followed by immediate regrowth, giving one or more additional cuts about 5–7 weeks apart through the growing season. In some places, five or even six cuts can be obtained in a good year, the first in late April and the last in September. In most years, however, silage grass is not ready for its first cut until late May.

FIG 129. Silage harvesting, south Scotland (Bobby Smith).

The change from hay to silage thus led to earlier, denser and faster grass growth, multiple cuts through the summer, lack of seeding by grasses, and loss of wild flowers and their seeds from the sward. All this increased the production of grass to unprecedented levels, so that silage largely replaced not only hay, but also oats and fodder root crops, as winter food for cattle and sheep. But because of the frequent cutting, silage fields provided a lethal habitat for nesting birds. Some species, including Skylark and in some places Corn Bunting, Yellow Wagtail, Whinchat, Grey Partridge, Corncrake, Lapwing, Oystercatcher and Curlew, occasionally nest in grass intended for silage, but seldom raise young.

The Skylark has been investigated in detail. In a study in Switzerland, where cuts of silage grass were made on a monthly basis, mowing accounted for 80% of all nest losses, and predation for only 10%. In one site, 95 out of 98 nests were destroyed, and the other three survived only because the grass was not cut properly (Jenny 1990). Any nests which survived the cut became exposed to predators and liable to fail soon afterwards. On average, from the 4–5 eggs laid in a clutch, only 0.14 chicks were produced, so that seven nesting attempts were needed to produce a single chick. Moreover, after cutting in this Swiss area, it took around two weeks for the grass to grow tall enough to tempt the birds into further nest-building, but the new nests were then destroyed at the next cut. If we assume that, after this two-week wait, nest-building takes at least a few days, and that the period from the laying of the first egg to chicks leaving the nest is about four weeks, this brings us to nearly seven weeks from the last cut. But allowing another two weeks for the fledged young to fly strongly brings us to nine weeks from the last cut. Even if Skylarks started nest-building immediately after a cut, they could still not rear a brood in the time available before the next cut. Clearly, Skylarks cannot stand such low productivity and, in the absence of continual immigration, populations must inevitably decline.

FIG 130. Skylark Alauda arvensis, the commonest victim of silage harvesting (Richard Chandler).

Other small songbirds also require some 5–7 weeks from nest-building to independence of young, so unless they happen to fit in their nesting attempts before the first cut in late May, or precisely within the gap of 5–7 weeks between subsequent cuts, they are doomed to fail. Immediately after each cut, the grass is in any case too short for Corn Buntings, Yellow Wagtails and Whinchats, and as mentioned above, usually also for Skylarks. The latter can sometimes manage to raise one early brood in silage grass if the first cut is delayed to the end of May, but the other three species begin nesting too late in the year for this (for Corn Bunting see Chapter 21).

Small wader species take around seven weeks between laying and fledging of chicks, while larger species take up to ten weeks. Lapwings and early individuals of other waders can hatch one clutch before the first silage cut and, although the chicks leave the nest soon after hatch, the dense tall grass sometimes makes it difficult for them to escape from the field. After rain they are also likely to become soaked and chilled in a way that would not happen in more open habitat with areas of shorter grass. Even in species as large as Black-tailed Godwit and Curlew, the chicks 'can hardly move in this "jungle" and after rainfall they often perish due to the cold' (Witt 1991). With their longer breeding cycles, Curlews need the grass to be left uncut until mid-July or later, if their young are to avoid the blades. Some pairs of waders and partridges manage to get their non-flying chicks out of silage fields to shorter grass, if it is available nearby, but they seem to be in the minority. Silage fields therefore act as 'sink' habitat for all these birds – habitat which is attractive because at a certain stage it is structurally suitable, but which offers little or no chance of reproductive success. Grass silage is worse than having a totally unattractive habitat, which would at least cause birds to move on and settle elsewhere.

In the south of Britain where the growth of grass begins early, Lapwings usually reject silage fields for nesting, preferring shorter and more open swards. It is in the north, where growth begins later, that Lapwings most often settle in early-stage silage fields, but then suffer the consequences. Along with other early-nesting species, Lapwings may also suffer from another danger, namely rolling, which is undertaken before the main period of grass growth and crushes any eggs that have been laid by then. This operation is intended to level the ground and prevent contamination of the growing grass by soil which can introduce Clostridium bacteria, making the silage rancid or toxic to livestock. This is less of a problem in haymaking, where contamination of grass by soil is not perceived as important.

During the cutting process, hirundines often feed above silage fields on any insects tossed into the air; gulls, Rooks, Jackdaws and Starlings are quick to pick up any insects left on the ground, while Kites search for voles and bigger insects. Probing birds also have access to soil-dwelling invertebrates which have been free of avian predation for at least several weeks. But this bonanza is short-lived. Surface prey are cleared up quickly, and with the removal of vegetation, the soil dries and soil-dwelling invertebrates retreat deeper, putting them beyond the reach of Rooks and other soil-probing birds (Devereux et al. 2006). It is for these reasons that birds normally feed heavily on silage fields for only a few days after mowing, and then gradually less. In northern England, 20 bird species were seen feeding on freshly cut fields, but usage declined by 50% by day 11 for corvids, by day 8 for aerial-feeders (hirundines), by day 6 for gulls, and by day 4 for Kestrels (Peggie et al. 2011). Furthermore, because silage contains so few seeds, it has little to offer sparrows, finches and buntings in either summer or winter. With frequent cuts, vole and shrew populations cannot build up as they do in hay, so that, apart from at cutting times, their predators seem to avoid silage fields.

The switch from hay to silage is clearly beneficial for livestock farmers, especially in high-rainfall areas where haymaking is difficult. Silage grass still requires warmth and frequent rain (or irrigation) to grow, and cannot be cut while wet, but it does not need a lengthy drying period. Harvested at an earlier growth stage, silage grass is not only more nutritious than hay, but with multiple crops per year, its overall yield is very much greater. The freshly cut grass is compressed for fermentation, often with molasses or other nutrients added, further enhancing its feed value. The development from the late 1980s of tractor-mounted machines to compress silage or haylage into conveniently sized bales wrapped in plastic only added to its popularity. With all these advantages, farmers are unlikely to revert to hay, and it is not surprising that the area of grass silage/haylage in Britain increased from 10% of total harvested grass in 1962 to 75–80% in the mid-1990s. The remaining harvested grass is still taken as hay, much of which is needed for riding horses, and variable summer weather can affect the ratio of hay to silage from year to year. But with hay, haylage and silage together, more than 40% of all lowland agricultural grassland in Britain – more than 870,000 ha – is mown at least once each year, within the bird breeding season. The other nearly 60% of lowland grassland remains as grazed pasture.

FIG 131. Haylage harvesting on Islay (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Much the same management is applied to grass grown for immediate consumption, whether it is cut piecemeal and carted on a daily basis to dairy cows kept in sheltered yards, or left in the fields for cows to graze each day between milkings, with their daily feeding range controlled by electric fences. Such grass supports a far higher density of cattle than traditional pastures, so that any birds that nest on the ground are likely to have their nests trampled. The net result of these changes is that few or no ground-nesting birds can expect to breed in intensively managed grass fields successfully.

CHANGE FROM MANURE TO FERTILISER

Both manure and inorganic fertilisers enhance the nutrient content of soil and vegetation, and hence the net productivity of the sward. However, manure releases its nutrients more slowly, and provides extra food for some soil-dwelling invertebrates, which are in turn eaten by birds (Chapter 5). Inorganic fertilisers also enhance the numbers of soil-dwelling organisms, but largely through the extra plant growth and subsequent decay that they promote (Edwards & Bohlen 1996). However, they also increase the density and uniformity of the sward, reducing the diversity of plant species, insects and birds that can live there.

Between the 1960s and 1990s, the annual amounts of inorganic nitrogen fertiliser applied to grassland in Britain increased several-fold (MAFF 1997). On permanent grass, between 1962 and 1985, the area treated annually increased from about 38% to more than 70%, while the amount applied to treated areas rose from about 20 to 120 kg/ha. On ley grass in the same period, the area treated increased from 65% to more than 90%, while the average amount rose from around 40 to more than 220 kg/ha (Shrubb 2003). In general, silage fields received more than twice as much nitrogen per hectare as hay fields (MAFF 1997). From the 1990s on, the average usage per hectare fell slightly (Chapter 4). These figures were from England and Wales, and usage on grassland in lowland Scotland was somewhat lower throughout, increasing overall from around 40% to more than 60% of area, and from around 20 to around 100 kg/ha. Into the 1990s, other factory fertilisers were also applied on about 67% of grassland annually at average rates of 15 kg phosphorus and 45 kg potassium per hectare. And if this were not enough, nearly half of mown grassland in recent decades also received annual applications of solid manure or liquid slurry.

FIG 132. Fertiliser spreading on silage field, south Scotland (Ricard & Barbara Mearns).

Many wild plants have evolved in situations that are nutrient-poor, and they either cannot tolerate high concentrations of nutrients or are out-competed by those species that can. Modern varieties of agricultural grasses have been bred to respond quickly to high nutrient levels, so they soon monopolise space and light, smothering other plants in the same sward (Smith 1987). A few broad-leaved plants, such as dandelions, docks and nettles, can thrive in high-nutrient soils, and are also strongly competitive. But most forbs and less competitive grasses begin to disappear from botanically diverse grasslands under inorganic nitrogen applied at 25 kg/ha per year, which is far lower than the amounts usually applied on British grassland. Phosphorus fertilisers can also severely reduce plant diversity. Across Europe, on both grassland and arable, the greater the nitrogen input, the fewer the plant species found there, after allowing for the effects of other variables (Kleijn et al. 2009). The loss of flowering plants from the countryside in turn translates into a loss of insects for many kinds of birds and of seeds for finches (Van Wingerden et al. 1992, Fenner & Palmer 1998).

In many districts slurry has now replaced farmyard manure as the main organic fertiliser available. This sloppy material releases its nutrients faster than manure, to the further detriment of botanical diversity. Seasons of application have also changed. In the past, manure was spread mainly in autumn, but today mainly in late winter and spring, providing the ground is firm enough. Applications in spring can cover the nests of early ground-nesting birds.

Despite its mainly negative impacts on bird populations, intensive management of grassland may have been a major factor contributing to the increase in Carrion Crows, Rooks and Jackdaws in Britain. All these species walk around and find their soil-dwelling prey more easily on short cultivated grass than on traditional rough grassland. Fertiliser use can promote higher earthworm densities in fields that are left unploughed, while the more frequent cutting and heavier grazing of improved grass fields ensures that short grass is available in abundance year-round, albeit in different fields at different times. The most recent national survey of Rooks in Britain during 1996 suggested a population of nearly 1.3 million pairs, 40% more than in the previous survey of 1975–77 (Marchant & Gregory 1999). However, many other feeding opportunities had increased for Rooks over that period, including refuse dumps, outdoor piggeries, game-bird feed sites, roadside carrion and garden bird-feeders.
