Temperature records suggest that, while the advancement in mowing dates before 1980 was largely due to agricultural intensification, after 1980 it was largely due to climate change. Up to around 1980, most godwit chicks hatched well before the onset of grazing and mowing, so they had safety and plenty of tall grass habitat to feed in. But nowadays the potential hatching peak occurs after most mowing has already taken place.

This has a number of implications (Kleijn et al. 2010). First, an increasing proportion of clutches and young chicks are exposed to mowing activities or grazing cattle. Correspondingly, the losses of godwit clutches increased nearly sevenfold between the late 1980s and the late 1990s. Secondly, hatched chicks now find themselves in landscapes that are largely devoid of their preferred tall-grass foraging habitat; and in recently cut or grazed fields with short grass the risk of predation is much greater. Thirdly, the vegetation on the remaining uncut fields is taller and denser at the time the chicks hatch, and therefore less suitable for foraging. Decline in the quality and availability of preferred habitat may explain why godwit chicks are currently in poorer condition than in the 1980s, and why reproductive success, and especially chick survival, has declined in this period. So to summarise, compared to the 1980s, nowadays: (1) a much greater proportion of eggs and chicks are lost to agricultural operations, (2) there is little good foraging habitat left when chicks hatch, and (3) partly because of climate change, the vegetation in the remaining foraging habitat is taller and denser and therefore less able to support chicks. It was suggested that an increase in godwit numbers could be achieved most efficiently by raising ground water levels to just below the field surface throughout the chick period. The resulting oxygen deprivation of plant roots would retard above-ground growth, independently of temperature or fertiliser levels, thus creating more open swards even in modern grasslands.

BREEDING AND POPULATION TRENDS

Since the 1970s, many studies have been made of breeding waders in Britain and western continental Europe, and almost all have shown that the production of young was too low to offset the usual annual mortality, so that populations were inevitably in decline. These findings came from grassland habitats where species were declining most strongly, and did not necessarily apply to other habitats. Among Lapwings in Britain, it was shown that, over a period of decline, no long-term change occurred in the annual adult mortality rate (as assessed from national ring recoveries), implying that population decline was entirely due to reduced reproductive output (Peach et al. 1994, Newton 2013a). This finding, based on BTO data at the national scale, was borne out by detailed local studies in Britain and elsewhere (Matter 1982, Galbraith 1988). The situation has changed in recent years, however, as the annual adult mortality of Lapwings in Britain has also increased slightly, presumably accelerating the rate of population decline (Robinson et al. 2014). In the lowlands, only on some nature reserves that were managed specifically for waders, and often where predators were also controlled, was reproduction high enough (more than 0.7 young per pair) to maintain Lapwing numbers (Merricks 2010). In a few other areas, reproduction was poor, but numbers were maintained, presumably by immigration. Some 25 sites surveyed in one year during the period 2003–05 held from 2 to 44 Lapwing pairs, but 10 of these sites produced no young at all. One of the non-productive sites held 32 pairs and another 22 pairs, but neither produced any young (Bolton et al. 2011).

While assessments of predation rates on eggs or chicks are usually not on their own sufficient to show that predation is reducing breeding numbers, rates can sometimes be so high that this conclusion is inescapable, even in the absence of information on adult survival. For example, Curlews in Northern Ireland declined by 58% over the period 1987–99. A study showed that 82–85% of all nesting attempts failed before hatching, with predation accounting for about 90% of the losses (Grant et al. 1999). Foxes appeared to be the main culprits in one area (in Co. Antrim), and Hooded Crows and Lesser Black-backed Gulls in another area (Lough Erne Islands). Annual breeding success of Curlews averaged 0.19 young per pair in Antrim and 0.38 young per pair on the Lough Erne Islands. If the breeding success in Antrim was typical of most of Northern Ireland, it was sufficient to account for the rate of population decline across the whole region (Grant et al. 1999). Among Curlews in Sweden, pairs nesting on farmland were much less productive than those on bogs (0.25 young per pair per year compared with 1.4), so farmland populations were probably maintained by surplus production on bogs (Berg 1994). So whatever the importance of habitat destruction in the 1960s–80s when population declines in waders began, lack of recovery and further decline since then can often be attributed largely to poor breeding success, of which predation is a major proximate cause. Nevertheless, for a given reduction in reproductive output, the naturally low annual mortality rates of waders, which are usually in the range 5–20%, would be expected to result in slower population declines than in species, such as Corncrake and small passerines, whose annual mortality rates are greater than 50%.

Dispersal and population declines

The reason that some waders continue to decline is that they persist in nesting in well-drained grass monocultures, even though their breeding success may be close to zero there. Such habitat looks good early in the season, but after the birds have started to nest, the fertilised grass grows so rapidly and thickly that they cannot raise young there. If the birds restricted themselves to traditional wet herb-rich grasslands, they would have much less habitat overall, but a breeding output that was at least high enough to maintain their numbers. The reduced population of wet meadows could then be sustained there in the long term. But while ever a substantial proportion of birds move each year to settle in the 'sink habitat' of modern grasslands, a continuing decline in overall numbers can be expected.

This problem of dispersal to poor habitat has been examined in Black-tailed Godwits in the Netherlands, where birds breed both in wet herb-rich meadows where breeding is good and in modern grass monocultures where breeding is poor (Kentie et al. 2014). Movements of birds between the two types of habitats were studied on the basis of 1,810 marked chicks and 531 marked adults in a study area of 8,500 ha. Both young and adult godwits moved at a higher rate from the grass monocultures to the few remaining meadows than the other way round, apparently preferring the better habitat. Yet some birds of both age groups still moved from meadows to monocultures. As explained in Chapter 12, such areas act as 'ecological traps' to which birds are attracted in spring, but in which they cannot subsequently raise enough young to maintain their numbers. If enough birds nest in this poor habitat, as opposed to good habitat, the overall population is bound to decline. In theory, the birds might in time evolve more effective behavioural avoidance of poor habitat, but this could be too slow a process to prevent the extinction of regional populations.

WATERFOWL ON WET GRASSLANDS

Of all the bird species found on wet grassland, wildfowl are often the first to suffer from drainage, because of their association with standing water. Well-drained floodplains lost nearly all their breeding waterfowl in the 1970s or later. In the absence of large ditches holding permanent water, standing flood-water in spring often induces ducks to nest, but survival of the young depends on surface water being available into summer. Where wet grasslands show big annual fluctuations in spring water levels, so too do the numbers of ducks that settle in spring to breed there (Thomas 1980).

FIG 148. Common dabbling ducks found on the water-filled ditches of wet grassland: upper left, Shoveler Anas clypeata (Keith Kirk); upper right, Mallard Anas platyrhynchos (Stan Wilson); lower left, Teal Anas crecca (Stan Wilson); lower right, Gadwall Anas strepera (Frank Snykers).

On the Ouse Washes nature reserve, breeding waterfowl densities over the period 1968–78 averaged 103 pairs per km2. The commonest species were Mallard and Shoveler, with smaller numbers of Gadwall, Teal, Garganey, Pintail, Tufted Duck, and a few Pochard and Shelduck. Numbers of Gadwall and Tufted Duck increased over the study period following the provision of permanent pools, while pre-breeding numbers of Mallard, Pintail, Coot and others were highest in years with most spring flood-water. The various dabbling duck species nested within grass tussocks located some 10–60 m from water, while the diving ducks usually nested in tall vegetation within 10 m from the water's edge. Coots built up their conspicuous nests within water, protected by the resulting 'moat'. But regardless of where they nested, most waterfowl took their broods to ditches and pools with permanent water, whereas adults without broods concentrated on temporary pools. All these duck species fed in the breeding season mainly on small crustaceans and chironomids obtained from water (Thomas 1980).

Turning to winter, any low-lying grassland that floods for periods soon attracts feeding and roosting waterfowl, in hundreds or thousands depending on the water surface available (Thomas 1976, 1982, Fuller 1982). In the Ouse Washes, mean winter duck usage increased from 1.27 million 'duck-days' in the 1950s to 5.35 million in the early 1970s. This increase was attributable partly to longer retention of winter flood-water as deliberate policy, and partly to reduced disturbance as areas were closed to wildfowling. The commonest wintering duck species included Mallard, Gadwall, Teal, Wigeon, Pintail and Shoveler, with Tufted Duck and Pochard on the ditches and other deeper areas.

FIG 149. Two diving ducks found on the water-filled ditches of wet grassland: left, Tufted Duck Aythya fuligula (Frank Snykers); right, Pochard Aythya ferina (Edmund Fellowes).

FIG 150. Two rare dabbling ducks of wet grassland in the breeding season: left, Pintail Anas acuta (Edmund Fellowes); right, Garganey Anas querquedula, a summer visitor to Britain (Chris Knights).

At each flooding, earthworms and other invertebrates displaced from the soil offered a temporary abundance of food for ducks and gulls, up to 300 worms per square metre having been recorded (Thomas 1976). In general, however, Wigeon, Gadwall, Moorhen and Coot ate mainly vegetation, especially grass leaves; Mallard, Pintail and Pochard fed extensively on seeds; while Shoveler, Tufted Duck and Pochard ate the largest quantities of invertebrates (Thomas 1982). Geese and swans roosted on flood-waters, but usually fed in drier fields nearby, as did many of the ducks. From November on, waste potato tubers in nearby fields were consumed by Mallard, Pintail, Whooper and Bewick's Swans, while swans and Wigeon grazed young cereal leaves. During unusually deep floods, dabbling ducks tended to leave the Washes to feed elsewhere, apart from Wigeon, which walked out onto the boundary banks, along with Coots, to graze the grass. As the floods subsided and drier ground became available in spring, large numbers of waders appeared, especially Lapwing and Snipe. Other birds such as Fieldfares, Redwings, Rooks, Jackdaws, Starlings and Golden Plovers fed in the same drying fields.

FIG 151. Coot Fulica atra, a common breeder in the ditches of wet grassland (Richard Chandler).

FIG 152. Bewick's Swans Cygnus columbianus, winter visitors to flooded grassland (Chris Knights).

FIG 153. Wigeon Anas penelope, grazing on grass (Chris Knights).

Away from the Ouse Washes, too, some impressive counts of waders have been made on partly flooded fields in winter. For example, some 6,500 Snipe were counted in a small part of the Somerset Levels in 1977, and 15,000 Lapwing and more than 1,000 Dunlin in another part, with up to 2,000 Whimbrel stopping on spring migration (Round 1978).

FIG 154. Golden Plovers Pluvialis apricaria on winter flooded grassland, Caerlavarock (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Given the spate of recent land drainage, it may seem surprising that waterfowl in Britain have not declined in the same way as waders. This is probably because, over the period that they lost much wet grassland habitat, they gained alternative habitat in the form of new reservoirs and gravel pits. Along with reduced shooting pressure, this enabled their overall populations to expand. Monitoring data suggest increases in nationwide breeding numbers during 1970–2012 of 92% for Mallard and 47% for Tufted Duck, and during 1994–2012 of 99% for Gadwall. Rarer duck species were less well monitored in the breeding season, but over the 25 years to 2013 summer Garganey numbers were estimated to have risen by 80%, Pintail by 38% and Pochard by 207%; however, Garganey and Pintail numbered just a few tens of pairs and Pochard just a few hundred (Hayhow et al. 2015a). Wet grasslands and their associated waters remain major breeding areas for both Shoveler and Garganey.

COASTAL GRASSLANDS

Compared with inland flood meadows, unimproved coastal marshes hold similar types of breeding birds, but many more Oystercatchers, Avocets and Ringed Plovers, and in winter they attract feeding and loafing waders from nearby intertidal areas (Chapter 11). With more limited open water, coastal marshes generally attract fewer waterfowl than inland flood meadows, but they hold bigger numbers of Shelduck, and also wintering Brent Geese. And since coastal marshes do not normally freeze, they can support birds in severe weather in a way that inland grasslands cannot. The largest areas of coastal grazing marsh remaining in Britain, comprising around one-fourth of the total, lie around the Solway estuary between England and Scotland, with other large areas in the Thames estuary and elsewhere.

Some remaining coastal grasslands still support good numbers of breeding Lapwings and Redshanks, as well as of Skylarks (Milsom et al. 2000, 2002). In the North Kent marshes in 1995–96, Skylarks were found at mean densities of 40 pairs per km2, rising to 160 pairs per km2 in the best areas. Such areas had structurally complex swards, no roads or powerlines, and grazing pressures equivalent to less than one cow per hectare (Milsom et al. 2001). On some coastal grasslands, the ground surface has never been levelled, so it remains uneven, giving the varied moisture regimes important to nesting waders. Nevertheless, drainage, agricultural intensification and sea-level rise have all resulted in decline of coastal grazing marshes and saltmarshes, and in the birds that nest on them. The numbers of Redshanks breeding on British saltmarshes fell by an estimated 53% over the 26 years between 1985 and 2011, declines being least severe on sites where grazing pressures had remained low (Malpas et al. 2013b). However, in contrast to breeding birds, some species which winter on coastal grasslands, such as Brent Geese, have increased in recent decades, although not necessarily because of any aspect of agricultural management.

FIG 155. Left, Saltmarsh at Gibraltar Point, Lincolnshire (Ian Newton); right, Brent Geese Branta bernicla feeding on winter saltmarsh (Chris Knights).

CREATION AND MANAGEMENT OF WET GRASSLAND NATURE RESERVES

Nowadays conservation bodies apply the lessons learned above to the creation and management of wet grassland nature reserves, which usually involves re-wetting previously drained land. Their aim is to combine water control and appropriate land management (especially grazing) to produce habitat suitable for at least several wader species: that is, extensive short tussocky grassland with pools and ditches. This is best achieved in places that were wet in the past, before they were drained. In some cases, simply reversing or limiting the outflow of water from a drainage ditch can bring the desired result, but in others a continuous input of water from elsewhere may be needed (Winspear & Davies 2005). Efforts are often compromised by surrounding agriculture and water management. In particular, lowered water tables to accommodate intensive agriculture in one part of a low-lying area make it difficult to raise or maintain water tables in another part in order to re-create wet grassland. This problem was encountered in the North Kent Marshes and Somerset Levels (Williams et al. 1983, Green & Robins 1993).

Invertebrates in flooded grassland

Long-term pastures free from flooding usually contain a high biomass of soil-dwelling invertebrates, comprising mainly various earthworms and leatherjackets. The situation differs on wet grasslands, especially on those subjected to winter flooding. In such areas the biomass of soil-dwelling invertebrates is generally lower than in dry pasture, comprising mainly a limited range of semi-aquatic earthworms, notably Allolobophora chlorotica, Eiseniella tetraedra, Lumbricus rubellus and Octolasion tyrtaeum (Ausden et al. 2001). So when dry grassland or arable land is flooded to re-create wet grassland, many soil invertebrates die, and it may take some years to gain a more appropriate invertebrate fauna (Callaway 1998). Most earthworms, tipulids and other invertebrates vacate the soil soon after the onset of flooding, and appear on the soil surface. Their emergence produces a rich but temporary food source for ducks and gulls attracted by the floods, but it reduces the soil-dwelling food items available to birds in the following summer. In one area, the sudden introduction of winter flooding to previously unflooded grassland reduced earthworm numbers by more than 90% and leatherjackets by more than 80% (Ausden et al. 2001).

Nevertheless, when worms are artificially confined in flooded soils, most species in the cold of winter can survive 3–4 months of continual submergence, providing the water remains aerated by surface agitation. In addition, the egg-containing cocoons of earthworms are apparently waterproof, enabling worm populations to re-establish themselves, but taking several months for newly hatched worms to reach a size suitable for birds. Moreover, high water tables in spring and early summer may confine any worms present to an upper layer within which they can be reached by the probing bills of waders. Remnants of winter floods that remain as pools in spring and early summer provide a rich source of chironomid midges and other aquatic invertebrates as important food sources for breeding ducks and waders and their chicks. Winter flooding may also remove voles, benefiting ground-nesting birds in the following summer, because it can take months for voles to return and even longer for their mammalian predators to re-colonise (Thomas 1980, Ausden et al. 2001). These predators would also eat the eggs and young of birds. But whatever the effects of winter flooding on invertebrates in soils, waders have long bred successfully in grasslands subject to regular and often prolonged submergence (Green 1986a, 1986b, 1988a, Green et al. 1990). The four most important sites for breeding Snipe in lowland England, namely the Ouse Washes, Nene Washes, Lower Derwent Valley and the Somerset Levels, are all extensively flooded in winter (Smith 1983).

FIG 156. The Nene Washes nature reserve under severe winter flooding. In this state they attract thousands of wintering waterfowl, some of which feed in the surrounding drier fields (Ian Newton).

Flooding during spring or summer is a different matter. As well as delaying or preventing breeding by waders, it has much more severe effects on soil-dwelling invertebrates. Under the higher temperatures that prevail in spring and summer, bacteria are more active and the soil can become anaerobic or toxic. Methane or hydrogen sulphide may then be emitted from rotting vegetation, killing most of the invertebrates present (Mather & Christensen 1988). It can then take months for their numbers to recover sufficiently to produce an adequate food supply for soil-probing birds.

Un-levelling land surfaces

One consequence of recent land drainage is that it allowed uneven land surfaces to be levelled, creating an ideal state for cultivation. But fields with varied topography provide mosaics of drier nesting places and wet feeding areas that dry out as the season advances. Gentle slopes provide a continuum of fresh wet-mud feeding areas as water levels recede during summer, with deeper places retaining water until June or beyond. This ensures that, throughout the drying period of late spring, there are always areas which are in ideal condition for a diversity of invertebrates, the staple food for wader chicks. Annual plants germinate on the margins, providing additional insect-food and cover for wader chicks; and the seeds from these plants later feed other birds, including wintering ducks.

The regular drying of pools in summer also ensures that fish cannot become established, as competitors with birds for the available insects. The conditions created by the periodic flooding and drying of ephemeral water bodies attract a limited range of invertebrates which, in the absence of fish, often reach prodigious numbers. High levels of organic matter from previous years promote high rates of invertebrate reproduction, providing lots of midge and beetle larvae to feed waders and their chicks. Such insects also benefit other farmland birds, such as Reed Buntings, Tree Sparrows, Song Thrushes, Pied and Yellow Wagtails. Uneven surfaces can be restored on previously levelled ground by re-excavating old drain systems or by creating a shallow sloping ridge-and-furrow system across the field.

On naturally well-draining soils, wetness of the surface layers can be maintained only by raising the water table, whereas on less permeable soils rainwater remains as surface pools for long periods. In re-wetted grassland, shallow pools (scrapes or wet flashes) can be created by reducing drainage from natural depressions, or by excavating new depressions at suitable places. Cattle can be used to graze the area and create the mosaic of tussocks and short turf favoured by several wader species, and to augment the invertebrate population by dunging. Normally the cattle are maintained at low density, or removed altogether for the nesting period to avoid clutches being trampled.

Grazing livestock

Grazing marshes are maintained by grazing, but as little as possible while birds are nesting. Many think that this can best be done with rare or traditional cattle breeds, but in reality, with large areas of wet grassland to be grazed, this is usually best done using animals from mainstream agriculture (P. Merricks, in litt.). Animals grazing such areas have to be part of a wider system which allows them to be moved elsewhere for wintering or fattening for slaughter, or simply to take the pressure off nesting birds. Grazing animals therefore need to be both readily available and readily saleable, so they can be acquired and moved on as needed.

Modern cattle, preferably with a Holstein parent, produce so much milk that they must graze constantly through the day, so a small number can keep the grass to the required shortness. Their calves, having a continental beef-breed father, are genetically programmed for rapid growth, and are able to drink all the milk produced by the dam. Old traditional slow-growing breeds can live on rougher less nutritious vegetation, but their demands are less, so greater numbers are required to keep the grass down. And greater numbers mean more nest trampling, if not by the cows themselves then by their more active calves.

Suckler cows are ideal for grazing during the breeding season, because they walk slowly over the ground (not running around like younger cattle), and are heavy enough to churn up the soft soil, creating additional feeding places for Lapwings. Protecting their calves, they also respond more readily to the mobbing behaviour of Lapwings, usually walking away from eggs or chicks (although they do crush some clutches). Sheep are less useful than cattle, because their trampling churns the soil less, their droppings are less attractive to insects, and they are less deterred by mobbing Lapwings.

Importance of rushes

Rushes are often a natural component of the damp grassland favoured by waders, and in fields with little plant diversity, rushes may be the only taller vegetation present providing cover for concealing nests and chicks, among shorter areas favoured for feeding. As a general guide, once rush cover exceeds 30% of a field's area, its value for breeding waders is reduced, although Lapwings, which need good all-round vision, are put off at lower levels of rush cover than Curlew or Snipe (Winspear & Davies 2005). In pasture, the tussocky structure suitable for nesting waders depends on the grazing pressure, with the sward becoming less tussocky as grazing increases. In fact, close grazing combined with summer mowing can eliminate rush clumps altogether, even in quite damp pastures (O'Connor & Shrubb 1986). The nutritional value of rushes is low, but cattle are better than sheep at grazing them down.

Predation control

Newly created wet grasslands usually attract Lapwings and other waders. The main problem is poor breeding success, which contributes to continuing national population decline. On many reserves, where livestock densities are limited, poor breeding can result from high predation on eggs and chicks. This problem can be resolved only by predation control, whether by killing predators (excluding legally protected ones), by removing potential nesting and denning sites, or by fencing – which works for mammalian predators but not for avian ones. Although effective fences lead to greater productivity in waders, they are expensive and need to be maintained, so it is difficult to build enough to deliver high productivity for a significant fraction of the wader population. Fox- and Badger-proof fences that do not require electricity are under development, and these may make larger-scale protection from mammal predators more feasible.

Despite the various management problems, declines in waders in recent decades have in general been much less marked on nature reserves than on similar habitat outside reserves. Compared to other waders, Snipe have declined most steeply on a national scale (Ausden et al. 2001, Ausden & Hirons 2002, Wilson et al. 2005c), although they persisted longest on soils that remained wet and soft through the breeding season (Smart et al. 2008).

CONCLUDING REMARKS

Traditional methods of managing wet grasslands by late grazing and haymaking clearly provided suitable conditions for breeding ducks and waders. But modern methods, involving drainage, fertiliser use and silage production, tend to produce drier, more uniform, dense swards unattractive or lethal to all ground-nesting birds, partly because they become ready for grazing or mowing earlier in the year (Chapter 12).

Drainage in the 1960s–90s caused the loss of around nine-tenths of all wet grassland from the lowlands of Britain. Waterfowl most dependent on standing water largely disappeared from these areas almost immediately, while waders often declined more slowly over a number of years. Levelling the ground to remove surface relief may have accentuated the effects of drainage, because it allowed the whole area to dry simultaneously in spring as the water table fell, leaving no damper areas for waders to feed. Drained soil dries earlier in spring, promoting earlier grass growth, and hence earlier grazing and mowing of the sward, with effects on wader nest success. On drained grassland, nesting attempts are mostly unsuccessful, owing to nest destruction by rolling or mowing, or by trampling from increased densities of livestock. Predation rates are often also higher in drained areas than in wetter ones, and because drained land dries out earlier in the year, soil-dwelling invertebrates more rapidly become inaccessible and the birds' breeding seasons are shortened.

In general, then, declines of waders and other birds on wet grassland can be attributed primarily to land drainage (affecting the period each breeding season in which soil probing is possible), with structural change in the vegetation to a more uniform sward (affecting its suitability for nesting), advancement of mowing or grazing dates (leading to more destruction of eggs and chicks), increased livestock densities (leading to more nest trampling and desertion), and reductions in soil-dwelling and surface-dwelling invertebrates as chick food. Other operations on short grassland, such as muck and slurry spreading or rolling and harrowing, can destroy the nests of ground-nesting birds in spring, although clutches lost at an early stage can in part be compensated by re-laying. Predation on the eggs and chicks of grassland waders is generally widespread, especially on drained land, and may have increased in recent decades in association with increases in the predators themselves or in the vulnerability of their eggs and chicks in the changed habitat. Crows and Foxes are some of the main culprits, but many other predators are involved in different places, including introduced Hedgehogs in the Outer Hebrides.

In populations of all grassland wader species studied, decline occurred because reproduction had fallen so low that insufficient young were produced to offset the usual adult mortality. Drainage and habitat loss may have caused the early declines of waders, during the 1960s–80s, but breeding success is now so low in most remaining wet grassland areas that, on prevailing adult mortality rates, further declines in numbers are inevitable, with much potential habitat unoccupied. The many studies of grassland waders in recent decades have given much information relevant to the management of wet grassland nature reserves.

## CHAPTER 14

## Insect Declines

DECLINES IN SOME OF THE food sources of birds on farmland, including soil-dwelling invertebrates, have been described in previous chapters. However, another major group of food organisms have not yet been discussed in detail, namely the above-ground insects. These small creatures are eaten by almost all farmland birds, and are crucial to the breeding of many. Declines in their abundance would therefore be expected to have major impacts on bird numbers and breeding success. Insects are active mainly in the warmer months, but the numbers of many seem to vary greatly from day to day, depending on the weather. Periods of cold and rain in summer can spell food shortage for many insectivorous birds. But overlying this seasonal and day-to-day fluctuation has been a long-term decline in insect abundance which has affected many birds. Overall, their declines may have been greater than those of birds.

Insects fill almost every conceivable ecological niche. While some species are herbivores, others are omnivores, predators, parasites or scavengers, consuming almost anything organic, dead or alive. Many small insects, including many flies, can complete their entire life cycles from egg to adult in less than a fortnight, so in ideal conditions, they can increase rapidly to take advantage of abundant food supplies. Others – mostly larger species – take the whole growing season to develop, or more than a growing season if they need a period of winter dormancy. Yet others take up to several years to develop, as shown by many beetles whose larvae live in the soil. Long life cycles make such insects especially vulnerable to the frequent disturbance caused by agricultural operations.

Insects are eaten by other insects and a vast array of other animals. Those that are especially important in the diets of birds, as larvae, pupae or adults, include beetles (Coleoptera), grasshoppers (Orthoptera), plant bugs (Hemiptera), butterflies and moths (Lepidoptera), flies (Diptera) and ants (Hymenoptera). Other arthropods, especially spiders (Araneae) are also important to many bird species.

FIG 157. The flower-rich meadows of the past were full of insects in summer (Richard & Barbara Mearns).

Anyone of appropriate age will remember a time when cleaning insects from car windscreens was a frequent task, and an invariable consequence of any long summer journey. Nowadays, in Britain, one can drive for weeks at any time of year without ever needing to do this. This is one of the most obvious manifestations of the massive decline in insect populations which has occurred in Britain since the 1970s. Studies imply that this is largely due to developments in agriculture.

Many people have noticed big reductions in conspicuous insects, such as butterflies and moths, bees, grasshoppers, cockchafers and other large beetles, but the declines extend to smaller insects too, including sawflies, leaf beetles, ants, weevils and others (Campbell & Cookeet al 1997, Wilson et al. 1999, Donald 1998, Potts 2012). A reminder of times past can be gained by walking through any remaining wild flower meadow or nature reserve in summer, when the sights and sounds of insects will be self-evident (Goulson 2014).

INSECTS OF VEGETATION

Among modern agricultural crops subject to pesticide use, cereals generally support most insects, beans and rape intermediate numbers, and potatoes fewest (Holland et al. 2011a). However, a much greater variety of species is found on the various weeds that develop within the crop. One of the initial causes of insect declines was the widespread use from the 1960s of selective herbicides to remove broad-leaved weeds (= wild flowers) from cereal crops. Most species of wild plants support several species of insect, which feed on the leaves, flowers or seed-heads, and others that suck the flowing sap. Some of these insects may be generalists that feed from a range of different plants, while others are restricted to a small number or even a single plant species. Close examination of any herbaceous plant at an appropriate time can reveal eggs, caterpillars, leaf beetles, aphids and plant suckers on the leaves, and a range of bees, butterflies and other insects on the flowers, all visited from time to time by predatory insects such as ladybirds and wasps. The destruction of these plants by herbicides thus removes a huge insect food supply, and the numbers and variety of insects are reduced accordingly (Potts 2012).

It is not just arable land that has lost most of its wild flora, but grassland too. Improvement in the productivity of old grassland usually involves ploughing and reseeding with cultivated grasses, followed by heavy nitrogen applications (Chapter 12). Most wild plants in these conditions cannot compete with grass, which, under the influence of extra nitrogen, grows so vigorously that it smothers the majority of broad-leaved herbs. One wild plant that does thrive in nitrogen-rich grassland is Dandelion, but it is evident only for a short time in spring when it flowers while the grass is still short. Other broad-leaved plants that can survive in modern grass fields, such as Creeping Thistle, can be readily eliminated by local herbicide applications. Most of the wild flowers of grassland, once so familiar, have thus disappeared from almost all the agricultural grassland in Britain, and with them their many dependent insects.

The second major factor in the decline of insects of arable land is the widespread use of insecticides to control crop pests. None of the chemicals used for this purpose is specific to pests, and all kill a wide range of other insects and other invertebrates at the same time (Chapter 8). Initially, these chemicals had two main agricultural uses: one as seed treatments, applied as a coating to seeds to protect them after sowing against insect attack, and the second as sprays against pests of fruit crops, such as codling moth and sawflies. But from the 1970s they became widely used also on cereal and other arable crops, often against aphids. In consequence, increasing areas of farmland were sprayed with insecticide year after year, further contributing to the widespread decline of insects and other arthropod populations. It is not only insects on the vegetation that were affected, but ground-dwelling species too, including ants and beetles.

FIG 158. Decline of the Grey Partridge Perdix perdix in the latter half of the 20th century was attributed primarily to herbicide use, which destroyed the weeds that supported the insects eaten by partridge chicks (Frank Snykers).

Most of the evidence for the declines of insects in the lowlands of Britain resides in the memories of farmers and naturalists, but some kinds of insects have been sufficiently well monitored to provide good quantitative evidence. One of the most influential studies has involved the insects of cereal fields in Sussex, as monitored annually by G. R. Potts and his colleagues in the GWCT (formerly the Game Conservancy Trust). Some of these insects formed the main food of young Partridge chicks, and poor chick survival resulting from shortage of suitable insects emerged as the primary driver of the widespread collapse of Grey Partridge populations in Britain from the mid-1950s on (Potts 1986, 2012). When this study began in 1969, insecticides had already been in use for more than 20 years and herbicides for more than 15 years, yet in the ensuing years overall arthropod numbers continued to decline by about 4% per year (equivalent to about 50% in the 20 years to 1989). Larger species were generally affected more than small ones, so that the overall biomass of insects in cereal fields had declined by 80%, and by 1990, this decline had reached 90% (Potts 1991, 2012, Ewald et al. 2015). This was the mean overall trend, and large annual fluctuations occurred in the abundance of some species, linked with weather. Overall declines were shown by sawflies (Symphyta), butterflies, bugs (except aphids), many beetle families (particularly leaf beetles Chrysomelidae and rove beetles Staphylinidae), money spiders (Linypiidae) and harvestmen (Opiliones), and parasitic wasps. Few of the insects involved were dependent on crop plants; most were found on weeds associated with the crops, so their declines were due more to herbicides than to insecticides. In the 1960s in cereal fields, 20 species of weeds could be found on every 2 × 2 m sample plot in the Sussex study area, mostly as small understorey plants, but these have now virtually gone, along with the insects they supported (Potts 2012). The decline of the Knotgrass Beetle – a favourite food of Partridge chicks and other birds – was especially severe.

Although these data came from a single large (62 km2) study area in Sussex, the findings seemed typical of events on cereal land throughout the lowlands of Britain (see also Greig-Smith et al. 1992). The declines in insects coincided with increases in the numbers and range of pesticide applications per year on the farms concerned, but it remained possible that other factors were also involved. However, some recovery in insect populations occurred within 1–2 years on arable land when pesticide use was experimentally curtailed. The density of weed cover then increased more than fourfold and insect numbers more than threefold, all with significant effects on the survival of young Grey and Red-legged Partridges and Common Pheasants (Sotherton 1991). This type of study, involving reduction of pesticide use, has been repeated many times subsequently, with similar results, as in flower-rich field margins created under agri-environment schemes (Chapter 20; Potts 2012). In addition, on organic farms free of pesticide use, insects as well as other animals are generally much more abundant (Chapter 9).

Other programmes monitoring insects have been organised from Rothamsted Research Station in Hertfordshire. In southern England, nocturnal moths sampled systematically by light trapping declined by 67% between 1933–50 and 1960–89 in arable land, but no change occurred in nearby woodland (Woiwood 1991). In a wider study, involving a network of about 100 light traps across Britain from 1968 to 2002, 66% of 337 large moth species declined significantly, half of these by 50% or more (Conrad et al. 2006). Later it was reported that the total numbers of larger moths in Britain had fallen by 28% between 1968 and 2007, the situation being particularly bad in southern Britain, where overall moth numbers were down by 40% (Fox et al. 2013). In northern Britain, decreases had been offset by other species spreading north. Overall, two-thirds of 337 species of common and widespread larger moths had declined over the 40-year study, while the remaining third had become more abundant, with 53 species (16% of the total) more than doubling their numbers. A similar report concluded that 70% of Britain's butterfly species had declined in occurrence and 57% in abundance over the same 40-year period (Fox et al. 2015). Some other species had expanded their distributions in this time, apparently in response to climate change. Widespread species generally fared better in Scotland than in England, mirroring trends reported in some other insects and birds. Other studies in parts of continental Europe under intensive agriculture gave similar results for other insects. For example, in Germany, some 50–80% of species of beetles and ants were effectively lost from arable land during 1951–81 (Heydemann 1983). These various declines coincided with increases in the numbers and range of pesticide applications per year in the areas treated, but it is not always possible to establish a firm causal link or to exclude other factors.

Some types of insects favoured by birds thrive on permanently short or sparse vegetation of a kind that is now rare on farmland. These include grasshoppers and ants, both of which require warmth from the sun, especially in early mornings. Grasshoppers feed on the green leaves of grass and other plants. They hatch in spring from eggs laid in dry soil during the preceding autumn, and grow through several nymph stages to produce winged adults in late summer. For egg-laying, they need warm dry soil undisturbed by cultivation, with suitable slope and orientation. These various requirements were widely available in the past, especially in rough unfertilised grassland, but now exclude them from most modern farmland (Chapter 12). They cannot persist in disturbed land, in any area treated with insecticides, or in thick dense grass or cereal crops which produce a microclimate at their level that is too cool and damp for them (Gardiner et al. 2008). Any that occur in grass intended for mowing suffer heavy mortality because the cutter blades pass at a height at which adults and nymphs tend to concentrate. Like butterflies, grasshoppers have now gone from intensive grass fields. Rich in fat and protein, they are eaten by a wide range of birds, from buntings and shrikes to corvids and Kestrels. Elsewhere, they are also eaten commonly by larger species, including storks, cranes and bustards.

Most common ant species also thrive on warm, well-drained soils, with short or sparse vegetation, but disappear from taller vegetation, such as ungrazed grass and cereals. They predominate in the diets of a small number of specialist bird species, such as the Green Woodpecker and Wryneck, but are also taken by many others. On dry unploughed soils, traditional tightly grazed grassland supports large colonies of ants, especially the Yellow Meadow Ant, whose bulging nursery mounds achieve a volume four times greater in tightly grazed areas than in ungrazed ones shaded by tall herbage (Potts 1970). Reduced grazing by sheep or Rabbits, resulting in a decline of these ants, has been suggested as a factor contributing to the declines of Grey Partridges in downland areas, and of Wrynecks in grassland areas with trees (Peal 1968, Potts 1970). Partridge pairs scratch into ant mounds to allow themselves and their chicks to feed on the pupae and workers. Some 86% of 346 food items found in chicks collected from grazed downland were ants, and brood sizes in grazed areas were 9.3 chicks per pair, compared with 2.9 in ungrazed downland where ants were scarce. This difference is so huge that other food items may also have been less available in ungrazed downland. The loss of traditional old grassland to ploughing has resulted in a corresponding loss of these large ant colonies from much of the country.

FIG 159. The Red-backed Shrike Lanius collurio was once found across farmland and heathland in southern Britain, feeding mainly on beetles, grasshoppers and other large insects. The species declined rapidly during the early 20th century, and although the causes are unknown, many of its prey species have become rare. No more than a few pairs now attempt to breed in Britain each year (Paul Hackett).

FIG 160. Ant-hills can be found on ancient grassland that has not been ploughed in recent times. The mounds themselves can be decades or centuries old, and in general, the bigger the anthills, the older the grassland. The ants form an important component in the diets of many grassland birds (Ian Newton).

FIG 161. Two ant specialists: above Green Woodpecker Picus viridis (Richard Chandler); below: Wryneck Jynx torquilla (Frank Snykers).

Many insects that are directly beneficial to agriculture have also declined in recent years, among them bees and other pollinators, on which much crop production (other than grass and cereals) depends. Poor pollination results in reduced yields, and poorly shaped orchard fruits which are usually un-saleable. It is not just Honey Bees that are involved in pollination, but a variety of wild bees too, including, in Britain, around 25 species of bumblebees. For bees to persist in any landscape, they need a supply of nectar-producing flowers throughout the growing season. In the past, wild flowers provided this resource, yielding a succession of nectar sources through the spring and summer. The needs of bees could have never been met by extensive cereal monocultures alone, or by favoured fruit or rape crops which are in flower for only a few weeks each year. In Britain, conditions offering an unbroken supply of nectar and pollen through the growing season are now found mainly in the semi-natural areas within farmed land, as in hedgerows, road verges, riversides and other uncropped areas, or in the gardens of towns and villages. Alternatively, they can be provided on farmland as 'nectar mixes', a range of flowering herbaceous plants sown in strips or patches among the crops specifically for the purpose of sustaining nectar-feeding insects through the summer (Chapter 20). Nevertheless, of the 97 food plants known to be preferred by bumblebees, at least 76% had declined significantly over the 70 years from 1930 (Carvell et al. 2006).

While destruction of habitat and food seems a likely cause of declines in bee and other pollinators, mortality and behavioural changes resulting from pesticide use may also be involved (Whitehorn et al. 2012). During their normal foraging behaviour, bees can be exposed to several different pesticides in a short time, giving the possibility of cumulative or combined effects. Honey Bees and wild bumblebees experimentally exposed to both pyrethroid and neonicotinoid pesticides showed increased mortality of workers (most died within four days of exposure), reduced production of workers, and reduced development of brood and colony growth, and reduced production of queens, which reduces the formation of future colonies (Gill et al. 2012). Individual worker bees exposed to neonicotinoids often showed a reduced ability to navigate and find their way home (Henry et al. 2012, Goulson 2013). Other factors involved in declines of Honey Bee populations include various viral diseases, mostly spread by the introduced varroa mite, but it is uncertain whether bees may be predisposed to such diseases by sub-lethal exposure to pesticides or inadequate food supply.

Much has been written in recent years about the effects of neonicotinoid pesticides on bees. As described in Chapter 8, rape seeds for sowing are treated with a neonicotinoid, which is absorbed into the growing plant, including the nectar and pollen consumed by bees. For years, the manufacturer (Bayer) denied that poison levels available in this way were high enough to harm bees, but eventually the evidence became overwhelming. Furthermore, a recent study examined the 20-year population trends of 62 different bee species in Britain according to whether or not they fed on rape flowers (a function of proboscis structure), and were therefore exposed to neonicotinoid pesticides. Population declines were on average three times stronger in the rape-feeding species than in the others (Woodcock et al. 2016).

In some situations, shortage of natural pollinators has been offset by importing hives into crop areas for the required pollination period. Commercial beekeepers provide this service, which is used in Britain mainly in fruit growing, and in North America also in the production of peas and beans, clover and alfalfa (lucerne). Seasonal shortages are avoided by moving the hives around between different crops and regions. This adds a cost to pollination which would not be incurred in a more natural system where wild bees were abundant. Despite their importance in pollination and seed production, bees do not form a major component of the diet of any bird species in Britain, except for the Honey-buzzard, which raids the nests for lumps of comb containing larvae. However, fewer than 50 pairs of Honey-buzzards are known to breed in Britain, so they cannot have a significant effect on bee populations. And nor can Bee-eaters, which hunt flying bees and breed sporadically in Britain, but only as occasional pairs.

Nowadays, partly owing to patterns of pesticide use, different crop types hold markedly different numbers of insects and other invertebrates. In studies in Hampshire and Lincolnshire in 1999–2000, break crops (oilseed rape and beans) often supported the most invertebrates and root crops the fewest. Regardless of crop, more invertebrates were found near the edges of fields than in the centres (Holland et al. 2002). Another study at Loddington in Leicestershire examined the abundance of 13 arthropod groups in different crops (cereals, beans, rape and grass), wild-bird cover and field boundaries (Moreby & Southway 2002). Overall, wild-bird cover contained the greatest numbers of arthropods important as bird foods, followed by wheat and then barley. These habitats were important for spiders, aphids and others (Homoptera), bugs (Heteroptera), leaf beetles (Chrysomelidae), soldier beetles (Cantharidae) and ground beetles (Carabidae). They were also the habitats containing the greatest numbers of sawfly larvae, which were particularly important for birds. Aphids were found in greatest numbers in cereals and also in some years in rape, while they were least abundant in wild-bird cover crops. However, the abundance of many kinds of insects varied greatly from year to year, probably in relation to weather and the timing of pesticide applications in the wider countryside.

Many of the insects that live in arable land are killed during cultivation and harvesting operations, and for part of each year have no crop or other field vegetation in which they can survive. They persist largely because of the presence of hedgerows and other undisturbed areas in which they can survive the winter, some colonising the crops afresh each year. As some hedges and other semi-natural areas were removed over the years, the overwintering habitats for insects were reduced accordingly, so that smaller areas of cropland were likely to be re-occupied in spring.

In summary, most kinds of insects and spiders that are found on field vegetation or the ground have declined greatly in recent decades, with reductions of 50–70% being recorded in many different groups. Many of these creatures figure prominently in the diets of birds. Declines have been attributed mainly to herbicide use removing food plants, fungicide use removing other insect food supplies, insecticide use removing insects directly, nitrogen-fuelled increased crop growth changing the structure and microclimate of field vegetation, and the removal from farmland of some refuge habitats, such as hedgerows and other semi-natural areas. Such pesticide-free habitats have been increased to some extent in recent years by agri-environment measures, such as provision of nectar-producing and other special crops in which insects can thrive (Chapter 20).

Impacts on birds

The most convincing evidence of the role of insect declines in bird declines relates to the Grey Partridge, discussed in Chapter 10. Through experiments, the breeding output of several other bird species, including Yellowhammer, Corn Bunting and Skylark, has been found to decline under shortage of insects, which can often lead to poor growth and starvation of nestlings (Brickle et al. 2000, Boatman et al. 2004, Morris et al. 2005, Hart et al. 2006), while observational evidence is available for others, such as Cirl Bunting (Evans et al. 1997). All these species collect their insect prey from vegetation or the ground. On the basis of their diets and ecology, at least 18 bird species are likely to have been affected indirectly by pesticide use in Britain (Campbell et al. 1997, Boatman et al. 2004). Almost all such species have declined substantially, but in the absence of more detailed studies, it is hard to say how much these declines were due to pesticide use, and how much to other agricultural changes that occurred at the same time.

AERIAL INSECTS

Insects on the move mostly travel by flying, and can be sampled from the airspace. Special equipment developed at Rothamsted Research Station was the first to be used in such monitoring and has been operated continuously since 1964. It consists of a pipe 12 m high on top of which sits a large pump that sucks in all insects and spiders that come within range. Following the Rothamsted example, other similar suction traps were built elsewhere, enabling the 'aerial plankton' to be sampled at widely spaced locations over periods up to several decades. The initial idea was mainly to monitor the abundance and distribution of travelling aphids, and provide an early warning system for farmers. But over the years these giant bug-suckers also gave information on the abundance of other small flying insects and drifting spiders, and their trends over the years. Although the catches at different localities often fluctuated in parallel from year to year, the mass of this aerial plankton declined most markedly over the years in areas where agriculture intensified most strongly. Some of the largest declines were in the small bibionid flies, whose larvae occur in grassland, feeding on dead and living plant roots, and which as flying adults are much favoured by Swifts and hirundines.

The annual catches of arthropods from a single suction trap near Stirling in central Scotland were examined for trends over 27 years (1972–98). The annual catches were compared with various measures of agricultural intensity and climate and also with the numbers of 15 farmland bird species, monitored in the breeding season (Benton et al. 2002). Twelve of 15 orders of arthropods showed significant downward trends over the 27-year period, their average abundance roughly halving in this time. These declining groups included seven of eight beetle families and 13 of 18 fly families. The remaining three orders showed big annual fluctuations over the years but no significant long-term trend. In general, farmland birds were more numerous in years with more abundant arthropods, or in the immediately following years, as would have been expected if arthropods had influenced bird breeding or survival. Moreover, arthropod numbers were in turn related to various measures of agricultural intensification, with bigger numbers in years when farming was less intensive. These relationships were partly modified by weather, but were consistent with the view that birds could be limited by insect availability, and that insect numbers were influenced by agricultural procedures.

Swifts, Swallows and martins all depend on airborne insects, but have somewhat different diets, depending partly on how high they fly, for bigger insects tend to fly at lower altitudes. Swallows feed relatively close to the ground, and take fewer and larger prey than martins and Swifts, including the flies associated with cattle. Sand Martins forage mainly over wetlands, often low over the water, and take insects of varying sizes. But House Martins and Swifts feed at higher altitudes, taking a lot of tiny items, including high-flying aphids. It is these two high-flying species that have most conspicuously declined in Britain over recent decades. In the House Martin, decline has become most evident in the southeast of Britain, and less marked towards the north and west where agriculture is less intense (Balmer et al. 2013). House Martins have even increased in parts of northwest Scotland, although in Britain as a whole the net change since 1970 has been a 47% decline (Hayhow et al. 2015a). No good index of Swift abundance in Britain was obtained before the start of the BBS in 1994, but from then to 2015 their numbers almost halved. Reduced nest sites may have caused some of this decline, but Swifts have also gone from many places where nest sites remain intact.

FIG 162. Two summer visitors to Britain which feed on aerial insects and have declined in recent decades: left, House Martin Delichon urbicum (Sean Gray, GrayImages); right, Swift Apus apus (Bobby Smith). Their breeding success varies from year to year according to the availability of small aerial arthropods which form their food, and both species have declined more markedly than Swallows, which feed on aerial insects nearer the ground.

Swallows have declined in southeast Britain, where cattle have gone from most farms, but increased in parts of the northwest. In one study, aerial invertebrate abundance over pasture fields was found to be more than double that over silage, and more than three and a half times greater than that over cereal fields (Evans et al. 2007). Pastures also hosted approximately twice as many foraging Swallows as both silage and cereal fields. It would be expected, therefore, that reductions in the amount of pasture in southeast England would have reduced the food supplies of Swallows, perhaps contributing to their decline in this region. Nationally, however, both Swallows and Sand Martins have shown substantial fluctuations and a slight net increase over past decades, although all three hirundine species have also shown annual fluctuations in relation to rainfall (and hence food supply) in their African wintering areas (Robinson et al. 2008).

Moreover, the breeding success of all these species has been found to fluctuate in relation to food supply (or in relation to weather which affects food supply) (for Swift see Lack 1956, for House Martin see Bryant 1975, for Swallow see Turner 2006). In addition, in areas of the Camargue in southern France that were sprayed with a microbial agent (Bti) to kill mosquitoes and midges, the clutch sizes and nestling survival of House Martins were lower than in control areas that were not sprayed, with mean brood sizes of 2.3 and 3.2 chicks respectively (Poulin et al. 2010). This gave direct experimental evidence of the effect of a bacterial insecticide on the productivity of House Martins, presumably mediated through reduction in food supply.

CONCLUDING REMARKS

Insects form a major dietary component of many farmland birds. Over much of Britain, their numbers have declined strikingly over recent decades, following the widespread introduction and continued use of agrochemicals. Many of the groups most favoured as food by birds have been affected. Insects tend to be generally more numerous on organic farms and other areas where pesticides are not used, and even on intensively managed farmland they can increase substantially if pesticide use is reduced or stopped. However, their declines are not due entirely to insecticide use, but also to herbicides, fungicides and fertilisers, which collectively destroy the habitat or food-base of many species. Large species which tend to have longer life cycles have proved most vulnerable to modern agriculture because they require longer periods of undisturbed conditions to complete their development, and not many areas of intensively used farmland are now left undisturbed for long, because of either autumn ploughing (which destroys many larvae in the soil) or frequent grass cutting (which destroys species that live among the grass).

Linking insect declines with bird declines has proved difficult, even though the two have coincided. Apart from the Grey Partridge, which has been the subject of experimental field studies, the evidence is mainly correlative. However, other experimental studies have shown that insect abundance can affect the breeding output of Yellowhammers, Corn Buntings and Skylarks. In these and other song-bird species, pairs with access to insect-rich feeding areas have produced more young than those without such access.

## CHAPTER 15

## Marshes and Land Drainage

IT IS ON LAND DRAINAGE THAT much of modern agriculture in Britain depends, and some of our most productive soils derive from the original marshland. The downside of land drainage at its present level has been the loss of most of the natural marshland of Britain and its associated wildlife, together with an increase in the frequency of damaging floods, as seen in recent years. This chapter examines the history of land drainage in Britain and its consequences for agriculture, wildlife and people.

At the start of the Neolithic period, as agriculture reached Britain, relatively small parts of the lowlands were suitable for cultivation. Large areas were probably waterlogged for at least part of the year. Marshland was much more extensive than it is now, and in winter water expanded to cover wider areas. Even many wooded areas were damp and seasonally flooded. Only when such wet areas were drained could they be cultivated. Nevertheless, wetlands have been exploited throughout human history for their fish, birds, and other resources.

Various marshlands around Britain were settled at least from Neolithic times. People lived around the edges or on islands and peninsulas, and built wooden track-ways through the swamps. In the Somerset Levels, such tracks, preserved under peat, date back approximately 6,000 years (as shown by radio-carbon dating of the wood) and remained in use through to the Iron Age or even later. Similar track-ways and artificial islands existed in the East Anglian fens, and the Bronze Age man-made island at Flag Fen near Peterborough is thought to be the biggest wooden structure ever built in Britain. People no doubt hunted in these marshes in even earlier times, though perhaps not from permanent settlements.

ORIGIN AND NATURE OF MARSHLAND

Natural wetlands exist through some combination of underlying geology, rainfall, springs and obstructed rivers. Or they arise on low-lying gently sloping coastlines of silt or sand, where high tides periodically cover the saltmarshes, and also cause low-lying rivers to back up and overflow neighbouring land with fresh water. Over time, many areas of lowland wetland gradually silt up and become shallower, which allows reeds and other emergent plants to establish, and as their remains accumulate through time, areas become raised and dry enough for trees, initially alders and willows, and later drier-land trees such as oak. This succession can be set back at any time by rises in water level from whatever source, and by floods which wash out some of the accreted material. Rivers may flow continuously through such areas, periodically changing course, and re-sculpting the land. At any one time, the ancient wetlands of lowland Britain contained a mixture of areas at various stages of succession, from open water to wet forest, as is borne out by pollen remains and by written descriptions of the ancient marshes. For example, the 8th-century Life of Saint Guthlac describes:

in the Midland district of Britain, a most dismal fen of immense size... now consisting of marshes, now of bogs, sometimes of black waters overhung by fog, sometimes studded with woodland islands and traversed by the windings of tortuous streams. (Gowland & Western 2011)

FIG 163. Reed-beds at Hickling Broad in Norfolk (Ian Newton).

Peat formation

Where plant remains are permanently waterlogged, they tend not to rot but to accumulate as peat, separating the living surface plants from the underlying mineral substrate. The depth of peat varies greatly between areas, reaching up to several metres in places, having accumulated over hundreds or thousands of years. In many regions of Britain, peat formation began to spread over wider areas some 5,000–6,000 years ago at a time of cooling and dampening climate, later increasing in upland areas under the influence of deforestation. On acid soils, this peat is relatively infertile, and occurs mainly as blanket bog on the hills and as raised bog on lower ground (Chapter 19). But on the neutral and alkaline soils found mainly in the lowlands, fen vegetation develops at the edges of shallow lakes or rivers or more widely on poorly drained alluvial floodplains. Such vegetation gives rise to peat which, when drained, can be very productive, providing some of our most fertile modern soils. Consisting entirely of decaying plant remains, the lack of stones makes this peat ideal for growing perfectly shaped root-crops such as carrots and parsnips.

In the past, large areas of peat formed in the inland parts of all the big low-lying coastal fens. Along the eastern and southern coasts were the East Anglian Fens, Hatfield Chase and Thorne Mere, the Isle of Axholme, the Hull Valley, the Vale of York and the Humberhead Levels, the Norfolk Broads, the Essex Marshes, Romney Marsh and the Pevensey Levels. On the west side of Britain, where the land is generally higher, there were the Lancashire mosses and meres, the Severn lowlands and the Vale of Berkeley, which merges into the Somerset Levels (Williams 1970). The distinctive individuality of these areas, largely imposed by their different topographical settings and water sources, is reflected in their regional names of fen, carr, level, broad and moss. All are fed by rain, but in addition some derive their water partly from inland catchments, and others partly from the sea, as in the East Anglian Fens and the Somerset Levels.

FIG 164. Common birds of reed-beds: left, Reed Warbler Acrocephalus scirpaceus (Frank Snykers); right, Sedge Warbler Acrocephalus schoenobaenus (Richard Chandler).

FIG 165. Rarer birds of reed-beds: left, Bittern Botaurus stellaris (Bobby Smith); right, Marsh Harrier Circus aeruginosus (Chris Knights).

Reed-beds are now the most widespread form of fen vegetation found in Britain, some having been deliberately planted for conservation reasons. Marsh Harriers, Bitterns and Bearded Tits depend almost entirely on large reed-beds, but other species, notably Reed and Sedge Warblers, are generally much more numerous and widespread, and are found in smaller as well as larger reed patches, including those in small farmland ditches. The drier margins of marshes are the main habitats for two less common passerines, the Marsh and Cetti's Warblers. Outside the breeding season, reed-beds and other fen habitats serve as roosts for thousands of Swallows, Sand Martins and Starlings, and also for buntings, pipits and wagtails. The grazing of fen habitat can produce lower vegetation suitable for ground-nesting waders.

FIG 166. Two uncommon marshland songbirds: left, Bearded Tit Panurus biarmicus; (Frank Snykers); right, Cetti's Warbler Cettia cetti (Frank Snykers).

FARMING AND DRAINAGE

Britain is blessed with good year-round rainfall, so water is not normally a major factor limiting the productivity of the land, or the profusion of plant and animal life (Chapter 5). Nevertheless, from a farming viewpoint, water has generally been considered more a nuisance than a blessing, and for centuries land drainage has been considered paramount. Land cannot be cultivated unless it is dry enough to provide a tilth and carry machines. Nor can pasture support livestock unless it is dry enough not to be churned into mud by constant treading. Improved drainage allows better plant growth, earlier cultivation or grazing in spring, and better take-up of fertilisers, thus enhancing plant productivity. Some 30–40% of improved farmland in Britain today is naturally free-draining and needs little or no artificial drainage, but on the remaining 60–70% draining is needed.

The process of lowering water tables can involve both the arterial drainage of major marshlands by cutting new drainage channels or improving existing ones (including natural rivers), and field drainage, which is achieved with networks of small ditches and other surface drains, or today mainly with porous pipes, buried deeper than plough depth. Whatever the system, water is carried by ditches into rivers or man-made drainage channels, to reach the sea or (less often) a low-lying lake from which water is lost by evaporation.

Historically, land drainage in lowland Britain has affected two main habitat types of significance to birds, namely (1) major areas of natural swamp with reed-beds and permanent water, and (2) the derived areas of damp grassland which flood in winter but can be used for grazing or hay production in summer. In the 19th and 20th centuries, field drainage allowed the expansion of relatively sophisticated farming over large areas of formerly wet clay and peat soils which had for centuries supported damp grassland.

DRAINAGE OF MAJOR WETLANDS

Shallow marshy wetlands are some of the most productive habitats on earth, as reflected in their plant and animal populations. In the past, the largest area of wetland in Britain was the fenland of East Anglia, which originally covered some 3,400–3,800 km2. Picture a vast pristine landscape of low-lying shallow lakes and extensive reed-beds and other marsh vegetation, Bog-myrtle clumps and occasional wet woods on silt, altogether as rich in fish and birdlife as the Danube delta today. Water levels would have fluctuated greatly through the year, expanding to flood wider areas in winter. Despite human presence and summer grazing round the edges, this region seems to have remained almost intact until Roman times, around 2,000 years ago, when the first major arterial drainage channels were dug. The Foss Dyke and the Car Dyke date from this period, as do the Reach and Wicken Lodes in Cambridgeshire, combining to remove water from huge areas of silt and peat. The Car Dyke was the biggest artificial watercourse that the Fens have ever had, skirting their western edge for 140 km between Lincoln and Cambridge. This dyke acted as a cut-off channel, intercepting lesser rivers so that they could no longer flow across the fen, making large areas habitable. People settled mainly on the silt-lands, which they cultivated, with farmsteads at least as numerous as today, while the peat fens were used for summer and autumn grazing (Rackham 1994). Similar management was applied in most other sizeable marshlands, including the Somerset Levels, which in Roman times covered some 680 km2.

After the Romans left, much of the drained fenland in East Anglia reverted to marshland, mainly through lack of maintenance and rise in sea level. However, the fens were never wholly abandoned, and by the end of the Anglo-Saxon period people were still sparsely distributed in many places. After the Norman Conquest further drainage was undertaken, and the human population of the fens expanded both eastward into former saltmarsh and westward into peatland. By Domesday times, about 50 villages lay in an arc around the Wash from Skegness to King's Lynn, situated on the highest belt of silt fen, while the inner fens were thinly populated, chiefly on islands in natural lakes, including Trundle Mere, Draymere and Whittlesea Mere – all valued as fisheries. By the 14th century, the fens had become one of the most prosperous parts of rural England, with an economy based mainly on grass and livestock (including domestic geese), but supplemented by sales of reed and sedge for thatching, of reed, sedge and peat for fuel, and of fish and wildfowl for food.

Although piecemeal drainage of small areas continued over the centuries, it was not until the 17th century that really large-scale drainage was again carried out. The incentive came from outsiders, notably the Earl of Bedford and his associates – the so-called 'Gentlemen Adventurers', intent on the money to be made from arable crops on the silt and from the rich grassland on the fen peat. Under the eventual guidance of a Dutch engineer, Cornelius Vermuyden, an elaborate system of drains and river diversions was dug. These included the Old and New Bedford Rivers (in 1637 and 1651), which were the biggest artificial watercourses dug since Roman times (Fig. 167). These straight channels diverted water from the River Great Ouse northeastwards to re-join the river further downstream at Denver, thereby drying huge areas which had previously flooded in winter. The Ouse Washes between the two Bedford Rivers still provide a vast holding area for flood-water in winter, protecting the neighbouring arable crops.

Through the digging of these huge ditches, great areas of fenland were thereby drained again, damaging their natural ecology, greatly reducing their fish and bird life, and destroying the way of life and common rights of the people who lived there. Moreover, the results were not always satisfactory, partly because banks sometimes broke at times of flood, causing inundation of the new farmland, and partly because insufficient allowance was made for the shrinkage and rotting of dried peat under cultivation. Many drained areas of the fens are now well below sea level, and water has to be pumped up into drains which run between elevated banks so that the water flows at levels metres higher than the cultivated fields. The original wind-powered pumps were replaced by more reliable steam-powered pumps from about 1820, and these were in turn replaced by diesel and electric pumps from the 1940s.

FIG 167. The New Bedford River at Welney, one of the major ditches dug in the 17th century to drain large areas of fenland (Ian Newton).

The last major feat of drainage in the East Anglian Fens involved Whittlesea Mere near Peterborough in 1851. In times of flood, this lake covered well over 1,000 ha and was surrounded by great reed-beds, 'abounding in wildfowl'. After it had gone, the remaining Huntingdonshire fens were quickly drained. Now the whole of the original fenland has gone, except for a few small patches, such as Holme Fen, Wickham Fen and Woodwalton Fen, preserved as nature reserves. These remnants are now drier and more tree-covered than in the past. They are biologically interesting, but do not reflect what was once there. Attempts are currently being made to join these patches together by re-creating wet fenland on the intervening land in the 'Great Fen Project'.

The present Holme Fen lies close to the original Whittlesea Mere. It houses a large vertical metal pole which in 1851 was pounded into the peat until its top was level with the surface. The pole now protrudes about 4 m above the ground (Fig. 168). The shrinkage of the peat has continued over the fenland of East Anglia ever since it was drained, so that the productive peat layer has become ever shallower, disappearing altogether from about half the original area (Holman 2009).

FIG 168. The Holme Fen Post. In 1851, when the neighbouring Whittlesea Mere was drained, this post was flush with the peat surface, but it now protrudes 4 m above it, reflecting the extent to which the peat has dried, shrunk and rotted over the past 165 years. The average rate of shrinkage is 2.4 cm per year, but it was most rapid to begin with, following the initial drainage, and slowed subsequently. The reclaimed farmland was abandoned to become birch woodland a century ago (Ian Newton).

Further loss of marshland from Britain

It is difficult to imagine now what a watery place Britain was up to the 17th century, or to appreciate the abundance of water-birds which historical accounts and other evidence reveal once lived here. All the original extensive fens and lowland peatlands listed above are now reduced to small drier remnants of their former selves. Smaller areas were found in most other counties, especially in wide river valleys and flat coastal areas. Many of them individually covered areas greater than 10 km2, and were capable of supporting viable populations of most marshland bird species (Shrubb 2003). Bird books of the 18th and 19th centuries describe the drainage of particular sites. They confirm that a massive amount of arterial drainage was carried out between about 1770 and the 1840s, comprising both new works and improvements to existing ones. In general, progress was more rapid in Scotland than in England and Wales, which may account for the earlier disappearance of the Bittern and other marshland birds from Scotland.

The total area of England and Wales drained by major channel systems has been estimated at around 8,000 km2, and to this could be added at least 2,000 km2 in Scotland, making a total for Britain of at least 10,000 km2, approaching 5% of the total land area. This can be taken as reflecting the total area of significant marshland present on low ground in Britain around 300–400 years ago, altogether covering an area about half the size of Wales (Marshall et al. 1978).

Turning to recent times, in CS2007, the total area of fen, marsh and swamp remaining in Britain was estimated to cover 3,920 km2, about 1.8% of the total land surface. This is a surprisingly large amount because, despite major drainage operations over recent centuries, it represents more than a third of that thought to be present 400 years ago. In the recent survey, about 60 km2 was reed-bed, much of it recently planted by conservation bodies.

Nowadays, the area of British farmland liable to periodic flooding is relatively small, being largely confined to major river valleys and coastal marshes. Only the peatlands of East Anglia are below sea level, but most are effectively pump-drained year-round, so as to maintain the water table a metre or more below the surface, in an ideal state for cereal and vegetable crops. The total length of major drainage channels in England and Wales has been calculated at 128,000 km (Marshall et al. 1978). At least until the 1950s, these channels supported a rich diversity of plant and animal life, but since the introduction of modern management, this abundance and variety has been much reduced.

Wetlands, peatlands and waterlogged soils have great capacity for storing carbon. This facility is much reduced in arable land, because organic matter is continually turned to the surface where carbon can be oxidised to carbon dioxide, contributing to climate warming.
