A re-examination of some of these sites in 2009–10 confirmed the trends, as waders were more often found and were generally more numerous on protected sites that were also subject to AE measures than on unprotected sites subject only to AE measures (Smart et al. 2014).

FIG 246. The Redshank Tringa totanus has benefited from the re-wetting of grasslands and other agri-environment measures (Richard Chandler).

A similar study in Scotland compared the numbers of nesting waders on 60 pairs of farmland areas that were first surveyed in 1992–93, before the implementation of AE measures, and again in 2005, after scheme implementation (O'Brien & Wilson 2011). Half the sites were subject to AES and the other half were not. Redshank breeding numbers increased slightly on scheme sites, while Lapwing breeding numbers declined less on scheme sites than on non-scheme ones. It seemed that nest destruction, by trampling or other means, was a major cause of poor performance on these farms, and benefits came mainly from reducing grazing and agricultural operations during the breeding season. It was estimated that appropriate management was benefiting only 2% of the Lapwing population on Scottish farmland, and to halt the general population decline, such management would need to be applied to around 44–54% of the overall population. This provided another example of measures effective at the field or farm scale applied on a total area too small to show a benefit for the overall population.

Seven studies on wet grasslands in the Netherlands and Germany found that waders either maintained their numbers or declined less rapidly on AES areas than on control areas, but in only one of these studies was the difference confirmed statistically (Kleijn & Sutherland 2003). Three other studies found no difference in population trends between areas inside and outside an AES. A later study concluded that high water tables and associated prey densities (earthworms and leatherjackets) had an overriding influence on wader nesting densities, regardless of other factors (Verhulst et al. 2007).

Findings from these various studies were consistent with previous research which indicated the importance for grassland waders of damp ground rich in invertebrate prey, maintaining dampness into June, low livestock densities on pastures, and late mowing on meadows (Chapter 13). However, many published studies looked only at breeding numbers and took no account of breeding success. Many areas of wet grassland are attractive to waders on arrival in spring, but subsequent reproduction is so poor (largely through predation or trampling) that numbers cannot be maintained in the longer term (Bolton et al. 2007, Merricks 2010, Chapter 13). Far from benefiting the birds, therefore, these areas act as population sinks, attracting birds but preventing them from breeding successfully, and the same may have been true of some of the AES areas studied.

BARE PLOTS FOR SKYLARKS AND LAPWINGS

Skylark plots are undrilled patches in autumn-sown cereal fields, each plot of at least 4 × 4 metres in area and usually positioned at two per hectare, so that they take up less than 0.5% of the total field area. They are created on a prepared seed-bed by switching off the seed-drill for the required distance during one pass, so that when the crop grows the unsown areas are left as bare patches within it. They provide places where Skylarks can settle and feed, and walk to their nests, which are usually placed a short distance into the crop. They continue to be used by the birds throughout the breeding season, even when the crop is tall. The plots are best placed in large fields, away from hedges, pylons and overhead wires, which Skylarks generally avoid.

FIG 247. A Skylark Alauda arvensis plot created by switching off the seed-drill for a certain distance to create bare or sparsely vegetated ground suitable for Skylarks, Yellow Wagtails Motacilla flava and other ground-nesters of cereal fields that are deterred by tall vegetation (Ian Newton).

In research trials, these patches held higher densities of some insect groups that birds feed on, but the main benefit was that any vegetation that developed was short and sparse, giving birds easy access to these prey items. Fields with two plots per hectare early in the breeding season had a density of nesting Skylarks at least 30% greater than in conventional cereal fields. Seasonal production of young was about 50% greater, partly because individual nests had larger broods in fields with bare patches, but mainly because pairs were able to continue breeding until later in the year, giving time for additional nesting attempts (Morris et al. 2004, Stoate & Moorcroft 2007). Pairs gradually abandoned conventional autumn-sown cereal fields from the end of May, as the crop grew, but some remained in patch-fields until harvest time in July or August. The Skylark chicks in fields with patches were also significantly heavier than those in conventional fields, and this difference widened during the course of the season. Their greater weights reflected better feeding and are likely to have increased their post-fledging survival over that of lighter individuals.

Broadly similar findings emerged from 15 experimental farms in Britain on which patches were trialled, and also on farms in Denmark and Switzerland. On the farms involved, Skylark numbers increased through time. The number of singing males counted on the RSPB's experimental farm in Cambridgeshire increased from 10 in 2000 to 34 in 2005, following the introduction of Skylark patches in 2001 (Donald & Morris 2005). Other birds which used these patches for feeding included Corn Buntings and Yellow Wagtails. However, Skylark plots proved unpopular with farmers, and were taken up on too small a scale to raise Skylark numbers nationally.

Larger patches of 2 ha or more are needed for Lapwings. Under AES, most have been created from overwinter stubble by cultivation in March to create a 'false seed-bed' that remained unplanted and unsprayed at least until 31 July. Some 212 large fallow patches (on 180 farms) were surveyed for breeding Lapwings and other birds, mostly with two visits several weeks apart during the breeding season (Chamberlain et al. 2009c). In total, 39% of fallow patches were found to be used by Lapwings during one or both visits, and breeding was proven or suspected on 25% of them. Other ground-nesting species recorded on Lapwing patches included Skylark (73% of plots), Red-legged Partridge (38%), Grey Partridge (17%) and Yellow Wagtail (6%). This study showed that fallow patches were taken up by Lapwings and other birds, but it did not measure breeding success or check what happened in subsequent years. Other studies indicate that, to achieve good nest success, bare patches should be sited as far as possible (more than 50 m) from field boundaries likely to harbour Carrion Crows and other predators, and that agricultural equipment should be kept off the plot during the breeding season to avoid destroying eggs and chicks (Sheldon et al. 2007).

Fallow fields were routine in farming at least into the 19th century, but they are much rarer now. It is chiefly fallow fields that provide for a time what many farmland birds seem to need, namely largely bare soil, with a sparse scattering of short plants. Habitat of this structure allows birds to walk freely over the ground, with all-round visibility, picking whatever they need from the ground or from the low-growing plants. Pigeons, thrushes, chats, wagtails, larks, finches, buntings and sparrows all feed freely in habitat of this structure, and plovers, Stone-curlews and others also nest in it. But in the nitrogen-loaded soil of modern farmland, few areas remain for long in such a sparsely vegetated state. One exception is the machair of the Outer Hebrides, where limited fertiliser use combined with rapidly draining sandy soil and a short growing season continues to produce sparse and biodiverse vegetation.

FIELD MARGINS

Crop margins are ideal places to expand wildlife habitats, because they are close to the hedges and ditches where much of the existing farmland wildlife persists. They are also lower yielding than the rest of the field, so their use for conservation purposes represents less financial loss to the farmer than would a similar area further into the field. Wild-bird seed mixes are often grown in field margins, as mentioned above, as are a range of other vegetation types discussed below.

Conservation headlands

So-called 'conservation headlands' are the outer margins of cereal crops (usually 6–24 m wide) which are sown with the crop like the rest of the field but do not receive insecticides or broad-spectrum herbicides after mid-March. This enables later-emerging broad-leaved weeds, such as Knotgrass, to develop, along with their associated insects. The additional step of using no fertiliser in the headlands gives a more open crop structure, making it easier for game-bird chicks to move through the vegetation, and also benefiting less competitive weeds, including some rare species. The best sites for weeds are on light or shallow soils that have had a long history of arable cropping but minimal inputs of agrochemicals. The weeds that develop provide an abundance of accessible insects for the chicks of Grey Partridges and many other birds, and seeds for various finches and Turtle Doves. Farmers are paid extra for not harvesting the conservation headland, and leaving the crop overwinter as bird food, but even where the headland is harvested along with the rest of the field, it is still valuable in summer and the resulting stubble (if unploughed) can provide seeds for birds in winter.

FIG 248. Weed growth on an unsown headland on sandy soil in Norfolk, producing an abundance of insects and seeds eaten by birds (Chris Knights).

Conservation headlands were developed by the Game Conservancy Trust (now GWCT) in the 1980s to enhance insect numbers on pesticide-treated farmland, and were eventually incorporated in various forms into agri-environment schemes. They can be managed so as to maintain useful weeds at acceptable levels, while controlling more troublesome ones, such as Cleavers, Barren Brome, Wild Oats and Black-grass. Herbicides to control these weeds are used in March, before more desirable weeds emerge. Where there is concern over the accumulation of weed seed, conservation headlands can be shifted periodically to different fields. At Loddington, a loss of cereal yield within the headlands of 7% was recorded relative to the rest of the field, averaged over three years. Across whole fields, therefore, the yield loss was very small (Stoate & Leake 2002).

The original aim of conservation headlands was to benefit Grey Partridges. A cereal crop provides an ideal structure allowing partridge chicks to forage within it, but with a canopy providing protection from weather and avian predators. In early studies, average chick production was nearly twice as high in unsprayed conservation headlands as in conventional sprayed headlands, enough to maintain adult breeding numbers and to provide a surplus for shooting (Potts 2012). Other studies revealed that conservation headlands are favoured feeding areas for Yellowhammers and Corn Buntings, and can influence their settlement patterns and breeding success (Brickle et al. 2000, Morris et al. 2005, Burgess et al. 2015).

In some modifications, other field margins are not cropped as they are in conservation headlands, but are deliberately sown with different seed mixtures and left for a year or more. This proved more acceptable to farmers, for many of whom allowing weeds to grow in arable crops was a step backwards (Potts 2012). Autumn sowings were more reliable, because plants sown in spring often failed to provide sufficient growth by mid-June, especially in dry years. Strips up to 6 m wide are ideal for partridges because they are next to hedgerow nest sites. The vegetation that consistently delivered the most insects suitable as chick-food comprised thinly sown perennial grasses and wildflowers, legume mixes and wild-bird seed mixes (Holland et al. 2011b). In summer, when the rest of the landscape is green, these habitats with their brightly coloured flowers are visibly alive with a variety of insects, especially bees, butterflies and grasshoppers. They also encourage natural enemies of crop pests, such as beetles and hoverflies, which can often keep pests below a critical threshold, making pesticide use unnecessary (Holland et al. 2012, Tschumi et al. 2016). The seed mix should ideally include only the less competitive grasses (Crested Dog's-tail and Sheep's Fescue) and not tussock-forming species such as Cock's-foot which would quickly swamp any flowering plants.

Nectar and pollen mixtures

Mixtures of plants rich in pollen and nectar are sown, often along with fine grasses, to provide a continuous supply of flowers for pollinating insects from March to September. They are targeted primarily at bumblebees, species of which have different lengths of proboscis, adapted to different plant species. A variety of plants is therefore desirable, including Phacelia and legumes such as Red and Alsike Clovers, Yellow Melilot, Bird's-foot Trefoil, Sainfoin, Lucerne, Common Vetch and Black Medick. Such mixtures are best planted in sunny places, such as the south side of hedgerows and along open field boundaries, kept free from fertiliser and pesticides. Small patches scattered across a farm benefit more insects and birds than one larger patch in a single location. Flower density declines over time, and patches need re-establishing about every five years. In trials, the number and diversity of bumblebees increased rapidly when wild-flower, pollen and nectar mixes were provided, the strength of the response varying with their proportion in the surrounding landscape (Carvell et al. 2011). Birds take advantage of the greater range of insects supported, and in one Swiss study, Skylarks fed more in wild-flower strips than in any other arable habitat present (Weibel 1998). Partridges nest in wild-flower strips near hedgerows, and Skylarks, Meadow Pipits and Corn Buntings nest in patches grown in the open. While all pollen and nectar mixes support an abundance of insects, in some trials only legume strips provided enough of the right kind to support developing game-bird chicks (Wood et al. 2013).

Grassy margins

Strips of native grasses around arable fields can support invertebrates in abundance, providing a winter refuge for insects and spiders, and allowing their numbers to build up through the summer and colonise neighbouring crops. They also provide seeds as winter food for buntings and other birds. Among insects, grasshoppers benefit from 6 m wide grassy margins established around 5–9 ha fields (Gardiner et al. 2008). However, high nitrogen inputs or bigger fields reduce this benefit, and the cutting of the grass margins in August removes all the habitat at once, leading to massive mortality of adult and nymph grasshoppers or to their emigration to less suitable areas. Cutting needs to be delayed until spring, if longer-term benefits are to accrue.

FIG 249. Grassy field margin, offering insects and seeds for a variety of bird species, and habitat for small mammals (Ian Newton).

Grassy margins provide good nesting cover for Grey and Red-legged Partridges, and when next to thick hedges, they also provide both nesting and foraging habitat for Yellowhammers and Whitethroats, while Corn Buntings feed in the grassy margins but usually nest in the crop. In contrast, margins close to hedgerows are normally shunned by Skylarks, Meadow Pipits and Yellow Wagtails.

Grassy margins also hold small rodents and shrews. In one study, small mammals were sampled in spring and autumn on grassy field margins of 2 and 6 m wide (Broughton et al. 2014). In both spring and autumn, species richness and abundance of small mammals was greater on wider margins than on narrow ones. Voles were not detected on any treatments in the initial period with only narrow margins, but Bank Voles rapidly became abundant thereafter, reaching peak densities after 2–3 years, while Field Voles increased more slowly over five years. Wood Mice were present at all times and in all situations, especially near hedgerows, but their overall spring abundance declined as vole numbers rose. The implication was that establishing more rough grassland, as field margins on farms, was effective in enhancing small mammal communities, which themselves support Barn Owls and other predators (Fig. 250, Box 22).

Beetle banks

Beetle banks are long strips of perennial grasses, extending across large arable fields and providing overwintering habitat for beetles and other predators of crop pests. Such banks are typically about 0.4 m high and 1.5–2.0 m wide. They are created on ridges produced using a plough, and are then seeded by hand, using a mixture of matt-forming grasses, especially Cock's-foot. They usually run to within a sprayer's width of the field boundary hedge. Leaving this gap saves interrupting farm work and also reduces access to the bank by mammalian predators which search along hedgerows for bird eggs and chicks. The birds that use beetle banks as a source of invertebrate food are mainly species such as Corn Bunting and Skylark that avoid feeding near tall hedgerows. Beetle banks also provide good nesting habitat for Grey Partridges and, depending on the sward structure, also for Skylarks, Corn Buntings and Reed Buntings. They have the potential to increase the breeding densities of these species by providing extra territory sites.

BOX 22. Barn Owls, grassy field margins and nest-boxes

In some areas, groups of enthusiasts have over several decades erected and maintained nest-boxes suitable for Barn Owls. But experience revealed that boxes were of little use to this species without the presence of rough grassy areas that provided habitat for Field Voles as the main prey. It soon became practice to provide boxes only to farmers who had sufficient rough grass, or who were prepared to create it as an agri-environmental measure. Both additions were needed for a farm to be reasonably sure of attracting Barn Owls. 'The Cheshire population was 240 pairs in 1932 but only 35 pairs in 1982–85 and just seven pairs in 1998 before local groups started working with landowners to create suitable feeding habitat in field margins and alongside watercourses. The birds bounced back to an estimated 150–200 breeding pairs' by 2012 (Norman 2013). Typically about 10–15% of the known Barn Owl nests in Cheshire were in natural sites, and the rest in boxes, about half attached to trees and the other half on old wooden telegraph poles erected in the corners of fields. Nest-boxes were easier to put up in trees, but were more susceptible to incursions by Grey Squirrels and Jackdaws than those on isolated poles. Similar experience with nest-boxes and grassy field margins developed in other parts of the country, mainly under the auspices of the Hawk and Owl Trust and the Barn Owl Trust. It has been estimated that some 25,000 nest-boxes have been erected for Barn Owls in Britain, but only a small proportion of them are occupied by Barn Owls, and a rather larger proportion by Jackdaws. Boxes with two compartments sometimes hold a pair of each (Barn Owl Trust 2012). The important point, however, is that two separate management actions were needed to deliver Barn Owls, although in this case only one derived from an agri-environment scheme. In various other areas, Kestrels have also shown a positive relationship with the amount of grassy field margin in 100 ha farmland sites (Henderson et al. 2010). Considering the effects of grassy field margins on Barn Owl numbers, it is surprising that Kestrel numbers continue to decline nationwide, suggesting that some other factor may be limiting their numbers. In their case, it is unlikely in most areas to be shortage of nest sites.

FIG 250. The Barn Owl Tyto alba benefits from the provision of wide grassy field margins which provide habitat for its main prey, the Short-tailed Field Vole Microtus agrestis (Chris Knights).

Beetle banks were developed by the GWCT to create a habitat across the middle of large arable fields, so that aphids and other pests in the crop could be controlled by beetles over a larger area. At Loddington, it took three years for the vegetation to develop into ideal condition for predatory beetles, and after five years beetle densities on the bank reached an incredible 2,000 per square metre (Stoate & Leake 2002). Beetles took more than two weeks to disperse out from the bank into the developing crop, but their effects on wheat aphids were apparent at more than 80 m out (Collins et al. 2002). Beetle banks were introduced into agri-environment schemes in limited areas in 1992, and more widely after 1996. Where the adjoining field supports a well-grown crop providing cover, beetle banks are also good places to position seed-hoppers for game birds, away from trees or other high perches suitable for raptors.

Comparison of different types of field margins

Field-margin habitats provide undisturbed nest sites for a few ground-nesting bird species, and food supplies for a much wider range. The best summer food supplies are created by measures that produce structurally and floristically diverse swards supporting an abundance and variety of insects. The best winter food supplies are created by measures that provide seed-rich habitats. Sown grass strips are limited in the food resources they offer, but potentially they provide seeds and, depending on the complexity of the sward structure, a range of arthropods, including predatory species able to control crop pests. Adding perennial forbs to a grass mixture gives more diverse plant and invertebrate food. Grass strips also support an abundance of small mammals as prey for predatory birds. All these food types are strongly influenced by management, especially cutting, cultivation and herbicide use. For grass margins, midsummer cutting has the most persistent negative effects on bird food supplies, autumn cutting less severe effects, and spring cutting the least severe (Feber et al. 2015). Cropped margins with reduced chemical inputs and wild-bird cover crops can provide relatively high arthropod densities and abundant seeds distributed within conventionally managed crops. However, in conservation headlands, which are cut at harvest, seeds are scarce in winter and arthropod abundance is usually lower than in uncropped margins. The width of field margins is also important. Wider margins hold greater densities of invertebrates and small mammals than narrow margins, as well as some species not usually found in narrow margins. No single margin type can provide a good year-round food supply for most bird species, so a mixture of different types of margins on the same farm, managed on rotation, benefits the greatest range of species.

Effects on crop yields

Hedgerows and patches of other semi-natural habitat within farmland act as refuges for bees and other pollinators, and for the natural predators of crop pests which in pre-pesticide times did much to control pest numbers. Many of these predators are themselves insects. By removing hedgerows and other semi-natural habitat from farmland over the past several decades, farmers have unwittingly destroyed this refuge habitat, and made it easier for pest species to build up to levels at which they can significantly damage crops (Rusch et al. 2016). The creation of pesticide-free crop margins through agri-environment measures has helped to redress this balance. In a study in which only the lower-yielding 3–8% of edge land within 50–60 ha blocks was used to create wildlife-friendly habitat, overall crop yields were actually increased, step by step over a six-year trial (Pywell et al. 2016). This effect was attributed to enhanced numbers of pollinating insects and predators of crop pests developed in the margins. No such benefit accrued in conventional fields lacking any specially created wildlife habitat. Compared to fields with wildlife margins, crop yields per hectare of conventional fields were lower by an average of 10% in wheat, 26% in beans and 38% in oilseed rape, the two latter crops being most susceptible to poor pollination. As a result of the wildlife margins, yields at the field scale were therefore maintained – and for some crops raised – despite the loss of part of the field for habitat creation. This study showed that wildlife-friendly management on some potential cropland is compatible with, and can even enhance, crop yields.

CONCLUDING REMARKS

As breeding birds have gradually declined and disappeared from farmed land, semi-natural and uncropped areas have come increasingly to hold most remaining lowland birds. Many agri-environment measures aim to preserve wildlife in semi-natural areas, such as hedges and other field boundaries. Such measures do not interfere with cropping, and are therefore usually acceptable to farmers. Nevertheless, under modern chemical-based agriculture the sacrifice of some potential cropland is essential to produce the food and nesting habitats that many species require. This is currently provided in the form of conservation headlands, wild-bird seed mixes, nectar mixes, grassy margins, beetle banks, bare patches and so on. Growth in bird populations can be achieved by increasing the areas of such uncropped habitats, and by managing them so that they support more birds. Other species benefit from a reversion to former management methods, as in the conversion of drained grassland back to wet grassland suitable for waders and others, or the switch from autumn-sown to spring-sown cereals to provide seed-rich winter stubble fields for some species and sparsely vegetated spring nesting areas for others. However, today's wet grasslands and stubble fields are seldom as good as their predecessors, for reasons discussed in earlier chapters.

Whatever agri-environment schemes offer in future, farmers can now produce crops and wildlife, not intermixed together on the same land as in the past, but largely on different parts of the same farm. Crop margins are ideal places to expand wildlife habitats, because they are closer to the hedges and ditches where much remaining wildlife persists. Trials have shown that: (1) margin habitats comprising perennial grasses and wildflowers, legume mixes and wild-bird seed mixtures provide the most insects suitable as chick food; (2) wild flowers and legumes also encourage bees, butterflies and pest-eating hoverflies; (3) in perennial mixes, broad-leaved plants support more insect life than grasses and cereals; (4) wild-bird seed crops produce most seeds for seed-eating birds, but also support other species; (5) autumn sowings provide more reliable establishment of field margin vegetation and its associated arthropod fauna; and (6) such margin patches benefit more birds in the breeding season if they are scattered around the farm rather than concentrated in one larger area. An important discovery is that the creation of these pesticide-free areas can, through supporting pollinating and predatory insects, increase crop yields in the rest of the field, sometimes even giving a net gain in crop production.

Another point to emerge from studies on the effects of agri-environment schemes is that diagnoses of the causes of declines in bird populations were basically correct. Otherwise species would not have responded repeatedly to the provision of extra habitat or food in the way they have. A major problem has been that, except in special cases, the extent of these beneficial habitats has typically been too small or too restricted in area to reverse national population declines. Bigger areas of agri-environment land are needed, an issue taken up in the next chapter.

## CHAPTER 21

## Agri-Environment Successes

THE PRECEDING CHAPTER gave a general review of the history and overall impact of agri-environment schemes (AES) on birdlife in Britain, and examined the effects of specific measures in some detail. This chapter provides further information, derived partly from focused studies on selected farms where agri-environment measures were applied to the full in a coordinated manner, and partly from detailed studies on particular rare species which for many years were subjected to intense management using AES. The chapter ends with a discussion of the main issues that have arisen from the application of AES in Britain, and makes suggestions for their future development.

RESEARCH ON INDIVIDUAL FARMS

On several farms managed for research or game rearing, various measures were applied over several years, while birds were regularly counted. Some such measures were trialled before being incorporated into wider agri-environment schemes. All such farms employed spring-sown crops (leaving winter stubble fields) and wild-bird seed crops, and managed field edges to provide nesting sites and food for birds. Details varied from farm to farm, and on those where game rearing was a priority (marked with an asterisk* below), predators were also controlled (apart from legally protected birds of prey). All these farms aimed to provide nesting cover, summer food and winter food for a range of bird species. They were all managed commercially, and profits from crops and livestock were maintained throughout.

On all the farms concerned, big increases in bird populations followed immediately from the instigation of agri-environment measures. The degree and rate of increase recorded in particular species varied between farms, according to the measures employed. On the RSPB's Hope Farm (Cambridgeshire), the species that were counted increased from 117 to 291 pairs in 10 years, with individual species increasing up to sevenfold in this time (RSPB data). At the GWCT's farm at Loddington (Leicestershire)*, total numbers of counted species increased from 749 to 1,437 pairs in eleven years, with up to fivefold increases recorded in individual species (Stoate & Leake 2002). On Titley Court Farm (Herefordshire), total bird numbers increased from 551 to 951 pairs in three years, with up to threefold increases recorded in individual species (Chapple et al. 2002). On Arundel Estate (Sussex)*, total numbers among counted species increased from 1,442 to 2,411 pairs over four years (Potts 2012). This mainly arable estate was managed primarily for Grey Partridges, which increased from 11 to a remarkable 375 pairs in eight years, while over the same period Corn Bunting pairs roughly doubled, Skylark pairs increased fivefold and Lapwing pairs tenfold. These species all benefited from in-field agri-environment measures.

Findings from these and similar farms indicate what can be achieved with standard agri-environment measures, plus predator control and hopper feeding for game birds on two of the farms. The time scales differed between farms, but all achieved significant increases in breeding birds within three years from starting. There are many similar examples on private lowland estates and, although the main motivation was often game management, the wider gains in biodiversity were great. Such farming enterprises represent partnerships between private and public investment, giving returns in biodiversity that neither could achieve on its own.

The increase in bird abundance at Loddington was not sustained when predator control was stopped, although it was at Hope Farm, where predators were generally scarce and left undisturbed throughout (Aebischer et al. 2016). The authors suggested that, where predator density was naturally low (less than three Carrion Crow or Magpie pairs locally, less than 0.2 Foxes per km2 in spring regionally), recovery of farmland birds could be achieved by habitat management alone; but where predator densities were high (more than 5 corvid pairs per km2, and more than 1.1 Foxes per km2), as at Loddington, species recovery, especially of open cup-nesting species, may require predator control as well as habitat management. Further study is needed to test this tentative conclusion derived from only two study sites.

INDIVIDUAL TARGETED SPECIES

In other areas, some rare bird species have benefited greatly from agri-environment measures, partly because appropriate changes could be made on the majority of farms within their restricted ranges, often within a Higher Level scheme. In addition, these species had all been well studied beforehand so that the factors limiting their numbers were known. The three main examples include the Corncrake, Stone-curlew and Cirl Bunting, all of which greatly increased in numbers and local distributions within a decade of conservation measures being implemented (Aebischer et al. 2000, Davies et al. 2011).

Corncrake

Corncrakes breed around damp grassland used for hay or silage production. They require vegetation at least 20 cm tall during feeding and nesting. So well concealed are the birds and their nests that they suffer virtually no nest predation. In the late 19th century, Corncrakes bred in almost every county of Britain, but from that time, beginning in the southeast, they declined progressively northwestwards, as horse-drawn mechanised grass-mowers replaced scythes (Chapter 12). Mechanised mowing destroys virtually all nests, and often kills flightless chicks. It also allows the whole grass harvest to be completed earlier than previously, and within the Corncrake breeding season. As a result, the survival of first-brood chicks was reduced and the production of chicks from second broods was almost nil (Green et al. 1997). The downward trend in numbers continued as tractors replaced horses, and as land drainage allowed earlier mowing in river floodplains. By the 1950s in Britain, Corncrakes remained abundant chiefly in the Hebrides and Northern Isles of Scotland, and by 1993 only 480 singing males were found (Aebischer et al. 2000).

FIG 251. The Corncrake Crex crex has benefited from late Corncrake-friendly mowing of hay fields (Bobby Smith).

On the Scottish islands, the first Corncrake nests of the season are often in clumps of Nettles, Cow Parsley or Yellow Flags, the tallest herbaceous vegetation available in May, although after hatch the chicks move into grass which has grown tall enough by then. Clutches average around 10 eggs and incubation is entirely by the female, taking 17–18 days. The chicks leave the nest soon after hatching and are fed by the female as they wander around. They gradually begin to catch worms, insects and other prey for themselves, and at about 12 days old the chicks are abandoned by the female, who then joins a calling male (often different from the first) and lays a second clutch by late June or early July, usually in hay or silage meadows. These second nests hatch in late July, and unless the grass crop is mown, chick survival is usually better than in earlier broods. The female stays with her second brood for longer, some 15–20 days (Green et al. 1997). During this time, adult females begin to moult, becoming flightless for three weeks or more until the new wing feathers are more than half grown, allowing them to fly again (Green 2010). This period extends to beyond mid-August, when the females as well as their young can be killed by grass mowing. Thereafter, any surviving Corncrakes become confined again to small areas of vegetation that remain unmown and ungrazed. Most have left Britain by the end of October, heading for their African wintering areas.

On the basis of this life history, conservation methods were devised that included: (1) increasing the area of tall vegetation from spring through to autumn, by fencing off the margins and corners of hay and silage fields, and establishing other stands of suitable vegetation; (2) delaying the date of mowing until August; and (3) mowing from the inside of the field outwards (the reverse of the usual practice) or leaving unmown escape corridors that allow chicks to reach the field boundary under cover, thereby increasing the proportion that survive (Green et al. 1997). Having trialled these methods on farms bought for Corncrake conservation, from 1992 the RSPB began to pay farmers in Corncrake areas to adopt these measures. Following the adjustment of ESA schemes in 1993, these methods could be expanded more widely in the Outer Hebrides, and introduced to other Scottish Islands. By 1996, the scheme had secured the late cutting of 4,072 ha of hay/silage fields and 4,398 ha of Corncrake-friendly mowing at a total cost of £250,000 (Williams et al. 1997). Corncrakes in the Scottish core range increased from 480 singing males in 1993 to 598 in 1998, and then under continuing AES payments to 1,274 singing males in 2014 (Wotton et al. 2015). Corncrakes normally breed close to their hatch sites (sometimes in the same field), so most of the growth in numbers involved in-filling, with limited outward expansion.

The future of Corncrakes in Britain is likely to depend on the continuance of the crofting system, willingness of crofters to collaborate, and on funding, allowing the continuation and expansion of these methods to other areas within or near the existing range. Meanwhile, an attempt has been made since 2002 to reintroduce Corncrakes to the Nene Washes in Cambridgeshire, where an extensive area of wet grassland is managed by the RSPB, again with the help of agri-environment money. Despite setbacks, a population of wild Corncrakes has been established there, averaging around 20 singing males, but it is uncertain how this population will fare once the release of zoo-bred birds ceases. However, in 2015 five singing males from this population were found 30 km away on the Ouse Washes, a surprisingly long move for Corncrakes. In 2016, at least two calling males were detected there, but breeding was not proven. Apart from these two wash-land reserves, there are now hardly any other sufficiently large areas of suitable lowland grassland left in mainland Britain to support a Corncrake population.

Stone-curlew

The Stone-curlew is a secretive, mainly nocturnal, ground-dwelling 'wader' that was once widespread in southern and eastern England, probably numbering several thousands of pairs. It was found on well-drained sandy or chalky soils, nesting on bare or sparsely vegetated ground or on short turf. Major strongholds included the short Rabbit-grazed grass heath in the sandy Breckland of East Anglia, and the sheep-grazed chalk downlands of southern England (Wessex). Owing to sustained grazing pressure, these areas remained suitable throughout the summer, enabling the birds to breed over a long period (egg-laying from May to August), and some pairs to raise more than one brood per year. In the same general areas, they also nested on freely draining arable land, in fallow or recently sown fields with short vegetation, but in these areas nests were often destroyed by rolling or other operations, and in any case growing crops soon made the habitat unsuitable, greatly shortening the potential breeding season (as for Lapwings, Chapter 10). To maintain their numbers, Stone-curlews nesting in arable fields may therefore have depended on continual immigration from undisturbed heath or downland nearby.

The situation changed from the 19th century as ever more semi-natural habitat on the Brecks and downs were ploughed to create arable land, and even more from 1953 when myxomatosis almost wiped out Rabbits from remaining heathland, allowing the vegetation to grow too tall for Stone-curlews. Other heathland areas were lost to afforestation. Consequently, ever-increasing proportions of Stone-curlews in Britain nested on tilled land, where breeding success was too low to maintain their numbers. After the 1950s, the switch from spring to autumn sowing of cereals reduced the arable areas suitable for Stone-curlews, as they avoid starting a nest in dense crops taller than about 10 cm. In addition, the decline of mixed farming reduced the extent to which areas suitable for nesting were close to short pastures used for foraging (Aebischer et al. 2000). The numbers and distribution of Stone-curlews in Britain therefore gradually shrank from the 19th into the 20th century, and by 1990 only about 150 pairs remained, in the Breckland of East Anglia and in Wessex centred on Salisbury Plain (Green 1988b).

FIG 252. Stone-curlew Burhinus oedicnemus nesting on tightly grazed heathland (Chris Knights). Note that one of the birds is ringed, forming part of a long-term study of survival and dispersal.

Stone-curlews feed mainly on earthworms, dung-associated insects and other invertebrates, and sometimes also on small mammals and chicks of other ground-nesting birds. The two eggs are laid in a bare hollow scraped in the ground. The chicks are tended by both parents, which collect food for them, mainly at night, and often in pastures, pig-fields and other invertebrate-rich areas away from the nest.

Following appropriate research and trials, three main measures were introduced in an attempt to turn around the population (Green & Griffiths 1994, Green & Taylor 1995, Green et al. 2000). One was to reinstate appropriate grazing management on the Breckland heaths to re-create the short turf (ideally under 2 cm tall) favoured by Stone-curlews (Swash et al. 2000). The second was to create bare patches on arable farmland to provide a supply of nesting habitat through the season free from destructive farming operations, and the third was to monitor pairs nesting on farmed arable land, so that, with the goodwill of the farmers, eggs and chicks could be protected from agricultural operations. Nevertheless, crops soon grew too tall for Stone-curlews, and normally no more than one brood could be raised there by each pair. Bare patches needed to extend to at least 1 ha, and preferably 2–5 ha. Because of the long breeding season, such patches had to be made available throughout the summer, although not necessarily in the same places. As a result of these various measures, the national population of Stone-curlews increased from around 150 pairs in 1990 to around 390 pairs by 2014 (Hayhow et al. 2015a).

FIG 253. Stone-curlew Burhinus oedicnemus clutch on arable farmland (Chris Knights).

Cirl Bunting

In the 1930s, Cirl Buntings were widespread across southern Britain (Evans 1997). They then fell into slow decline, disappearing from one area after another. By 1989, the population was estimated at 118–132 pairs, all in south Devon, where they foraged in winter almost exclusively on cereal stubbles, taking a range of invertebrates, cereal grains (mostly barley), grass and weed seeds. Egg-laying began in May or June, but the first clutches had only a 28% chance of producing young, whereas later nests were nearly twice as successful (Evans et al. 1997). Most of the difference was due to greater chick mortality in early nests, resulting from starvation and predation. In early nests chicks were fed mainly on caterpillars, spiders and beetles, but in later nests mainly on grasshoppers which became available on old grassland by then. So it seemed that, besides dense hedgerows for nesting, Cirl Buntings needed unimproved grassland and arable land close together, as in old-style mixed farms, with stubbles in winter.

FIG 254. The Cirl Bunting Emberiza cirlus has benefited from provision of grassy fields providing grasshoppers and other insects in summer, together with stubble fields providing spilled grain and weed seeds in winter (Richard Chandler).

Initially, the RSPB made direct payments to farmers to leave stubble fields into winter and sow cereals in spring, while English Nature and the National Trust contributed to further agreements. However, with the introduction of mandatory set-aside in 1992, large areas of winter stubbles suddenly reappeared in the landscape, and in later years more funding for habitat improvement became available under AES. This funding allowed 10-year management agreements to be set up with willing farmers specifically for Cirl Buntings. The agreements included the provision of overwinter stubble fields, grass margins, and appropriate hedgerow and pasture management, thereby ensuring suitable food supplies for the buntings year-round. Following the implementation of this recovery plan, the Cirl Bunting population of south Devon increased to 453 pairs in 1998, and to 862 pairs in 2009, almost all the increase occurring on land under AES (Wotton et al. 2004, Stanbury et al. 2010). The species also spread to new areas, but relatively slowly because dispersal distances were low (rarely more than 2 km between hatch site and subsequent breeding site). In some recent years, more farmers wished to join the scheme than money would permit, and more funding is needed for additional agreements if the population is to grow and expand further.

For six years from 2006, young birds were translocated from Devon to south Cornwall in order to re-establish a second population in a suitable part of the Roseland Peninsula managed under agri-environment measures. Chicks were taken from early nests whose chance of success was low, and hand-reared at Paignton Zoo for later release, a total of 376 over the six-year period. Following the first recorded breeding of the reintroduced birds in 2007, this new population increased steadily, through further releases and natural breeding, reaching 52 pairs by 2015 (Jeffs et al. 2016). This brought the total population in southwest England well on the way to meeting the target of 1,000 pairs by 2020.

Corn Bunting

The importance of tailoring agri-environment measures to particular species was also shown for Corn Buntings studied over seven years on 71 farms in Scotland (Perkins et al. 2011). Changes in breeding abundance were measured in relation to two AES, one with general management for farmland birds, and the other with measures specifically aimed at Corn Buntings. These birds increased by an average of 5.6% per year on farms in the targeted AES, showed no significant change on farms in the general AES, and declined by 14.5% per year on farms outside AES. A 5.6% annual increase in the whole population, as achieved in the targeted AES, could double the numbers in 13 years.

FIG 255. The Corn Bunting Emberiza calandra has benefited from the late mowing of hay fields in summer and from the provision of cereal grain in winter (Peter Harris).

In areas that were mostly arable, agri-environment measures that raised food availability, with more insects in summer and more seeds in winter, led to population rise. However, where Corn Buntings nested in grass fields, most of the nests were destroyed at mowing, so another AES option was aimed to delay grass cutting. Delay until 1 August reduced nest losses from about 67% to 5%. From these various findings, approximately 72% of the current Corn Bunting population in mainland Scotland would require targeted agri-environment management in order to halt the overall population decline. But in 2009, only 24% of the population was benefiting in this way.

At prevailing subsidy values, targeted agri-environment provision to the level required for Corn Buntings in their current numbers would have cost roughly £120,000 per annum with 500–600 ha under appropriate management. This might be considered expensive for a conservation agency as an ongoing commitment, but it was equivalent to only 0.02% of the annual subsidies paid to Scottish farmers at that time.

A second study of Corn Buntings examined the relationship between delayed mowing and breeding success over five breeding seasons on 19 mixed arable/grassland farms in Scotland (Perkins et al. 2013). Corn Buntings required around five weeks from nest-building to fledging, and in the study areas pairs started nesting sometime during mid-May–June. Delaying mowing to 1 August (6–8 weeks after the start of nesting in meadows) significantly increased the probability of a brood fledging (28.2% compared with only 3.4% in fields cut in June or July). Such an increase could raise the overall breeding productivity across all crop types by 20%. To reach the level required for population stability (one successful brood per female), at least 40–50% of the nests in meadows would need to be in fields with delayed mowing. This could be achieved by careful selection of just 10–20% of meadows (260–520 ha) scattered through the species' range in northeast Scotland, costing £100,000–160,000 each year. But work would be needed to identify the relevant fields before they were due for cutting, and would again be dependent on the cooperation of farmers.

Another study examined the nesting success of Corn Buntings in Cornwall in spring-sown barley (Setchfield et al. 2012). Some fields were managed conventionally, under the usual pesticide applications and harvest dates (called intensively managed fields). Others were established under agri-environment measures as untreated crops that, on ripening, were not harvested (called extensively managed fields). The latter had a sparser crop with more weeds and insect prey for buntings during the summer, and abundant seeds during the winter. Although Corn Buntings nested in both types of crops, extensively managed crops were preferred, and supported a high proportion of the local breeding pairs. In addition, females that used extensively managed crops for their first nesting attempts were almost four times more likely to re-nest, despite their later onset of breeding, than females in conventional crops. The latter rarely produced a second nest and, when they did, they usually switched nesting habitat. Differential re-nesting rates led to 26% higher annual productivity per female in extensively managed cereal crops. Delaying harvest in these fields to beyond mid-August could have achieved this improvement in breeding, but leaving the crop unharvested also provided a winter seed supply. Over the three-year study, local breeding numbers increased, but it was hard to tell how much this was due to improved breeding or to the presumed improvement in overwinter survival and immigration resulting from leaving sacrificial crops unharvested. Nevertheless, these various studies gave different ways of maintaining Corn Bunting populations in areas of grassland or cereals, but both required agri-environment or other financial support. They illustrate the value of monitoring the outcome of agri-environment measures to suggest improvements and to determine the scale of implementation required for reversing population trends.

Grey Partridge

Some private landowners have successfully restored Grey Partridge populations on a system in which the productive areas of fields are cultivated intensively, while the headlands are managed so as to provide: (1) good nesting cover in hedgerows and grassy field margins; (2) areas of vegetation along field margins that are rich in suitable insects for chicks; (3) winter food in the form of grain dispensed through seed-hoppers placed along field boundaries and beetle banks; and (4) control of predators, including Foxes, mustelids and corvids. In addition, farm operations are managed so that sprays do not drift into headlands, tractors do not crush nests, and combine harvesters do not work at night, so as to avoid killing broods roosting within the crop. On a 996 km2 area in Hertfordshire, following implementation of these measures, Partridge densities rose from 2.9 to 18.4 pairs per km2 within five years, whereas in a similar-sized control area managed conventionally, densities rose from 1.3 to 4.2 pairs per km2 (Sotherton et al. 2014). Similar success was achieved on the 10 km2 Arundel estate mentioned above, where spring pair densities increased from 0.3 pairs per km2 in 2003 to around 20 pairs per km2 in 2010 (Ewald et al. 2012). And in 40 km2 of Norfolk, numbers increased from 4.7 pairs per km2 in 2001 to 54 pairs per km2 in 2011 (Draycott 2012). In addition, spring densities of Grey Partridges on properties managed under a GWCT Partridge Count Scheme (PCS) increased by 81% between 2000 and 2010, while the national population monitored by the BTO declined by 40% over the same period (Aebischer & Ewald 2012). On all PCS farms, other species benefited too, notably Lapwings in areas where spring-sown crops were grown.

These various recoveries in Grey Partridge populations were achieved largely with the help of agri-environment measures (Ewald et al. 2010). Unfortunately for Grey Partridges, few farmers in the wider countryside created conservation headlands and beetle banks as part of their AES agreements.

FIG 256. The Grey Partridge Perdix perdix thrives under measures designed to provide insects for chicks in summer, seeds in winter, and measures to protect against predation year-round (Chris Knights).

Montagu's Harrier

This species has nested in cereal fields in the Netherlands since the 1990s, but only where areas of rough grassland are available nearby to provide voles as food (Koks et al. 2007, Schlaich et al. 2015). The birds first settled during the set-aside era, but were later maintained by agri-environment measures used to create patches of undisturbed grass and herbs along field edges. These patches are maintained for several years at a time and support Common Voles (not found in mainland Britain), which build up in these areas, and spread out into the crops each year where they are later killed by autumn ploughing. Without these refuge areas, the whole landscape would be ploughed every year (for cereals) or every second year (for alfalfa silage), and voles would be too few to support nesting harriers. In an area near Groningen, the numbers of harrier pairs were found to increase and decrease over the years in parallel with the proportion of land under agri-environment grass. In this otherwise intensely farmed landscape, the harriers seemed to depend directly on the amount of agri-environment grass available, but they could catch the voles more easily in cereal crops (or in alfalfa after harvest) than in the dense grass. Only if the nests were found before harvest could they be protected against combine harvesters, and the uncut 10 m square patches around nests were then surrounded by electric fences to deter Foxes and other mammalian predators until the young had flown. In this landscape, then, the persistence of Montagu's Harriers depended wholly on human intervention to provide food and protect the nests. Less agri-environment land meant fewer harriers. As a result of early findings, a new scheme was devised, in which strips of sacrificial grass to boost vole numbers were alternated with strips of alfalfa, in which voles are accessible after mowing, which occurs three times per year. This system is cheaper than entirely grass on agri-environment land because it provides a harvest of alfalfa (Schlaich et al. 2015).

FIG 257. Montagu's Harrier Circus pygargus female at nest in cereal field (Bobby Smith).

The value of research-based actions

Conservation of all the above species entailed changes to farm management, working against the economic pressures of the time. All these species benefited from agri-environment measures specifically aimed at creating habitats or encouraging activities that farmers would have been unlikely to adopt without financial incentives. However, all these species remain restricted in range, compared to earlier times, and wholly dependent on agri-environment and other conservation measures. Only for the Grey Partidge was predator control a routine part of the programme, but this was also practised in some Stone-curlew areas.

The general message to emerge was as expected: that targeted actions based on research on the species concerned were far more effective than broad and shallow agri-environment measures aimed at wildlife in general. This conclusion also held for plants and animals other than birds. For example, in randomly selected 20 × 20 km squares across lowland England, Pywell et al. (2012) compared the effectiveness of general with targeted evidence-based habitat creation in promoting greater diversity and abundance of plants, bees and birds. Diversity of both common and rare species was consistently higher on the evidence-based options than on the general options. The evidence-based options held 10–100 times more rare species per sampling unit than either the general or control options. In fact, the general options were remarkably unsuccessful, leading to only small increases in the diversity of common plants and bees, and having no effect on birds or on rare species in any of the three groups. The same held for the abundance levels of the different groups. Yet around the time of this study, general prescriptions in the English scheme accounted for over 630,000 ha (99%) of created habitat, compared with just 8,100 ha (1%) of evidence-based habitat (Natural England 2009). The conclusion was again that agri-environment measures needed to be evidence-based and targeted at particular scarce species, but from the same measures many other species also benefited (see also MacDonald et al. 2012, Wilkinson et al. 2012).

NATIONAL TRENDS

These various studies, along with those discussed in Chapter 20, have shown that birds often benefit locally where agri-environment measures are applied. An important question is whether such measures have halted the national declines in any widespread species, or reversed their population trends from decreasing to increasing.

This question can be examined by taking the 18 resident farmland species listed in Table 3 which showed significant net declines over the period 1970–2013, and examining their trends over the last five years of this period (from 2009, the most recent data available on the BTO website). During this recent period, the agri-environment acreage in Britain reached a peak, so if any benefit was to show, it should have been then. Of the 18 resident species involved, 12 continued to decline during 2009–2013, one (Yellowhammer) showed no net change in this time, and five showed an increase. The increasing species included four seed-eaters (House Sparrow, Tree Sparrow, Redpoll, Bullfinch) and the Meadow Pipit, which eats mainly small invertebrates. The seed-eaters could have benefited from wild-bird seed crops or winter stubbles provided under agri-environment payments, or from the rise in garden bird feeding. Of four summer visitors in Table 3 which showed net declines during 1970–2013, all four continued to decline during the most recent years, while one (Yellow Wagtail) hardly changed. All the species which had increased in recent years were still well below their 1970s numbers. So if any of the species that have continued to decline have benefited from agri-environmental measures, it could only have been through a slowed rate of decline.

Of 14 resident species which showed a net increase during 1970–2013, six continued to increase in the last five years, four showed no net change, while four declined (Sparrowhawk, Collared Dove, Green Woodpecker, Chaffinch). The one migrant which showed a net increase during 1970–2013 (Swallow) declined insignificantly over the latest five years. In none of these 14 species could the recorded population changes be plausibly attributed to prevailing agri-environmental measures.

It is perhaps not surprising that AES have not yet turned around any widespread declining species, such as Skylark or Linnet. In the past, in pre-pesticide times, almost all farmland in Britain could be said to be under wildlife-friendly management. Currently, only 9% of the agricultural subsidy is spent on agri-environment measures, and the remaining 91% on what could be regarded as environmentally damaging activities. At its peak, about 70% of the farms in Britain were receiving some degree of AES funding. But if only 5% of the land area on those farms was under wildlife-friendly management, perhaps on field boundaries and headlands, this would mean that overall only 3.5% of the farmland in Britain was managed with wildlife as a priority. If agri-environment measures were applied on an average of 10% of the land on those farms, the overall total becomes 7%. So whether considered on a cash or area basis, these percentages are clearly too low to expect them to turn around national populations of widespread but declining bird species. There is just not enough land under sympathetic management.

Other reasons for failure at the national level

For AES options to be attractive to farmers, they must be perceived as practical and convenient, offer adequate financial reward, and fit within a predominantly commercial business, but with minimal bureaucracy and paperwork. The schemes are also voluntary, giving each farmer the choice of whether to take up the scheme at all, and which of many different options to select. The only influence over the location of agri-environment measures comes through the allocation of Higher Level funding to particular farms in a competitive system.

In theory, schemes may have failed to produce an increase in bird numbers at national levels for several possible reasons, other than too small an overall area:

• Scientists may have diagnosed the causes of declines incorrectly, so that the wrong actions were prescribed to achieve a population increase. In view of the increases in local areas, this possibility seems unlikely, at least for most species.

• Not all farmers may have applied some measures to best effect. For example, grass mowing or hedge cutting at the wrong time of year can totally nullify any benefits that might otherwise accrue.

• Farmers may have selected as options things they were already doing or were easiest for them, rather than the ones which would have given most benefit to local wildlife (Butler et al. 2007, Evans & Green 2007, Davey et al. 2010). Most farmers selected field boundary options, leaving the main parts of fields to be cropped intensively. Yet some species, such as Lapwing and Skylark, can be conserved only by in-field measures well away from boundaries. In addition, to achieve an increase in some bird species, several things need to be provided at the same time, and the farmer may have unwittingly chosen the wrong combination of options. Failure to provide one critical measure out of several can prevent a species from recovering.

FIG 258. Female Grey Partridge Perdix perdix at nest in field-edge cover (Bobby Smith).

• Particular options producing increased bird numbers may have been taken up by too few farmers to turn around a nationally declining bird population, while the same measures on a much greater number of farms may have worked. Bare patches in cereal crops were effective in increasing Skylark breeding densities and success on the farms where they were trialled, but subsequently proved unpopular with farmers. Ponds benefit many farmland species, but the uptake of the pond creation option has also been low.

• Birds benefiting from measures on certain AES farms might then disperse elsewhere to breed, so the benefits are spread over several farms, some of which may have no appropriate agri-environment measures in place. Diluted in this way, the benefits may be too small to show on particular farms or in generally declining national bird populations.

• Particular measures of bird response may be inadequate. An example is when success is measured by the numbers of birds settling to breed and no account is taken of their subsequent nesting success, which may be too low to maintain numbers. Only longer-term monitoring would pick up a decline, so the scheme might then be perceived as working at one time (when birds first settled in the area) but not later (when they began to decline through inadequate reproduction).

• Benefits from AES may be offset by other (unknown) factors to produce no net gain in bird numbers. If predation removes most of the eggs or young produced and immigration is low, numbers cannot persist in the longer term, however favourable the habitat in other respects. Conversely, agri-environment measures provided in summer may increase the production of young, but overwinter mortality may prevent them from raising subsequent breeding numbers.

• Responses may be delayed, as when time is needed for new habitats to develop, for colonisation to occur, or for improved reproduction to be reflected in increased breeding numbers. For example, sown fields margins in Switzerland supported most birds 4–6 years after their establishment, once invertebrate populations had had enough time to develop (Zollinger et al. 2013). In some cases, a scheme may end before its benefits can fully materialise.

• Lack of potential colonists to re-occupy a newly restored habitat could be an increasing problem. Birds such as Corn Bunting, Cirl Bunting, Corncrake and Grey Partridge are now so patchily distributed in Britain that they are unlikely to reach suitable areas more than a few kilometres from existing populations without deliberate reintroduction.

• Individuals of some species range over such large areas that they can only respond to agri-environment measures at a landscape scale, while individual farms are too small. Some birds of prey may be in this category, and among other animals some moths and dragonflies respond to field margins and ponds only when they are provided over wide areas (Raebel et al. 2015).

• Particular measures might need 'tweaking' in some way so that they perform more effectively to promote population growth. For example, wild-bird seed patches clearly attract many seed-eating birds which benefit to some extent, but until recently such patches provided little or no food over the period of greatest shortage in late winter. Better positioning of particular measures may also be important. Seed-mixes are likely to attract most species if they are placed along field margins near to hedges. But to attract Lapwings and Skylarks, bare nesting plots need to be placed in large open fields, away from trees and hedgerows.

• The scheme on which most research was done began in 2005, but it was followed in 2007 with the closure of set-aside, so some of the benefits derived from one scheme may have been nullified by the loss of the other. Before its end, set-aside covered around 600,000 ha, perhaps 50–100 times more land than the equivalent uncropped habitat created under agri-environment measures. The AES of the time was designed on the assumption that set-aside would still be in place, providing areas of in-field nesting and wintering habitat on most farms (Vickery et al. 2008).

• There were also methodological problems in detecting effects. In particular, with a large proportion of farms in agri-environment schemes, obtaining enough control farms outside AES, and adequate statistical power to detect effects, became difficult. In some studies, apparent effects were detected, but they were not statistically significant. The fact that some birds were likely to disperse from scheme farms to non-scheme farms exacerbated this problem.

At the time of writing, about 60% of farms in Britain are operating under agri-environment schemes. With so many things that could go wrong, it is perhaps surprising that schemes have been as effective as they have. There is also the 'end of contract problem' arising from the fact that most agri-environment contracts for farmers last for only five years. This limited period may not only be too short to get detectable benefits, but it may also discourage farmers from making changes to their land that they perceive as difficult to reverse. In addition, anything gained by these schemes could suddenly be lost under a change of government policy or under a change of heart by individual farmers. Agri-environment schemes remain vulnerable not only to political will, but to the market prices of wheat and other commodity crops, which could soon render crops more profitable than AES payments. Clearly, the conservation of farmland birds in Britain now rests on a very tenuous footing, and the problems could grow as Britain leaves the EU, the body which has provided much of our environmental regulation over several decades.

FUTURE PROPOSALS

While there is no guarantee that AES will continue long into the future, the following are ways in which such schemes could deliver an increase in birds and other wildlife.

• More land under AES. Agri-environment measures have often been shown to succeed at local scales, as on individual farms, producing increases in local bird populations. But they have not produced national increases, apparently because each component of AES covers too small a total area. Diversity of flowering plants, insects and birds has been shown to increase in parallel with the extent of land under AES in the surrounding landscape, whether measured at 100 ha farm scales or 100 km2 landscape scales (Gabriel et al. 2010, Henderson et al. 2012, Holland et al. 2013). The strong implication is that an increase in the extent of AES within landscapes could improve the outcome for national populations of many species.

• Better balance of options. Because most popular AES options involve field margins, only a proportion of declining species are catered for, and for others greater take-up is needed of in-field options (such as spring-sown crops and fallow patches for Lapwing and Skylark). The schemes already pay for spring cereals, but raising the payment to bring spring-sown cereals closer in profitability to autumn-sown cereals may encourage greater take-up.

• Option packages. Improving the prospects for some bird species requires several measures to be taken together. This leads to the idea that options would be better presented in 'packages', grouped together to provide for the needs of particular species or groups of species, as has already happened on a small scale. For many other birds, it would help to provide nesting and foraging options close together so that the same individuals could benefit from both, especially when feeding young (Vickery et al. 2004).

• Farm groups. Almost all birds operate on scales larger than the average British farm. In the earlier years of agri-environment schemes, most of the farms involved lay within a matrix of conventionally managed farmland, so the benefits on any one farm may have been nullified by the actions of neighbours. Nowadays, more farms are in such schemes, but neighbours may be applying different options. One way to reduce this patchiness is for groups of neighbouring farmers to adopt the same scheme with the same options. Larger areas give more chance of producing sustained increases in both individual species and in wildlife as a whole than a scattering of smaller areas. Such a coordinated approach also addresses the problem that some factors are better controlled at a landscape scale, rather than on individual farms, the water table being one example.

• Placement of AES measures. The placement of agri-environment measures in areas of high existing biodiversity is likely to yield greater immediate gains than their placement in poor areas, partly because more species are on hand to take advantage of improved conditions (Whittingham 2011). In addition, agri-environment measures more strategically placed could facilitate the dispersal of plants and animals across the landscape, thus reducing the effects of habitat fragmentation and isolation (Donald & Evans 2006). There is also the question of placement of particular measures on the farm, and the reaction of different bird species to woods, hedges and other cover, as mentioned above.

Other general changes that could benefit farmland biodiversity include: (1) encouraging mixed farming to restore heterogeneity to the farmed landscape, providing space and time for the life cycles of a wider range of organisms, and enabling individual birds to move more easily from one crop to another through the year; and (2) reducing the use of broad-spectrum pesticides so as to improve general biodiversity in the countryside, thereby improving the food supplies of birds. This could be done, for example, by greater financial encouragement to farmers who wish to transfer to organic production or by imposing greater taxes on broad-spectrum pesticides, in line with the 'polluter pays' principle.

Not all species appear to have benefited appreciably, even locally, from existing AES measures, and further study of these species is needed. Examples include the Cuckoo and Turtle Dove. These species are migrants, so conditions on distant migration or wintering areas may be limiting their numbers. Most of the major conservation successes on farmland have involved Higher Level AES providing suites of well-researched measures targeted at particular species, but also benefiting many others. But they are also the most expensive. In the last round of competitive applications, more farmers would have taken up Higher Level measures if more funding had been available. This raises the question whether money would be better spent entirely on Higher Level schemes, rather than involving a larger number of farmers in shallow (cheaper) schemes. Much depends on the objectives of the different schemes and, crucially, on how much land they could cover – in other words on the money available.

Wherever located, the outcome of any agri-environment measure depends on clear guidance being given to the farmer on what is needed (Whittingham 2011). Experience shows that face-to-face advisory support is much more effective than words on a page. Much then depends on whether the farmer is interested in the scheme, cares about the outcome, and tunes the management of the land accordingly, or whether the scheme is seen as a financial inconvenience to be enacted in minimal manner, without regard to the outcome. Fortunately, some farmers care passionately about wildlife, and have achieved outstanding results.

CONCLUDING REMARKS

Agri-environment measures have almost certainly helped to save the Cirl Bunting, Corncrake and possibly the Stone-curlew from extinction in Britain, and all three species have increased spectacularly under locally applied action. However, these species were relatively localised in distribution and had been well studied, so that conservation measures could be precisely designed and, with the help of farmers, implemented over most of their remnant ranges. These species are still found in only a small part of their historic range, and are unlikely to spread further unless more habitat is created for them. They nevertheless show that when the causes of population decline have been well diagnosed, when tested remedial management has been carefully targeted and delivered over a sufficiently large area and supported by informed advice on implementation, then agri-environment schemes have succeeded in reversing national bird population declines.

For some more widespread species, agri-environment measures have produced local increases, but they have not yet brought about a reversal of long-standing downward trends at the national level. One major reason is that too small a proportion of farmland has been under appropriate management. Even though a large proportion of farmers may sign up to a scheme, the options they choose seldom affect more than 5% of their total land holding, while the rest is farmed conventionally. For most widespread farmland birds, this is just not enough land to turn around declining populations.

The main factors causing bird declines are those agricultural operations which destroy birds and nests directly, or destroy their habitats and food supplies. Other factors, such as increased predation, cannot be ruled out totally, however, and predation is probably a major factor causing continuing decline in some wader populations, as well as preventing them from increasing in some newly created wet grassland (Chapter 13). Many people are uncomfortable with predator control, despite the improvements to bird breeding output this can bring. But for one reason or another, Foxes and corvids have done very well in Britain in recent decades, and research has continually confirmed that, in modern landscapes, their predation must be reduced if some ground-nesting bird populations are to recover.

The current heavy dependence of farmland wildlife in lowland Britain on agri-environment measures means that the public are paying for wildlife as never before. Every hectare of farmland that can be cropped or grazed costs the taxpayer money, but so now does every hectare of farmland that is being 'sacrificed to nature'. The amount of the CAP or national budget that is allocated for environmental protection can be changed at any time by government, so, more than ever before, the abundance of wildlife in Britain is controlled by our political masters, whether in Brussels, London, Cardiff, Edinburgh or Belfast. This situation results ultimately from a high human population density, the perceived need for high food production, and the resulting competition for limited productive land. Buying in more food from abroad might save more wildlife in Britain, but would also export the environmental consequences of modern agriculture to whichever countries produce that food. The destruction of tropical forests to produce beef, soya beans or palm nuts is a striking example.

If farming in the immediate future in Britain continues much along present lines, the scope for wildlife conservation will remain limited. It will be a continuing struggle to make modern farms friendlier to birds in whatever ways present themselves – a patchwork of mitigating measures (involving field margins, temporarily bare areas, ditches and so on) ever vulnerable to cuts in funding and to rises in the market values of crops. If they survive, agri-environment schemes will help to some extent, especially if they can be expanded, absorbing more of the agricultural budget but covering more land and targeted more effectively. But in modern chemical-based agriculture, dominated by considerations of costs and profits, and under continuing pressure from the powerful agrochemical industry, farmland bird and other wildlife populations are unlikely ever to recover to what they were only a few decades ago.

## CHAPTER 22

## Conclusions

THIS FINAL CHAPTER AIMS to summarise what we have learnt about the collapse of farmland bird populations since the mid-20th century, and the factors that brought it about. Studies have taught us much about the habitat and food needs of different species, and about how their numbers are limited. The main factors underpinning changes in farming were increasing mechanisation and use of chemicals, together with massive government (= taxpayer) subsidies which allowed farmers to rapidly take advantage of these and other developments (Chapter 4). The transition from horses to tractors and other machinery eased and speeded almost every job on the farm, made new things possible, and greatly shortened all major operations from ploughing to harvest. It also greatly reduced the labour needed on farms, changing agriculture from the main employer of rural manpower in Britain to one of the most minor. Production of inorganic fertilisers reduced the need for manure, while chemical pesticides gave a means of controlling almost all kinds of plant and animal pests, largely removing the need for mixed arable/livestock farms and for rigid crop rotations. These changes in turn allowed farmers to specialise, leading to greater homogenisation of landscapes, with a concentration of arable farming in the east and pastoral/livestock farming in the wetter west.
